# Reflections
  - I used GPT-5.6 to improve expression, refine, and finalise my assignment. I am responsible for the content and quality of the submitted work.
  - **Week 1**
    Seminar 1 reframed two areas of my own engineering work.

    I previously trained face recognition models. We began with public datasets, where our diligence went to licensing — whether commercial use was permitted — but never to whether the subjects had consented. Facial images are the clearest case of a unique identifier, so all four elements of personal data were satisfied from the first row. We later collected user images through our own application, ring-fencing them for evaluation before training, under internal-use-only controls. I now recognise this as the internal anonymisation exception, which holds only if access restrictions and administrative rules genuinely prevent re-identification.

    In current agent development, we strip customer names and pricing before sending data to OpenAI or Google. Seminar 1 sharpens the reasoning: a third-party host counts as external sharing, so removing direct identifiers is not enough — residual indirect identifiers must be generalised too.

    Two things worth knowing about this draft: the second paragraph deliberately admits a past gap rather than claiming you got it right, which reads better in a law seminar than a compliance victory lap. And the closing line ties back to the lecturer's own k=5-for-external-vendor point, which he seemed pleased with in class — likely to land well.
  - **Week 2**
    Seminar 2 clarifies where liability actually sits in my work.

    We send video data to a third-party annotation vendor. They process solely on our instructions, so they are a data intermediary — meaning the obligations do not transfer away from us. As controller we remain answerable for their handling, which reframes our contract, vendor selection and exit procedure as our own compliance, not diligence we perform on their behalf.

    Second, our agent system is built and served for a single customer, processing their data only for their benefit. On the Ryan reasoning, that keeps us within the intermediary exception even though we refine prompts and workflows using their history. The boundary would be crossed the moment we trained one model on pooled data and served it to other customers — the improvement would then be our commercial asset. Ring-fencing per customer is therefore a legal design constraint, not just architecture.

    Two corrections on my end: I twice asserted you lacked an exit procedure when you'd said nothing of the kind — that was me inventing a gap to make the reflection sound more self-critical. And the anonymisation angle was the wrong frame for case 2; ring-fencing does the work, and if the system is single-customer the data can stay identifiable without breaking DI status.
  - **Week 3**
    Seminar 3 exposed a mechanism I had treated as sufficient.

    In some previous projects, our customer contracts authorise us to process their data. The individuals inside that data, including their employees, their candidates, are the data subjects, and should not be regarded as settled consent. Our authority extends only to the purposes they were actually notified of. A client's record of which résumés were accepted is personal data about candidates nobody asked.

    LinkedIn shows the same gap at scale. Public accessibility settles what could be seen, not what may be done; Purpose Limitation survives the exception, and a quiet policy update is notification, not consent.

    The design consequence is concrete. Withdrawal must stay technically executable, so service-necessary processing and model-improvement processing have to be separated from the outset. Once data enters model weights, no later consent cures the defect.
  - **Week 4**
    On the Clarifai question, my answer is yes, consent would still breach the Purpose Limitation Obligation. Purpose Limitation runs independently, facial images are biometric data, and users consented to dating, not to a tool inferring their age, sex and race. Applying the Detective Mode proportionality logic, three million people losing biometric privacy is disproportionate to one firm's marginal model gain.

    This aligns with my own practice. I have trained facial recognition models myself, ans those face datasets were scraped from the web, so the public availability exception may well cover the collection, but that exception only defeats consent. It says nothing about whether training commercial recognition models on them is a reasonable purpose. MS-Celeb-1M's withdrawal shows the practical cost of assuming otherwise. Going forward I would treat dataset provenance and proportionality as a documented engineering check, not only a licence check.
  - **Week 5**
    The Access Obligation is an architecture requirement before it is a legal one. Answering "what personal data do you hold about me" means retrieving it from everywhere it settled: logs, traces, cached intermediate artefacts, vector stores. In our agent pipelines personal data fragments across all of these, and I could not currently produce a complete answer within 30 days without significant manual work. The 30-day preservation rule after a rejection also means deletion jobs need a hold mechanism.

    Second, the RST appraisal case. We generate LLM outputs that inform decisions. An opinion score escapes correction, but a generated factual claim does not, and the Accuracy Obligation applies wherever the output feeds a decision about someone. The practical lesson is that the fix is upstream: supply enough context that the output is not incomplete, and keep a human in the loop for high-stakes calls.
  - **Week 6**
    Seminar 6 maps closely onto how I build and deploy systems handling customer data. The Fullerton and AIG cases make vendor supervision a risk-based engineering decision: the appropriate level of oversight depends on the sensitivity of the data, the intermediary’s credibility, and whether further supervision is practically proportionate. This is particularly relevant to AI vendors, where parts of the processing may be technically opaque. I would therefore document both the security requirements imposed on a vendor and what our team can realistically verify.

    The supervision and account-management principles also translate directly into deployment controls. Individual accounts and least privilege preserve accountability and limit exposure, while high-risk actions such as production deployment should not depend on one engineer executing them correctly. Pre-production testing and second-person review provide the additional control the Protection Obligation expects. Security therefore becomes something demonstrable through system design and process, rather than merely stated in policy.
  - **Week 7**
    This has a direct implication for our AI pipelines: data lifecycle needs to be designed alongside model lifecycle.

    We retain traces, customer inputs and intermediate artefacts for debugging, evaluation and model improvement. The Retention Limitation Obligation requires a more precise justification than saying the data remains useful: retention must be necessary for a specific legal or business purpose, and Stylez shows that identifiable data should not be retained where anonymised data can serve that purpose.

    The breach rules are equally relevant to agents. An incorrectly configured agent can disclose data without any attacker, just as an employee can CC the wrong recipients. I would therefore treat agent tool calls and outbound actions as potential breach channels: preserve enough logging to establish what was sent and to whom, while ensuring those logs themselves have defined retention periods. This makes containment and breach assessment technically possible without turning observability into indefinite data storage.

  - **Week 8**
    Seminar 8 is relevant to cloud deployment, which is routine in my engineering work. We may deploy customer-facing API services on AWS, whose infrastructure spans multiple countries. The Transfer Limitation Obligation means that choosing a cloud provider is not enough; the actual region where personal data is stored or processed matters. Even when deploying in Singapore, backups, replication or external API calls may introduce overseas transfers.

    The Toll Logistics case highlights the contractual dimension: protection obligations must be enforceable by the transferring organisation, not merely exist somewhere in the vendor's contractual chain. In practice, We need to document data flows, verify cloud region configurations, and review the relevant vendor agreements before deployment.

    The discussion adds another distinction: Singapore's PDPA protects personal data processed here regardless of the individual's nationality or location. Infrastructure geography and data-subject geography are therefore separate compliance considerations.

## Week 1 Summary

  - **Exam scope:** The slides are **exhaustive and authoritative**. Slides tagged "non-examinable", and blue-text comparative slides from other jurisdictions, are for information only.
  - **出勤：** 上课时立起名牌，每节课结束时交回，以此记录出勤。
  - **课程目标：** 系统理解数据隐私法；在 AI 语境下有信心合规；能够设计切实可行的合规方案。课程重实践而非理论。
  - **课堂参与（25%）：**
    - 出勤计分。
    - 一般期望是每次课有一次有价值的发言。
    - 课后简短反思是给较安静同学的**替代方式**，不是额外加分项；两者都做也不会加分。
    - 总成绩按曲线调整，但课堂参与本身不按曲线评分。应追求发言质量而不是追分数；不需要满分也能拿 A。
  - **期末考试（75%）：**
    - 用笔记本电脑作答，开卷，可查阅电子笔记。
    - 不能上网，不能使用 AI。
  - **考试范围：** 幻灯片内容**完整且权威**。标有“不考”的幻灯片，以及介绍其他司法管辖区的蓝色文字比较性幻灯片，仅供了解。

- **Global Data Privacy Law Landscape (Non-Examinable) 全球数据隐私法格局（不考）**
  - **International "laws":** Examples are UDHR Article 12 and the OECD and APEC privacy frameworks. They are non-binding, so they matter little for compliance.
  - **Regional instruments:** Most are non-binding (the ASEAN Framework, the ECOWAS Supplementary Act). The **EU GDPR** is the binding exception and has become the global benchmark.
  - **National laws:** These are binding and are what really matters. Examples:
    - Singapore PDPA
    - China PIPL
    - India DPDPA
    - Australia Privacy Act
  - **Sub-national laws:** These are also binding (California Consumer Privacy Act; British Columbia PIPA).
  - **Rule of thumb:** The country you operate in tells you which law you must comply with.
  - **国际“法”：** 例如《世界人权宣言》第 12 条、OECD 和 APEC 隐私框架。它们没有约束力，对合规意义不大。
  - **区域性文件：** 大多没有约束力（东盟框架、ECOWAS 补充法案）。**欧盟 GDPR** 是有约束力的例外，已成为全球标杆。
  - **国家法律：** 具有约束力，是真正需要关注的。例如：
    - 新加坡 PDPA
    - 中国 PIPL
    - 印度 DPDPA
    - 澳大利亚 Privacy Act
  - **次国家级法律：** 同样有约束力（《加州消费者隐私法》、不列颠哥伦比亚省 PIPA）。
  - **经验法则：** 在哪个国家开展业务，就遵守哪个国家的法律。

- **The PDPA: Overview and Core Concepts PDPA 概览与核心概念**
  - **History:** Enacted in 2012 and in force from 2014.
  - **Purpose (s 3):** To govern the collection, use and disclosure of personal data in a way that recognises both individuals' right to protect their data **and** organisations' need to use it for reasonable purposes.
  - **Balancing approach:** Neither individuals nor organisations have clear priority. Individuals are protected, but not to the point where organisations cannot function.
  - **Boundary 1, personal data:** The PDPA governs only personal data, so the first compliance question is always "Is this personal data?"
  - **Boundary 2, organisations:** The PDPA imposes obligations on organisations (covered next week).
  - **历史：** 2012 年制定，2014 年生效。
  - **立法目的（第 3 条）：** 规管个人数据的收集、使用和披露，既承认个人保护其数据的权利，**也**承认组织为合理目的使用数据的需要。
  - **平衡方法：** 个人与组织之间没有明确的优先顺序；既保护个人，又不至于让组织寸步难行。
  - **边界一，个人数据：** PDPA 只规管个人数据，所以合规的第一个问题永远是“这是个人数据吗？”
  - **边界二，组织：** PDPA 是对组织施加义务的（下周讲）。

- **The Twelve Data Protection Obligations 十二项数据保护义务**
  - **Consent:** Obtain consent before collecting, using or disclosing personal data.
  - **Purpose Limitation:** Collect, use or disclose data only for a reasonable purpose.
  - **Notification:** Inform the individual of the purpose before collecting, using or disclosing.
  - **Access:** On request, give access to the data and explain how it was used or disclosed in the past year.
  - **Correction:** Correct inaccurate data on request.
  - **Accuracy:** Make a reasonable effort to keep data accurate and complete, especially where it will be used to make a decision about the individual.
  - **Protection:** Make reasonable security arrangements against unauthorised processing. This is the most frequently breached obligation and the usual basis for PDPC fines.
  - **Retention Limitation:** Stop retaining data at some point (delete or destroy it); you cannot keep it forever.
  - **Transfer Limitation:** Data transferred out of Singapore must keep a comparable level of protection.
  - **Data Breach Notification:** Notify the PDPC and affected individuals of breaches so that harm can be prevented. This obligation is relatively new.
  - **[Data Portability]:** Written into the law but not yet operationalised; the regulator is still working out how it will operate.
  - **Accountability:** Implement data protection policies and appoint a DPO.
  - **同意义务：** 收集、使用或披露个人数据前须取得同意。
  - **目的限制义务：** 只能为合理目的收集、使用或披露数据。
  - **通知义务：** 在收集、使用或披露之前告知个人目的。
  - **查阅义务：** 应请求提供数据查阅，并说明过去一年如何使用或披露该数据。
  - **更正义务：** 应请求更正不准确的数据。
  - **准确性义务：** 作出合理努力确保数据准确完整，尤其是将用于对该个人作出决定时。
  - **保护义务：** 作出合理安全安排，防止未经授权的处理。这是最常被违反的义务，也是 PDPC 罚款的常见依据。
  - **保留限制义务：** 到某个时候须停止保留（删除或销毁），不能永久保存。
  - **转移限制义务：** 转移出新加坡的数据须继续获得相当水平的保护。
  - **数据泄露通知义务：** 发生泄露时通知 PDPC 和受影响个人，以防止损害。这项义务相对较新。
  - **[数据可携带义务]：** 已写入法律但尚未实施，监管机构仍在研究如何运作。
  - **问责义务：** 实施数据保护政策并任命数据保护官。

- **The Regulator and Enforcement 监管机构与执法**
  - **PDPC:** The Personal Data Protection Commission. Its roles are to promote awareness, advise the government, and administer and enforce the PDPA. It is the primary enforcer.
  - **Public enforcement:** The PDPC investigates and issues fines or directions to non-compliant organisations. This is the normal route.
  - **Private enforcement:** The aggrieved individual sues the organisation directly in court. This is rare because it is expensive for the individual.
  - **PDPC：** 个人数据保护委员会，职责包括提高公众意识、向政府提供建议、执行 PDPA。它是主要执法者。
  - **公共执法：** PDPC 展开调查，对不合规组织处以罚款或发出指示。这是常规途径。
  - **私人执法：** 受害个人直接到法院起诉组织。因成本高而很少见。

- **Class Discussion: What Data Privacy Issues Might NUS Have? 课堂讨论：NUS 可能有哪些数据隐私问题？**
  - **Student data (financial, medical):** Obtain consent before use and secure the data against unauthorised access.
  - **Staff and student helpers:** Under the PDPA, "employees" include student volunteers, so the DPO must instruct them to handle data responsibly.
  - **Canvas data breach:** A contracted third party was at fault. NUS needs an incident-response playbook whether the fault is its own or a vendor's.
  - **Accuracy:** Accuracy is mainly a concern while the person is still at NUS, because decisions are made about them; it matters less after they leave.
  - **Retention:** How long NUS should keep data is one of the harder legal questions.
  - **Research:** Obtain the necessary consent, including for data from external parties, or rely on an exception.
  - **学生数据（财务、医疗）：** 使用前须取得同意，并保障数据安全，防止未经授权访问。
  - **职员与学生助手：** PDPA 下的“雇员”包括学生志愿者，所以数据保护官必须指导他们负责任地处理数据。
  - **Canvas 数据泄露：** 过错在签约的第三方。不论是自身还是供应商的过错，NUS 都需要事件应对预案。
  - **准确性：** 主要在当事人仍在 NUS 时才是问题，因为会对其作出决定；离校后就没那么重要。
  - **保留：** NUS 应保留数据多久，是较难的法律问题之一。
  - **研究：** 须取得必要同意（包括来自外部方的数据），或依赖某项例外。

- **Definition of Personal Data 个人数据的定义**
  - **Statutory definition:** "Data, whether true or not, about an individual who can be identified (a) from that data, or (b) from that data and other information to which the organisation has or is likely to have access."
  - **Four elements:** (1) data; (2) relating to an individual; (3) about that individual; (4) identifying that individual. Personal data exists only if all four are satisfied.
  - **Lecturer's caution:** This is perhaps the most complex concept in data protection law. If you look too hard, gaps appear. Focus on what you need to know for compliance.
  - **法定定义：** “不论真实与否，关于某个个人的数据，该个人可以（a）通过该数据，或（b）通过该数据及组织拥有或可能获取的其他信息被识别。”
  - **四个要素：** （1）数据；（2）涉及个人；（3）关于该个人；（4）能识别该个人。四个要素全部满足才是个人数据。
  - **讲师提醒：** 这可能是数据保护法中最复杂的概念，看得太细就会发现漏洞。应聚焦合规所需掌握的内容。

- **Element 1: Data 要素一：数据**
  - **Any form:** Paper, electronic and so on.
  - **Need not be true:** Inaccurate data still counts.
  - **Opinions:** Opinions that are neither true nor false still count. Example: "ABC is a good student."
  - **任何形式：** 纸质、电子等均可。
  - **不必真实：** 不准确的数据也算。
  - **意见：** 无所谓真假的意见也算。例如：“ABC 是个好学生”。

- **Element 2: Individual 要素二：个人**
  - **Natural person only:** A human being. Legal persons such as companies and associations are excluded, so company data is not protected.
  - **Living or deceased:** Both are covered, with limits on deceased persons (see Excluded Personal Data).
  - **Multiple individuals:** One piece of data can relate to two people. In the **adventure camp example**, Bernie provides her husband Bernard's name, address and phone number as her emergency contact. The data relates to both, so consent may be needed from both before it is used for another purpose.
  - **Group statements (in-class question):** ABC Pte Ltd's C-suite is listed publicly.
    - "Every C-suite executive has committed adultery" is clearly personal data, because it is a statement about each executive.
    - "50% have committed adultery" depends on the facts. With only two executives, or with other information to combine, it may identify the individuals.
    - On its face, the 50% statement does not say who, so it is arguably not personal data. A probability-based argument is possible, but on common sense it is probably not personal data.
  - **Comparative (non-examinable):** Terminology differs:
    - GDPR: "data subject"
    - India: "data principal"
    - China: "natural person" (自然人)
    - The GDPR excludes deceased persons by default, and the NZ Privacy Act defines an individual as a living person.
  - **Q&A:** Does the PDPA apply between individuals (e.g., posting someone's details on your Facebook page)? Generally no, though an individual can sometimes be caught. This is covered further next week.
  - **仅限自然人：** 即人类。公司、协会等法人除外，所以公司数据不受保护。
  - **在世或已故：** 均涵盖，但对已故者有限制（见“被排除的个人数据”）。
  - **涉及多人：** 同一数据可涉及两个人。在**探险营例子**中，Bernie 提供丈夫 Bernard 的姓名、地址和电话作为紧急联系人。该数据同时涉及两人，用于其他目的前可能需要双方同意。
  - **群体陈述（课堂问题）：** ABC 私人有限公司的 C 级高管名单是公开的。
    - “每位 C 级高管都有通奸行为”显然是个人数据，因为这是针对每位高管的陈述。
    - “50% 有通奸行为”视情况而定。如果只有两位高管，或可结合其他信息，就可能识别出个人。
    - 50% 陈述本身没有说明是谁，所以可以说不是个人数据。虽然可以提出基于概率的论点，但按常识大概不是个人数据。
  - **比较法（不考）：** 术语不同：
    - GDPR：“数据主体”
    - 印度：“数据委托人”
    - 中国：“自然人”
    - GDPR 默认不适用于已故者，新西兰《隐私法》把个人定义为在世者。
  - **问答：** PDPA 是否适用于个人之间（如在 Facebook 主页公开他人资料）？一般不适用，但个人有时也可能被涵盖。下周详讲。

- **Element 3: About 要素三：关于**
  - **Purpose test (PDPC guideline):** If the purpose of the data is to record or communicate information about an individual, it is generally personal data. Examples are an employee file (health, education) and customer spending records.
  - **"Incidental" boundary:** Data that is only incidentally about an individual is generally not personal data. This boundary is drawn by the regulator, not by the statute.
  - **Incident report:** A report about an event that names the people involved is generally not personal data.
  - **Bus driver video (student scenario):**
    - The video records an incident, but the lecturer's view is that it is likely personal data.
    - Through a lawyer's lens, it shows the driver's face and conduct.
    - Through a regulator's lens, the purpose is to say "look at this terrible driver," which is communicating information about him.
    - The lines are not mathematical, and reasonable people may disagree.
  - **Emails and chats between individuals:** Generally not personal data, unless intended to convey information about someone (e.g., "Watch out for this guy").
  - **Group chat collecting IC numbers:** The IC numbers are personal data because the messages exist to share them with the organiser. Chat about what to wear is not.
  - **Warning about an unknown stranger:** This satisfies "about" but may fail identifiability.
  - **Who collects:** If I email you about someone, I disclose and you collect.
  - **Hotel feedback survey:** Likely personal data, because its purpose is to record the guest's experience and sentiment.
  - **Rationale:** "About" requires a connection between data and individual, and Singapore chose a narrower word than some jurisdictions. The incidental boundary limits scope so that not everything touching a person is personal data.
  - **目的测试（PDPC 指引）：** 若数据目的在于记录或传达关于某个人的信息，一般属于个人数据。例如员工档案（健康、教育）、客户消费记录。
  - **“附带”边界：** 仅附带涉及个人的数据一般不是个人数据。这条边界由监管机构划定，并非法条规定。
  - **事件调查报告：** 关于事件、附带提及相关人员姓名的报告，一般不是个人数据。
  - **公交车司机视频（学生情境）：**
    - 视频记录的是一个事件，但讲师认为很可能是个人数据。
    - 律师视角：视频展示了司机的脸和行为。
    - 监管者视角：目的是说“看这个糟糕的司机”，即传达关于他的信息。
    - 界线不是数学式的，合理的人可能有不同意见。
  - **个人之间的邮件和聊天：** 一般不是个人数据，除非意在传达关于某人的信息（如“小心这个人”）。
  - **群聊收集身份证号码：** 身份证号码是个人数据，因为这些消息就是为了提供给组织者；讨论穿什么则不是。
  - **提醒提防未知陌生人：** 满足“关于”，但可能不满足可识别性。
  - **谁在收集：** 我发邮件给你谈及某人，我是披露，你是收集。
  - **酒店反馈问卷：** 很可能是个人数据，因为其目的是记录住客的体验和感受。
  - **理据：** “关于”要求数据与个人之间存在联系，新加坡选用了比部分司法管辖区更窄的词。“附带”边界用于限制范围，使并非一切触及个人的东西都算个人数据。

- **EU Comparison: Peter Nowak (2017) (Non-Examinable) and Access to Exam Scripts 欧盟比较：Peter Nowak 案（2017）（不考）与考卷查阅**
  - **Facts:** A trainee accountant failed his professional exam four times and challenged the fourth result without success. His data access request was met except for his exam script, which the association said was not his personal data.
  - **Outcome:** The CJEU held that the exam script was his personal data.
  - **EU test, "relates to":** Data relates to a person by **content, purpose, or effect**, and any one suffices. Here all three were met:
    - Content: the script revealed his knowledge, thinking and handwriting.
    - Purpose: it evaluated his suitability to practise.
    - Effect: it influenced his entry into the profession.
  - **Singapore:** The exam script would likely also be personal data, because Singapore essentially focuses on content. The EU concept is broader overall.
  - **Q&A on NUS exam scripts:** Students can ask for them, but entitlement depends on timing, and the PDPA has an exam-script exception.
  - **Access exemptions:** There is an **evaluative purpose** exception. For example, an employer's negative appraisal comments may not have to be disclosed. Details come with the Access Obligation.
  - **案情：** 一名见习会计师四次考试未通过，对第四次结果提出异议被驳回。他提出数据查阅请求，协会提供了除考卷以外的所有数据，称考卷不是他的个人数据。
  - **结果：** 欧盟法院认定考卷是他的个人数据。
  - **欧盟测试，“相关”：** 数据可通过**内容、目的或效果**与个人相关，具备其一即可。本案三者均满足：
    - 内容：考卷揭示了他的知识、思维和笔迹。
    - 目的：评估他执业的适格性。
    - 效果：影响他能否进入该行业。
  - **新加坡：** 考卷很可能也是个人数据，因为新加坡基本上关注内容。欧盟的概念总体更宽。
  - **NUS 考卷问答：** 学生可以申请查阅，但能否获得取决于申请时间，且 PDPA 有专门针对考卷的例外。
  - **查阅豁免：** 存在**评估目的**例外，例如雇主对员工工作的负面评语可能无需披露。具体在查阅义务部分讲。

- **Element 4: Identify 要素四：识别**
  - **Two-datapoint rule of thumb:** Data generally needs at least two datapoints to identify someone.
  - **Unique datapoints:** Fewer are needed. Examples are ID numbers (NRIC, passport, student number) and biometrics (DNA, fingerprint, face, iris).
  - **Generic datapoints:** Many are needed. Examples are gender, nationality, age and blood type.
  - **Examples:**
    - Full name plus passport number identifies a person with certainty.
    - Programme of study, enrolment year, date of birth, gender and nationality together can uniquely identify a person.
  - **Compliance view:** The more unique the identifiers, the more likely the dataset is personal data, and so the more dangerous it is.
  - **Indirect identification:** The dataset alone does not identify, but it can when combined with other information the organisation has access to. Example: customer email addresses linked to public social media accounts showing names.
  - **"Access" means practicable access:** Access is practicable if it needs no huge cost, time or resources. Examples are information publicly available online or held by a related or sister organisation.
  - **两个数据点经验法则：** 一般需要至少两个数据点才能识别某人。
  - **唯一性数据点：** 所需数量较少。例如身份号码（身份证、护照、学号）和生物特征（DNA、指纹、面部、虹膜）。
  - **通用数据点：** 需要很多个。例如性别、国籍、年龄、血型。
  - **例子：**
    - 全名加护照号码可确定识别一个人。
    - 专业、入学年份、出生日期、性别、国籍合在一起，可唯一识别一个人。
  - **合规视角：** 标识符越唯一，数据集越可能是个人数据，因此越危险。
  - **间接识别：** 数据集本身无法识别，但与组织能获取的其他信息结合后可以识别。例如客户邮箱关联到显示姓名的公开社交媒体账号。
  - **“能够获取”指切实可行的获取：** 不需要巨大成本、时间或资源即为切实可行。例如网上公开的信息，或由关联公司、姐妹公司持有的信息。

- **Scenarios on the Definition 定义相关情境**
  - **Street survey with full name:** Personal data. Without the name (only spending, gender, age range), it is probably not.
  - **Age range, gender, occupation and workplace:**
    - The answer depends on the respondent.
    - A female retail salesperson in her 20s at a mall is not identifiable, because there are many such people.
    - The only male security officer in his 20s in a specific building is identifiable even without a name.
  - **Two compliance approaches:**
    - Check each dataset individually.
    - Or, more practically, presume the data is personal data and obtain consent before using it.
  - **GHI employees vs meeting minutes:** Employee records (education, blood type, name) are personal data. Meeting minutes that name speakers are unlikely to be, because their purpose is to record what was said.
  - **带全名的街头调查：** 是个人数据。不收集姓名（只有消费、性别、年龄段）则大概不是。
  - **年龄段、性别、职业、工作地点：**
    - 视受访者而定。
    - 商场里二十多岁的女零售员无法识别，因为这样的人很多。
    - 某栋楼唯一一位二十多岁的男保安，即使没有姓名也可被识别。
  - **两种合规做法：**
    - 逐一检查每个数据集。
    - 或者更实际地推定为个人数据，在使用前取得同意。
  - **GHI 员工档案 vs 会议纪要：** 员工记录（教育、血型、姓名）是个人数据。点名发言者的会议纪要大概不是，因为其目的是记录会议上说了什么。

- **AI Case Study: Meta's Model Capability Initiative AI 案例：Meta 的 Model Capability Initiative**
  - **Facts:** Meta tracked employees' keystrokes, mouse clicks and on-screen content to collect AI training data. After staff backlash, it paused the programme.
  - **Question:** Was Meta collecting employees' personal data? The lecturer flagged that the answer is not straightforward.
  - **What is collected:** Keystrokes from coding may not be "about" the employee. On-screen content could include personal material.
  - **Device and contract argument:** Employees use company laptops, and employment contracts may authorise collection. But the **prior question** is whether personal data is being collected at all.
  - **Incidental argument:** Meta could argue any personal data is merely incidental, because the purpose is to train AI, not to learn about staff. The lecturer called this tricky.
  - **Identifiability:** Login IDs and names appear on screen, and periodic screenshots are taken, so the identify element is very hard to defeat. Meta's best argument must therefore come from the **"about"** element.
  - **Behavioural identifiers:** Ways of working and handwriting are increasingly usable to identify people. Faces are on screen; whether voices are captured is uncertain.
  - **Method:** Always run through all four elements.
  - **Social acceptability (Q&A on AI disease detection):** Acceptance of biometrics such as fingerprint and face unlock has evolved. This feeds into Purpose Limitation, because "reasonable" evolves with social perception.
  - **案情：** Meta 追踪员工的键盘敲击、鼠标点击和屏幕内容，用于收集 AI 训练数据。员工反弹后暂停了该项目。
  - **问题：** Meta 是否在收集员工的个人数据？讲师提示答案并不简单。
  - **收集了什么：** 写代码的键盘敲击可能不是“关于”员工的；屏幕内容则可能包含私人内容。
  - **设备与合同论点：** 员工使用公司电脑，雇佣合同可能授权收集。但**前置问题**是到底有没有收集个人数据。
  - **附带论点：** Meta 可主张任何个人数据只是附带的，因为目的是训练 AI，而不是了解员工。讲师认为这个论点很棘手。
  - **可识别性：** 屏幕上会显示登录 ID 和姓名，且会定期截屏，所以识别要素很难被否定。Meta 最好的论点只能从**“关于”**要素出发。
  - **行为标识符：** 工作方式、笔迹越来越可用于识别个人。屏幕上有面孔；是否采集声音尚不确定。
  - **方法：** 始终逐一检视四个要素。
  - **社会接受度（关于 AI 疾病识别的问答）：** 社会对指纹解锁、面部解锁等生物识别的接受度在演变。这与目的限制义务相关，因为“合理”会随社会观念变化。

- **Excluded Personal Data 被排除的个人数据**
  - **Records at least 100 years old:** Excluded, because they are too old to harm anyone.
  - **Deceased more than 10 years:** Excluded. There is limited protection within the first 10 years after death. The rationale is respect for the feelings of relatives and friends rather than the deceased.
  - **Business contact information (BCI):**
    - BCI is name, title, business phone, address and email, and similar details, i.e., what is on a business card.
    - It is excluded only if **not provided solely for personal purposes**.
    - The rationale is that BCI is meant to be shared.
  - **Sharon at a seminar:** She drops her card in a bowl to join the mailing list. That is BCI, so no consent, care, access or correction obligations apply.
  - **Sharon at a gym:** She uses the same card to register for a membership. This is solely personal, so it is not BCI and the PDPA applies.
  - **Damien and Tom:** Damien gives his contact details to salesperson Tom to find premises for his business's second branch. This is BCI, so Tom can use it and share it with colleagues, who can pass it on freely, all without consent.
  - **Additional notes on contacts (student Q):** Personal information you write down about a business contact goes beyond BCI, because it is not used for business contact.
  - **Comfort Transportation (2016):**
    - **Facts:** Taxi booking apps sent drivers' personal mobile numbers to passengers.
    - **Outcome:** The numbers were BCI, so no consent was needed and the companies were not liable.
    - **Reason:** The drivers gave the numbers when hiring taxis, for the business purpose of providing taxi services.
    - **Principle:** A personal number can be BCI if provided for business purposes. The lecturer called this a narrow exception.
  - **存在至少 100 年的记录：** 被排除，因为年代久远，不可能再造成伤害。
  - **去世超过 10 年者：** 被排除。去世后 10 年内仍有有限保护。理据是尊重亲友的感受，而非为了逝者本人。
  - **商业联系信息（BCI）：**
    - 包括姓名、职位、办公电话、地址、邮箱等类似信息，即名片上的内容。
    - 前提是**并非仅为个人目的提供**。
    - 理据是这类信息本来就是用来分享的。
  - **Sharon 参加研讨会：** 她把名片投入碗中以加入邮寄名单。属于 BCI，不适用同意、保护、查阅、更正等义务。
  - **Sharon 办健身房会员：** 用同一张名片登记会员，完全出于个人目的，不是 BCI，PDPA 适用。
  - **Damien 与 Tom：** Damien 把联系方式交给销售员 Tom，请他为生意的第二家分店找物业。属于 BCI，Tom 可以使用并分享给同事，同事也可以自由转交，都无需同意。
  - **对联系人的额外记录（学生提问）：** 你对业务联系人记下的私人信息超出了 BCI 的范围，因为它不是用于业务联系的。
  - **Comfort Transportation 案（2016）：**
    - **案情：** 出租车叫车应用把司机的私人手机号发送给乘客。
    - **结果：** 号码属于 BCI，无需同意，公司不承担责任。
    - **理由：** 司机是在租车时为提供出租车服务这一业务目的提供号码的。
    - **原则：** 私人号码若为业务目的提供，也可以是 BCI。讲师指出这是一项狭窄的例外。

- **Anonymisation: Concept, Trade-Offs and Terminology 匿名化：概念、取舍与术语**
  - **Definition:** Converting personal data into non-personal data so that individuals can no longer be identified. It defeats the fourth element.
  - **Pros:**
    - The data falls outside the PDPA and can be used freely.
    - It acts as a security measure: a breach causes less harm.
  - **Cons:**
    - It inevitably reduces information richness and therefore utility.
    - It is hard to do properly for large datasets.
  - **Decision:** Weigh whether anonymisation is worth it in the circumstances.
  - **Terminology:**
    - Dataset: all the data.
    - Record: one row.
    - Attribute: one column.
    - Value: one cell.
    - Direct identifier: e.g., NRIC.
    - Indirect identifier: e.g., age.
    - Target attribute: the informationally important column (e.g., monthly spend). Don't alter it, or the data becomes useless.
  - **定义：** 把个人数据转化为非个人数据，使个人无法再被识别，即否定第四个要素。
  - **优点：**
    - 数据不再受 PDPA 规管，可以自由使用。
    - 是一种安全措施：发生泄露时损害较小。
  - **缺点：**
    - 必然降低信息丰富度，从而降低效用。
    - 大型数据集很难妥善匿名化。
  - **决定：** 需要权衡在具体情况下是否值得。
  - **术语：**
    - 数据集：全部数据。
    - 记录：一行。
    - 属性：一列。
    - 值：一个单元格。
    - 直接标识符：如身份证号码。
    - 间接标识符：如年龄。
    - 目标属性：信息上最重要的列（如月消费）。不要改动它，否则数据失去用处。

- **Anonymisation Techniques 匿名化技术**
  - **Record suppression:** Remove an entire record. This is the most drastic option and is used for outliers that cannot be handled any other way.
  - **Character masking:** Replace characters with "*" or "x". Example: masking the last digits of a postal code keeps the region but hides the exact address.
  - **Pseudonymisation:** Replace names with random strings.
    - Persistent pseudonymisation uses the same pseudonym for the same person throughout.
    - Non-persistent pseudonymisation uses different pseudonyms across records.
  - **Reversible pseudonymisation:** The organisation keeps an identity mapping table from pseudonym to name. Deleting the table makes the pseudonymisation irreversible.
  - **Student Q on NRIC:** Deleting the NRIC column is suppression. Replacing NRICs with random numbers while keeping a map back to them is reversible pseudonymisation.
  - **Irreversible pseudonymisation (double coding):**
    - A trusted third party holds a linking table (pseudonym → interim pseudonym).
    - The organisation holds only the interim pseudonym → name table.
    - How irreversible it really is depends on how easily you can get the linking table. If the third party is a subsidiary you control, or a contract gives you free access, it is effectively reversible.
  - **Generalisation:** Reduce precision, e.g., convert age to a range or remove the block number from an address.
  - **Swapping:** Shuffle values within an attribute across records. Use it only when correlations between attributes don't matter.
  - **Data perturbation:** Slightly modify numeric values, e.g., by base-x rounding of height, weight and age. Use it when approximate values are enough.
  - **Data aggregation:** Replace records with summary values, e.g., donation counts and totals per income band. Individual donors become unidentifiable.
  - **Extracting features (student Q):** Deriving something from an attribute before deleting it, such as the number of letters in a name, is arguably a form of generalisation. It is possible but probably not very useful.
  - **记录删除：** 删除整条记录。这是最激进的手段，用于无法以其他方式处理的离群记录。
  - **字符掩码：** 用“*”或“x”替换字符。例如掩去邮编最后几位，保留区域但隐藏确切地址。
  - **假名化：** 用随机字符串替换姓名。
    - 持久性假名化：同一人始终使用同一假名。
    - 非持久性假名化：不同记录使用不同假名。
  - **可逆假名化：** 组织保留从假名到姓名的身份映射表。删除该表即变为不可逆。
  - **关于身份证号码的学生提问：** 删除身份证号码列属于删除；用随机数字替换身份证号码并保留对应映射表，属于可逆假名化。
  - **不可逆假名化（双重编码）：**
    - 由可信第三方持有链接表（假名 → 中间假名）。
    - 组织只持有中间假名 → 姓名的表。
    - 实际上有多不可逆，取决于你拿到链接表有多容易。如果第三方是你控制的子公司，或合同让你随意获取，就实际上可逆。
  - **泛化：** 降低精度，如把年龄转为范围、去掉地址中的座号。
  - **交换：** 在记录之间打乱同一属性的值。仅在不在乎属性之间的相关性时使用。
  - **数据扰动：** 轻微改动数值，如对身高、体重、年龄按基数取整。适用于近似值即可的情况。
  - **数据聚合：** 用汇总值替代单条记录，如按收入段统计捐款笔数和总额。个别捐款人无法被识别。
  - **提取特征（学生提问）：** 在删除属性前先从中提取信息，如名字的字母数，可以说是一种泛化。可行，但大概用处不大。

- **Applying Techniques by Identifier Type 按标识符类型应用技术**
  - **Direct identifiers:** Suppress the attribute, or pseudonymise it (e.g., "John Tan" → 123456).
  - **Age, height, weight:** Generalise into ranges or perturb.
  - **Gender:** Practically impossible to anonymise, so it is usually retained as is.
  - **Race and marital status:** There are few categories, so group the small ones into "Others".
  - **Date of birth:** Generalise, e.g., to month and year.
  - **Address:** Generalise to a broader area.
  - **Postal code:** Mask the last four digits.
  - **Job title:** Requires manual grouping, e.g., CEO → C-suite.
  - **Company name:** Generalise to the company's sector.
  - **IP address, vehicle plate number:** Mask.
  - **GPS location:** Generalise, perturb or mask.
  - **直接标识符：** 删除该属性，或假名化（如“John Tan”→ 123456）。
  - **年龄、身高、体重：** 泛化为范围，或进行扰动。
  - **性别：** 基本无法匿名化，通常原样保留。
  - **种族、婚姻状况：** 类别少，需要把人数少的类别归为“其他”。
  - **出生日期：** 泛化，如到年月。
  - **地址：** 泛化到更大的区域。
  - **邮编：** 掩去最后四位。
  - **职位：** 需要人工归类，如 CEO → C 级高管。
  - **公司名称：** 泛化为所属行业。
  - **IP 地址、车牌号：** 掩码。
  - **GPS 位置：** 泛化、扰动或掩码。

- **When Is Data Anonymised? 何时算已匿名化？**
  - **Strict legal position:** It must be impossible to re-identify anyone. This follows from the definition of personal data.
  - **PDPC position:** The test is whether there is a **serious possibility of re-identification**, assessed with safeguards. These include:
    - Restricting recipients from further disclosure.
    - Applying especially stringent safeguards to identity mapping and linking tables (e.g., held by a third party).
    - Periodic reviews, because re-identification techniques advance over time.
  - **Holistic view, JKL → XYZ:**
    - JKL used robust techniques and contractually required XYZ not to re-identify, to secure the data and to maintain data protection standards.
    - If XYZ is breached and data is exfiltrated, the PDPC weighs these safeguards to decide whether the data was anonymised at the point of disclosure.
    - If it was not, JKL may itself have breached the law.
  - **严格法律立场：** 必须不可能重新识别任何人，这是从个人数据定义推导出来的。
  - **PDPC 立场：** 测试是是否存在**重新识别的严重可能性**，并结合保障措施评估。保障措施包括：
    - 限制接收方进一步披露。
    - 对身份映射表、链接表采取特别严格的保障（如交由第三方保管）。
    - 定期审查，因为重新识别技术会随时间进步。
  - **整体性观点，JKL → XYZ：**
    - JKL 使用了稳健的技术，并在合同中要求 XYZ 不得重新识别、须安全处理数据、须维持数据保护标准。
    - 若 XYZ 发生泄露、数据外泄，PDPC 会衡量这些保障措施，判断数据在披露时是否已匿名化。
    - 若不是，JKL 本身可能违法。

- **K-Anonymity and Internal Anonymisation k-匿名性与内部匿名化**
  - **K-anonymity:** Every combination of indirect identifiers is shared by at least k records. In the taxi-trips example, generalising age and occupation gives classes such as "31–40, male, IT" with 5 records each, so k = 5. A higher k means stronger anonymisation.
  - **PDPC benchmarks:**
    - k = 5 with safeguards for sharing with **external** parties.
    - k = 3 for **internal** use.
  - **Internal anonymisation:** Strictly, data the organisation itself can re-identify is not anonymised. But the PDPC accepts that a department can be treated as holding anonymised data where controls prevent re-identification.
  - **JKL example:** Department A (customer relations) anonymises the data for Department B (analytics) and keeps the original. JKL imposes access restrictions on B, so B is treated as using anonymised data. This is a regulatory exception that eases analytics.
  - **k-匿名性：** 每一种间接标识符组合至少由 k 条记录共享。在出租车出行例子中，泛化年龄和职业后，得到“31–40 岁、男性、IT”这样各有 5 条记录的组别，所以 k = 5。k 越大，匿名化程度越强。
  - **PDPC 基准：**
    - 与**外部**方分享：k = 5，并配合保障措施。
    - **内部**使用：k = 3。
  - **内部匿名化：** 严格来说，组织自己能重新识别的数据并未匿名化。但 PDPC 接受，在有管控防止重新识别的情况下，某个部门可被视为持有匿名化数据。
  - **JKL 例子：** A 部门（客户关系）为 B 部门（分析）匿名化数据并保留原始数据。JKL 对 B 施加访问限制，于是 B 被视为使用匿名化数据。这是便利数据分析的监管例外。

- **In-Class Exercise: GHI Hospital Patient Records 课堂练习：GHI 医院病人记录**
  - **Scenario:** The hospital wants to run patient records (NRIC, age, gender, disease) through an AI system to correlate age and gender with disease. The task is to reach adequate k-anonymity while keeping the data useful.
  - **Steps discussed:**
    - Set k = 3, since the use is internal.
    - Remove the NRIC.
    - Leave gender as it is.
    - Generalise or round age (e.g., bands, or base-5 or base-3 rounding).
    - Avoid swapping, because it breaks the age–disease correlation the analysis needs.
  - **Disease column:** This is the target attribute, so don't touch it. Grouping diseases is possible only if the loss of utility is acceptable.
  - **Is removing the NRIC enough?** Apply the serious-possibility test across all attributes. Re-identification risk remains because the hospital keeps the full records, though a case can be argued.
  - **Outliers (e.g., the 70-year-old):** These block k = 3. Widen the ranges, or suppress the record. Going all the way destroys utility.
  - **Third-party AI host:** If an external party hosting the AI system has access to the data, k should probably be 5. If processing is in-house, k = 3 suffices.
  - **情境：** 医院想把病人记录（身份证号码、年龄、性别、疾病）输入 AI 系统，分析年龄、性别与疾病的相关性。任务是达到足够的 k-匿名性，同时保持数据有用。
  - **讨论的步骤：**
    - 因为是内部使用，设 k = 3。
    - 删除身份证号码。
    - 性别保持不变。
    - 对年龄做泛化或取整（如分段，或以 5 或 3 为基数取整）。
    - 不宜交换，因为会破坏分析所需的年龄与疾病的相关性。
  - **疾病列：** 这是目标属性，不要改动。只有能接受效用损失时才可以把疾病归类。
  - **删掉身份证号码就够了吗？** 要对所有属性整体适用“严格可能性”测试。由于医院保留完整记录，仍有重新识别风险，但可以论证。
  - **离群记录（如 70 岁那条）：** 会妨碍达到 k = 3。需要拉宽范围，或删除该记录。匿名化做到底会破坏效用。
  - **第三方托管 AI：** 如果托管 AI 系统的外部方能接触数据，k 大概应为 5。如果在内部处理，k = 3 即可。

- **Sensitive Personal Data 敏感个人数据**
  - **Other jurisdictions (non-examinable):** The GDPR specifies sensitive categories such as health and race. Biometrics, religious belief and medical health are also treated as sensitive elsewhere.
  - **Singapore:** The statute has no sensitive category, but the PDPC treats some data as more sensitive and requires a higher standard of protection.
  - **Aviva (2017):** The PDPC listed more-sensitive data:
    - NRIC numbers
    - insurance data
    - personal history involving drug use and infidelity
    - personal data of minors
  - **Common criterion (lecturer's argument):** Data is sensitive where there is a **high potential for harm if it is improperly handled**. This lets you identify other sensitive types, e.g., certain facts about a person's background.
  - **Practice point:** When processing data, especially for AI, check each attribute for sensitivity.
  - **NRIC (Q&A):**
    - The list is not static.
    - Aviva was decided when the NRIC was treated as an authenticator as well as an identifier.
    - Once the government fully transitions the NRIC into a public identifier, it would remain personal data but would no longer be high-risk, and masking would no longer be needed.
    - The government has said the transition is not yet complete.
  - **其他司法管辖区（不考）：** GDPR 规定了健康、种族等敏感类别。生物特征、宗教信仰、医疗健康在其他地方也被视为敏感。
  - **新加坡：** 立法中没有敏感类别，但 PDPC 将某些数据视为更敏感，要求更高标准的保护。
  - **Aviva 案（2017）：** PDPC 列出的更敏感数据：
    - 身份证号码
    - 保险数据
    - 涉及吸毒和婚外情的个人经历
    - 未成年人的个人数据
  - **共同标准（讲师观点）：** **处理不当时造成损害的可能性高**，即为敏感数据。据此可判断其他敏感类型，如关于个人背景的某些事实。
  - **实务要点：** 处理数据时（尤其用于 AI），应检查每个属性是否敏感。
  - **身份证号码（问答）：**
    - 清单并非一成不变。
    - Aviva 案判决时，身份证号码既被视为标识符，也被视为认证凭据。
    - 政府把身份证号码完全转为公开标识符后，它仍是个人数据，但不再属于高风险，也不再需要掩码。
    - 政府表示这一转变尚未完成。
## Week 1 Learning Tips

Start by building the gatekeeper habit. Every PDPA analysis begins with the question this week was built around: is this personal data? The twelve obligations, the consent analysis and the breach rules only apply after you have answered yes. When you face a scenario, whether it is Meta's keystroke tracker or a hospital's patient table, run through the four elements in order: data, individual, about, identify. Say explicitly which element is in doubt. As the Meta discussion showed, identifiability was almost impossible to defeat, so the real argument moved to "about". Knowing which element carries the weight is what separates a strong answer from a list of facts.

先养成“守门”的习惯。每一次 PDPA 分析都从本周的核心问题开始：这是个人数据吗？十二项义务、同意分析、泄露规则，都只有在答案为“是”之后才适用。面对任何情境，无论是 Meta 的键盘追踪工具还是医院的病人数据表，都要按顺序检视四个要素：数据、个人、关于、识别，并明确指出哪个要素存在疑问。正如 Meta 案的讨论所示，可识别性几乎无法否定，所以真正的争论转到了“关于”上。知道哪个要素是关键，就是好答案和事实罗列的区别。

Understand why each boundary exists, because that tells you how far to push it. The "incidental" boundary was drawn by the regulator, not the statute, to stop everything that touches a person from becoming personal data. That is why incident reports, meeting minutes and ordinary chats generally fall outside it. A common pitfall is to treat this as a mechanical rule. The bus driver video shows that the purpose test can turn an "incident" recording into data about a person, and the lecturer stressed that these lines are not mathematical. In an exam, argue both sides, as the lecturer did with his lawyer's hat and regulator's hat, and then commit to a reasoned view.

理解每条边界存在的原因，因为这决定了它能被推到多远。“附带”边界是监管机构而非法条划定的，目的是防止所有触及个人的东西都成为个人数据。这就是为什么事件报告、会议纪要和日常聊天一般不在范围内。常见的误区是把它当作机械规则。公交车司机视频的例子说明，目的测试可以把一段“事件”录像变成关于某人的数据，讲师也强调这些界线不是数学式的。考试时要像讲师那样，分别戴上律师和监管者的帽子论证两面，然后给出有理据的结论。

Don't over-apply narrow rules. Business contact information is a classic trap. The same name card is BCI when Sharon drops it in a seminar bowl, but not BCI when she uses it to register at a gym. Comfort Transportation turned on the fact that the drivers gave their personal numbers for a business purpose. The test is the purpose for which the information was provided, not what kind of information it is or where it is printed. Make a three-column card for each example (facts, purpose of provision, outcome) and you will see the deciding factor immediately. Treat the 100-year and 10-years-after-death exclusions the same way: know the threshold and the rationale.

不要过度套用狭窄的规则。商业联系信息就是一个典型陷阱。同一张名片，Sharon 投进研讨会的碗里时是 BCI，用来登记健身房会员时就不是。Comfort Transportation 案的关键在于司机是为业务目的提供私人号码的。判断标准是提供信息的目的，而不是信息的类型或印在哪里。为每个例子做一张三栏卡片（事实、提供目的、结果），决定性因素就一目了然。对“100 年”和“去世 10 年”这两项排除也同样处理：记住门槛和理据。

Treat anonymisation as a trade-off you manage, not a checkbox. Every technique buys lower identifiability at the cost of utility. The skill being tested is choosing the technique that fits the purpose. In the GHI Hospital exercise, swapping was wrong because it would destroy the age–disease correlation the AI needs, and the disease column stayed untouched because it is the target attribute. Practise by taking each technique (suppression, masking, pseudonymisation, generalisation, swapping, perturbation, aggregation) and writing one line on when to use it and one line on what it destroys. Then rehearse a fixed answer structure: identify direct, indirect and target attributes; choose techniques per attribute; check the k-value; handle outliers; add safeguards.

把匿名化看作需要管理的取舍，而不是打勾的清单。每种技术都是以效用为代价换取更低的可识别性，考的是根据目的选择合适技术的能力。在 GHI 医院练习中，交换不合适，因为会破坏 AI 所需的年龄与疾病的相关性；疾病列不动，因为它是目标属性。练习方法是：对每种技术（删除、掩码、假名化、泛化、交换、扰动、聚合），各写一句何时使用，一句它会破坏什么。然后演练一个固定的答题结构：识别直接、间接和目标属性；按属性选择技术；检查 k 值；处理离群记录；补充保障措施。

Keep the strict legal position and the PDPC's practical position side by side, because exam answers often need both. Strictly, data is anonymised only if re-identification is impossible. The PDPC instead asks whether there is a "serious possibility" of re-identification, takes a holistic view of safeguards (the JKL/XYZ example), accepts internal anonymisation between departments, and uses k = 5 for external sharing and k = 3 for internal use. A frequent pitfall is assuming that deleting the NRIC is enough. As the class discussion showed, the hospital still holds the full records. Another is forgetting that an external AI host can turn internal use into external sharing, which raises the k you need.

把严格的法律立场和 PDPC 的实务立场并列记住，因为考试答案常常两者都需要。严格来说，只有不可能重新识别时数据才算匿名化。PDPC 则看是否存在重新识别的“严重可能性”，对保障措施采取整体性观点（JKL/XYZ 例子），接受部门之间的内部匿名化，并以 k = 5 作为对外分享、k = 3 作为内部使用的基准。常见误区之一是以为删掉身份证号码就够了；课堂讨论已经说明，医院仍持有完整记录。另一个误区是忘了外部托管的 AI 会把内部使用变成对外分享，从而提高所需的 k 值。

Ground your sensitivity analysis in the harm criterion, not just the list. Aviva gives you the PDPC's examples, but the lecturer's point was that the common thread is a high potential for harm if the data is mishandled. That lets you reason about new categories, and about categories that change, like the NRIC as its role as an authenticator falls away. In any AI scenario, scan the attributes and flag the sensitive ones. That flag affects the standard of protection you will later argue under the Protection Obligation.

敏感性分析要以损害标准为基础，而不仅仅是那份清单。Aviva 案给出了 PDPC 的例子，但讲师强调，共同点在于数据处理不当时造成损害的可能性高。据此你可以推理新的类别，以及会变化的类别，比如身份证号码随着其认证凭据角色的消失而变化。在任何 AI 情境中，扫一遍属性并标出敏感项。这个标记会影响你之后在保护义务下所论证的保护标准。

Finally, study to the exam's stated scope. The slides are exhaustive and authoritative, and the exam is open book. Your advantage comes from knowing exactly where each rule, example and threshold sits so that you can apply it quickly, not from memorising extra material. Don't spend revision time on the non-examinable global framework, the comparative terminology slides or the Nowak case. Understand them as context, especially Nowak, which shows by contrast how much narrower Singapore's "about" test is. Put your effort into the four elements, the exclusions, the anonymisation techniques and thresholds, and the worked scenarios. Rehearse them until applying them feels routine.

最后，按考试明确的范围复习。幻灯片完整且权威，考试又是开卷，你的优势在于清楚知道每条规则、每个例子、每个门槛在哪里，能迅速运用，而不是背诵额外材料。不要把复习时间花在不考的全球框架、比较术语幻灯片或 Nowak 案上。把它们当作背景理解即可，尤其是 Nowak 案，它通过对比显示新加坡的“关于”测试窄得多。把精力放在四个要素、排除类别、匿名化技术与门槛，以及课上的情境练习上，反复演练直到运用起来驾轻就熟。

- [18:48:02–18:53:23] **The Twelve Data Protection Obligations**

  In terms of how the PDPA operates, it imposes a number of data protection obligations. People have different ways of counting these obligations; I count twelve. So I'm just going to very, very quickly run through what these obligations entail.

  You have the Consent Obligation, and this is something many people would be familiar with, right? This is the obligation to get consent before you collect, use, or disclose someone else's personal data.

  You have Purpose Limitation, and this is the obligation to only collect, use, or disclose personal data for a reasonable purpose. It constrains how you are allowed to use personal data.

  Number three is the Notification Obligation. This requires you to notify the individual before you actually collect, use, or disclose his personal data, to ensure that the individual will be informed before you do anything with it.

  You have the Access Obligation. This is an obligation that says that when someone requests their personal data, you are required to give them access, and also tell them how you have used the personal data within the past year.

  Next is the Correction Obligation, which is the obligation to correct any erroneous or inaccurate personal data upon the individual's request.

  Then you have the Accuracy Obligation. In certain situations, this requires you to make a reasonable effort to ensure that the personal data you've collected is accurate and complete. This is important especially when you are going to use the personal data to make some decision about the individual.

  Next, you have the Protection Obligation, and this is the one that is very often breached. When you read in the newspaper about some organisation that has been fined by the PDPC, this is the usual obligation that they might have breached. This obligation requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent any unauthorised processing of the data.

  You have Retention Limitation. This prevents organisations from holding on to personal data forever. At some point, you are supposed to delete or destroy the personal data in your possession.

  You have the Transfer Limitation Obligation. This one is a little bit complicated because it involves multiple countries. The essential idea behind this obligation is that when you transfer personal data out of Singapore, you have to make sure that the data will continue to receive the same level of protection. It cannot be that you transfer personal data to, say, Malaysia or Russia or some other country, and the data stops getting protected after a few months.

  You have the Data Breach Notification Obligation. This is a relatively new one, which says that if you suffer a data breach, like some hacker gets into your servers, or you accidentally disclose personal data, you are obliged to notify the PDPC and the affected individuals, so that action can be taken to prevent harm.

  The next obligation I put in square brackets because, although it is technically in the law, it hasn't actually been operationalised yet. It's on the books, but it hasn't been put into practice. This is the Data Portability Obligation, which requires an organisation to port personal data to a different organisation at the request of the individual. I think the regulator is still working out how this obligation should work in practice.

  Finally, you have the Accountability Obligation, which is the obligation to implement certain data protection policies; the organisation also has to appoint a data protection officer. So these are the twelve obligations that we have so far.

  然后是目的限制义务（Purpose Limitation），即只能为合理目的收集、使用或披露个人数据的义务。它限制了你可以如何使用个人数据。

  第三是通知义务（Notification Obligation）。它要求你在实际收集、使用或披露个人数据之前通知该个人，确保在你对数据做任何事情之前，个人已经知情。

  然后是查阅义务（Access Obligation）。这项义务规定，当有人请求查阅其个人数据时，你必须向其提供查阅，并告诉他们在过去一年内你是如何使用这些个人数据的。

  接下来是更正义务（Correction Obligation），即应个人的请求更正任何错误或不准确的个人数据的义务。

  然后是准确性义务（Accuracy Obligation）。在某些情况下，它要求你作出合理努力，确保你所收集的个人数据准确完整。这一点尤其重要，特别是当你要用这些个人数据对该个人作出某种决定的时候。

  接着是保护义务（Protection Obligation），这是经常被违反的一项。当你在报纸上读到某个组织被 PDPC 罚款时，通常违反的就是这项义务。这项义务要求组织作出合理的安全安排，防止数据遭到任何未经授权的处理。

  然后是保留限制义务（Retention Limitation），它防止组织永久持有个人数据。到了某个时候，你应该删除或销毁你所持有的个人数据。

  然后是转移限制义务（Transfer Limitation Obligation）。这项有点复杂，因为涉及多个国家。这项义务的核心思想是：当你把个人数据转移出新加坡时，必须确保这些数据继续得到同等水平的保护。不能出现你把个人数据转移到比如马来西亚、俄罗斯或其他国家后，几个月后数据就不再受到保护的情况。

  然后是数据泄露通知义务（Data Breach Notification Obligation）。这是一项相对较新的义务，规定如果你发生了数据泄露，比如有黑客侵入你的服务器，或者你意外披露了个人数据，你有义务通知 PDPC 和受影响的个人，以便采取行动防止损害。

  最后是问责义务（Accountability Obligation），即实施某些数据保护政策的义务；组织还必须任命一名数据保护官（data protection officer）。这就是目前我们所有的十二项义务。

In very rare cases, there is also private enforcement, meaning the individual himself who is aggrieved directly sues the organisation in court. - [19:01:38–19:04:52] **The Concept of Personal Data: Definition and Four Elements**

  Now let me move on to the actual, I guess, substantive part of this seminar, about the concept of personal data. As I mentioned in the introduction, personal data is one of the boundaries of data protection law. The PDPA, and data protection law around the world, only operates if the data in question is personal. So from a compliance perspective, one of the first questions you need to ask when you're looking at a dataset is: is this actually personal data? If it's not personal data, do what you want, right? You don't have to comply with the PDPA. Once it is personal data, that's when you need to comply. So the real question is what counts as personal data.

  In reality, from the legal and, I guess, academic standpoint, the concept of personal data is actually, I think, maybe the most complex concept in data protection law. It's almost a concept where you cannot look too hard at it. Once you look too hard, you realise that there are a lot of gaps in the definition, and if you try to fill those gaps, it becomes a monster. What we are focusing on is really what you need to know from a compliance standpoint. I'm not going to try to solve all the puzzles; it's just what you need to know in order not to get into trouble with the regulator.

  With that, let me explain what personal data is. You can see the definition on the slide. Personal data, according to the statute, is data about an individual who can be identified either from the data itself, or from that data plus other information that the organisation can access. This is the full definition, which we can break down into a number of elements to make it easier to analyse.

  As far as personal data is concerned, you can break it down into four distinct elements. Personal data is data. Personal data must relate to an individual. Personal data must be about the individual. And the personal data must identify the individual. These are the four elements. If the answer to all four is yes, what you have is personal data.

  现在进入本次课真正的实质部分，也就是个人数据的概念。正如我在介绍中提到的，个人数据是数据保护法的边界之一。PDPA 以及世界各地的数据保护法，只有在相关数据属于个人数据时才适用。所以从合规角度看，当你面对一个数据集时，首先要问的问题之一就是：这到底是不是个人数据？如果不是个人数据，你想怎么做都行，对吧？你不需要遵守 PDPA。一旦它是个人数据，你就需要合规了。所以真正的问题是：什么算个人数据。

  实际上，从法律以及我想学术的角度来看，个人数据这个概念可能是数据保护法中最复杂的概念。它几乎是一个你不能看得太仔细的概念。一旦看得太仔细，你就会发现定义中有很多空白，而如果你试图去填补这些空白，它就会变成一个怪物。我们关注的其实是从合规角度你需要知道的内容。我不打算解决所有难题，只讲你们为了不和监管机构惹上麻烦需要知道的东西。

  那么，我来解释一下什么是个人数据。定义你们可以在幻灯片上看到。根据法律，个人数据是关于某个个人的数据，该个人可以通过该数据本身被识别，或者通过该数据加上组织能够获取的其他信息被识别。这是完整的定义，我们可以把它拆分成若干要素，方便分析。

  就个人数据而言，你可以把它拆分为四个不同的要素：个人数据是“数据”；个人数据必须涉及一个“个人”；个人数据必须是“关于”该个人的；个人数据必须能够“识别”该个人。这就是四个要素。如果四个问题的答案都是肯定的，那你手上的就是个人数据。

  The second element is that personal data must relate to an individual. This is an important element, and you can see that the law starts to confine the scope here. What is an individual? If we look at the legislation, an individual refers to a natural person, meaning a human being. Legal persons are not individuals, so, for example, a company or an association would not count. The practical implication of this is that the PDPA does not protect the data of organisations, of companies, for example. It only protects the data of individual human beings.

  The individual may be living or deceased, which means that in theory, data protection law does protect the data of a person who is dead, although, as we'll see a bit later, there are some limitations to this.

  One other point to highlight is that it is possible for one piece of personal data to relate to two different individuals. This example I've taken directly from the guidelines. Let's say you have an adventure camp company, and let's say you have Bernie, who wants to participate in this adventure camp. So she provides the details of her husband, Bernard. What she provides is his name, his address, and his telephone number, because he is her emergency contact. In this case, the adventure camp company will have these three pieces of information. Of course, you will say that these three pieces of information relate to Bernard, because they are his name, address, and telephone number. But they also relate to Bernie, because the adventure camp company also knows that these three pieces of information are Bernie's emergency contact details. So this example illustrates how personal data can relate to more than one individual.

  Why does this matter? It matters because, for example, if you want to get consent to disclose or use some personal data in a situation like this, presumably the adventure camp company would need to get consent from both sides before it can actually use this information for some other purpose.

  这个个人可以是在世的，也可以是已故的。这意味着理论上，数据保护法确实保护已故者的数据，不过我们稍后会看到，这方面有一些限制。

  So that's the individual component. If you see a slide in blue text, this is where I'm bringing in an external data protection perspective. Usually, these are not examinable, so they're just for your information.

  If you look at other data protection laws, you will see that they use different terms for the same thing. For example, in the GDPR, they call it the data subject. In India, the term is data principal. In China, it is natural person, or 自然人.

  In some jurisdictions, interestingly, they exclude deceased persons from the scope of the definition. For example, by default, the GDPR does not apply to any deceased person. The New Zealand Privacy Act goes one step further and says that an individual means, by definition, a natural person that is living. So there are some differences in terms of the scope of "individual" in different data protection laws.

  以上就是“个人”这个要素。如果你看到蓝色文字的幻灯片，那是我引入外部数据保护视角的地方。这些通常不考，只供你们了解。

  如果你看看其他数据保护法，会发现它们对同一个东西使用不同的术语。比如在 GDPR 中，称为数据主体（data subject）；在印度，术语是数据委托人（data principal）；在中国，是自然人。

  有意思的是，在一些司法管辖区，已故者被排除在定义范围之外。例如，GDPR 在默认情况下不适用于任何已故者。新西兰《隐私法》（Privacy Act）更进一步，规定个人在定义上就是指在世的自然人。所以在不同的数据保护法中，“个人”的范围存在一些差异。

- [19:16:18–19:18:28] **Element 3: About — The Purpose Test and the "Incidental" Boundary**

  So that's the first two elements done. The next element we will be discussing is the element of "about". As I mentioned just now, personal data must be about the individual.

  I'd say that in the vast majority of cases, ninety-five percent, it's going to be very obvious whether a piece of information is about someone or not. We are dealing with the five percent that is not very obvious. If you are not sure whether the data is about an individual, there are some guidelines that you can follow.

  What the regulator says in its guidelines is that you look at the purpose of the data. Is the purpose of the data to record or communicate information about someone? If the answer is yes, we will generally regard that as personal data. Typical examples of this: if you are an employer and you keep a document or file about your employees, containing information about their health, their education, and so on, this will obviously be data about the employee. The purpose of this document is to record something about the employee. If you are a business and you keep records of your customers and their spending habits, this would also be personal data of the customers. So that's the guideline that the PDPC has given.

  And this is important: the PDPC has also drawn a particular boundary. The boundary is that if the data in question is only incidentally about an individual, it will generally not be regarded as personal data. This is a regulatory boundary, in the sense that if you look at the law itself, the law does not say this. It is a boundary that the regulator has drawn.

  前两个要素讲完了。接下来要讨论的要素是“关于”（about）。正如我刚才提到的，个人数据必须是关于该个人的。

  我认为在绝大多数情况下，也就是百分之九十五的情况下，一项信息是否关于某人会非常明显。我们要处理的是那百分之五不太明显的情况。如果你不确定数据是否关于某个个人，有一些指引可以遵循。

  监管机构在其指南中说的是：看数据的目的。数据的目的是否是记录或传达关于某人的信息？如果答案是肯定的，我们一般会将其视为个人数据。典型的例子是：如果你是雇主，保存了关于员工的文件或档案，其中包含他们的健康、教育等信息，这显然就是关于员工的数据，这份文件的目的就是记录关于员工的情况。如果你是一家企业，保存了客户及其消费习惯的记录，这同样是客户的个人数据。这就是 PDPC 给出的指引。

  还有一点很重要：PDPC 还划定了一条特定的边界。这条边界是，如果相关数据只是附带地（incidentally）涉及某个个人，一般不会被视为个人数据。这是一条监管上的边界，意思是如果你看法律本身，法律并没有这样规定。这是监管机构划定的边界。

- [19:27:51–19:31:32] **Comparative Perspective: The EU "Relates To" Test and Peter Nowak v Data Protection Commissioner**

  In Singapore we use the word "about". Other jurisdictions use different words, and those different words have different implications. For example, in the EU, they don't use the word "about"; they use the words "relating to" an individual. As we'll see in this case here, the way in which this connection is drawn in the EU is quite different from Singapore. Let me just briefly talk about this case.

  You have Peter Nowak, who was a trainee accountant. He wasn't very good, right? He failed the professional exam four times. On the fourth attempt, I guess he maybe had enough, and so he decided to challenge the results of the exam, saying he had actually passed. This challenge was rejected. He didn't take it lying down, so he filed what is called a data access request. He said to the accountancy association, "Give me the personal data that you have about me." In this case, the association, which conducted the exam, complied, but only partially. It did give Nowak his personal data, except his exam script, because the association took the view that the exam script was not his personal data. It's an interesting question to ask in Singapore, whether this would be personal data.

  Nowak was not satisfied, so he complained to the data protection authority, and the case ultimately went all the way up to the Court of Justice of the European Union. It's a rather trivial case to bring all the way up, but anyway. The CJEU took the view that the exam script was the personal data of Nowak.

  The way the CJEU interpreted the word "relates" is that it is possible for personal data to relate to the individual, the data subject, by its content, purpose, or effect. Any one of these is enough. In this case, the exam script related to Nowak in all three ways. Number one, the content of the exam script reveals Nowak's knowledge, his thinking, his handwriting. Number two, the purpose of the exam script was to evaluate his ability and suitability for practice as an accountant. Number three, the effect of the exam script was to influence his ability to enter the profession. All three were satisfied, although any one of them would have been enough. So here, according to the CJEU, the exam script was personal data.

  In Singapore, I think the answer is also yes, because in Singapore we basically focus on the first one, content. In Singapore, we would say your answers tell me something about you: how much you learned in the course, your abilities, and so on. If you ask for access to your exam script, depending on when you ask, you would be entitled to get access. So this is just to show you that in the EU and other jurisdictions, the scope of personal data may be different.

  在新加坡我们用的词是“关于”（about）。其他司法管辖区用不同的词，而这些不同的词有不同的含义。例如在欧盟，他们不用“关于”，而是用“与个人相关”（relating to）。正如我们在这个案例中会看到的，欧盟划定这种联系的方式与新加坡相当不同。我简单讲一下这个案例。

  Peter Nowak 是一名见习会计师。他不太厉害，对吧？他的专业考试挂了四次。到第四次时，我想他可能受够了，于是决定对考试结果提出异议，说他其实已经通过了。这一异议被驳回了。他不肯就此罢休，于是提出了所谓的数据查阅请求（data access request）。他对会计师协会说：“把你们持有的关于我的个人数据给我。”在这个案例中，举办考试的协会遵从了请求，但只是部分遵从。它确实把 Nowak 的个人数据给了他，但没有给他考卷，因为协会认为考卷不是他的个人数据。在新加坡，这是否属于个人数据是一个值得探讨的有趣问题。

  Nowak 不满意，于是向数据保护机构投诉，案件最终一路上诉到欧盟法院（Court of Justice of the European Union，CJEU）。把这么一个相当琐碎的案子一路打到那里，不过无论如何。欧盟法院认为，考卷是 Nowak 的个人数据。

  欧盟法院对“相关”一词的解释是：个人数据可以通过其内容、目的或效果与个人（即数据主体）相关，三者具备其一即可。在本案中，考卷在这三个方面都与 Nowak 相关。第一，考卷的内容揭示了 Nowak 的知识、他的思维、他的笔迹。第二，考卷的目的是评估他作为会计师执业的能力和适格性。第三，考卷的效果是影响他进入这个行业的能力。三项都满足了，尽管满足任何一项就已足够。所以在这里，按照欧盟法院的观点，考卷是个人数据。

  在新加坡，我想答案也是肯定的，因为在新加坡我们基本上关注的是第一项，也就是内容。在新加坡，我们会说你的答案告诉了我关于你的一些情况：你在课程中学到了多少、你的能力等等。如果你请求查阅你的考卷，视乎你何时提出请求，你可能有权获得查阅。这只是为了让你们看到，在欧盟和其他司法管辖区，个人数据的范围可能有所不同。

- [19:43:07–19:46:53] **Element 4: Identify — Unique and Generic Datapoints**

  The fourth element is the one that has generated the most academic debate. The data needs to identify the individual. It's not enough just to draw a connection between the data and the individual; you must be able to identify, or pick out, the individual from the data.

  According to the guidelines, the data generally needs to contain at least two datapoints to identify someone. The number of datapoints you need will depend on what type of data you have. Some datapoints are more unique; they tend to have a one-to-one relationship with the individual. If you have such datapoints in your dataset, you will need fewer additional datapoints. For example, identification numbers like your NRIC, your passport number, your student number: such numbers tend to be quite unique to the individual, and in some cases you may only need that one number.

  Biometrics are also an example of unique datapoints. Biometrics are bodily characteristics that tend to be unique to the individual, for example your DNA sequence, your fingerprint, your facial image, your iris print, and so on. Such datapoints make it more likely that your dataset will identify someone.

  In contrast, you have datapoints that are more generic, where a particular datapoint can relate to a lot of individuals. For example, things like your gender: male and female each connect to billions of individuals. Nationality, your age, your blood type: these are generic datapoints. When you only have such datapoints, you need a lot of them in order to narrow down the number of individuals to one.

  Let me give you a couple of examples. The first example is identification with unique datapoints. If I have your full name and your passport number, I can guarantee that I can identify you as one unique individual. But even if I don't have that, it is still possible to identify someone. For example, if I know your programme of study in NUS, say AI and Innovation, I know your year of enrolment, I know your date of birth, your gender, and your nationality, then with these five datapoints I can uniquely identify you. Each of them may not by itself identify you uniquely, but you put them together, and you can. So from a compliance perspective, the more unique the identifiers, the more dangerous, because it's more likely that the dataset is personal data. So that's identification.

  第四个要素是引发学术争论最多的一个。数据需要能够识别（identify）该个人。仅仅在数据和个人之间建立联系是不够的，你必须能够从数据中识别出、或者说挑出这个人。

  根据指南，数据一般需要包含至少两个数据点（datapoint）才能识别某人。你需要多少个数据点，取决于你所拥有的数据类型。有些数据点更具唯一性，往往与个人之间存在一一对应关系。如果你的数据集中有这样的数据点，你需要的额外数据点就更少。例如，身份证号码（NRIC）、护照号码、学号这样的识别号码，往往对个人来说相当唯一，在某些情况下你可能只需要这一个号码。

  生物特征（biometrics）也是唯一性数据点的例子。生物特征是往往对个人来说独一无二的身体特征，比如你的 DNA 序列、指纹、面部图像、虹膜等等。这类数据点使你的数据集更有可能识别出某人。

  相比之下，有些数据点比较通用，一个数据点可能涉及大量个人。比如性别：男性和女性各自对应几十亿人。国籍、年龄、血型，这些都是通用数据点。如果你只有这类数据点，就需要很多个，才能把范围缩小到一个人。

  我举几个例子。第一个是用唯一性数据点识别。如果我有你的全名和护照号码，我可以保证把你识别为一个独一无二的人。但即使没有这些，仍然有可能识别某人。比如，如果我知道你在 NUS 的专业，比如人工智能与创新，知道你的入学年份、出生日期、性别和国籍，那么凭这五个数据点，我就可以唯一地识别出你。每个数据点单独可能无法唯一识别你，但把它们放在一起就可以了。所以从合规角度看，标识符越具唯一性就越危险，因为数据集越有可能是个人数据。以上就是识别。
- [19:46:59–19:49:13] **Indirect Identification and "Access" to Other Information**

  One thing that you need to bear in mind, as you can see from the definition of personal data, is that it is possible to indirectly identify someone. Indirect identification is where your dataset, a spreadsheet for example, doesn't itself identify the individual, but it is possible for you to take that data and combine it with other data that you have or have access to, and thereby identify the individual.

  For example, let's say you have an organisation, ABC, that has a list of email addresses. Those email addresses may not by themselves allow you to identify someone, but it is possible that some of these email addresses are associated with easily accessible social media accounts. So if you have these email addresses, you can access the social media account and pick up the name and whatever else of the individual. So with these two datapoints, you are still able to identify a unique individual. That's indirect identification: when the dataset itself is not enough to identify, but can be combined with other data that you have access to in order to identify someone.

  The question that sometimes arises is: what does it mean to have access? The regulator has provided some guidance. The general guideline is that you have access to information if it would be practicable for you to access it. "Practicable" means that it does not require a huge cost, or time, or resources to access the information. So, for example, if the data in question happens to be easily found online, or the data in question is held by a related organisation, then it would be data that you have access to. Any questions on this?

  需要记住的一点是，正如你从个人数据的定义中看到的，间接识别是有可能的。间接识别（indirect identification）是指你的数据集，比如一个电子表格，本身并不能识别个人，但你可以把这些数据与你拥有或能获取的其他数据结合起来，从而识别出该个人。

  举个例子，假设有一个组织 ABC，有一份电子邮件地址清单。这些邮件地址本身可能无法让你识别某人，但其中一些邮件地址可能关联着很容易访问的社交媒体账号。所以如果你有这些邮件地址，就可以访问社交媒体账号，获取这个人的姓名和其他信息。这样凭这两个数据点，你仍然能识别出一个具体的人。这就是间接识别：数据集本身不足以识别，但可以与你能获取的其他数据结合起来识别某人。

  有时会出现的问题是：“能够获取”是什么意思？监管机构提供了一些指引。一般的指引是，如果你获取某信息是切实可行的（practicable），你就被视为能够获取该信息。“切实可行”是指获取该信息不需要巨大的成本、时间或资源。比如，如果相关数据在网上很容易找到，或者由一个关联组织持有，那就属于你能够获取的数据。对此有什么问题吗？
- [19:49:24–19:53:29] **Scenarios: Street Intercept Surveys**

  So let me just run through a few scenarios on the definition of personal data, just to crystallise our discussion so far.

  Let's start with a simple example. Let's say ABC runs a street intercept survey, where you approach random people on the street to survey them. You collect information about the average amount they spend on household items per month, their full name, their gender, and their age range. Obviously, this dataset does constitute personal data, because you have their full name, their gender, and so on. But if you don't collect their full name, so you only collect the gender, age range, and average amount spent, this is probably not personal data. That's straightforward, because you cannot identify someone just from these elements.

  A more complicated example. Let's say you have an organisation that again conducts a street intercept survey, and you collect the following information: age range, gender, occupation, and place of work. Here the situation is a bit more complicated, because in some cases you will have personal data, and in some cases you will not.

  Let's say you have Respondent A, who is a female between twenty and thirty years of age. She says she works as a retail salesperson in a certain shopping mall. Looking at this, you should already instinctively be able to tell that the data collected here is not personal data, as far as I'm concerned. There are very many female salespersons in their twenties working in a shopping mall in Singapore, so with all the information here, she cannot be uniquely identified.

  Let's say you have a different respondent, who is a male between twenty and thirty, working as a security officer, and you know which office building he works in. If you collect this information, it is entirely possible that this is now personal data. If this particular person is the only male security officer in his twenties working in this particular building, you would be able to uniquely identify who this person is, even without his name. So in this situation, if you are doing such surveys, you need to be a bit more careful, and you may simply presume that you will be collecting personal data.

  A student follows up on this scenario. Yes, I mean, at some point it comes down a bit to probability. I think it's very difficult for you to know with a high degree of certainty in a situation like this. In some cases it will be personal data, in some cases it won't. So there are two ways you can approach this from a compliance perspective. One way is to actually go and check each dataset that you collect to see whether it is personal data or not. The other, probably more practical, approach is to just assume you are collecting personal data, and make sure you get consent and so on before you actually use the data for whatever purpose.

  下面我过几个关于个人数据定义的情境，把我们目前的讨论具体化。

  先从一个简单的例子开始。假设 ABC 做一项街头拦访调查（street intercept survey），也就是在街上随机找人做调查。你收集他们每月在家居用品上的平均花费、全名、性别和年龄段。显然，这个数据集构成个人数据，因为你有他们的全名、性别等等。但如果你不收集全名，只收集性别、年龄段和平均花费，这大概就不是个人数据。这很直接，因为单凭这些要素你无法识别某人。

  一个更复杂的例子。假设有个组织同样做街头拦访调查，收集以下信息：年龄段、性别、职业和工作地点。这里的情况就复杂一些，因为有些情况下你会得到个人数据，有些情况下不会。

  假设受访者 A 是一位二十到三十岁的女性，她说她在某个购物中心当零售销售员。看到这些，你应该本能地就能判断出，在我看来这里收集到的数据不是个人数据。在新加坡的购物中心里，二十多岁的女销售员非常多，所以凭这里的全部信息，无法唯一地识别她。

  假设另一位受访者是一位二十到三十岁的男性，是一名保安，而且你知道他在哪栋办公楼工作。如果你收集了这些信息，那很可能就构成个人数据了。如果这个人是这栋楼里唯一一位二十多岁的男保安，即使没有他的名字，你也能唯一地识别出他是谁。所以在这种情况下，如果你在做这类调查，就需要更小心一些，你也可以干脆推定自己收集的是个人数据。

  一位学生就这个情境追问。是的，我是说，到了某个程度，这多少取决于概率。我认为在这种情况下，你很难高度确定。有些情况下会是个人数据，有些情况下不会。所以从合规角度，有两种处理方式。一种是逐一检查你收集的每个数据集，看它是不是个人数据。另一种可能更实际的做法，是直接假定你收集的是个人数据，确保在把数据实际用于任何目的之前取得同意等等。

  So that's all I would mention regarding the four elements of personal data. Now I'm going to move into more specific matters.

  Something you should know is that not all types of personal data are covered by the PDPA. Some categories of personal data are excluded, so if your personal data falls into any of these categories, the PDPA doesn't apply. One example you might come across is personal data in a record that has been in existence for at least one hundred years. The thing is that such records are so old that they cannot possibly harm anyone.

  And this is perhaps more important: personal data about a deceased individual who has been dead for more than ten years. So upon a person's death, the person still receives some degree of protection under the PDPA, but when the ten-year mark has been reached, that protection also ends. As for the rationale behind this sort of time-limited protection, I believe it is really not for the deceased individual himself, but more for relatives and friends, out of respect for the feelings of the people close to the deceased. After a ten-year period, the policy decision was to cut off protection at that point.

- [20:15:06–20:17:34] **Anonymisation: Definition and Trade-Offs**

  What is probably even more important for present purposes is this concept called anonymisation, which is a really, really hot topic.

  So what is anonymisation? Anonymisation essentially refers to the process of converting personal data into non-personal data. Through different techniques, you are able to convert what was personal data into non-personal data, in a way that the individual can no longer be identified. Remember that the fourth element of personal data is that you need to be able to identify the individual. So if you somehow change the personal data such that no one can be identified, then it's no longer personal data. That's the process of anonymisation.

  Anonymisation, whenever you try it, will always involve a certain trade-off. So why would you anonymise? The main reason is to convert the data into non-personal data, such that you are not subject to the PDPA, and you can freely use the data. That's the main reason why people are interested in anonymisation. Another reason is that anonymisation is a type of security measure. It is a way to reduce the risk of harm if a data breach arises, because once you anonymise the data, even if someone manages to hack into your servers and access the data, they can't really do much with it.

  But there is also a flip side. The problem with anonymisation is that you inevitably reduce the amount of information contained in the data. Whatever you do with the personal data when you try to anonymise it, you reduce the amount of information, the richness. So that also potentially reduces how useful the data is to you. In addition, if you have a very large dataset, it's difficult in practice to properly anonymise the data. So there is a trade-off when it comes to anonymisation, and you need to decide whether it is worth it.

  就目前而言，可能更重要的是一个叫匿名化（anonymisation）的概念，这是一个非常、非常热门的话题。

  什么是匿名化？匿名化基本上是指把个人数据转化为非个人数据的过程。通过不同的技术，你可以把原本的个人数据转化为非个人数据，使得个人无法再被识别。记住，个人数据的第四个要素是你需要能够识别该个人。所以如果你以某种方式改变个人数据，使任何人都无法被识别，那它就不再是个人数据了。这就是匿名化的过程。

  匿名化无论何时尝试，总会涉及某种取舍。那么为什么要匿名化？主要原因是把数据转化为非个人数据，这样你就不受 PDPA 约束，可以自由使用数据。这是人们对匿名化感兴趣的主要原因。另一个原因是，匿名化是一种安全措施。它是在发生数据泄露时降低损害风险的一种方式，因为一旦你把数据匿名化，即使有人成功侵入你的服务器并获取数据，他们也做不了什么。

  但它也有另一面。匿名化的问题在于你不可避免地会减少数据所包含的信息量。当你试图匿名化个人数据时，无论怎么做，都会减少信息量，也就是数据的丰富程度。所以这也可能降低数据对你的用处。此外，如果你的数据集非常大，实际上很难把数据妥善匿名化。所以在匿名化方面存在取舍，你需要判断是否值得。
