- [20:29:03–20:31:19] **Techniques: Generalisation and Swapping**

  This next technique is called generalisation. Generalisation refers to a reduction in the precision of data. Basically, you are converting precise data into a range. For example, let's say you have this dataset containing a serial number, the person's pseudonym, the age, as well as the address. Say you want to anonymise it further. What you can do is, instead of specifying the exact age, specify a range. For the address, what you can do is take away part of the precise address, for example the block number of the house. With this generalisation, you end up with this, which is less easy to identify.

  The next one is swapping. Swapping basically means you are shuffling the data. Specifically, you are mixing up the data in a particular attribute, switching values between the records. You do this when you don't care about maintaining the correlation between the different attributes. So if you just want to run an analysis of one particular attribute, then you don't need the correlation. For example, you have this dataset: the person, job title, date of birth, membership type, and how many times this person visits in a month. If you don't care about maintaining the relationships between them, what you can do is swap around the attributes. Once you have done this, you won't be able to identify anyone from this data, because it's all been anonymised.

  下一种技术叫泛化（generalisation）。泛化是指降低数据的精确度。基本上就是把精确的数据转换成一个范围。比如，假设你有一个数据集，包含序号、人的假名、年龄和地址。假设你想进一步匿名化。你可以不写确切年龄，而是写一个年龄段。对于地址，你可以把精确地址的一部分去掉，比如房屋的座号。经过这样的泛化，你就得到这样的结果，更难识别出个人。

  下一种是交换（swapping）。交换基本上就是打乱数据。具体来说，就是把某个属性中的数据打乱，在记录之间互换数值。当你不在乎保持不同属性之间的相关性时，就可以这样做。所以如果你只想分析某一个属性，就不需要这种相关性。比如，你有这样一个数据集：人名、职位、出生日期、会员类型，以及这个人每月到访的次数。如果你不在乎保持它们之间的关系，就可以把这些属性打乱互换。一旦这样做了，你就无法从数据中识别出任何人，因为全部都已经匿名化了。
- [20:31:28–20:33:24] **Techniques: Data Perturbation and Data Aggregation**

  The next one is data perturbation. Data perturbation means that you change the values in your dataset slightly. You would do this with numbers, where you don't need the numbers to be exact, but you still want them to be approximately right. Say you have this dataset with the height, the weight, and the age of various people, and you want to make it more difficult to identify someone. What you could do is, for example, round the height to the nearest multiple of five, and do something similar for the weight and the age. Then you get this slightly modified data, from which you should not be able to identify the exact person, because the values have been modified slightly.

  Then you have data aggregation. You just compress the data into summarised values, and you don't need the exact records. Let's say you have this dataset containing donors, the individual donors' monthly income and how much they donated. Say you want to write up an analysis of this, and you don't really care about the individual records. What you can do is aggregate. For example, for monthly income of one thousand to one thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine, you have the number of donations and the total amount donated. From the original dataset, you can identify a donor; from the aggregated one, you cannot. That's another way of anonymisation. So these are just some of the more common techniques.

  下一种是数据扰动（data perturbation）。数据扰动是指对数据集中的数值作轻微改动。你会对数字这样做，即你不需要数字完全精确，但仍希望它们大致正确。假设你有一个数据集，包含不同人的身高、体重和年龄，你想让识别某人变得更困难。你可以比如把身高四舍五入到最接近的五的倍数，体重和年龄也做类似处理。这样你就得到了轻微改动过的数据，从中应该无法识别出具体的人，因为数值已经被轻微修改了。

  然后是数据聚合（data aggregation）。你只是把数据压缩成汇总数值，不需要具体的记录。假设你有一个捐款人的数据集，包含每位捐款人的月收入和捐款金额。假设你想写一份分析，并不在乎单条记录。你可以做聚合。比如，月收入在一千到一千九百九十九之间的，列出捐款笔数和捐款总额。从原始数据集你能识别出某位捐款人，而从聚合后的数据则不能。这是另一种匿名化方式。以上只是一些较常见的技术。
- [20:33:45–20:37:43] **Applying Techniques to Direct and Indirect Identifiers**

  Okay, so how then do you use these techniques to deal with certain identifiers? For direct identifiers, generally what you are required to do is to suppress the attribute completely, or you can pseudonymise if you want to replace the name with some sort of string. For example, pseudonymisation would be replacing John Tan with one, two, three, four, five, six.

  For indirect identifiers, there are different techniques. For age, height, and weight, you can do certain things, for example generalisation. What this means is, let's say you have the records twenty-four, thirty-nine, eighteen. For each age, you can generalise into age ranges. Or you can do data perturbation, changing the numbers slightly.

  Gender is basically not possible to anonymise, so you can probably just retain this attribute as it is.

  Race and marital status: there are not that many categories, so depending on your dataset, you may need to do creative things. For example, let's say you have this dataset with Indian, Chinese, Malay, and Eurasian. How do you anonymise this? You probably have to do something like grouping some of them into "Others", and this makes it more difficult to specifically identify one individual.

  Date of birth is similar to age and height, in the sense that you can generalise it, for example to the month and year. For addresses, generalisation basically means removing the precise details, so you can generalise an address to a broader area. For postal codes, the usual way is character masking, so you hide the last four digits of the postal code to remove the exact location.

  Job titles are tricky again, because there are many different job titles, so you need to actually take a look at what job titles you have and work out how to group them together in order to generalise. For example, CEO can be generalised to C-suite or senior leadership. Company names are again not that easy, but you can generalise them to the sector the company is in.

  For things like IP addresses and vehicle licence plate numbers, the typical way is masking. For GPS location, again there are different methods: generalisation, perturbation, and masking as well. If you want to find out about this in detail, you can look at the guide.

  那么，如何用这些技术处理不同的标识符呢？对于直接标识符，一般要求你把这个属性完全删除，或者如果你想用某种字符串替换姓名，也可以做假名化。比如，假名化就是把 John Tan 替换成 123456。

  对于间接标识符，有不同的技术。对于年龄、身高和体重，你可以做一些处理，比如泛化。意思是，假设你有二十四、三十九、十八这几条记录，可以把每个年龄泛化成年龄段。或者你可以做数据扰动，轻微改动这些数字。

  性别基本上无法匿名化，所以你大概可以直接保留这个属性原样。

  种族和婚姻状况：这些类别并不多，所以视乎你的数据集，你可能需要做一些有创意的处理。比如，假设你的数据集里有印度族、华族、马来族和欧亚裔。怎么匿名化？你大概需要把其中一些归入“其他”，这样就更难具体识别出某一个人。

  出生日期与年龄、身高类似，可以泛化，比如泛化到年和月。对于地址，泛化基本上就是去掉精确细节，可以把地址泛化到更大的区域。对于邮政编码，常用的方法是字符掩码，隐藏邮编的最后四位数字，去掉确切位置。

  职位名称同样棘手，因为职位名称五花八门，你需要实际看看手上有哪些职位名称，想办法把它们归类以便泛化。比如，CEO 可以泛化为 C 级高管或高层领导。公司名称同样不太容易处理，但可以泛化为公司所属的行业。

  对于 IP 地址、车牌号码之类的，典型做法是掩码。对于 GPS 位置，同样有不同的方法：泛化、扰动，还有掩码。如果你想详细了解，可以看那份指南。
- [20:37:49–20:40:49] **When Is Data Anonymised? The Strict Legal Position and PDPC Safeguards**

  So far, I've talked about how you anonymise using different techniques. The question people want to know is: when can we consider the personal data to be anonymised? How anonymised is enough? From a strict legal standpoint, the answer is that it must not be possible to re-identify any individual, which follows from the definition of personal data.

  The PDPC guidelines set out several criteria. You should implement certain safeguards to further reduce the possibility of re-identification. For example, if you share anonymised data with someone, you should restrict them from further disclosing the data; that would be a safeguard that reduces the risk that someone out there is able to re-identify. You should also implement especially stringent safeguards on datasets that can be used to re-identify. This refers specifically to the identity mapping table and the linking table; for example, keeping these with a third party makes re-identification even more difficult. Finally, you should conduct periodic reviews to make sure the anonymisation is still effective. The concern here is that over time, resources and techniques to reverse anonymisation can develop, so you go back and review your current anonymisation to see whether it's still good enough.

  到目前为止，我讲了如何用不同的技术进行匿名化。大家想知道的问题是：什么时候可以认为个人数据已经被匿名化了？匿名到什么程度才够？从严格的法律立场来看，答案是必须不可能重新识别出任何个人，这是从个人数据的定义推导出来的。

  PDPC 的指南列出了若干标准。你应该采取某些保障措施，进一步降低重新识别的可能性。比如，如果你和别人分享匿名化数据，应限制对方进一步披露数据；这就是一项能降低外界有人重新识别出个人的风险的保障措施。你还应对可用于重新识别的数据集采取特别严格的保障措施。这具体指身份映射表和链接表；比如把它们交由第三方保管，会让重新识别变得更加困难。最后，你应该定期审查，确保匿名化仍然有效。这里的担忧是，随着时间推移，逆转匿名化的资源和技术可能会发展起来，所以你要回头审查目前的匿名化，看它是否仍然足够好。
- [20:40:55–20:42:23] **The PDPC's Holistic View: The JKL and XYZ Example**

  So, just to give one example of what this looks like in practice. The PDPC has said that it will take a holistic view, so it will consider these criteria. In this example, you have JKL, which discloses a dataset that has been anonymised to XYZ. What JKL does to reduce the risk of re-identification is things like making sure they use robust anonymisation techniques, contractually requiring XYZ not to attempt re-identification, requiring XYZ to put in place protections to ensure that the dataset is securely handled, and requiring XYZ to maintain certain data protection standards. So these are safeguards that JKL puts in place.

  In the event that there is a data breach and the dataset somehow gets exfiltrated, the PDPC will investigate, and these will be the things the PDPC considers to determine whether the dataset was anonymised or not. If it was not sufficiently anonymised, then it may be that JKL actually breached data protection law.

  举一个例子说明这在实践中是什么样子。PDPC 表示会采取整体性的观点（holistic view），也就是会考虑这些标准。在这个例子中，JKL 把一个已经匿名化的数据集披露给 XYZ。JKL 为降低重新识别风险所做的事情包括：确保使用稳健的匿名化技术，在合同中要求 XYZ 不得尝试重新识别，要求 XYZ 采取保护措施确保数据集得到安全处理，以及要求 XYZ 维持一定的数据保护标准。这些都是 JKL 采取的保障措施。

  如果发生数据泄露，数据集不知怎么被窃取外泄，PDPC 会展开调查，而这些就是 PDPC 判断该数据集是否已匿名化时会考虑的因素。如果匿名化不充分，那么 JKL 可能实际上违反了数据保护法。
- [20:43:55–20:46:18] **K-Anonymity as the PDPC's Benchmark**

  The PDPC uses k-anonymity as a benchmark. Let me explain k-anonymity with this example, which will be a bit simpler. Let's say you have this particular dataset with a serial number, age, gender, occupation, and the average number of trips per week, about people taking taxis, and we are trying to anonymise it.

  Let me show you what this looks like. Here you have the anonymised table. The target attribute, the average number of trips, you don't touch, because that's the important information. Here you can see that in the occupation column, after generalisation, you have data protection officer: one, two, three, four, five. Similarly, for this particular combination of attributes, thirty-one to forty, male, IT, there are one, two, three, four, five records. So we say that k equals five in this case. The bigger the k, the more anonymised the dataset. What the PDPC has said is that if you want to share data with external parties, you should achieve a k-anonymity of five.

  PDPC 把 k-匿名性（k-anonymity）作为基准。我用这个例子来解释 k-匿名性，会简单一些。假设你有这样一个数据集，包含序号、年龄、性别、职业和每周平均乘车次数，是关于搭出租车的人的，我们要把它匿名化。

  我给你们看看是什么样子。这是匿名化后的表格。目标属性，也就是平均乘车次数，你不去动，因为那是重要信息。你可以看到在职业这一列，经过泛化后，“数据保护官”有一、二、三、四、五条。同样，对于“三十一到四十岁、男性、IT”这个属性组合，有一、二、三、四、五条记录。所以我们说在这个例子中 k 等于五。k 越大，数据集的匿名化程度越高。PDPC 的说法是，如果你想与外部方分享数据，应达到 k 等于五的匿名性。
- [20:47:32–20:49:47] **Internal Anonymisation within an Organisation**

  This next point is also quite interesting, because the lawyer and the regulator will say different things. From the strict legal point of view, if the organisation itself can re-identify the data that it anonymised, you cannot strictly say the data has actually become anonymised, because I myself can reverse it.

  Interestingly, the PDPC has taken the view that you can consider some data to be internally anonymised. How this works is that you split the organisation into different departments, treated almost like different organisations. One department has the full dataset; it anonymises it and creates the anonymised dataset, which is then processed in a different department. In this scenario, the organisation as a whole can still re-identify, since they're all in the same company, but the PDPC's view is that within the department that has only the anonymised dataset, the data is treated as anonymised. This makes data analysis easier for organisations.

  So, for example, say you have Departments A and B, both in the same company, JKL. Department A uses the data for customer relations. Department B then wants to use the data for some business analysis. So what Department A does is anonymise the dataset, keeping a copy of the original, and hand the anonymised data to B for its data analysis. JKL also puts in place certain controls, such as access restrictions and so on. In this scenario, even though technically both departments are in the same organisation, Department B can be considered to be using anonymised data. It's a sort of exception that has been made.

  下一点也很有意思，因为律师和监管机构会给出不同的说法。从严格的法律角度看，如果组织自己能够重新识别它所匿名化的数据，你就不能严格地说这些数据已经真正被匿名化了，因为我自己就能逆转它。

  有意思的是，PDPC 的观点是，你可以把某些数据视为“内部匿名化”（internally anonymised）。具体做法是把组织划分为不同的部门，几乎当作不同的组织来对待。一个部门持有完整的数据集，把它匿名化，生成匿名化数据集，然后在另一个部门进行处理。在这种情况下，组织作为一个整体仍然可以重新识别，因为都在同一家公司，但 PDPC 的观点是，在只持有匿名化数据集的那个部门内，这些数据被视为已匿名化。这让组织做数据分析更容易。

  举个例子，假设有 A 部门和 B 部门，都在同一家公司 JKL。A 部门把数据用于客户关系。B 部门想把数据用于某种业务分析。于是 A 部门把数据集匿名化，保留一份原始数据，把匿名化后的数据交给 B 部门做数据分析。JKL 还采取了某些管控措施，比如访问限制等等。在这种情况下，尽管严格来说两个部门在同一个组织里，B 部门仍可被视为在使用匿名化数据。这算是被开出的一种例外。

  In Singapore, we don't have that in the legislation itself, but the PDPC has specified that there are in fact certain types of data that are more sensitive. The key case to look at is Aviva. My own argument is that the common criterion is that there's a high potential for harm if the data is improperly handled. High-risk data is sensitive data. If you accept this as the criterion, then you will be able to figure out what other types of data you also need to treat as sensitive. For example, certain facts about a person's background may well also be sensitive, if disclosed in an unintended way that could cause harm.

# Seminar 2 Singapore PDPA organisation concept
## Week 2 Readings
  - AGKCP at 6.1-6.34.
  - GMDI.
## Week 2 Summary

- **The Concept of "Organisation" 机构的概念**
  - **Definition:** an **organisation** is any individual, company, association or body of persons, corporate or unincorporated, whether or not formed, resident or based in Singapore. It is **deliberately extremely broad** and covers any natural or legal person anywhere in the world.
  - **Why it matters:** the PDPA places its obligations on **organisations**, so being an organisation is what brings you under the PDPA's obligations.
  - **Two ways out of the PDPA:**
    - Show that the data is **not personal data**.
    - Show that you are an **excluded organisation** that falls within one of the exceptions.
  - **定义：** **机构**指任何个人、公司、协会或人士团体，不论是否法人，也不论是否在新加坡成立、居住或设有营业地点。这个定义**有意设计得极其宽泛**，涵盖世界任何地方的任何自然人或法人。
  - **重要性：** PDPA 把义务施加在**机构**身上，所以一旦属于机构，就要承担 PDPA 的义务。
  - **摆脱 PDPA 的两种途径：**
    - 证明相关资料**不是个人资料**。
    - 证明自己是**被排除的机构**，适用其中一个例外。

- **Comparative Perspectives on "Organisation" (Non-examinable) 机构概念的比较视角（不考）**
  - **Different terms:** the EU GDPR uses **"controller"**, China's PIPL uses **个人信息处理者 (personal information processor)**, and India's DPDPA uses **"data fiduciary"**.
  - **Not merely terminology:** an EU **controller** is whoever **determines the purposes and means** of processing, so the EU must first ask who decides the "how and why". Singapore never has to ask this, because **anyone is an organisation**.
  - **Tiering by size or significance:** Singapore applies the **same rules to everyone**. Other jurisdictions differ:
    - **India** adds a higher tier, the **significant data fiduciary**. The government designates one by looking at the volume and sensitivity of data, risk, and impact on sovereignty, democracy, security and public order. Once designated, it must appoint a DPO and an independent data auditor and carry out assessments and audits.
    - **Australia** carves out **small businesses** (annual turnover of $3m or less). They are outside the Privacy Act unless they do certain activities, such as providing health services or trading in personal data.
  - **术语不同：** 欧盟 GDPR 用 **"控制者（controller）"**，中国 PIPL 用 **个人信息处理者**，印度 DPDPA 用 **"数据受托人（data fiduciary）"**。
  - **不只是用词差异：** 欧盟的**控制者**是**决定处理目的和方式**的人，所以欧盟首先要问由谁决定"怎么处理、为何处理"。新加坡不需要问这个问题，因为**任何人都是机构**。
  - **按规模或重要性分级：** 新加坡**对所有人适用同一套规则**，其他法域则不同：
    - **印度**增设更高一级的**重要数据受托人**。政府根据资料数量和敏感度、风险，以及对主权、民主、安全和公共秩序的影响来认定。一旦被认定，就必须委任数据保护官和独立数据审计员，并进行评估和审计。
    - **澳大利亚**排除**小型企业**（年营业额 300 万澳元或以下）。它们不受《隐私法》管辖，除非从事某些活动，例如提供医疗服务或买卖个人资料。

- **Excluded Organisations: Overview 被排除的机构：概览**
  - **Why exclusions exist:** the definition is so broad that the PDPA must carve out people it should not cover.
  - **The four main exclusions:**
    - The **personal and domestic exception**.
    - The **employee exception**.
    - The **public agency exception**.
    - The **data intermediary exception**.
  - **Each works differently:** the four exclusions do not operate the same way, so analyse each one separately.
  - **Only the excluded organisation benefits:** the exclusion does **not** extend to anyone dealing with the excluded organisation.
    - **Travel agency example:** Tom books a holiday and gives the agency data about his wife Jane. Tom is exempt because he acts in a personal capacity, but the agency must still comply for both Tom's and Jane's data.
    - **Collecting from the government:** if you collect personal data from the government, you must still comply. The government is exempt, but you are not.
  - **设立排除情形的原因：** 机构定义过于宽泛，PDPA 必须把不应涵盖的人排除在外。
  - **四个主要排除情形：**
    - **个人及家庭例外**。
    - **雇员例外**。
    - **公共机构例外**。
    - **数据中介例外**。
  - **运作方式各不相同：** 四个排除情形的运作方式不一样，需要逐一分析。
  - **只有被排除的机构本身受益：** 排除**不会**延伸到与被排除机构打交道的人。
    - **旅行社例子：** Tom 预订家庭度假，把妻子 Jane 的资料交给旅行社。Tom 以个人身份行事所以获得豁免，但旅行社对 Tom 和 Jane 的资料仍须遵守 PDPA。
    - **从政府收集资料：** 如果你从政府那里收集个人资料，你仍须遵守 PDPA。政府获得豁免，但你没有。

- **Personal and Domestic Exception: The Basic Rule 个人及家庭例外：基本规则**
  - **Rule:** an **individual** acting in a **personal or domestic capacity** is not bound by the PDPA.
  - **Personal capacity:** activities done for your own purposes, for example:
    - Filming a fight on the train.
    - Posting a group selfie from a dinner with friends.
    - Making a photo completely public on Facebook, which is still personal.
  - **Domestic capacity:** activities for your home or family, for example:
    - Installing a home CCTV camera.
    - Registering your child for tuition. You are exempt, but the tuition centre is not.
  - **Rationale:** without this exception, the PDPA would clamp down on most everyday activities.
  - **Two-part test:** being an individual is **not enough**. You must also be acting in a personal or domestic capacity, and that second limb is usually where the argument lies.
  - **规则：** 以**个人或家庭身份**行事的**个人**不受 PDPA 约束。
  - **个人身份：** 为自己的目的进行的活动，例如：
    - 在地铁上拍下打架事件。
    - 发布与朋友聚餐的合照。
    - 把照片在 Facebook 上完全公开，这仍属个人性质。
  - **家庭身份：** 为家庭或家人进行的活动，例如：
    - 在家安装闭路电视。
    - 为孩子报名补习班。家长获得豁免，补习中心则不获豁免。
  - **理由：** 没有这个例外，PDPA 会限制大多数日常活动。
  - **两步测试：** 仅仅是个人**并不足够**，还必须是以个人或家庭身份行事，而争议通常就在这第二步。

- **Personal and Domestic Exception: Business vs Personal Capacity Cases 个人及家庭例外：商业身份与个人身份案例**
  - **Business purpose defeats the exception — Sharon Assya Qadriyah Tang (2018):**
    - **Facts:** S, a telemarketer, bought leads (names, NRIC numbers, mobile numbers, income ranges) for her work. She later resold them to supplement her income.
    - **Outcome:** S could not rely on the exception and breached the **Consent Obligation**.
    - **Reason:** reselling for profit is a **business capacity**, even when done by an individual or sole proprietor.
  - **Giving leads away for free (class Q&A):** the lecturer suspects the answer is **still no** if the data is passed to a friend in the same line of work. Giving it away is altruistic, but the **overarching purpose is still business**, because the friend will use it for profit.
  - **Buying leads (class Q&A, previewing the consent topic):** buyers usually rely on the **seller's consent**. The short answer was that a buyer can still be treated as having obtained consent if it took **reasonable care** to check that the seller had the required consent, even if the seller turns out not to have done things properly.
  - **Capacity is fixed at the time of collection — Ang Rui Song (2017):**
    - **Facts:** A, a financial consultant with Prudential, obtained client documents at work. After leaving, he dumped them in a plastic bag next to a public bin.
    - **Outcome:** A could not rely on the exception and breached the **Protection Obligation**.
    - **Reason:** data obtained in a **business capacity** stays held in that capacity. You cannot later switch to "personal" on your own.
  - **Why Prudential was not liable (class Q&A):** this was a special case, because its consultants were **independent agents, not employees**. If they had been employees, Prudential would have been liable.
  - **Employers' burden (class Q&A):** employers must put in procedures so that employees do not mishandle personal data. If employees do, the employer answers for it, which previews the employee exception.
  - **Non-commercial activity can qualify — Grabcar / GrabHitch (2019):**
    - **Facts:** GrabHitch carpool drivers posted passengers' personal data on social media after disputes.
    - **Outcome:** the drivers **could** rely on the exception, even though they received money.
    - **Reason:** the platform rules made the activity non-commercial. Drivers could not solicit passengers, were limited to two rides, could only recover costs (no profit), and could only carry passengers incidentally on their own journey.
  - **Distinguishing factors:**
    - **Profit motive** (Sharon) points to business capacity.
    - **The capacity in which the data was first obtained** (Ang) carries forward.
    - **Structural limits that remove any profit** (GrabHitch) point to personal capacity.
  - **商业目的使例外不适用 — Sharon Assya Qadriyah Tang（2018）：**
    - **事实：** 电话推销员 S 为工作购买销售线索（姓名、身份证号码、手机号码、收入范围），后来转售以补贴收入。
    - **结果：** S 不能依赖该例外，违反了**同意义务**。
    - **理由：** 为获利而转售属于**商业身份**，即使行为人是个人或独资经营者。
  - **免费送出线索（课堂问答）：** 讲师认为，如果把资料送给同行朋友，答案**很可能仍是不能**。送出资料虽属利他行为，但**总体目的仍是商业性的**，因为朋友会用它来获利。
  - **购买线索（课堂问答，预告同意义务）：** 买方通常依赖**卖方取得的同意**。简短的回答是：只要买方采取了**合理注意**去确认卖方已取得所需同意，即使卖方后来被发现做得不妥，买方仍可被视为已取得同意。
  - **身份在收集时确定 — Ang Rui Song（2017）：**
    - **事实：** A 是 Prudential 的理财顾问，在工作中取得客户文件。离职后，他把文件装进塑料袋放在公共垃圾桶旁。
    - **结果：** A 不能依赖该例外，违反了**保护义务**。
    - **理由：** 以**商业身份**取得的资料会继续以该身份持有，事后不能单方面改为"个人身份"。
  - **Prudential 为何无须负责（课堂问答）：** 这是特殊情况，因为它的顾问是**独立代理人而非雇员**。如果是雇员，Prudential 就要负责。
  - **雇主的负担（课堂问答）：** 雇主必须建立程序，防止雇员不当处理个人资料。雇员如果这样做，由雇主承担责任，这一点预告了雇员例外。
  - **非商业活动可以适用 — Grabcar / GrabHitch（2019）：**
    - **事实：** GrabHitch 顺风车司机在纠纷后把乘客的个人资料发到社交媒体。
    - **结果：** 司机**可以**依赖该例外，即使他们收了钱。
    - **理由：** 平台规则使这项活动属于非商业性质。司机不得招揽乘客，只能搭载两趟，只能收回成本（不得获利），并且只能在自己的行程中顺路搭载乘客。
  - **区分因素：**
    - **营利动机**（Sharon）指向商业身份。
    - **最初取得资料时的身份**（Ang）会延续下去。
    - **排除任何利润的结构性限制**（GrabHitch）指向个人身份。

- **Personal and Domestic Exception: Grey-Area Q&A 个人及家庭例外：灰色地带问答**
  - **Grab drivers who drive for a living:** whether they are employees is **debatable**. Grab says they are independent, which would leave a data breach as the drivers' own problem.
  - **Airbnb host with surveillance cameras:**
    - **Employee question:** hosts are clearly **not Airbnb employees**, because Airbnb is just a platform. That is a separate question from capacity.
    - **Capacity question:** the lecturer leans towards **business capacity**, because hosting allows profit and many people run it like a business, unlike GrabHitch's cost recovery.
    - **Qualification:** this is a grey area, and a full answer needs Airbnb's specific terms and how far hosts make profits.
  - **以开车为生的 Grab 司机：** 他们是否属于雇员**存在争议**。Grab 称他们是独立司机，这样一来资料违规就是司机自己的问题。
  - **装有监控摄像头的 Airbnb 房东：**
    - **雇员问题：** 房东显然**不是 Airbnb 的雇员**，因为 Airbnb 只是平台。这是与身份问题分开的另一个问题。
    - **身份问题：** 讲师倾向于认为属于**商业身份**，因为出租可以获利，很多人当作生意经营，不同于 GrabHitch 的收回成本。
    - **保留意见：** 这属于灰色地带，完整的答案需要看 Airbnb 的具体条款以及房东获利的程度。

- **In-Class Exercise: Armin's AI-Generated Portfolio Website 课堂练习：Armin 的 AI 生成作品集网站**
  - **Scenario:** Armin, a graduating web design student, vibe-codes a public sample corporate website for a future job portfolio. He makes no money from it and has not yet used it. The AI tool inserted a real person's face and name (James) into the "Our People" page, and James complained to the PDPC.
  - **Arguments for "yes" (he can rely on the exception):**
    - He makes no money and runs no ads.
    - The website has not yet been used for anything.
    - He is a graduating student building a **personal portfolio**, so the activity is personal development rather than work.
  - **Arguments for "no":**
    - The intended use is to **get a job**, and **employment is definitely business**, so it is not a 100% personal purpose.
    - Making the site **public** may indicate a work purpose. Publicity alone does **not** defeat the exception in Singapore, but it can support that inference.
  - **Being an individual is not enough:** the analysis must address the **capacity limb**.
  - **Personal data argument:** saying "the purpose wasn't to communicate personal data" is unlikely to persuade the PDPC. A real person's face and name on a website, published accidentally or deliberately, is very hard to argue is not personal data.
  - **AI lookalike images:** this is an ongoing debate. It depends on **how closely the image resembles the person**. A photo-realistic likeness is that person's personal data, whether it was photographed, hand-drawn or AI-generated.
  - **Who did what:** the AI tool **created** the image, and Armin **published or disclosed** it.
  - **Intention:** generally **irrelevant**. Not knowing that something is personal data does not avoid responsibility.
  - **Career development vs business (debated, open):** the lecturer's view is that purely developing skills or growing as an individual is personal. Students countered that the portfolio's purpose is to show employers his ability to win paid employment. The question did not say whether the job is with an NGO or a commercial company.
  - **Lecturer's lean:** **probably yes**. In an investigation, Armin would likely present a non-business narrative and probably get away with it. Both sides are arguable, and the question was designed to provoke debate.
  - **James's position:** in Singapore, there is not much he can do to get the image taken down where the poster is not harassing him. Some other countries have easier takedown rules.
  - **情境：** 即将毕业的网页设计学生 Armin 用"氛围编程"做了一个公开的示范企业网站，准备将来求职时作为作品集。他没有从中赚钱，也还没有使用它。AI 工具在"Our People"页面放入了真人 James 的面孔和名字，James 向 PDPC 投诉。
  - **支持"可以"（可依赖例外）的论点：**
    - 他没有赚钱，也没有广告。
    - 网站尚未被用于任何用途。
    - 他是在制作**个人作品集**的应届毕业生，这属于个人发展而非工作。
  - **支持"不可以"的论点：**
    - 预期用途是**求职**，而**就业绝对属于商业**，所以并非百分之百的个人目的。
    - 网站**公开**可能显示工作目的。在新加坡，公开本身**不会**使例外失效，但可以支持这一推论。
  - **仅是个人并不足够：** 分析必须处理**身份这一要件**。
  - **个人资料论点：** 主张"目的并非传达个人资料"不太可能说服 PDPC。无论是意外还是故意发布，网站上真人的面孔和名字都很难被说成不是个人资料。
  - **AI 相似图像：** 这是仍在进行的争论，取决于**图像与本人的相似程度**。逼真的肖像就是该人的个人资料，无论是拍摄、手绘还是 AI 生成。
  - **各自角色：** AI 工具**生成**了图像，Armin **发布或披露**了图像。
  - **意图：** 一般**无关紧要**。不知道某样东西是个人资料，并不能避免责任。
  - **职业发展与商业（有争议，未有定论）：** 讲师认为纯粹提升技能、作为个人成长属于个人性质。同学们反驳说，作品集的目的是向雇主展示能力以获得有薪工作。题目也没有说明工作是在非政府组织还是商业公司。
  - **讲师的倾向：** **大概可以**。在调查中，Armin 很可能会提出一个非商业的说法，并可能全身而退。双方都有理据，这道题本就是为了引发讨论而设计的。
  - **James 的处境：** 在新加坡，如果发布者并非骚扰他，他很难让对方删除图像。其他一些国家有更便利的删除规则。

- **Personal and Domestic Exception Abroad (Non-examinable) 其他法域的个人及家庭例外（不考）**
  - **Similar exceptions:** the GDPR, PIPL and India's DPDPA all have one, for the same reason as Singapore.
  - **Same words, different scope — Ryneš (CJEU, 2014):**
    - **Facts:** R's home security camera covered his entrance, the public footpath and the house opposite. It recorded suspects breaking his window, and he gave the footage to the police. The Czech data protection office found he had breached data protection law.
    - **Outcome:** the exception did **not** apply.
    - **Reason:** the exception covers only **purely** personal or household activity, and surveillance that covers public space is not purely personal.
  - **Contrast with Singapore:** the same case would almost certainly be **yes** in Singapore. Whether Singapore's position is right is debatable.
  - **类似的例外：** GDPR、PIPL 和印度 DPDPA 都有，理由与新加坡相同。
  - **措辞相同，范围不同 — Ryneš（欧盟法院，2014）：**
    - **事实：** R 的家用安保摄像头拍到自家入口、公共人行道和对面房屋，录下了嫌疑人打破窗户的画面，他把录像交给警方。捷克数据保护办公室认定他违反了数据保护法。
    - **结果：** 该例外**不**适用。
    - **理由：** 该例外只涵盖**纯粹**的个人或家庭活动，而覆盖公共空间的监控不属于纯粹个人活动。
  - **与新加坡对比：** 同样的案子在新加坡几乎肯定会判**可以**。新加坡的立场是否正确，存在争论。

- **Employee Exception 雇员例外**
  - **Rule:** an employee acting **in the course of employment** is not bound by the PDPA. The act is treated as the **employer's own**, whether or not the employer knew of it or approved it.
  - **Rationale:** responsibility shifts from the employee to the employer, because the employer controls employees' work and must ensure compliance.
  - **The decisive question:** whether the act was done **in the course of employment**.
    - **If yes:** the employer is liable and the employee is not.
    - **If no** (own time, or during work hours but not part of the work): the employee is personally liable and the employer is not.
  - **Simple case — Reggie at ABC:** Reggie is an admin assistant whose job is mailing customer letters. He carelessly sends Bert's letter to Annie. This is literally his job, so he is not liable under the PDPA, although ABC may discipline him internally. ABC is treated as having sent the letter and is responsible.
  - **Test — Reed v Bellingham (2022):** a **factual inquiry** that looks at two things:
    - **Job scope:** compare what the employee did with what the job required. Acts within job scope point to the course of employment.
    - **Deliberate evasion:** did the employee **deliberately evade practices the employer set up** to stop the act? A rogue employee flouting a responsible employer's PDPA policies is likely outside the course of employment.
  - **Who is an employer (class Q&A):** an individual (such as a sole proprietor) or a company. Whether someone is an employee turns on how much control the company has over what they do.
  - **One-person company (class Q&A):** where the director is the only person, the lecturer suspects that person would not be treated the same way. This was a tentative view.
  - **规则：** 在**受雇过程**中行事的雇员不受 PDPA 约束。该行为被视为**雇主本身**的行为，不论雇主是否知情或批准。
  - **理由：** 责任从雇员转移到雇主，因为雇主控制雇员的工作，必须确保合规。
  - **关键问题：** 该行为是否在**受雇过程**中作出。
    - **如果是：** 雇主负责，雇员不负责。
    - **如果不是**（在私人时间，或在工作时间内但不属于工作的一部分）：雇员个人负责，雇主不负责。
  - **简单案例 — ABC 的 Reggie：** Reggie 是行政助理，工作是寄信给客户。他粗心地把给 Bert 的信寄给了 Annie。这就是他的本职工作，所以他不用承担 PDPA 责任，但 ABC 可以在内部处分他。ABC 被视为寄信的一方，须承担责任。
  - **测试 — Reed v Bellingham（2022）：** 属于**事实问题**，看两点：
    - **工作范围：** 比较雇员做了什么与工作要求他做什么。行为属于工作范围，就指向受雇过程。
    - **故意规避：** 雇员是否**故意规避雇主为阻止该行为而设立的做法**？如果雇主尽责地制定了 PDPA 政策，而"流氓"雇员公然违反，这名雇员很可能不在受雇过程中。
  - **谁是雇主（课堂问答）：** 个人（如独资经营者）或公司。某人是否雇员，取决于公司对其所做之事的控制程度。
  - **一人公司（课堂问答）：** 如果公司只有董事一人，讲师猜测此人不会被以同样方式对待。这只是初步看法。

- **Employee Exception: PBPL vs GCPL (Progressive Builders, 2021) 雇员例外：PBPL 与 GCPL（Progressive Builders，2021）**
  - **Facts:** a list of operators was involved.
    - PBPL's officer, **on his own initiative**, shared the list in his **private WhatsApp group**.
    - GCPL's officer received it there and told his safety coordinator to put a copy in the guardroom.
    - The coordinator misunderstood and pasted it on the **external façade** of GCPL's worksite.
  - **PBPL — not liable:** PBPL never told the officer to share the list, and he breached his employment contract's confidentiality requirement. He acted **outside the course of employment**, so **he** is liable, not PBPL.
  - **GCPL — liable:** both the officer and the coordinator acted **in the course of employment**, ultimately trying to keep the workplace safe. They simply did it **wrongly**.
  - **Lesson:** doing your job badly is still doing your job. Acting on your own, for no employer purpose and against the contract, takes you outside it.
  - **事实：** 涉及一份作业员名单。
    - PBPL 的主任**自作主张**，把名单分享到他的**私人 WhatsApp 群组**。
    - GCPL 的主任从群里收到名单，吩咐安全协调员把一份副本放在警卫室。
    - 协调员误解了指示，把名单贴在 GCPL 工地的**外墙**上。
  - **PBPL — 无须负责：** PBPL 从未叫主任分享名单，而他违反了雇佣合同中的保密要求。他是在**受雇过程之外**行事，所以由**他本人**负责，而不是 PBPL。
  - **GCPL — 须负责：** 主任和协调员都是在**受雇过程中**行事，最终目的都是确保工作场所安全，只是**做错了**。
  - **启示：** 把工作做砸仍然是在做本职工作。自作主张、没有任何雇主目的、并且违反合同的行为，才会落在受雇过程之外。

- **In-Class Exercise: Elena the CEO and the Misconfigured AI Agent 课堂练习：CEO Elena 与配置错误的 AI 智能体**
  - **Scenario:** CEO Elena gives an AI agent access to DEF's customer database to "find patterns of consumption". Because it is misconfigured, the agent emails all customers about their future purchases, and customers complain. DEF's policy requires a superior employee's permission to access the database, but Elena has **no superior employee** and no practical access limits.
  - **Arguments for "yes" (class majority; lecturer leans yes):**
    - A CEO's job includes strategy and improving profit, so finding consumption patterns fits her **job scope**.
    - The policy is **ineffective** against her. With direct, unrestricted access, she is not deliberately evading anything; she is "going straight through".
  - **Arguments for "no" (harder to make):**
    - Argue she **violated the data protection policy**, even though it is flimsy, and so acted outside the scope of employment.
    - Argue that **experimenting** is not a CEO's job and is lower-level marketing or technical work. The lecturer called this a hard sell, because experimenting alone does not take an act outside job scope.
  - **Key distinction:** a **negligent mistake** goes to whether there was a **breach**. **Scope of employment** is a separate question. An employee can act within scope but badly, which makes the employer liable.
  - **Policy strength is a sliding scale:** there is no bright line for when a policy is strong enough. The simpler question is what the policy says about the specific act.
    - A clear rule (for example, "do not use tool X on personal data") that the person deliberately ignores makes flouting easier to argue.
    - **Real technical controls** that she bypassed would make the argument stronger still.
  - **Board as superior (class Q&A):** technically the board is the CEO's superior, which is why the policy deliberately said "superior **employee**". Had it said just "superior", there would be an argument that the policy is effective against the CEO.
  - **Wider relevance:** this pattern is likely to be common, with any employee encouraged to experiment with AI where something goes wrong.
  - **Exam framing:** you **must take a position**. Either is acceptable; what is marked is the **reasoning**.
  - **情境：** CEO Elena 让 AI 智能体访问 DEF 的客户数据库，以"找出消费模式"。由于配置错误，智能体给所有客户发邮件询问未来的购买意向，客户纷纷投诉。DEF 的政策规定，访问数据库须经上级雇员许可，但 Elena **没有上级雇员**，访问也没有任何实际限制。
  - **支持"可以"的论点（多数同学；讲师倾向于可以）：**
    - CEO 的工作包括制定战略、提高利润，所以寻找消费模式属于她的**工作范围**。
    - 政策对她**无效**。她拥有直接、不受限的访问权，并没有故意规避什么，只是"径直穿过"。
  - **支持"不可以"的论点（较难论证）：**
    - 主张她**违反了数据保护政策**（即使政策形同虚设），因此是在受雇范围之外行事。
    - 主张**做实验**不是 CEO 的工作，而是低层营销或技术人员的事。讲师认为这很难让人信服，因为仅仅是做实验，并不会使行为落在工作范围之外。
  - **关键区分：** **疏忽错误**关系到是否构成**违规**。**受雇范围**则是另一个问题。雇员可以在范围内行事但做得很差，此时由雇主负责。
  - **政策强度是渐变尺度：** 没有明确界线说明政策何时算足够强。更简单的问题是：政策对这个具体行为是怎么规定的？
    - 有明确规定（例如"不得把工具 X 用于个人资料"）而当事人故意无视，就更容易论证她是在公然违反。
    - 如果她绕过了**实际的技术控制**，论点会更有力。
  - **董事会是否算上级（课堂问答）：** 严格来说董事会是 CEO 的上级，所以政策特意写成"上级**雇员**"。如果只写"上级"，就可以论证政策对 CEO 有效。
  - **更广泛的意义：** 这种模式可能会很常见，任何受鼓励去尝试 AI 的雇员都可能遇到出错的情况。
  - **考试作答：** 你**必须选定立场**。哪一方都可以，评分看的是**推理过程**。

- **Public Agency Exception 公共机构例外**
  - **Rule:** **public agencies** are outside the PDPA. They include:
    - The **government** (ministries, departments, agencies, organs of state).
    - Tribunals and courts.
    - Statutory bodies.
  - **Internal rules:** public agencies follow their own internal rules instead.
  - **Effect:** Singapore's PDPA is **purely private-sector regulation**, unlike the EU, whose rules cover both public and private sectors.
  - **规则：** **公共机构**不受 PDPA 管辖，包括：
    - **政府**（各部、部门、机构、国家机关）。
    - 审裁庭和法院。
    - 法定机构。
  - **内部规则：** 公共机构改为遵守自己的内部规则。
  - **效果：** 新加坡的 PDPA **纯属私营部门监管**，不同于同时涵盖公共和私营部门的欧盟。

- **Data Intermediary Exception 数据中介例外**
  - **Definition:** a **data intermediary (DI)** is an organisation that **processes personal data on behalf of another organisation** (the **data controller**). Employees of the controller are not DIs.
  - **Processing:** almost any operation on data, such as recording, holding, organising, and so on.
  - **When it arises:** whenever a company outsources data processing.
  - **Effect:** the DI is **mostly exempt**, and the controller bears the same obligations as if it had processed the data itself.
  - **Rationale:** the same as the employee exception, because the controller controls the DI.
  - **Common examples raised in class:**
    - Storage.
    - Survey firms.
    - Call centres (taking customer calls for the controller).
    - Payment processors.
    - Outsourced HR or payroll.
  - **Not a complete exemption — the DI still owes three obligations:**
    - **Protection:** secure the data.
    - **Retention Limitation:** don't keep the controller's data once its function is fulfilled.
    - **Data Breach Notification:** notify the controller, which then notifies the PDPC or the individuals.
  - **Not universal:** the exception covers the DI only when it processes **on behalf of** a controller. Processing for its **own purposes** gets no exemption.
  - **定义：** **数据中介（DI）**是**代表另一机构**（**数据控制者**）**处理个人资料**的机构。控制者的雇员不是数据中介。
  - **处理：** 几乎对资料的任何操作，例如记录、持有、整理等等。
  - **何时出现：** 每当公司把数据处理外包出去时。
  - **效果：** 数据中介**大部分获得豁免**，控制者承担的义务与自行处理该资料时相同。
  - **理由：** 与雇员例外相同，因为控制者控制着数据中介。
  - **课堂提出的常见例子：**
    - 存储服务。
    - 调查公司。
    - 呼叫中心（代控制者接听客户来电）。
    - 支付处理商。
    - 外包的人力资源或薪资处理。
  - **并非完全豁免 — 数据中介仍须履行三项义务：**
    - **保护义务：** 保障资料安全。
    - **保留限制义务：** 完成职能后不得继续保留控制者的资料。
    - **数据泄露通知义务：** 通知控制者，再由控制者通知 PDPC 或相关个人。
  - **并非普遍适用：** 只有在**代表**控制者处理资料时才受例外保护。为**自己的目的**处理资料则不获豁免。

- **Data Intermediary: Worked Examples and Q&A 数据中介：示例与问答**
  - **Market research:** ABC surveys people to produce a report solely for XYZ. ABC is a DI **even though** the contract does not specify methods or whom to survey, as long as everything is done on XYZ's behalf and for XYZ's purposes.
  - **Courier (unexpected):** a delivery company given a recipient's name, address and phone number is the sender's DI for that delivery. Its mishandling remains the sender's responsibility.
  - **Corporate group payroll:** XYZ is a DI when processing sister companies' employee data under their instructions. It is **not** a DI for its **own employees'** data, so it must comply fully there.
  - **Public agency as controller (Q&A):** the DI relies on the DI exception, and the agency relies on the public agency exception.
    - **Practical consequence:** this looks like nobody is liable, but the agency and the responsible public servants face **internal consequences**, just not through the PDPA.
    - **Suing the government:** you can still sue the government, just not for data protection.
  - **Parent and subsidiary (Q&A):** the corporate relationship is irrelevant. The only question is **who processes on behalf of whom**.
  - **市场调查：** ABC 进行调查，专为 XYZ 制作报告。即使合同**没有**规定方法或调查对象，只要一切都是代表 XYZ、为 XYZ 的目的而做，ABC 就是数据中介。
  - **快递（出人意料）：** 收到收件人姓名、地址和电话号码的送货公司，就该次送货而言是寄件人的数据中介。它处理不当，仍由寄件人负责。
  - **企业集团薪资处理：** XYZ 按姊妹公司的指示处理其雇员资料时是数据中介，但处理**自己雇员**的资料时**不是**，在这方面必须全面遵守 PDPA。
  - **公共机构作为控制者（问答）：** 数据中介依赖数据中介例外，公共机构依赖公共机构例外。
    - **实际后果：** 表面上似乎无人负责，但公共机构及负责的公务员会面对**内部后果**，只是不通过 PDPA。
    - **起诉政府：** 你仍可起诉政府，只是不能以数据保护为由。
  - **母公司与子公司（问答）：** 公司之间的关系无关紧要，唯一的问题是**谁代表谁处理资料**。

- **In-Class Exercise: Ryan's AI Fraud-Triage Startup 课堂练习：Ryan 的 AI 欺诈分流初创公司**
  - **Scenario:** insurers send Ryan claim data, which includes personal data. He triages it for fraud with his proprietary AI model, and also uses the insurers' accuracy feedback together with the personal data to improve his model.
  - **Answer — split by purpose:**
    - **Triaging:** processing **on behalf of** the insurers, so he is a DI and the exception applies.
    - **Model improvement:** processing for **his own purposes**, so the exception does not apply.
  - **The contract can change this:** if the contract expressly requires him to improve the model for the insurer's benefit (for example, separate per-insurer models kept apart), the whole activity can count as processing on the insurer's behalf.
  - **Mere permission is not enough:** an insurer saying "go ahead, use it to improve your model" is just permission. It does not make the training processing on the insurer's behalf.
  - **Unwritten "benefit exchange":** if both sides informally agree that Ryan can train on the data in return, he faces an **evidential problem** with the PDPC. Substantively, he is still processing for himself, **even if the insurer fully knows**.
  - **Locate the breach:**
    - A breach in the **triage stage** is covered by the exception.
    - A breach in the **training stage** is not, for example where an individual asks why their details were used without consent.
  - **Are the two processes separable? (class Q&A):** the lecturer suspects that asking a model to improve its output does not change the underlying model, unless he is mistaken.
  - **Location:** where the insurer is located (for example, Europe) is irrelevant to this exception.
  - **情境：** 保险公司把理赔资料（含个人资料）发给 Ryan。他用自己的专有 AI 模型进行欺诈分流，同时利用保险公司的准确度反馈连同个人资料来改进模型。
  - **答案 — 按目的拆分：**
    - **分流：** 是**代表**保险公司处理，所以他是数据中介，例外适用。
    - **改进模型：** 是为**自己的目的**处理，例外不适用。
  - **合同可以改变结论：** 如果合同明确要求他为保险公司的利益改进模型（例如为每家保险公司分别建立、彼此分开的模型），整个活动都可算作代表保险公司处理。
  - **单纯许可并不足够：** 保险公司说"去吧，用来改进你的模型"只是许可，并不会使训练变成代表保险公司的处理。
  - **未写入合同的"利益交换"：** 如果双方非正式同意 Ryan 可以用资料训练模型作为回报，他在 PDPC 面前会面对**证据问题**。实质上他仍是为自己处理资料，**即使保险公司完全知情**。
  - **确定违规所在：**
    - 发生在**分流阶段**的违规受例外保护。
    - 发生在**训练阶段**的违规则不受保护，例如个人质问为何未经同意使用其资料。
  - **两个过程能否分开？（课堂问答）：** 讲师认为，要求模型改进输出并不会改变底层模型，除非他理解有误。
  - **所在地：** 保险公司在哪里（例如欧洲）与这个例外无关。

- **Data Intermediary Management Lifecycle (Non-examinable) 数据中介管理生命周期（不考）**
  - **Purpose:** the controller is responsible for its DI, so it must manage the DI. The PDPC recommends a four-stage lifecycle.
  - **Stage 1 — Governance and risk assessment (before appointing a DI):**
    - Set the business objectives and requirements.
    - Determine the scale of outsourcing and the type and sensitivity of the data.
    - Identify the risks that guide which DI to choose.
    - Identify requirements to put in the contract.
    - Involve **senior management** with decision-making power.
    - **Childcare example:** 800 children's family details, medical history and parents' information is sizeable and sensitive, so the controller should consider whether a smaller, cheaper DI is too risky.
  - **Choosing the DI:** look at three indicators:
    - Its data protection policy and staff training.
    - Its security arrangements.
    - **External validation** such as certifications.
  - **Stage 2 — Policies and practices:**
    - **Contracts** should define the scope of processing and the data protection requirements. Example: a cloud provider with data centres in Singapore and Hong Kong promises Singapore-level protection wherever the data goes.
    - **Standard operating procedures** add operational detail. Example: a print-and-mail vendor of personalised financial reports must test delivery programmes, check that data is accurate, and specify how data is transferred.
    - **Reporting** includes regular reports and **ad hoc incident reports**. Example: an IT vendor fixed a disclosure bug without telling the controller, which found out only when customers contacted it.
  - **Stage 3 — Service management:** onboarding and training, management meetings, proactive monitoring by the DI, audits, and simulations.
    - **Scale to the DI:** with a giant like Microsoft, none of this is feasible or needed. With a smaller local DI you don't fully trust, these steps may be necessary.
  - **Stage 4 — Exit management:** make sure the DI stops retaining the data, documents all its work, and migrates data securely.
  - **目的：** 控制者要为其数据中介负责，所以必须管理数据中介。PDPC 推荐一个四阶段的生命周期。
  - **第一阶段 — 治理与风险评估（委任数据中介之前）：**
    - 确定业务目标和要求。
    - 确定外包规模以及资料的类型和敏感度。
    - 识别有助于选择数据中介的风险。
    - 确定要写入合同的要求。
    - 让有决策权的**高级管理层**参与。
    - **托儿中心例子：** 800 名儿童的家庭详情、病史和父母信息，数量可观且敏感，所以控制者要考虑选择规模较小、较便宜的中介是否风险过高。
  - **选择数据中介：** 看三个指标：
    - 它的数据保护政策和员工培训。
    - 它的安全安排。
    - **外部验证**，例如认证证书。
  - **第二阶段 — 政策与实践：**
    - **合同**应界定处理范围和数据保护要求。例子：在新加坡和香港设有数据中心的云服务商承诺，资料无论去到哪里都享有新加坡水平的保护。
    - **标准作业程序**加入操作细节。例子：负责打印和寄送个性化财务报告的供应商，必须测试寄送程序、确保资料准确，并说明资料如何传输。
    - **报告**包括定期报告和**临时事故报告**。例子：某 IT 供应商修复了资料披露漏洞却没有告知控制者，控制者直到客户联系才知道。
  - **第三阶段 — 服务管理：** 入职培训、管理会议、数据中介主动监控、审计和模拟演练。
    - **视中介而定：** 面对 Microsoft 这类巨头，这些都做不到也不需要。面对不完全信任的较小本地中介，这些步骤可能是必要的。
  - **第四阶段 — 退出管理：** 确保数据中介停止保留资料、记录所有工作，并安全迁移资料。

- **Intermediaries Elsewhere and Network Service Providers 其他法域的中介与网络服务提供商**
  - **Equivalents abroad (non-examinable):**
    - EU GDPR **"processor"**.
    - China PIPL **受托人 (entrusted party)**.
    - India DPDPA **"data processor"**.
  - **Network service provider exception:** an ISP or telco (such as Singtel or M1) merely acting as a **conduit** for third-party material is outside the PDPA for that transmission. The lecturer said it is not important and was included only for completeness.
  - **其他法域的对应概念（不考）：**
    - 欧盟 GDPR 的 **"处理者（processor）"**。
    - 中国 PIPL 的 **受托人**。
    - 印度 DPDPA 的 **"数据处理者（data processor）"**。
  - **网络服务提供商例外：** 仅作为第三方内容**通道**的 ISP 或电信公司（如 Singtel、M1），就该传输而言不受 PDPA 管辖。讲师表示这并不重要，只是为完整起见才提及。

- **Subordination of the PDPA 个人资料保护法的从属性**
  - **Rule 1:** the PDPA does **not affect** any authority, right, privilege, duty, obligation or limitation imposed by **other law**. Example: the hotel licensing regulations require hotels to collect every guest's full name, nationality and ID, which overrides the PDPA's consent requirement.
  - **Contracts are not law:** a contractual obligation is **not an excuse** for breaching the PDPA. Other laws override the PDPA; contracts do not.
  - **Rule 2:** other written law **prevails** to the extent it is **inconsistent** with the PDPA. Example: where a bank can rely on section 47 of the Banking Act to disclose customer information, the PDPA does not apply.
  - **AI:** there is no AI-specific law overriding the PDPA yet. Future regulations, for example requiring data sharing, could override parts of it.
  - **One-line takeaway:** most laws will override the PDPA.
  - **In other jurisdictions (non-examinable):** data protection can have a **superior**, not subordinate, status. In the EU, it is a fundamental right under the EU Charter.
  - **规则一：** PDPA **不影响**其他**法律**所赋予的任何权力、权利、特权，或施加的义务、责任、限制。例子：酒店执照规例要求酒店收集每位住客的全名、国籍和身份证件号码，这凌驾于 PDPA 的同意要求之上。
  - **合同不是法律：** 合同义务**不能作为**违反 PDPA 的**借口**。其他法律可以凌驾于 PDPA 之上，合同则不行。
  - **规则二：** 其他成文法在与 PDPA **不一致**的范围内**优先适用**。例子：银行可依据《银行法》第 47 条披露客户信息时，PDPA 不适用。
  - **AI：** 目前没有专门针对 AI、凌驾于 PDPA 之上的法律。将来的规例（例如要求数据共享）可能会凌驾于其部分条文之上。
  - **一句话总结：** 大多数法律都会凌驾于 PDPA 之上。
  - **在其他法域（不考）：** 数据保护可以具有**优先**而非从属的地位。在欧盟，它是《欧盟基本权利宪章》下的基本权利。
## Week 2 Learning Tips

Start with the architecture of this week. Singapore defines "organisation" so broadly that almost anyone is caught, and then carves people out through exclusions. That design tells you how to approach any problem question: the default is that the PDPA applies, and the work lies in proving an exception. Each exclusion has its own logic. The personal and domestic exception protects everyday life. The employee and data intermediary exceptions move liability to whoever has control. The public agency exception keeps the PDPA a private-sector regime. Once you see these purposes, the tests stop feeling arbitrary. Ask what problem each exception solves, and you will usually see which way a borderline case should go.

先把握本周的整体结构。新加坡把"机构"定义得极其宽泛，几乎人人都被涵盖，然后再通过排除情形把一些人剔除出去。这个设计告诉你如何处理任何问题题：默认 PDPA 适用，功夫在于证明某个例外成立。每个排除情形都有自己的逻辑。个人及家庭例外保护日常生活。雇员例外和数据中介例外把责任转移给有控制权的一方。公共机构例外使 PDPA 保持为私营部门制度。一旦看清这些目的，这些测试就不再显得武断。问一问每个例外要解决什么问题，你通常就能看出边界案例应该怎么判。

The single most common trap this week is stopping at the first limb of a test. Being an individual does not get you the personal and domestic exception; you must also be acting in a personal or domestic capacity, and that is where Sharon, Ang and GrabHitch were decided. Being an employee does not get you the employee exception; you must also be acting in the course of employment, which is where PBPL and GCPL split. Being an outsourced vendor does not get you the data intermediary exception; you must be processing on someone else's behalf, which is why Ryan's model training falls outside it. In every answer, identify the status, then spend most of your words on the second limb.

本周最常见的陷阱，是在测试的第一步就停下来。是个人并不能让你自动适用个人及家庭例外，你还必须以个人或家庭身份行事，而 Sharon、Ang 和 GrabHitch 案正是在这一点上作出裁决。是雇员并不能让你自动适用雇员例外，你还必须在受雇过程中行事，这正是 PBPL 和 GCPL 结果不同的地方。是外包供应商也不能让你自动适用数据中介例外，你必须是代表他人处理资料，这就是为什么 Ryan 的模型训练落在例外之外。每个答案都要先确认身份，再把大部分篇幅放在第二步上。

A second pitfall is confusing the breach with the exception. In the Elena discussion, the lecturer separated two questions: whether a negligent mistake caused a breach of the PDPA, and whether the act fell within the scope of employment. An employee can act within scope and still do the job badly, as GCPL's safety coordinator did. Making a mistake does not, by itself, take you outside the course of employment. The same discipline applies to intention under the personal data question: not knowing the image showed a real person did not help Armin. Keep the questions "was there a breach?" and "who is responsible?" in separate paragraphs of your answer.

第二个陷阱是把违规与例外混为一谈。在讨论 Elena 时，讲师区分了两个问题：疏忽错误是否导致违反 PDPA，以及该行为是否属于受雇范围。雇员可以在范围内行事却把工作做得很差，就像 GCPL 的安全协调员那样。犯错本身并不会让你落在受雇过程之外。同样的区分也适用于个人资料问题中的意图：不知道图像是真人，并不能帮到 Armin。在答案中，请把"是否违规"和"由谁负责"放在不同的段落里处理。

Build a contrast table for the cases. Use columns for facts, the factor that decided the case, and the outcome. Personal and domestic: Sharon (profit motive, so no), Ang (capacity fixed when the data was obtained, so no), GrabHitch (cost recovery and solicitation limits, so yes), and Ryneš as the stricter EU contrast. Employee: Reggie (literally his job, so the employer is liable), PBPL (own initiative and a breach of confidentiality, so the employee is liable), GCPL (a wrongly executed job task, so the employer is liable). Then add a one-line "lesson" card for each. The cases are useful for their distinguishing factors, and the table forces you to state them.

为案例制作一张对比表。栏目包括事实、决定案件的因素和结果。个人及家庭例外：Sharon（营利动机，不能适用）、Ang（身份在取得资料时确定，不能适用）、GrabHitch（收回成本和不得招揽的限制，可以适用），再加上更严格的欧盟对照案例 Ryneš。雇员例外：Reggie（就是本职工作，由雇主负责）、PBPL（自作主张并违反保密义务，由雇员负责）、GCPL（工作任务执行错误，由雇主负责）。然后为每个案例写一张一句话的"启示"卡片。这些案例的价值在于它们的区分因素，而这张表会迫使你把这些因素写出来。

Rehearse the three in-class problems with a fixed structure: identify the exception, state the test, argue the "yes" side, argue the "no" side, then commit to a conclusion. The lecturer was explicit that in the exam you must take a position, and that what earns marks is how you reason to it. For Armin, the hinge is whether seeking employment is business. For Elena, it is whether an ineffective policy can be "deliberately evaded", and why the drafting "superior employee" matters. For Ryan, it is splitting the processing by purpose, then asking what the contract says. Notice how small changes in the facts flip the answer: an express contract term or an effective control would change the result. Practise writing these variations yourself.

用固定结构演练课堂上的三道题：识别例外、陈述测试、论证"可以"的一方、论证"不可以"的一方，然后得出结论。讲师明确表示，考试时你必须选定立场，而得分的关键在于你如何推理得出这个立场。Armin 一题的关键在于求职是否属于商业。Elena 一题的关键在于一份无效的政策能否被"故意规避"，以及"上级雇员"这一措辞为何重要。Ryan 一题的关键在于按目的拆分处理活动，再看合同怎么规定。注意事实上的细微改变会如何扭转答案：一个明确的合同条款或一项有效的控制措施就会改变结果。自己动手写出这些变化版本来练习。

Keep the lecturer's hedges intact rather than turning them into rules. Airbnb hosts sit in a grey area. Whether full-time Grab drivers are employees is debatable. The one-person company was only a tentative view. Career development versus business was left open, and so was the AI-lookalike question, which depends on how closely the image resembles the person. Writing "this is debatable because…" and then reasoning through it shows more understanding than a confident one-word verdict. Equally, don't over-extend narrow points. That publicity does not defeat the exception, and that contracts never override the PDPA while other laws usually do, are precise statements. Learn them precisely.

保留讲师的保留措辞，不要把它们变成规则。Airbnb 房东处于灰色地带。全职 Grab 司机是否属于雇员存在争议。一人公司的问题只是初步看法。职业发展与商业的关系没有定论，AI 相似图像的问题也是如此，它取决于图像与本人的相似程度。写下"这一点有争议，因为……"然后逐步推理，比给出一个自信的单词结论更能显示你的理解。同样，不要过度延伸狭窄的论点。"公开并不会使例外失效"，以及"合同永远不能凌驾于 PDPA 之上而其他法律通常可以"，都是精确的表述。请精确地掌握它们。

Finally, budget your revision according to scope. The comparative material is non-examinable: India's significant data fiduciaries, Australia's small businesses, the EU controller definition, Ryneš, foreign equivalents of intermediaries, and the superior status of data protection in the EU. The lecturer also said the data intermediary management lifecycle does not need revising, and that the network service provider exception is not important. Read these once for context; they help you understand why Singapore's choices matter. Spend your real effort on the definition of organisation, the four exclusions and their tests, the decided cases, the three in-class problems, and the two subordination rules.

最后，按考试范围分配复习时间。比较法材料不考：印度的重要数据受托人、澳大利亚的小型企业、欧盟控制者的定义、Ryneš 案、其他法域的中介概念，以及数据保护在欧盟的优先地位。讲师还表示，数据中介管理生命周期不需要复习，网络服务提供商例外也不重要。这些内容读一遍了解背景即可，它们能帮助你理解新加坡的选择为何重要。真正的精力应放在机构的定义、四个排除情形及其测试、已裁决的案例、三道课堂练习题，以及两条从属性规则上。

- [18:38:49–18:42:49] **Comparative Perspectives: Terminology and Tiering of Organisations**

  Before we go into the exceptions, I want to highlight some comparative or international aspects of this concept. The light is not too bright, so you can still see the slide, right?

  One thing I want to point out is that some jurisdictions use different words for "organisation". For example, in the EU, the GDPR refers to the "controller". In China, the PIPL refers to the 个人信息处理者, or "personal information processor". In India, the term they like to use is "data fiduciary". By and large, you can kind of treat them as the same as organisation, but I would highlight that sometimes it is not exactly the same. When the EU GDPR uses the word "controller", it is not exactly the same as "organisation" in Singapore, because if you look at the definition of controller, it refers to the person or body which, alone or together with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data. So in the EU, one of the first questions you need to ask is: who is the one that determines the how and the why of processing? In Singapore, that is a question you don't actually need to answer, because anyone is an organisation.

  Another comparative point to highlight is that Singapore treats all organisations the same, but some jurisdictions differentiate between different types of organisations based on their size or significance. For example, in India, there is the concept of a "significant data fiduciary". The way this works is that the government can decide that you are a significant data fiduciary based on a number of factors: things like how much personal data you are processing, what the sensitivity of the data is, what risks your processing poses, and potential impacts on India's sovereignty, integrity, democracy, security, public order, and so on. So the Indian government can look at these factors to identify someone as a significant data fiduciary. Once you are identified as one, you are then subject to extra obligations: you must now appoint a data protection officer, you must appoint an independent data auditor, you must undertake assessments and audits, and so on. So what India does is create a new, higher tier of organisation.

  Australia does the opposite. Australia carves out certain insignificant organisations from the scope of its law. In the Australian Privacy Act, there is the concept of a "small business", which refers to any business with an annual turnover of three million dollars or less. Once you are a small business in Australia, you are not covered by the Privacy Act, unless you are doing certain types of activities, like providing health services or trading in personal data. So Australia says, "If you're a small business, generally we don't care about you; you don't have to comply with data privacy regulation." As far as Singapore is concerned, Singapore does not discriminate, so the same rules apply to everyone.

All of these are fairly important and fairly significant, and they operate in somewhat different ways, so we need to explore each of them one by one.

  Before I go into each exclusion, one thing I need to highlight, which should be quite obvious, is that only the excluded organisation itself can benefit from the exclusion. The exclusions or exceptions don't extend to any organisation that is dealing with the excluded organisation. Take this example here, which is taken from the guidelines.   Another example, which I sometimes get questions about: if I collect personal data from the government, do I need to comply with the PDPA? - [18:45:48–18:48:07] **The Personal and Domestic Exception: Basics**

  So let me go into the first exclusion, which is the personal and domestic exception. This exception is actually pretty straightforward. Any individual, like you and me, acting in a personal or domestic capacity does not need to comply with the PDPA. In your everyday life, you don't need to care about data protection rules.

  What is "personal" and what is "domestic"? When you act in a personal capacity, you undertake activities for your own purposes. For example, when you are taking the train and you see some incident happening, like someone fighting someone else, you do the Singaporean thing: you whip out your phone. That is recording personal data in your personal capacity. When you do that, you are not bound by the PDPA. You don't have to ask the people fighting for their consent. So that's one. If you have dinner with friends, take a group selfie and post it online, that's also in your personal capacity. You don't have to comply with the PDPA, and we all do these things.

  The other part of this exception is the domestic part. Domestic refers to family, refers to home. For example, when you install a CCTV camera to protect your home, that counts as acting in a domestic capacity. So when that camera records personal data on a day-to-day basis, you don't have to comply with the PDPA. If you register your child for tuition classes, this is something you are doing in your domestic capacity. You don't have to comply with the PDPA, but of course the tuition centre does.

  The reason for this exception is pretty obvious. If this exception did not exist, then the PDPA would clamp down on most of our everyday activities, which is not what we want.

  下面我讲第一个排除情形，也就是个人及家庭例外（personal and domestic exception）。这个例外其实相当直接。任何个人，比如你和我，在以个人或家庭身份行事时，都不需要遵守 PDPA。在日常生活中，你不需要理会数据保护规则。

  什么是“个人”，什么是“家庭”？当你以个人身份行事时，你是在为自己的目的从事活动。比如，你在坐地铁时看到发生了某件事，比如有人在和别人打架，你就做了新加坡人都会做的事：掏出手机。那就是以个人身份记录个人资料。你这样做时，不受 PDPA 约束。你不需要征求打架的人的同意。这是一个例子。如果你和朋友吃饭，拍了一张合照并发到网上，那也是以个人身份进行的。你不需要遵守 PDPA，而我们都会做这些事。

  这个例外的另一部分是家庭部分。家庭指的是家人、家。比如，你安装闭路电视摄像头来保护你的家，这算是以家庭身份行事。所以当这个摄像头日复一日地记录个人资料时，你不需要遵守 PDPA。如果你为孩子报名补习班，这是你以家庭身份在做的事。你不需要遵守 PDPA，但补习中心当然需要。

  这个例外存在的原因相当明显。如果没有这个例外，PDPA 就会限制我们大部分的日常活动，而这并不是我们想要的。

  是的。我很确定我提到过这一点。至少有两种方法可以让你不必遵守 PDPA。一种是证明你处理的资料不是个人资料。另一种是说你属于被排除的机构，你可以使用其中一个例外。无论哪种方式，你都可以避免遵守 PDPA。
- [18:52:20–18:54:24] **Q&A: Buying Leads and Relying on the Seller's Consent**

  A student points out that this case is different because Sharon was selling as a business.   Your question goes towards what we will cover in the next seminar, which is the consent obligation, and how you can obtain consent properly. Organisations that buy personal data often rely on the consent that was obtained by the seller. The seller should have gotten consent from the individuals whose personal data they're selling, and then they sell it, and you can rely on that consent to use the personal data for what you plan to use it for.

  The student follows up: what if the seller actually has a problem with its consent? Would the buyer still be okay?

  Well, the short answer is yes, as long as you yourself have taken reasonable care to make sure that the seller has obtained the requisite consent. So even if the seller turns out not to have done things properly, if you have taken reasonable care, you can still be counted as having obtained consent. I think we'll get to that question when we go to the consent obligation.

- [18:54:28–18:56:24] **Data Obtained in a Business Capacity: Ang Rui Song**

  The next part of this exception. We've talked about how you cannot use this exception if you're acting in a business capacity. In addition, if you previously obtained the personal data in a business capacity, you cannot later turn around and use it for a personal or domestic use. If the way in which you obtained the data was in a business capacity, you can never rely on this exception.

  The example given here is Ang Rui Song, which is also a PDPC case. Here, the individual, Ang, was a financial consultant associated with Prudential. While he was working as a financial consultant, he of course got a lot of client personal data. Subsequently, he stopped being a financial consultant with Prudential, and after that, he disposed of these client documents. Unfortunately, the way he disposed of the documents was to simply put them in a plastic bag and leave them next to a public bin, which is certainly a breach of the Protection Obligation, which we will look at in a subsequent seminar.

  Again, one of the questions that arose in this case was: can Ang rely on the personal and domestic exception, given that he was no longer acting as a financial consultant? The answer the PDPC gave was that he obtained the documents in the course of his business as a financial consultant. That being the case, he could not simply change the capacity in which he held the documents. He cannot later say, "Oh, I'm no longer a financial consultant, so I can do whatever I want with this." As long as you start holding it in a business capacity, you must continue to hold it in a business capacity. Therefore, he could not rely on the exception.

  这个例外的下一部分。我们已经讲过，如果你是以商业身份行事，就不能使用这个例外。此外，如果你之前是以商业身份取得个人资料的，你之后就不能转过头来把它用于个人或家庭用途。如果你取得资料的方式是以商业身份进行的，你就永远不能依赖这个例外。

  这里举的例子是 Ang Rui Song 案，这也是一个 PDPC 案件。这里的个人 Ang 是一名与 Prudential 有关联的理财顾问。在做理财顾问期间，他当然取得了大量客户的个人资料。后来，他不再担任 Prudential 的理财顾问，之后他处置了这些客户文件。不幸的是，他处置文件的方式是直接把它们装进一个塑料袋，放在一个公共垃圾桶旁边，这当然违反了保护义务（Protection Obligation），我们会在之后的研讨课中讲到这个义务。

  同样，这个案子中出现的问题之一是：既然 Ang 已经不再以理财顾问身份行事，他能否依赖个人及家庭例外？PDPC 给出的答案是，他是在作为理财顾问开展业务的过程中取得这些文件的。既然如此，他不能单方面改变他持有这些文件的身份。他不能事后说：“哦，我已经不是理财顾问了，所以我可以随意处置这些东西。”只要你一开始是以商业身份持有，你就必须继续以商业身份持有。因此，他不能依赖这个例外。
- [18:56:32–18:57:54] **Q&A: Why Prudential Was Not Liable, and Employers' Responsibility**

  A student asks: so in that case, Prudential is not liable, only the individual consultant?

  Actually, the reason why Prudential is not liable is a special case, and this is because these financial consultants, or insurance agents, are not really employees of Prudential. They are more like independent agents. If they were employees, Prudential would be liable.

  The student follows up: so employers have to make sure all their employees comply, even though they have no control over what the employees do?

  That will be addressed in the next exception, which is the employee exception, but the short answer to the question is yes. If you're an employer, you have to put in the necessary procedures to make sure that your employees don't go around doing something risky with personal data. If they do, you are the one who will be held responsible.

  一位同学问：所以在那个案子里，Prudential 不需要承担责任，只有那位顾问个人要承担？

  其实，Prudential 不承担责任的原因是一个特殊情况，因为这些理财顾问，或者说保险代理，其实并不是 Prudential 的雇员。他们更像是独立代理人。如果他们是雇员，Prudential 就要承担责任。

  这位同学追问：那么雇主就必须确保所有雇员都遵守规定，即使他们无法控制雇员的行为？

  这会在下一个例外，也就是雇员例外（employee exception）中讲到，但简短的回答是：是的。如果你是雇主，你必须建立必要的程序，确保你的雇员不会拿个人资料去做有风险的事。如果他们这样做了，被追究责任的就是你。
- [18:58:02–19:00:36] **Non-Commercial Capacity: The GrabHitch Case**

  The next case is an interesting one because it sits in the grey area. We've talked about how you cannot rely on the personal and domestic exception if you're acting in a business capacity. So when can you rely on it? This case highlights that if you are acting in a non-commercial capacity, then you are likely to be able to use this particular exception.

  The case is the Grabcar case. You have an organisation that operates an app, and on the app there is a carpooling function called GrabHitch. This GrabHitch function allows a driver who is driving to work to pick up passengers along the way, and the passengers pay the driver a certain amount of money for this hitching or ride service. So basically, the driver is already going to travel to a location, and he's just saying, "Anyone along the way, I can pick up."

  Here, the complainants, two individuals, were passengers who had used this GrabHitch function. Basically, both of them complained that their respective drivers had posted their personal data on social media without asking for their permission. I assume this is because there was some sort of dispute between driver and passenger.

  Same question: the drivers here are individuals; can they rely on the personal and domestic exception? Interestingly, the PDPC says yes, even though they are being paid money, because the drivers here were driving on a purely non-commercial and non-profit basis. That's because of the rules of the GrabHitch function. The drivers cannot solicit passengers, so they cannot go looking for passengers. They cannot offer more than two rides. They can only collect payments on a cost-recovery basis, so no profit, just cost recovery. And they can only carry passengers as an incidental part of the journey they're already taking. Given these restrictions, the drivers are not acting commercially. They are just, I suppose, trying to subsidise their own journey. So here, the drivers are acting in a personal capacity, and they can rely on the exception.

  下一个案子很有意思，因为它处于灰色地带。我们讲过，如果你以商业身份行事，就不能依赖个人及家庭例外。那么什么时候可以依赖它呢？这个案子说明，如果你是以非商业身份行事，那么你很可能可以使用这个例外。

  这个案子是 Grabcar 案。有一个机构运营一个应用程序，应用程序上有一个叫 GrabHitch 的顺风车功能。这个 GrabHitch 功能让一个开车上班的司机可以顺路搭载乘客，乘客为这种顺风车服务付给司机一定金额。所以基本上，司机本来就要前往某个地点，他只是说：“顺路的人，我都可以载。”

  这里的投诉人是两个人，他们都是使用过 GrabHitch 功能的乘客。基本上，两人都投诉各自的司机在没有征求他们许可的情况下，把他们的个人资料发到了社交媒体上。我猜这是因为司机和乘客之间发生了某种纠纷。

  同样的问题：这里的司机是个人，他们能否依赖个人及家庭例外？有意思的是，PDPC 说可以，即使他们收了钱，因为这里的司机是在纯粹非商业、非营利的基础上驾驶的。这是因为 GrabHitch 功能的规则。司机不能招揽乘客，所以他们不能主动去找乘客。他们不能提供超过两趟的搭载。他们只能按收回成本的方式收费，所以没有利润，只是收回成本。而且他们只能把搭载乘客作为自己本来行程的附带部分。鉴于这些限制，司机并不是在从事商业行为。我想，他们只是在补贴自己的行程。所以在这里，司机是以个人身份行事，可以依赖这个例外。

Grab is what they call a ride-share company, a taxi company, and this particular GrabHitch function is meant specifically for this type of non-commercial carpooling. For Grab drivers who drive for a living, I think it's a bit debatable whether or not they count as employees. Grab of course says they don't count as employees; they're independent drivers, and therefore if they breach data protection law, that's their problem. I think it's debatable as to whether that is correct.

  一位同学问，Grab 司机实际上是否被视为该机构的雇员，还是被视为以个人身份行事。

Speaking about Airbnb, I think the answer is that you are working in a business capacity.   The student points out that the owners don't work for Airbnb.

  Correct, yes. Airbnb is just a platform.

  The student adds that the owner is simply renting out the place, and the guests are staying in the owner's own place, and asks further about the cameras capturing the guests.

  Right. So if you're asking the question, "Are they employees?", I think clearly the answer is no. They aren't employees of Airbnb. But that's a separate question.   在这里，正如我提到的，这就开始进入灰色地带了。某件事到底是个人性质还是商业性质，并不是很清楚。就 Airbnb 而言，我认为答案是你是以商业身份行事。我猜 Airbnb 并不限于收回成本；它实际上允许你赚取利润，而且很多人把这当作生意来经营。我同意，在这个例外是否适用的问题上，这有点灰色地带。要完整回答这个问题，我们需要看 Airbnb 的具体条款，以及房东获利的程度。

  对。所以如果你问的是“他们是不是雇员？”，我认为答案显然是否定的。他们不是 Airbnb 的雇员。但这是另一个问题。一个问题是：他们是雇员吗？答案：不是。第二个问题是：他们是否以个人或家庭身份行事？这一点就有点争议了。
- [19:04:07–19:09:08] **In-Class Exercise: Armin's AI-Generated Portfolio Website**

  So let's look at an example that is perhaps more relevant to the AI context. Some of you may relate to this.

  Here we have Armin, who is a graduating university student majoring in web design. He wants to show off his AI competency and his aesthetics, so he vibe-codes a sample corporate website. Armin makes no money from the website, because it's just a sample; it doesn't contain any advertising. He is merely using this website as part of his portfolio when he applies for jobs at various companies. He hasn't actually used the website for that purpose yet; that is in the future.

  On the website, there's a web page entitled "Our People", like most corporate websites have. It is meant to contain fake corporate profiles: fake faces, made-up names. Unfortunately, the AI tool, for whatever reason, included a real person's face and name in one of the profiles, and we'll call that person James. James has since complained to the PDPC that Armin is disclosing his personal data without his consent. Do you think Armin can rely on the personal and domestic exception?

  Take maybe five minutes to think about this question. This is a small example of what you might have to do when dealing with data privacy concepts. The way you approach this question is, I guess, to start with your intuition: do you think the exception applies? But don't stop there. Go into the reasoning: why do you think the exception applies, or why do you think it does not? Just take a few minutes, and we'll come back and share thoughts.

  那我们来看一个也许和 AI 背景更相关的例子。你们当中有些人可能会有共鸣。

  这里有 Armin，他是一名即将毕业、主修网页设计的大学生。他想展示自己的 AI 能力和审美，所以他用“氛围编程（vibe-coding）”做了一个示范企业网站。他用一个 AI 工具和一系列提示词制作了这个示范网站，并把它放到网上供公众浏览。Armin 没有从这个网站赚钱，因为它只是一个样本，没有任何广告。他只是打算在向各家公司求职时，把这个网站作为作品集的一部分。他其实还没有把网站用于这个目的，那是将来的事。

  网站上有一个名为“Our People（我们的团队）”的网页，大多数企业网站都有。这个页面本来应该放的是虚构的企业人员简介：假的面孔、编造的名字。不幸的是，那个 AI 工具不知为何在其中一份简介里放进了一个真实人物的面孔和名字，我们就叫这个人 James。James 后来向 PDPC 投诉，说 Armin 在未经他同意的情况下披露了他的个人资料。你们认为 Armin 能依赖个人及家庭例外吗？

- [19:09:22–19:14:19] **Exercise Discussion: Arguments For and Against Armin**

  Right, I think we have a bit of time to pick up on this problem. Can I get a show of hands? Who thinks the answer is yes, he can rely on the exception? And who thinks he cannot? Good, that means I made a good question. So, someone who said yes, he can rely on the exception: what are you saying?

  A student who said yes explains that the crucial point is that the portfolio use is only something in the future.

  So I think one of the things you would highlight about this is that he's not actually making any money from it. No money, no advertising, nothing. At the moment, he hasn't actually used the website for anything; it's just sitting there on the internet.

  Another student raises the point that his future use of it is for a job, and that could be a job with a commercial purpose.

  So the counter-argument would be: you're not making any money from it, but your intention is to use this as part of your portfolio to get a job, and that clearly counts as a business purpose.

  Another student argues in Armin's favour that he is acting as an individual, so it is in his personal capacity.

  Yes, so it's true that he's acting as an individual. But I suppose that doesn't quite fully answer the question, because you must be an individual, plus you must be acting in a personal or domestic capacity. That second part is the thing you need to address in this particular question.

  Another student adds to the counter-argument: he showed the website to the public. If it were within the personal and domestic exception, you'd probably only open it to a certain group of friends who could see it. The fact that he is showing it to the public suggests that it includes a commercial or business purpose.

  So that would be something the PDPC might consider: the fact that he made it public. We'll talk about this a bit later, but at least in Singapore, the fact that you made something public does not by itself prevent you from relying on the exception. For example, if you take a photo and put it on Facebook, completely public, that's still personal; that's still using data in your personal capacity. Of course, you could point to the public nature of this website as indicating that he intends to use it for some work or business purpose in the future. I think you can make that argument there.

  A student offers one more point: the purpose of the website is not to communicate anyone's personal data, so the photo shouldn't count as personal data.

  So that would be an interesting argument: the purpose of this is not to communicate any personal data, so it is not personal data. I suspect it would be quite difficult to convince the PDPC of that. It's clearly an accident; Armin didn't intend to disclose anyone's personal data. But if you put up someone's facial photo and name on your website, whether accidentally or deliberately, it will be hard to argue that that doesn't constitute personal data, even if you point to the purpose as a reason why it's not personal data.

  好，我想我们还有一点时间来讨论这个问题。可以举手示意一下吗？谁认为答案是可以，他能依赖这个例外？谁认为他不能？很好，这说明我出了一个好问题。那么，认为他可以依赖例外的同学，你怎么说？

  一位认为可以的同学解释说，关键在于作品集的用途只是将来的事。

  所以我想你会强调的一点是，他实际上没有从中赚钱。没有钱，没有广告，什么都没有。目前，他还没有把这个网站用于任何用途，它只是放在网上而已。

  另一位同学提出，他将来是要用它来求职的，而那份工作可能具有商业目的。

  所以反方论点会是：你没有从中赚钱，但你的意图是把它作为作品集的一部分去找工作，而这显然算是商业目的。

  另一位同学为 Armin 辩护，认为他是以个人身份行事，所以属于个人身份。

  另一位同学补充反方论点：他把网站公开给公众。如果属于个人及家庭例外，你大概只会开放给某一群朋友看。他把它公开给公众这一事实，表明其中包含商业或业务目的。

- [19:26:26–19:28:41] **The Employee Exception: Introduction**

  Let me start by introducing the next exception, and then we can pause for a bit. We talked about the personal and domestic capacity. The next important exception is known as the employee exception.

  What this exception says is that if you are an employee acting in the course of your employment, doing your work as you are required to do, then you are not bound by the PDPA. Instead, if you do something in the course of your employment that happens to breach the PDPA, it is the employer who is regarded as responsible, and this is whether or not the employer knew that the act was done, or whether or not the employer approved of the act. What this exception does is shift responsibility from the employee to the employer. It is ultimately the employer who has control over the employee and what they do in the course of their work, so the law says that the employer is the one responsible for making sure that they are compliant.

  For this exception to apply, one of the most important things is to decide whether the person in question is an employee. Usually, it's very easy to decide whether someone is an employee. The biggest part is trying to decide whether what the employee did was done in the course of employment, and you'll see some examples of when this is contested. So to make it clear: if the employee is acting in the course of employment, the employee is not liable; the employer is liable. If the employee does something outside the course of employment, like on his own time, or even during work time but not as part of his work, then it is the employee who is liable, not the employer.

  这个例外的意思是，如果你是雇员，在受雇过程中行事，按要求做你的工作，那么你不受 PDPA 约束。相反，如果你在受雇过程中做了某件事，而这件事恰好违反了 PDPA，那么被视为负有责任的是雇主，而且不论雇主是否知道这一行为，也不论雇主是否批准了这一行为。这个例外的作用是把责任从雇员转移到雇主身上。归根结底，是雇主控制着雇员以及他们在工作过程中所做的事情，所以法律规定，雇主才是负责确保合规的那一方。

- [19:36:55–19:39:58] **The Employee Exception in Practice and the "Course of Employment" Test**

  Back to the employee exception. As I mentioned, the employee exception shifts responsibility from the employee to the employer. Let me give one simple example of how this works. Say you have Reggie, who works as an administrative assistant at ABC. Reggie is the employee and ABC is the employer. Reggie's job involves mailing letters to ABC's customers. Because he is careless, he accidentally sends Annie a letter that was meant for Bert. What this means, of course, is that Bert's personal data has been disclosed to Annie without his consent.

  This is a very clear case where Reggie is acting in the course of his employment. This is literally his job. So he falls within the employee exception, and he will not be legally liable for breaching the PDPA, although of course ABC may choose to punish him internally. Reggie is covered by the exception, but ABC is now regarded as the one who sent the letter, and ABC becomes responsible under the PDPA. That's how the exception works in most cases.

  But there will be some cases where you are not really sure whether what the person did was in the course of employment or not, so you will sometimes need to ask whether what the employee was doing was part of his job. The case of Reed v Bellingham says that this is a factual inquiry, and you can consider a few things. The obvious thing to consider is what the employee was doing and what the employee's job required him to do. Were the employee's acts part of his job scope? If the answer is yes, then it is quite likely that he was acting in the course of employment. So look at what he did: was it within his job scope? If yes, then he's doing it in the course of his employment.

  Another thing you are allowed to consider is whether the employee deliberately tried to evade practices that the employer set up to stop employees from doing that act. If the employer was responsible and implemented policies to make sure its employees comply with the PDPA, and then this particular rogue employee found ways to evade those policies, it's likely that the law will treat the employee as not acting in the course of employment, because he is really flouting the employer's policies.

  回到雇员例外。正如我提到的，雇员例外把责任从雇员转移到雇主。我举一个简单的例子说明它如何运作。假设有一个人叫 Reggie，他在 ABC 担任行政助理。Reggie 是雇员，ABC 是雇主。Reggie 的工作包括给 ABC 的客户寄信。由于粗心，他不小心把一封本来要寄给 Bert 的信寄给了 Annie。这当然意味着，Bert 的个人资料在未经他同意的情况下被披露给了 Annie。

  这是一个非常清楚的案例，Reggie 是在受雇过程（course of employment）中行事的。这实实在在就是他的工作。所以他属于雇员例外，不会因为违反 PDPA 而承担法律责任，虽然 ABC 当然可以选择在内部处分他。Reggie 受到例外的保护，但 ABC 现在被视为寄出这封信的一方，因此 ABC 要根据 PDPA 承担责任。大多数情况下，这个例外就是这样运作的。
