- [19:41:31–19:45:12] **When the Line Is Not Obvious: PBPL and GCPL**

  So here is an interesting case. This is a case where the line was not obvious.

  PBPL's officer had the list of operators. On his own, he decided to share it in his own private WhatsApp group with his fellow officers. This of course constitutes a disclosure of the complainants' personal data without their consent. GCPL's officer then receives the list from this WhatsApp group. He sees the names, and he tells his safety coordinator to put a copy of the list in the guardroom. However, the safety coordinator somehow misunderstands the instructions, and pastes the list instead on the external façade of GCPL's worksite, which results in a disclosure of the complainants' personal data, again without their consent.

  So the question here is: are PBPL and GCPL responsible, or are the respective officers responsible? Of course, it depends on whether these officers were acting in the course of their employment.

  Starting with PBPL's officer, the PDPC says that this officer was not acting in the course of his employment. Remember that this officer shared the list of operators in his own WhatsApp group. It is clear that PBPL didn't tell the officer to share the list. He was clearly acting in breach of his employment contract, because he was required to keep such information confidential. So here he was acting outside the course of his employment, and therefore it is he who is liable, not PBPL.

  Contrast this with GCPL's officer. Here, he was acting in the course of his employment when he instructed the safety coordinator to put up the list, and so was the coordinator who put up the list. Both of them were actually acting in the course of their employment; they just did it wrongly. They were ultimately trying to make sure that the workplace was safe. So the PDPC says that GCPL is the one responsible for the actions of its officers. This case illustrates how you might apply the employee exception.

- [20:02:05–20:03:15] **The Public Agency Exception**

  So that's the employee exception. The next exception is actually very straightforward, so I won't spend much time on it, and this is the public agency exception. It's very simple: if you are a public agency in Singapore, you don't fall under the PDPA. That includes the government, any tribunal or court, and any statutory body; all of these count as public agencies. So those don't get caught by the PDPA. There are some internal rules that they follow.

  What this means is that in Singapore, our data protection rules are purely for the private sector. This is actually quite different from many other countries. The EU, for example: their data protection rules cover both the public and the private sector. We choose to draw a line: private sector, you get caught by the PDPA; public sector, you comply with your own internal rules. So that one is quite simple.

  这意味着，在新加坡，我们的数据保护规则纯粹针对私营部门。这其实和很多其他国家相当不同。比如欧盟，它们的数据保护规则同时涵盖公共部门和私营部门。我们选择划一条线：私营部门受 PDPA 约束；公共部门则遵守自己的内部规则。所以这一个相当简单。
- [20:03:22–20:06:20] **The Data Intermediary Exception: Definition and Common Examples**

  The next one is a bit more complicated, and this is the data intermediary exception. This one needs a little bit of explanation. What is a data intermediary? This is relevant whenever you see a company outsourcing some of its data processing. A data intermediary refers to an organisation that is processing personal data on behalf of another organisation, which most people call the data controller, but it does not include an employee of the data controller. So this would be a situation where the data controller outsources some data processing to a data intermediary, a different company, for example. Processing is basically anything you do with data: recording, holding, organisation, and so on and so forth.

  So what happens when an organisation acts as a data intermediary? What happens is similar to the employee exception. Because the data intermediary is acting on behalf of the data controller, it is generally exempt from the PDPA. It's the data controller who will be held liable if something wrong is done with the data. The rationale is again quite similar to that for the employee exception: the data controller is the one who has control over the intermediary, so it should be held responsible.

  Can anyone name some common examples of data intermediary relationships that you may have come across?

  A student suggests storage.

  Yes, storage is a very common data intermediary relationship.

  Another student suggests social security and health insurance, and another suggests surveying firms and call centres.

  So, surveying firms and call centres. Take the call centre example: the call centre is basically taking calls from customers on behalf of the data controller.

  Another student suggests payment processors.

  Payment processors, yes. A payment processor is again an intermediary, because it's taking in payment information, credit card details, on behalf of its customer.

  Another student suggests that it could be any function of a business that is outsourced to a third-party firm, for example HR payroll processing.

  Yes, payroll processing or general HR responsibilities can also potentially be outsourced, and those would be data intermediary relationships.

  下一个例外稍微复杂一些，那就是数据中介例外（data intermediary exception）。这个需要稍作解释。什么是数据中介？每当你看到一家公司把部分数据处理外包出去时，这个概念就相关了。数据中介指的是代表另一个机构处理个人资料的机构，而另一个机构大多数人称为数据控制者（data controller），但数据中介不包括数据控制者的雇员。所以这就是数据控制者把某些数据处理外包给数据中介，比如另一家公司的情况。处理（processing）基本上就是你对资料所做的任何事：记录、持有、整理，等等。

  那么，当一个机构作为数据中介行事时会怎样？情况和雇员例外类似。由于数据中介是代表数据控制者行事，它一般不受 PDPA 约束。如果资料处理出了问题，被追究责任的是数据控制者。其理由同样和雇员例外相当类似：数据控制者是对中介有控制权的一方，所以应该由它承担责任。

  有谁能举出一些你们可能遇到过的常见数据中介关系的例子吗？

  一位同学提出存储服务。

  对，存储是一种非常常见的数据中介关系。

  另一位同学提出社会保障和医疗保险，还有一位同学提出调查公司和呼叫中心。

  调查公司和呼叫中心。以呼叫中心为例：呼叫中心基本上就是代表数据控制者接听客户的来电。

  另一位同学提出支付处理商。

  支付处理商，对。支付处理商同样是一种中介，因为它代表它的客户接收支付信息、信用卡资料。

  另一位同学提出，可以是企业外包给第三方公司的任何职能，比如人力资源的薪资处理。

  对，薪资处理或一般的人力资源工作也有可能被外包，那些就会是数据中介关系。
- [20:06:27–20:08:03] **Not a Complete Exemption: The Three Remaining Obligations and the Exception's Limits**

  One thing to keep in the back of your mind, and we will explore these obligations later on: the exemption is not complete. If you are a data intermediary, you are still bound by a few obligations. Number one is protection, meaning you are supposed to secure the personal data, and if you fail to, you are liable. Number two is retention limitation: you are not allowed to keep retaining the data controller's personal data once you have fulfilled your function; you are supposed to limit it. Number three is data breach notification: if there is a data breach, the data intermediary must notify the data controller, and the data controller then proceeds with notifying the PDPC or the individuals. You don't know the details of these obligations yet; you just have to be aware that the data intermediary does still need to comply with some obligations.

  But one important thing to note about the data intermediary exception is that it is not some kind of universal exception that covers you. It only covers you as a data intermediary, only if you are processing personal data on behalf of a controller. Whenever you process personal data on your own behalf, for your own purposes, you don't get to enjoy the exception.

  有一点大家要放在心里，我们之后会再探讨这些义务：这个豁免并不是完全的。如果你是数据中介，你仍然受几项义务约束。第一是保护（protection），意思是你应当保障个人资料的安全，如果做不到，你就要承担责任。第二是保留限制（retention limitation）：一旦你完成了你的职能，就不得继续保留数据控制者的个人资料，你应当加以限制。第三是数据泄露通知（data breach notification）：如果发生数据泄露，数据中介必须通知数据控制者，然后由数据控制者去通知 PDPC 或相关个人。你们现在还不知道这些义务的细节，只需要知道数据中介仍然需要遵守某些义务。

  但关于数据中介例外，有一点很重要：它不是某种无论如何都覆盖你的普遍例外。它只在你作为数据中介时覆盖你，也就是只有当你代表控制者处理个人资料时才适用。每当你为了自己、出于自己的目的处理个人资料时，你就不能享有这个例外。
- [20:08:15–20:12:42] **Examples: Market Research, Courier Services, and Corporate Groups**

  So, some examples of data intermediary relationships. Let's say you have organisation ABC, which is engaged by organisation XYZ. ABC is a market research survey firm. The written contract says that ABC is engaged to collect personal data on behalf of XYZ and produce a report, basically to see the correlation between certain characteristics of the people surveyed. So XYZ is basically asking ABC to go and collect survey information. The contract also says ABC must collect the telephone number and residential address of each person surveyed.

  Here, it is clear that ABC is the data intermediary of XYZ, and this is even though the contract doesn't actually say how ABC should be doing the survey, and even though the contract doesn't specify who ABC should be reaching out to. As long as ABC can show that all it is doing is done on behalf of XYZ and for XYZ's purposes. In this case, ABC is doing everything in order to produce a report for XYZ. So that would be a standard example.

  Another interesting example, perhaps a little more unexpected, is the courier situation. You have XYZ, which provides courier or delivery services, and ABC uses XYZ to deliver a parcel to someone. ABC gives XYZ the name, address and telephone number of the person who should be receiving the parcel. Here, XYZ is a data intermediary. It's a bit strange, because XYZ is not what you'd think of as a data processing company; it is a delivery company. But because what it is doing is taking the recipient's personal data and processing it for a particular purpose, for ABC's purpose, XYZ is still counted as a data intermediary as far as this delivery is concerned. So if XYZ mishandles this personal data, it will still be ABC's responsibility.

  Yet another situation is the corporate group context. It is quite common that within a group of companies, there is one particular company that handles all the administration for the other sister companies. In this example, you have XYZ, which does payroll administration for a number of organisations, including its sister companies. Here, XYZ holds records of those organisations' employees, such as their names, duration of employment, and so on. XYZ processes the personal data solely for the purpose of payroll administration, in line with the instructions given to it by the data controllers. So here, XYZ is the data intermediary.

  But, and this is the important thing to bear in mind going from this example: it's true that XYZ is a data intermediary whenever it is processing the personal data of other data controllers' employees. But when it is processing the personal data of its own employees, it cannot rely on the exception. When XYZ processes the personal data of its own employees, it is not doing it on behalf of others; it's doing it on its own behalf. So it is not a data intermediary as far as that is concerned, and it cannot rely on the exemption, as I mentioned just now.

  下面是一些数据中介关系的例子。假设有一家机构 ABC，受机构 XYZ 委托。ABC 是一家市场调查公司。书面合同规定，ABC 受委托代表 XYZ 收集个人资料并制作一份报告，基本上是要看受访者某些特征之间的相关性。所以 XYZ 基本上是请 ABC 去收集调查资料。合同还规定，ABC 必须收集每位受访者的电话号码和住址。

  在这里，ABC 显然是 XYZ 的数据中介，即使合同实际上没有规定 ABC 应该如何进行调查，即使合同没有指定 ABC 应该联系哪些人。只要 ABC 能证明它所做的一切都是代表 XYZ、为了 XYZ 的目的而做的。在这个案例中，ABC 所做的一切都是为了给 XYZ 制作一份报告。所以这会是一个标准的例子。

  另一个有意思的例子，也许有点出人意料，是快递的情况。XYZ 提供快递或送货服务，ABC 利用 XYZ 把一个包裹送给某人。ABC 把收件人的姓名、地址和电话号码交给 XYZ。在这里，XYZ 就是数据中介。这有点奇怪，因为 XYZ 并不是你会想到的那种数据处理公司，它是一家送货公司。但由于它所做的是拿着收件人的个人资料，为了特定目的，也就是 ABC 的目的去处理，所以就这次送货而言，XYZ 仍然算是数据中介。所以如果 XYZ 处理不当这些个人资料，责任仍然在 ABC。

  还有一种情况是企业集团的情境。在一个公司集团内部，由某一家公司为其他姊妹公司处理所有行政工作，这相当常见。在这个例子中，XYZ 为若干机构，包括它的姊妹公司，处理薪资行政工作。在这里，XYZ 持有这些机构雇员的记录，比如他们的姓名、受雇期限等等。XYZ 处理这些个人资料纯粹是为了薪资行政，并且是按照数据控制者给它的指示进行的。所以在这里，XYZ 是数据中介。

  但是，从这个例子出发，有一点很重要需要记住：XYZ 在处理其他数据控制者雇员的个人资料时，确实是数据中介。但当它处理自己雇员的个人资料时，它就不能依赖这个例外。XYZ 处理自己雇员的个人资料时，并不是代表他人，而是为了自己。所以就这一点而言，它不是数据中介，不能依赖这个豁免，正如我刚才提到的。

  If the data controller is a public agency, what happens in that scenario is that the data intermediary is able to enjoy the data intermediary exemption, and the public agency relies on a different exception: the public agency will rely on the public agency exception to avoid liability.

  The student follows up: what if there's a lapse that has nothing to do with anything in the data intermediary's contract, and the agency did not give specific instructions?

  So this particular scenario makes it look like nobody is responsible. The data intermediary is not responsible because of its exception, and the public agency is not responsible per se because of the public agency exception. But I think practically, what will likely happen is that the public agency itself, and the public servants who are responsible for this, would have to contend with the public agency's internal rules. There will be consequences; it just won't be done through the legal mechanism of the PDPA.

  The student asks: so I cannot sue the government?

  No, you can sue the government. Just not for data protection.

  Another student asks how it works if it is a parent company and a subsidiary.

  Same thing. It doesn't matter what the relationship between the two companies is. The only question is: is one company processing personal data on behalf of the other? It could be the subsidiary processing for the parent. The main question is who is processing on behalf of whom; that tells you who is the data intermediary and who is the data controller.

  有什么问题吗？

  一位同学问：如果数据控制者是公共机构，而数据中介是一家私营的市场调查公司呢？那时数据中介的义务会怎样？

  如果数据控制者是公共机构，那么在这种情况下，数据中介可以享有数据中介豁免，而公共机构则依赖另一个例外：公共机构会依赖公共机构例外来避免承担责任。

  这个情境让人觉得好像没有人要负责。数据中介因为它的例外而不用负责，公共机构本身也因为公共机构例外而不用负责。但我认为实际上可能发生的是，公共机构本身以及负责此事的公务员，必须面对公共机构的内部规则。会有后果的，只是不会通过 PDPA 这个法律机制来处理。

  这位同学问：那我就不能起诉政府了吗？

  不，你可以起诉政府。只是不能以数据保护为由。

  另一位同学问，如果是母公司和子公司，又是怎样的情况。

  一样的道理。两家公司之间是什么关系并不重要。唯一的问题是：是否有一家公司在代表另一家公司处理个人资料？可能是子公司为母公司处理。主要的问题是谁在代表谁进行处理，这就告诉你谁是数据中介、谁是数据控制者。

  Another student wants to clarify: if he has a proprietary model that he built by himself, and he just takes the data, runs it, and gives the results back to the insurance company, without doing any training, because the model already works perfectly, would that be fine and within the exception?

  A student asks: what if the companies actually authorise Ryan to use the data to improve the model?

  No, because here, even if these companies just say, "Go ahead, use the personal data to improve your model more," it is just the company giving permission. You can't really say that he is processing the personal data on their behalf.

  The student refines the question: what if the company tells him to use the data to improve the model, so as to provide better service to the customer?

  So it is based on what the contract is, like I mentioned.   Yes. So the answer here is to determine which breaches he can rely on this exception for, and which he cannot. If the breach of the PDPA happens at the first stage, he's safe, because he can rely on the exception. Whereas if the breach happens at the training stage, where someone says, "Why are you using my details without my consent?", there he cannot rely on the exception.

- [20:28:34–20:32:45] **The Data Intermediary Management Lifecycle: Governance and Risk Assessment**

  So that's the data intermediary exception. The next few slides are not examinable, but I think it's also important for you to know what things look like from the controller's perspective.

  As I mentioned, when you have a controller–intermediary relationship, the responsibility lies with the controller. So, as the controller, you need to be able to manage your data intermediary, and one way by which data controllers manage their intermediaries is using this suggested data intermediary management lifecycle. It's a kind of system that has been recommended by the PDPC as a method for data controllers to properly manage their data intermediaries. There's a four-stage process, which I will go through. Again, you don't have to revise this for the exam.

  So how does this lifecycle work? The first stage of the lifecycle is governance and risk assessment. This is the stage before you actually appoint the data intermediary. What the controller needs to do is understand the nature of the intermediary relationship. There are a few things the controller will typically do. First, figure out the business objectives: what are the requirements for the data processing outsourcing that we want to do? Number two, figure out the scale of the outsourcing and what type of personal data the intermediary is going to access. Number three, identify potential risks, because that determines whom you should take on as your data intermediary. Number four, see what requirements you can put into your contract with the data intermediary. So it's a kind of scoping out of the nature of the data intermediary relationship.

  Generally, what the PDPC recommends is that at this particular stage, the senior management of the data controller should be involved, because you need someone who is able to make decisions about the intermediary relationship, not just someone with no executive power running this stage.

  It is, I think, especially important to figure out the scale of the outsourcing and the type of personal data you're looking at, because that tells you what you need to require from the data intermediary. For example, here your organisation XYZ runs childcare centres, and it wants to engage a data intermediary for its personal data. So the management of XYZ would look at the personal data in question. In this case, XYZ needs someone who is able to process data for 800 children, which is a sizeable number, plus the personal data in question includes things like family details, medical history, and parents' information, which is on the sensitive side. Knowing this, XYZ can then properly evaluate what kind of data intermediary it requires: can I take a risk with a smaller, cheaper intermediary, or do I need to go a bit higher? That's one of the things the controller would have in mind when deciding which data intermediary to choose.

  以上就是数据中介例外。接下来几张投影片不在考试范围内，但我认为让你们了解从控制者的角度看事情是什么样子，也很重要。

  正如我提到的，当存在控制者与中介的关系时，责任在控制者身上。所以，作为控制者，你需要能够管理你的数据中介，而数据控制者管理中介的一种方式，就是使用这个建议的数据中介管理生命周期（data intermediary management lifecycle）。这是 PDPC 推荐的一种体系，作为数据控制者妥善管理其数据中介的方法。它是一个分四个阶段的过程，我会逐一讲解。同样，考试不需要复习这部分。

  这个生命周期是怎么运作的呢？生命周期的第一个阶段是治理与风险评估（governance and risk assessment）。这是在你真正委任数据中介之前的阶段。控制者需要做的是了解这个中介关系的性质。控制者通常会做几件事。第一，弄清楚业务目标：我们想要外包的数据处理有什么要求？第二，弄清楚外包的规模，以及中介将会接触什么类型的个人资料。第三，识别潜在风险，因为这决定了你应该选谁作为你的数据中介。第四，看看你可以在与数据中介的合同中加入哪些要求。所以这是一种对数据中介关系性质的界定。

  一般来说，PDPC 建议在这个阶段，数据控制者的高级管理层应该参与，因为你需要一个能够就中介关系作出决定的人，而不只是一个没有执行权力的人来主导这个阶段。

  我认为，弄清楚外包的规模和你所涉及的个人资料类型尤其重要，因为这会告诉你需要对数据中介提出什么要求。比如，这里你的机构 XYZ 经营托儿中心，它想为它的个人资料聘请一个数据中介。所以 XYZ 的管理层会看相关的个人资料。在这个案例中，XYZ 需要一个能够处理 800 名儿童资料的中介，这是一个相当可观的数量，而且相关的个人资料包括家庭详情、病史以及父母的信息，这些都属于比较敏感的。知道这些之后，XYZ 就可以妥善评估它需要什么样的数据中介：我能冒险选一个规模较小、比较便宜的中介，还是需要选更高档次的？这是控制者在决定选择哪个数据中介时会考虑的事情之一。
- [20:33:00–20:36:04] **Choosing the Intermediary, and Stage Two: Contracts**

  Having gone through this process of thinking, you will of course need to make sure that you choose the correct data intermediary, someone who is able to meet your requirements. To determine whether the data intermediary in question meets your requirements, there are a few indicators you can look at. First, you can request that the data intermediary give you their data protection policy. Generally, it should provide you with their data protection framework and tell you how they train their staff. Two, you want to look at the security arrangements the intermediary is able to implement; they will tell you these things if they have arrangements in place. Number three, and this is something you may or may not want to do, is to see whether the data intermediary's practices are subject to some sort of external validation: any certificates that indicate that someone else, some auditor, has looked at their policies and decided that they meet a certain standard.

  Logically, the second stage of this lifecycle is to look at the data intermediary's policies and practices. Once you have chosen the data intermediary, you have to make sure that you subject the data intermediary to certain policies and practices, and you can do this using contracts, or you can do it using standard operating procedures.

  The main way by which a data controller controls the data intermediary is through the contract. Generally, inside the service contract, there will be provisions telling the data intermediary what it is required to do as far as data protection is concerned. The contract should at least clearly define, number one, the scope of the outsourced data processing: what exactly are you asking this intermediary to do? And number two, what data protection requirements you are imposing. So, for example, you have organisation ABC, which appoints DEF as a cloud service provider, and DEF has data centres in Singapore and Hong Kong. ABC would then include a clause in their contract under which DEF promises to protect the personal data wherever it goes, to the same extent as the personal data would be protected in Singapore.

  经过这个思考过程之后，你当然需要确保选对数据中介，选一个能够满足你要求的中介。要判断相关的数据中介是否满足你的要求，有几个指标可以参考。第一，你可以要求数据中介提供他们的数据保护政策。一般来说，这份政策应该向你说明他们的数据保护框架，并告诉你他们如何培训员工。第二，你要看中介能够实施哪些安全安排；如果他们有相关安排，他们会告诉你。第三，这是你可做可不做的，就是看看数据中介的做法是否经过某种外部验证：有没有任何证书表明有其他人、某个审计师审查过他们的政策，并认定他们符合某种标准。

  按逻辑，这个生命周期的第二个阶段是看数据中介的政策与实践（policies and practices）。一旦你选定了数据中介，你就必须确保数据中介受到某些政策和做法的约束，你可以通过合同来做到，也可以通过标准作业程序（standard operating procedures）来做到。

  数据控制者控制数据中介的主要方式是通过合同。一般来说，在服务合同里，会有条款告诉数据中介在数据保护方面需要做什么。合同至少应该清楚界定：第一，外包数据处理的范围，也就是你到底要这个中介做什么？第二，你所施加的数据保护要求是什么。比如，机构 ABC 委任 DEF 作为云服务提供商，而 DEF 在新加坡和香港都有数据中心。ABC 就会在合同里加入一个条款，DEF 据此承诺，无论个人资料去到哪里，都会以与在新加坡同等的程度保护这些个人资料。
- [20:36:18–20:39:17] **Stage Two Continued: Standard Operating Procedures and Reporting**

  Apart from contracts, another method the data controller can rely on is standard operating procedures. This would include providing for certain operational procedures. For example, let's say ABC, which is a financial institution, engages XYZ to print and send financial reports to its customers. ABC wants to provide these reports personalised to each customer. ABC has a contract with XYZ telling them to implement the necessary data protection measures. But ABC then decides that this may not be enough, so it might go a bit deeper. What ABC might do is require XYZ to have a specific operational procedure governing how they create and how they deliver the reports. For example, ABC might require someone from XYZ to test any delivery programme to make sure that reports are sent to the correct person. It might require XYZ to have some sort of process to make sure that the personal data they are receiving is accurate. It might ask XYZ to tell it exactly how XYZ is going to transfer the data. This would be your standard operating procedure.

  Standard operating procedures can also include things like reporting. So you, as the data controller, might require the data intermediary to submit reports on a regular basis to update the data controller on what it has done, or you can request ad hoc incident reports, meaning the data intermediary must report whenever something has gone wrong. In this example here, you can see that ABC has an IT vendor, DEF. Here, the app accidentally discloses a customer's personal data. In this case, DEF fixed the error but didn't notify ABC, and ABC only became aware of the incident after customers contacted it. Ideally, what ABC should do is have some sort of arrangement with DEF saying that in the event of any incident, you should report to us promptly.

  So this is the second stage of the lifecycle, which is to make sure that you have policies and practices in place to manage the data intermediary.

  除了合同之外，数据控制者可以依靠的另一种方法是标准作业程序。这包括规定某些操作程序。比如，假设 ABC 是一家金融机构，它聘请 XYZ 打印并寄送财务报告给它的客户。ABC 想为每位客户提供个性化的报告。ABC 和 XYZ 签了合同，要求他们实施必要的数据保护措施。但 ABC 后来认为这可能还不够，所以它可能会更深入一些。ABC 可能会要求 XYZ 制定一套具体的操作程序，规范他们如何制作和寄送报告。比如，ABC 可能会要求 XYZ 的人测试任何寄送程序，确保报告寄给了正确的人。它可能会要求 XYZ 建立某种流程，确保他们收到的个人资料是准确的。它可能会要求 XYZ 说明他们具体将如何传输资料。这就是你的标准作业程序。

  标准作业程序还可以包括报告之类的内容。所以你作为数据控制者，可能会要求数据中介定期提交报告，向数据控制者汇报它做了什么；或者你可以要求临时事故报告，也就是每当出了问题时，数据中介都必须报告。在这里的例子中，你可以看到 ABC 有一个 IT 供应商 DEF。在这里，应用程序意外披露了一位客户的个人资料。在这个案例中，DEF 修复了错误，但没有通知 ABC，ABC 是在客户联系它之后才知道这起事故的。理想的做法是，ABC 应该和 DEF 有某种安排，规定一旦发生任何事故，你都应该及时向我们报告。

  这就是生命周期的第二个阶段，也就是确保你有适当的政策和做法来管理数据中介。
- [20:39:29–20:41:50] **Stages Three and Four: Service Management and Exit Management**

  The next stage, the third one, is service management. Basically, after you have the policies and practices, you need to make sure that the intermediary actually follows them, so that's what you do at this stage. There's a range of things the controller could do: for example, conduct onboarding training, hold management meetings, instruct the data intermediary to conduct proactive monitoring, conduct audits, or conduct simulations.

  You can't always do these things, because this really depends on who your data intermediary is. If your intermediary is Microsoft, you can basically forget about doing any of these things, and you wouldn't need to, because they are fairly well established and will have sufficient protections in place. But if you're contracting with a smaller local intermediary that you don't quite trust to have their house in order, then these are some things you might need to do to make sure they comply with the policies. I think these points are fairly easy to understand, so I'll just run to the last step, which is exit management.

  Exit management is the final stage, and this refers to ending the data intermediary relationship when you no longer want the outsourcing arrangement. During this stage, you will do certain things: make sure the data intermediary stops keeping the personal data; make sure the data intermediary records or documents all the work it has done; and if you need to migrate data back to yourself or to some other intermediary, make sure it's done securely.

  So that was the so-called data intermediary management lifecycle, which is not tested but could be useful if you happen to be sitting on the controller's side. For even more details, you can look at the guidelines, which I've put up in the references.

  下一个阶段，也就是第三个阶段，是服务管理（service management）。基本上，在你有了政策和做法之后，你需要确保中介真的遵守它们，这就是你在这个阶段要做的事。控制者可以做一系列事情：比如进行入职培训、举行管理会议、指示数据中介进行主动监控、进行审计，或者进行模拟演练。

  你不一定总能做这些事，因为这真的取决于你的数据中介是谁。如果你的中介是 Microsoft，你基本上可以不用考虑做任何这些事，而且你也不需要，因为他们相当成熟，会有足够的保护措施。但如果你是和一家规模较小的本地中介签约，而你不太相信他们把一切都管理得井井有条，那么这些就是你可能需要做的事，以确保他们遵守政策。我认为这几点相当容易理解，所以我直接讲最后一步，也就是退出管理（exit management）。

  退出管理是最后一个阶段，指的是当你不再需要这个外包安排时，结束与数据中介的关系。在这个阶段，你会做一些事情：确保数据中介不再保留个人资料；确保数据中介记录或存档它所做的所有工作；如果你需要把资料迁移回自己这里或迁移到其他中介，要确保迁移是安全进行的。

  以上就是所谓的数据中介管理生命周期，这部分不考，但如果你恰好站在控制者一方，可能会有用。如果想了解更多细节，可以看我放在参考资料里的指南。
- [20:42:04–20:43:29] **Data Intermediaries Elsewhere, and the Network Service Provider Exception**

  One final point as far as data intermediaries are concerned is that this concept of a data intermediary also exists in other jurisdictions. In the EU, you have the so-called processor, who is the person who processes personal data on behalf of the controller, so very similar to what we have in Singapore. In China, you have the concept of the 受托人, or entrusted party: the person to whom personal data has been entrusted. In India, you also have the similar concept of a data processor. So this idea of a processor or intermediary does appear in other places as well.

  The last exception is really not important, but I include it just for completeness. The basic idea behind this exception is that if you are an ISP, like Singtel, M1, a telco, you create the infrastructure, and personal data passes through it from one person to another. You are not under the PDPA for that transmission, because you're just serving as a conduit. That's the network service provider exception, which you don't really need to know.

  关于数据中介，最后一点是，数据中介这个概念在其他法域也存在。在欧盟，有所谓的处理者（processor），也就是代表控制者处理个人资料的人，所以和我们在新加坡的概念非常相似。在中国，有受托人（entrusted party）的概念，也就是被委托处理个人资料的人。在印度，也有类似的数据处理者（data processor）概念。所以处理者或中介这个概念在其他地方也确实存在。

  最后一个例外其实并不重要，我只是为了完整起见才把它放进来。这个例外背后的基本理念是，如果你是互联网服务提供商（ISP），比如 Singtel、M1 这类电信公司，你建设了基础设施，个人资料经由它从一个人传到另一个人。就这种传输而言，你不受 PDPA 管辖，因为你只是充当一个通道。这就是网络服务提供商例外（network service provider exception），你们其实不太需要了解。
- [20:43:39–20:46:49] **Subordination of the PDPA to Other Laws**

  So that's all for this part about organisation. Just a couple more slides, because I also want to address the concept of subordination.

  What is subordination? Subordination refers to the nature of the PDPA, which is subordinate to other laws. How do these rules operate? Number one, the data protection provisions do not affect any authority, right, privilege, duty, obligation or limitation that is imposed by other law. Basically, if there's some other rule of law that creates an obligation or creates a right, that overrides the PDPA. For example, if we look at the hotel licensing regulations, all licensed hoteliers must collect the full name, nationality and ID of every guest. So here, even though the PDPA says you must get consent, that is overridden by the regulations.

  That being said, you cannot rely on a contractual obligation as an excuse for breaching the PDPA. Contractual obligations don't override the PDPA, so you cannot create a contract and say, "Oh, there's this contract now, I have to comply with it, so I don't have to obey the PDPA." That's not allowed. Other rules of law do override the PDPA, but contracts don't.

  The second point is that whenever the provisions of a different law, let's say the Banking Act, are inconsistent with the PDPA, they will override the PDPA. For example, the Banking Act provides that a bank can disclose customer information for certain purposes. So to the extent that the bank can rely on section 47 of the Banking Act, the PDPA does not apply. So this is how the PDPA becomes subordinated to other laws.

  As far as AI is concerned, there isn't yet any rule of law that applies specifically to AI and overrides the PDPA. But it is possible that in future we may see some regulations, for example regulations requiring data sharing, that could override portions of the PDPA. But for now, none of those exist.

  So this part is very straightforward. If you want just one sentence: most laws will override the PDPA.

  关于“机构”这一部分就讲到这里。还有几张投影片，因为我还想讲一下从属性（subordination）这个概念。

  什么是从属性？从属性指的是 PDPA 的性质，也就是它从属于其他法律。这些规则是怎么运作的？第一，数据保护条款不影响其他法律所赋予的任何权力、权利、特权，或施加的义务、责任或限制。基本上，如果有其他法律规则创设了一项义务或一项权利，它就会凌驾于 PDPA 之上。比如，看看酒店执照规例（hotel licensing regulations），所有持牌酒店经营者都必须收集每位住客的全名、国籍和身份证件号码。所以在这里，即使 PDPA 说你必须取得同意，这一点也被这些规例所凌驾。

  话虽如此，你不能以合同义务作为违反 PDPA 的借口。合同义务不能凌驾于 PDPA 之上，所以你不能订立一份合同，然后说：“哦，现在有这份合同，我必须履行它，所以我不用遵守 PDPA。”这是不允许的。其他法律规则确实可以凌驾于 PDPA 之上，但合同不行。

  第二点是，每当另一部法律，比如《银行法》（Banking Act），其条文与 PDPA 不一致时，它就会凌驾于 PDPA 之上。比如，《银行法》规定银行可以为某些目的披露客户信息。所以，只要银行可以依赖《银行法》第 47 条，PDPA 就不适用。这就是 PDPA 如何从属于其他法律。

  就 AI 而言，目前还没有任何专门适用于 AI、并凌驾于 PDPA 之上的法律规则。但将来我们可能会看到一些规例，比如要求数据共享的规例，可能会凌驾于 PDPA 的部分条文之上。但目前，这类规例都还不存在。

  所以这部分非常直接。如果你只想要一句话：大多数法律都会凌驾于 PDPA 之上。

# Seminar 3
## Week 3 Readings

## Week 3 Summary
- **Structure of the Consent Obligation 同意义务的结构**
    
    - **Core rule:** Organisations must have consent before collecting, using or disclosing personal data. There are three routes:
        - **Actual consent:** the organisation asks the individual and gets their consent. This is the standard route.
        - **Deemed consent:** the law lets the organisation assume consent even though none was actually given.
        - **Exceptions:** no consent is needed at all, for example in emergencies where there is an overriding necessity.
    - **Withdrawal:** Actual and deemed consent can always be withdrawn. When an organisation relies on an exception, there is nothing to withdraw.
    - **Other jurisdictions:** The EU treats consent as one of six legal bases for processing. The structure differs from Singapore's, but in practice it works the same way: you get consent unless you rely on something else.
    - **Cross-border activity:** The rules that apply depend on where the activity happens. A Singapore company collecting data in the UK follows UK rules.
        - **Purchased data:** the seller must comply with the rules where it collected the data (e.g. Spain), and the buyer complies with Singapore's rules when it receives the data.
        - **Online publication:** this is tricky because it is unclear whether the disclosure happens in Singapore or in every country where the page is read. Multinationals usually rely on a standard consent box that works in most countries, though the lecturer said this is an oversimplification.
    - **核心规则：** 组织在收集、使用或披露个人数据之前必须取得同意。共有三种途径：
        - **实际同意（actual consent）：** 组织询问个人并取得其同意，这是标准途径。
        - **视为同意（deemed consent）：** 即使个人实际上没有给出同意，法律也允许组织假定已经同意。
        - **例外（exceptions）：** 完全不需要同意，例如存在压倒性必要性的紧急情况。
    - **撤回：** 实际同意和视为同意都可以随时撤回。组织依赖例外时，不存在可撤回的东西。
    - **其他司法管辖区：** 欧盟把同意作为六种处理依据之一。结构与新加坡不同，但实际运作相同：除非依赖其他依据，否则就要取得同意。
    - **跨境活动：** 适用哪套规则取决于活动发生在哪里。新加坡公司在英国收集数据，就要遵守英国的规则。
        - **购买的数据：** 卖方在收集地（如西班牙）必须守法，买方在新加坡接收数据时遵守新加坡的规则。
        - **网上发布：** 情况比较棘手，因为不清楚披露是发生在新加坡，还是发生在每个能读到网页的国家。跨国组织通常依靠一个在大多数国家都适用的标准同意框，不过讲师说这是一种简化。
- **Valid Actual Consent and Unreasonable Tying 有效实际同意与不合理捆绑**
    
    - **Two requirements:** First, notify the individual of the purposes; this is essentially the Notification Obligation. Second, the individual must consent to those specific purposes. The regime is purpose-based.
    - **Unreasonable tying (first way to invalidate consent):** An organisation makes a product or service conditional on consent that goes beyond what is reasonably necessary to provide it. The vice is force: a "yes" given under compulsion is not meaningful.
    - **Spa example (Sarah):** The spa refuses service unless Sarah accepts every term, including the sale of her data to third parties. Selling her data is not necessary for spa services, so the consent is invalid even if she signs. The fix is to separate necessary purposes from optional ones.
    - **Cookie banners:** Requiring "essential cookies" while leaving the other checkboxes optional is fine.
    - **Facebook debate:** In Europe, Facebook argued that consent to targeted advertising is necessary because ads fund the free service. The lecturer was unsure whether this would work in Singapore, called it controversial, and suspected the PDPC might accept it if pressed.
    - **Permissible compulsion:**
        - **Reasonably required data:** e.g. a telco plan needs the customer's name, address and service data.
        - **Legal mandates:** e.g. passport checks for phone numbers. This can be framed as necessary, but more straightforwardly the other law overrides the PDPA on that point.
        - **Incentives (quid pro quo):** discounts, offers or lucky draws in exchange for consent. The organisation is effectively buying the consent.
    - **Exhibition example:** Making entry conditional on sharing your data with exhibitors is probably unreasonable, unless there is a real reason the sharing is necessary.
    - **Discount vs penalty:** A 20% discount for consenting is an acceptable incentive. A 30% surcharge for refusing looks like a penalty. The line is unclear: the PDPC would ask whether it is a real discount, likely by looking at the history of the organisation's pricing.
    - **"Necessary information" checkboxes:** Singapore does not strictly require organisations to declare the exact personal data they collect, unlike some other jurisdictions. Websites usually show the details if you look.
    - **两项要求：** 第一，告知个人目的，这本质上就是通知义务；第二，个人必须同意这些具体目的。这是一个以目的为基础的制度。
    - **不合理捆绑（使同意无效的第一种方式）：** 组织把提供产品或服务与超出合理必要范围的同意挂钩。问题在于强迫：在强迫下说的"是"没有意义。
    - **水疗中心例子（Sarah）：** 水疗中心要求 Sarah 接受全部条款（包括把她的数据卖给第三方）才提供服务。出售数据并非提供水疗服务所必需，所以即使她签了字，同意也无效。正确做法是把必要目的和可选目的分开。
    - **Cookie 横幅：** 只强制要求"必要 cookies"，其他勾选框保持可选，这是可以的。
    - **Facebook 争议：** Facebook 在欧洲主张，定向广告的同意是必要的，因为广告为免费服务提供资金。讲师不确定这在新加坡是否行得通，认为有争议，并猜测 PDPC 若被逼表态可能会接受。
    - **可以强制要求同意的情形：**
        - **合理必需的数据：** 例如电信套餐需要客户的姓名、地址和服务数据。
        - **法律强制要求：** 例如办电话号码时核查护照。可以说成是必要的，但更直接的理由是另一部法律在这一点上凌驾于 PDPA 之上。
        - **激励（对价交换）：** 用折扣、优惠或幸运抽奖换取同意。组织实际上是在购买这个同意。
    - **展览会例子：** 把入场与向参展商分享数据挂钩，很可能不合理，除非确实有必要分享。
    - **折扣与惩罚：** 同意就打八折，是可以接受的激励；拒绝就加价 30%，看起来像惩罚。界线并不清楚：PDPC 会判断这是否真是折扣，很可能会查看组织的定价历史。
    - **"必要信息"勾选框：** 与一些其他司法管辖区不同，新加坡并不严格要求组织声明具体收集哪些个人数据。网站通常会在某处列明，只要你去查。
- **Deception 欺骗**
    
    - **Second way to invalidate consent:** Obtaining consent through false or misleading information, or through deceptive practices.
    - **Deceptive practices:**
        - **Outright lies.**
        - **Weasel words:** purposes stated in vague or inaccurate terms.
        - **Illegible fonts:** purposes printed so small they cannot be read, even if technically accurate.
        - **Obscure placement:** purposes put in a hard-to-find location.
    - **使同意无效的第二种方式：** 用虚假或误导性信息，或用欺骗性做法取得同意。
    - **欺骗性做法：**
        - **直接撒谎。**
        - **含糊措辞：** 用模糊或不准确的说法陈述目的。
        - **难以辨认的字体：** 目的印得小到无法阅读，即使内容在技术上准确。
        - **隐蔽位置：** 把目的放在难以找到的地方。
- **Consent from Minors and Representatives 未成年人与代表的同意**
    
    - **Spring College International (2018):** A private school posted on Facebook about students' admission to secondary schools, including a child's photo, full name, primary school and how long he had studied there. All the students featured were under 13. No consent was sought at all, and the PDPC found a breach.
    - **Test for minors:** Does the minor have "sufficient understanding of the nature and consequences of giving consent"? The lecturer framed this for anyone below 21.
    - **Rule of thumb:** A person aged 13 or above is typically able to consent. This cannot be assumed in every case; complex or potentially harmful purposes need a closer look.
    - **Representatives:** Parents or guardians can consent on a child's behalf. The organisation must do due diligence (proof of parenthood or guardianship). To be extra safe, it can ask both the child and the parent.
    - **Spring College International（2018）：** 一所私立学校在 Facebook 上发帖宣传学生考进中学，帖子包括一名孩子的照片、全名、就读小学和在该校学习的时长。被展示的学生都在 13 岁以下。学校完全没有征求同意，PDPC 认定违规。
    - **未成年人测试：** 该未成年人是否"对给出同意的性质和后果有足够理解"？讲师把这一标准用于 21 岁以下的人。
    - **经验法则：** 13 岁或以上通常能够给出同意。但不能在每个案例中都这样假定；目的复杂或可能造成伤害时，需要更仔细地评估。
    - **代表：** 父母或监护人可以代孩子同意。组织必须做尽职调查（证明父母或监护关系）。为了格外稳妥，可以同时询问孩子和家长。
- **Form of Consent: Written vs Verbal, Express vs Implied 同意的形式：书面与口头、明示与默示**
    
    - **No prescribed form:** The PDPA does not prescribe a form, but the form must be appropriate.
    - **Verbal consent:** This is valid, e.g. over the phone. It is good practice to confirm it later in writing. Reasons raised in class:
        - **Proof:** it shows that consent was given at all.
        - **Searchability:** written records are easier to find than recordings.
        - **Content:** it records what exactly was consented to.
        - **Date and time:** it records when consent was given.
        - **Memory:** people forget over two or three years.
    - **Recorded calls:** Banks rely on the consent given at account opening. For phone-only consent, the company must be able to prove that every recording starts with the consent statement and that the caller stayed on the call. The insurance cooling-off period is statutory and not a data protection rule.
    - **German European School Singapore (2019):** The school did random drug testing and threatened expulsion if a student refused the hair sample or tested positive.
        - **Outcome:** no breach. Bye-law 5.8 mandated drug testing, the parents had access to the bye-laws, and they had enrolled the child for about 10 years. That amounted to implied consent. The tying argument was also rejected as not unreasonable.
    - **Risks of implied consent:**
        - **Understanding:** the individual must actually know what they are getting into, and people may have forgotten rules they read long ago.
        - **Proof:** there is no signature or tick box, so consent must be proved some other way.
    - **CCTV signs at condos:** Walking in after seeing a sign is implied consent, but only if the sign is impossible to miss. A hidden sign is not enough.
    - **没有规定的形式：** PDPA 没有规定同意的形式，但形式必须恰当。
    - **口头同意：** 有效，例如通过电话给出。良好做法是事后以书面确认。课堂上提出的理由：
        - **证明：** 证明确实给出了同意。
        - **可检索：** 书面记录比录音更容易查找。
        - **内容：** 记录具体同意了什么。
        - **日期和时间：** 记录何时给出同意。
        - **记忆：** 两三年后人们会忘记。
    - **通话录音：** 银行依赖开户时取得的同意。如果只有电话同意，公司必须能证明每段录音都以同意声明开头，并且来电者留在了通话中。保险冷静期是法定要求，不属于数据保护规则。
    - **German European School Singapore（2019）：** 学校进行随机药物检测，并威胁说学生若拒绝提供头发样本或检测呈阳性就会被开除。
        - **结果：** 不违规。章程第 5.8 条规定了药物检测，家长能查阅章程，并让孩子就读约 10 年，这构成默示同意。捆绑论点也被驳回，认定并非不合理。
    - **默示同意的风险：**
        - **理解：** 个人必须真正知道自己面对的是什么，而人们可能早已忘了很久以前读过的规则。
        - **证明：** 没有签名或勾选框，必须用其他方式证明同意。
    - **公寓闭路电视告示：** 看到告示后走进去属于默示同意，但前提是告示不可能被错过。藏起来的告示不算。
- **Positive vs Negative Consent 积极同意与消极同意**
    
    - **Definitions:**
        - **Positive consent:** the individual acts, e.g. signs a form or ticks a box.
        - **Negative consent:** the individual fails to act, e.g. does not untick a pre-ticked box or stays silent when asked whether they object.
    - **PDPC position:** Avoid pre-ticked boxes.
    - **Core problem: ambiguity.** Not unticking could mean agreement, but it could also mean misunderstanding, text too small to read, being in a rush, simply missing it, or not understanding the language.
    - **Practical position:** Negative consent can be valid, but often will not be. If used, it must be super obvious, for example very prominent, or a repeated confirmation statement next to the OK button.
    - **Lecturer's own legal argument:** The PDPA already prescribes a specific opt-out mechanism (deemed consent by notification), so a separate informal opt-out should not count. This is his argument, not settled law; the cases and guidelines still allow negative consent.
    - **Language:** Singapore law generally does not care whether you could read what you signed, but language barriers make negative consent even more dangerous.
    - **Comparison (non-examinable):** The EU GDPR and India's DPDPA require consent that is free, specific, informed and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action. That expressly rules out negative consent.
    - **定义：**
        - **积极同意：** 个人采取了行动，例如签表格或勾选方框。
        - **消极同意：** 个人没有采取行动，例如没有取消预先勾选的方框，或被问是否反对时保持沉默。
    - **PDPC 立场：** 应避免预先勾选的方框。
    - **核心问题：模糊。** 没有取消勾选可能表示同意，也可能是误解、字太小看不清、赶时间、单纯漏看，或看不懂语言。
    - **实务立场：** 消极同意可以有效，但往往无效。如果使用，必须极其显眼，例如非常醒目，或在"确定"按钮旁重复一遍确认声明。
    - **讲师本人的法律论点：** PDPA 已规定了一种特定的选择退出机制（通过通知视为同意），所以另外的非正式选择退出不应被承认。这是他个人的论点，不是定论；案例和指引目前仍允许消极同意。
    - **语言：** 新加坡法律一般不在意你能否读懂所签的东西，但语言障碍让消极同意更加危险。
    - **比较（不在考试范围内）：** 欧盟 GDPR 和印度 DPDPA 要求同意是自由、具体、知情、明确的，并通过明确的肯定性行动给出。这明确排除了消极同意。
- **In-Class Question: EFG University Proctoring 课堂题：EFG 大学监考**
    
    - **Scenario:** Students had consented to webcam recording reviewed by human proctors. EFG then added AI cheating detection by a third party (IHG) through a privacy-policy amendment that made consent mandatory.
    - **Problems identified:**
        - **No effective notice:** nobody reads an updated policy, so EFG had to bring the change to students' attention.
        - **Bigger scope:** moving from a human reviewer to third-party AI is a large change in purpose and scope, so consent should be re-obtained.
        - **Possible tying:** it is debatable whether AI proctoring is necessary for the education service, and the lecturer said it was unclear which side would win.
        - **No real purpose stated:** "we will analyse recordings using an algorithm" describes a method, not a purpose. A proper purpose would be "to check for potential cheating".
    - **"We may update this policy" clauses:** The lecturer doubted these are legitimate, because if they worked everyone would use them to amend at will.
    - **Fix:** New students get the updated consent form. Current students, who signed the old version, get a direct email with checkboxes for the specific new purpose.
    - **场景：** 学生已同意摄像头录像由人工监考员审看。EFG 随后通过修改隐私政策，加入了第三方（IHG）的 AI 作弊检测，并把同意定为强制。
    - **发现的问题：**
        - **没有有效通知：** 没有人会去读更新后的政策，所以 EFG 必须让学生注意到这一变化。
        - **范围扩大：** 从人工审看改为第三方 AI 分析，是目的和范围上的重大变化，应重新取得同意。
        - **可能构成捆绑：** AI 监考是否为教育服务所必需存在争议，讲师说不清楚哪一方会胜出。
        - **没有真正说明目的：** "我们会用算法分析录像"描述的是方法而不是目的。恰当的目的应是"检查潜在的作弊行为"。
    - **"我们可能更新本政策"条款：** 讲师怀疑这类条款是否正当，因为如果有效，人人都会用它随意修改。
    - **补救：** 新生改用更新后的同意表格。签过旧版本的在读学生，则直接发电邮，附上针对新的具体目的的勾选框。
- **Deemed Consent: Third Party, Conduct, Contractual Necessity 视为同意：第三方、行为、合同必要性**
    
    - **From a third party:** If the individual consented to A disclosing their data to B, they are deemed to consent to B collecting it.
        - **Due diligence:** B must check that A really had that consent, typically with a written undertaking and, if B wants more, evidence such as the signed form.
        - **Example:** Sarah refers her friend Jane to the spa. The spa asks Sarah whether Jane knew her data was being shared; that light check is adequate.
    - **By conduct:** The individual voluntarily provides data for a purpose, and it is reasonable that they would do so. The purpose must be so clear that a reasonable bystander would assume the individual would ordinarily consent.
        - **Examples:** handing over a credit card to pay $49.99 for a facial; going ahead with a clinic health check after being told what it collects; giving a name and number to a taxi hotline so you can be told when the taxi arrives.
        - **Limit:** taxi marketing is not covered, because it is not an obvious purpose.
    - **Actxa (2018):** A smart scale whose app sent both registration data and body data to the company's servers.
        - **Registration data:** deemed consent applies, because the purpose of registering for the app is obvious.
        - **Body data:** no deemed consent. Stepping on the scale was voluntary, but the organisation's purpose for collecting the data was not clear. Result: breach.
    - **By contractual necessity:** Data given to A for a transaction can be disclosed to B, and onward to C, D and so on, where reasonably necessary to perform the contract. Example: the spa's card payment passes through banks and payment processors.
        - **Overlap with data intermediaries:** a payment processor can also be a data intermediary, but not every intermediary is doing something necessary for a contract, and those that are not cannot rely on this route.
    - **来自第三方：** 如果个人同意 A 把其数据披露给 B，则视为同意 B 收集这些数据。
        - **尽职调查：** B 必须核实 A 确实取得了该同意，通常是取得书面承诺；如果 B 想进一步查，可以要求证据，例如签好的表格。
        - **例子：** Sarah 把朋友 Jane 推荐给水疗中心。水疗中心询问 Sarah，Jane 是否知道自己的数据被分享；这种轻度核查已经足够。
    - **通过行为：** 个人为某个目的自愿提供数据，而且这样做是合理的。目的必须清楚到合理旁观者会认为个人通常都会同意。
        - **例子：** 交出信用卡支付 49.99 元的面部护理费；在被告知收集什么之后继续做诊所体检；向出租车热线提供姓名和号码，以便车到时得到通知。
        - **界限：** 出租车公司的营销不在此列，因为那不是显而易见的目的。
    - **Actxa（2018）：** 一款智能体重秤，其应用程序把注册数据和身体数据都传到了公司服务器。
        - **注册数据：** 适用视为同意，因为注册应用程序的目的很明显。
        - **身体数据：** 不构成视为同意。站上秤是自愿的，但组织收集这些数据的目的并不清楚。结果：违规。
    - **基于合同必要性：** 为交易提供给 A 的数据，在履行合同合理必要的范围内，可以披露给 B，并继续传给 C、D 等。例如：水疗中心的刷卡付款要经过银行和支付处理商。
        - **与数据中介重叠：** 支付处理商也可以是数据中介，但并非每个中介都在做合同所必需的事，不是的就不能依赖这一途径。
- **Deemed Consent by Notification 通过通知视为同意**
    
    - **Mechanism:** The organisation notifies the individual of the intended collection, use or disclosure, and the individual does not opt out. It is a statutory opt-out regime with safeguards.
    - **Three conditions plus one bar:**
        - **Adverse effect assessment:** the organisation must assess whether the processing is likely to harm the individual.
        - **Adequate notification:** the organisation must take reasonable steps to notify.
        - **Reasonable opt-out period:** the individual must have enough time to opt out.
        - **No direct marketing:** this route cannot be used for direct marketing, because otherwise every marketer would use it.
    - **Assessment steps:**
        - **Step 1:** determine the purposes.
        - **Step 2:** determine how to notify.
        - **Step 3:** assess likely adverse effects, considering how sensitive the data is, whether the purpose is reasonable, the likely impact on the individual, and how to reduce the likelihood of harm.
        - **Step 4:** after the mitigation measures, decide whether any likely adverse effect remains. If yes, you cannot use this route; if no, proceed. A ready-made checklist is in Annex B of the Key Concepts guidelines.
    - **Notification content:** the intention to collect, use or disclose; the purpose; and a reasonable period and method to opt out (e.g. "you have 14 days").
    - **Notification method:** No method is prescribed; the notice just has to be effective. Consider:
        - **Usual mode of communication:** if you normally email, send it by email.
        - **Direct channels:** email, phone, SMS or WhatsApp, rather than a notice on a website.
        - **Number of people:** a million people may need broader channels; three people can just get a text.
        - **Example:** a health app notifies users inside the app, and also by email and social media to reach inactive users.
    - **Opt-out period:** No period is prescribed. It can be shorter when you interact often, communicate directly, and offer a convenient opt-out channel. Processing must wait until the period has expired.
    - **Cannot be used:**
        - **Exhibition sensors:** collection starts the moment a visitor walks in, so no real opt-out period is possible.
        - **Adversarial relationships:** e.g. fraud detection that may lead a bank to freeze an account is likely to have adverse effects, so the organisation needs another exception.
    - **Distinction:** Deemed consent is a legal fiction that lets you assume consent nobody gave. Implied consent is actual consent, given by action rather than words.
    - **机制：** 组织把拟进行的收集、使用或披露通知个人，个人没有选择退出。这是一种附有保障措施的法定选择退出制度。
    - **三个条件加一项禁止：**
        - **不利影响评估：** 组织必须评估处理是否可能伤害个人。
        - **充分通知：** 组织必须采取合理步骤进行通知。
        - **合理的选择退出期：** 个人必须有足够时间选择退出。
        - **不得用于直接营销：** 这一途径不能用于直接营销，否则每个营销者都会用它。
    - **评估步骤：**
        - **第一步：** 确定目的。
        - **第二步：** 确定如何通知。
        - **第三步：** 评估可能的不利影响，考虑数据是否敏感、目的是否合理、对个人的可能影响，以及如何降低伤害的可能性。
        - **第四步：** 采取缓解措施后，判断是否仍有可能的不利影响。有，则不能使用这一途径；没有，则可以继续。《关键概念指引》附件 B 有现成的评估清单。
    - **通知内容：** 收集、使用或披露的意图；目的；合理的选择退出期限和方式（例如"你有 14 天时间"）。
    - **通知方式：** 没有规定方式，只要求有效。需要考虑：
        - **惯常沟通方式：** 平常用电邮沟通，就用电邮发出。
        - **直接渠道：** 电邮、电话、短信或 WhatsApp，而不是在网站上贴通知。
        - **人数：** 通知一百万人可能需要更广的渠道；三个人发短信即可。
        - **例子：** 健康应用程序在应用内通知用户，同时通过电邮和社交媒体通知不活跃用户。
    - **选择退出期：** 没有规定期限。互动频繁、直接沟通且退出渠道方便时，期限可以较短。必须等期限届满后才能开始处理。
    - **不能使用的情形：**
        - **展览会传感器：** 访客一走进场地收集就开始了，不可能有真正的选择退出期。
        - **对立关系：** 例如可能导致银行冻结账户的欺诈检测，很可能产生不利影响，组织需要依赖其他例外。
    - **区分：** 视为同意是一种法律拟制，让你假定一个实际上没人给出的同意。默示同意则是实际同意，只是通过行动而非言语给出。
- **Withdrawal of Consent 撤回同意**
    
    - **Rule:** Actual or deemed consent can be withdrawn at any time; consent is never permanent.
    - **Withdrawal policy:** It should be clear and accessible, and should state:
        - **How:** the form and manner of giving notice.
        - **Where:** the person or mechanism that receives the notice.
        - **Which purposes:** which purposes are necessary for the service and which are optional, so individuals can withdraw only the optional ones.
        - **No obstruction:** the policy must not make withdrawal unnecessarily complicated.
    - **Process:** The individual gives notice. The rule of thumb is that 10 business days is a reasonable time to act on it; if more time is needed, tell the individual. The organisation must then:
        - **Explain consequences:** tell the individual the likely consequences of withdrawing.
        - **Stop processing:** stop collecting, using and disclosing the data within a reasonable time.
        - **Instruct intermediaries:** make its data intermediaries and agents stop too.
    - **No deletion right:** There is no right in Singapore to force deletion. Data must eventually be deleted under a separate retention rule, and the organisation can keep data it needs for legal or business purposes.
    - **Y Electronics example (Andy):** Andy withdraws consent to marketing. Y Electronics must stop its own marketing, stop disclosing his data, and instruct its marketing agent. It need not inform the independent third parties it already disclosed to, because it is not responsible for them unless they are its intermediaries or agents.
    - **No prohibiting withdrawal, but legal consequences remain:** A contract cannot forbid withdrawal. Withdrawal can still trigger legal consequences. Example: withdrawing consent from a telco on a two-year plan means the service can't continue, so the contract terminates early and early termination charges may apply.
    - **Fees:**
        - **Not allowed:** a direct fee for withdrawing, which amounts to prohibiting it, or a "processing cost" for handling the withdrawal.
        - **Allowed:** a genuine fee that follows as a consequence, such as early termination. The regulator would likely look at whether the fee is real or meant to deter withdrawal, and a fee far above the actual cost is less likely to be seen as genuine.
    - **Degrading service:** This is fine where the data is genuinely linked to the quality of the service. Degrading service purely to punish the individual is an attempt to prohibit withdrawal.
    - **Incentives:** Continuing to reward people who keep consenting is fine. Charging people who withdraw is risky. An organisation that bought consent has to accept that some people may take the reward and then withdraw.
    - **When to state consequences:** Consequences need not be stated upfront in the contract, but must be stated when the withdrawal notice is received.
    - **规则：** 实际同意或视为同意可以随时撤回；同意从来不是永久的。
    - **撤回政策：** 应清晰且易于获取，并说明：
        - **方式：** 发出撤回通知的形式和方式。
        - **途径：** 接收通知的人员或机制。
        - **目的区分：** 哪些目的是服务所必需的，哪些是可选的，让个人可以只撤回可选目的。
        - **不得阻碍：** 政策不得让撤回变得不必要地复杂。
    - **流程：** 个人发出通知。经验法则是 10 个工作日内处理是合理的；如需更长时间，应告知个人。组织随后必须：
        - **说明后果：** 告诉个人撤回可能带来的后果。
        - **停止处理：** 在合理时间内停止收集、使用和披露数据。
        - **指示中介：** 让其数据中介和代理也停止处理。
    - **没有删除权：** 在新加坡，个人无权强制删除数据。数据最终须依另一条保留规则删除，组织也可以保留法律或业务上需要的数据。
    - **Y Electronics 例子（Andy）：** Andy 撤回对营销的同意。Y Electronics 必须停止自己的营销、停止披露他的数据，并指示其营销代理照做。它不需要通知已经收到数据的独立第三方，因为除非它们是其中介或代理，否则它不对它们负责。
    - **不得禁止撤回，但法律后果仍然存在：** 合同不能禁止撤回，但撤回仍可引发法律后果。例子：在两年期电信套餐中撤回同意，服务无法继续，合同提前终止，可能产生提前终止费用。
    - **费用：**
        - **不允许：** 直接为撤回收费（这等于禁止撤回），或以"处理成本"为名为处理撤回收费。
        - **允许：** 作为后果而产生的真实费用，例如提前终止费。监管机构很可能会审视费用是否真实，还是意在阻止撤回；远超实际成本的费用不太可能被视为真实。
    - **降低服务质量：** 如果数据确实与服务质量相关，降低是可以的。纯粹为惩罚个人而降低服务，等于试图禁止撤回。
    - **激励：** 持续奖励继续同意的人是可以的；向撤回的人收费则有风险。买下同意的组织必须接受，有些人可能拿了好处之后就撤回。
    - **何时说明后果：** 不必在合同中预先写明后果，但收到撤回通知时必须说明。
- **Real-Life Question: LinkedIn AI Training 真实题目：LinkedIn AI 训练**
    
    - **Scenario:** LinkedIn updated its policy to use user content to train generative AI, with the setting on by default. Opting out does not affect training that has already happened. Many users said they received no notification, the PDPC sought proof of consent, and training may also be done by another provider.
    - **LinkedIn's best case:** "We disclosed it in the policy update and gave users an opt-out."
    - **Problems identified:**
        - **Negative consent:** it relies on users not opting out.
        - **Ineffective opt-out:** opting out does not undo past training.
        - **Hidden notice:** the change was buried in the data collection policy, an indirect channel.
        - **Unread updates:** people do not reread amended policies.
        - **Inactive users:** many never see the setting at all.
        - **Unexpected purposes:** generative-AI training is a new purpose for a networking platform, and so is sharing data with an outside AI provider. Unexpected purposes need prominent notice.
    - **Possible counter-argument:** Training improves the existing service, so it might fit within purposes users already consented to. Whether that works depends on what users agreed to when they signed up.
    - **Outcome:** Nothing much seems to have come of it. LinkedIn probably backpedalled a little, and the PDPC appeared to take a cautious "ask questions first" approach. There was still a negative public reaction.
    - **Doing it properly:**
        - **Actual consent:** explicit agreement, possibly with an incentive such as access to a new AI feature. It is valid but burdensome to track across millions of users.
        - **Deemed consent by notification:** adverse effect assessment, direct notice and an opt-out period. It is valid but carries reputational risk.
        - **Either way:** consent cannot be made a condition of keeping the service. Choosing between the two is a business decision.
    - **Organ donation (HOTA) aside:** Singapore's default opt-in for organ donation, with lower priority for those who opt out, reflects different public policy considerations. The government makes a trade-off with personal autonomy.
    - **场景：** LinkedIn 更新政策，用用户内容训练生成式 AI，设置默认开启。选择退出不影响已经完成的训练。许多用户说没收到通知，PDPC 要求提供同意的证明，训练也可能由另一家提供商进行。
    - **LinkedIn 最好的论点：** "我们在政策更新中披露了，并给了用户选择退出的权利。"
    - **发现的问题：**
        - **消极同意：** 依赖用户不选择退出。
        - **无效的退出：** 选择退出不能撤销过去的训练。
        - **隐藏的通知：** 变更被埋在数据收集政策里，是一种间接渠道。
        - **没人重读：** 人们不会重读修改后的政策。
        - **不活跃用户：** 很多人根本看不到这个设置。
        - **意料之外的目的：** 对一个社交人脉平台来说，生成式 AI 训练是新的目的，与外部 AI 提供商分享数据也是。意料之外的目的需要醒目的通知。
    - **可能的反驳：** 训练是在改进现有服务，因此可能属于用户已同意的目的。这能否成立，取决于用户注册时同意了什么。
    - **结果：** 似乎没有什么下文。LinkedIn 可能稍有退让，PDPC 看来采取了谨慎的"先提问"做法。但公众还是有负面反应。
    - **正确做法：**
        - **实际同意：** 明确的协议，可以配合激励（例如使用新 AI 功能）。这有效，但在数百万用户中追踪很麻烦。
        - **通过通知视为同意：** 不利影响评估、直接通知和选择退出期。这有效，但有声誉风险。
        - **无论哪种：** 都不能把同意作为继续享受服务的条件。两者之间的选择是商业决定。
    - **器官捐献（HOTA）题外话：** 新加坡的器官捐献默认加入，选择退出者优先次序较低，这反映了不同的公共政策考量。政府在个人自主方面做出了取舍。
- **Notification Obligation (Self-Study) 通知义务（自学）**
    
    - **Scope note:** This was not covered in class because of time. The lecturer said the slides are comprehensive, the topic is not complicated, and it is mostly best practice on how to present the notification. Questions can be brought to him directly.
    - **范围说明：** 因时间关系课堂上没有讲。讲师说幻灯片已相当全面，这个主题并不复杂，大部分内容是关于如何呈现通知的最佳做法。有问题可以直接找他。
## Week 3 Learning Tips
Start by holding the whole map in your head: actual consent, deemed consent, exceptions, and withdrawal across all of them. Almost every scenario this week becomes manageable once you ask, in order: which route is the organisation relying on, did it meet that route's specific test, and can the individual withdraw? The EFG and LinkedIn questions were both, at heart, cases of an organisation acting as if it had actual consent when its facts looked more like a defective attempt at deemed consent by notification. Practise naming the route before you analyse anything else.

先在脑中建立整体框架：实际同意、视为同意、例外，以及适用于它们的撤回。本周几乎每个场景，只要按顺序问几个问题就能理清：组织依赖的是哪种途径？是否满足该途径的具体测试？个人能否撤回？EFG 和 LinkedIn 两道题本质上都是组织表现得像是取得了实际同意，而事实看起来更像是一次有缺陷的"通过通知视为同意"。分析任何内容之前，先练习说出它依赖的是哪条途径。

Understand the "why" behind each validity rule, because the lecturer kept pushing on it. Unreasonable tying is invalid because forced consent is not a meaningful choice. That one idea explains why necessity, legal mandates and incentives make compulsion acceptable, and why the discount-versus-penalty and fee-for-withdrawal questions are hard: each asks whether pressure is a genuine trade or disguised coercion. Negative consent is problematic because inaction is ambiguous. If you can explain these two rationales, you can reason through new facts rather than matching them to memorised examples.

要理解每条有效性规则背后的"为什么"，因为讲师一直在追问这一点。不合理捆绑之所以无效，是因为被强迫的同意不是有意义的选择。这个理念解释了为什么必要性、法律强制和激励能让强制要求变得可以接受，也解释了为什么"折扣还是惩罚"和"撤回收费"的问题很难：它们都在问，压力究竟是真正的交换，还是变相的强迫。消极同意之所以有问题，是因为不作为是模糊的。能讲清楚这两个理由，你就能对新的事实进行推理，而不是去套背下来的例子。

Watch for three pitfalls this material invites. First, don't confuse implied consent (actual consent given by conduct, as in German European School and the condo CCTV sign) with deemed consent (a statutory fiction where no consent was given). Second, don't over-apply deemed consent by conduct: Actxa shows that a voluntary act, stepping on a scale, does not carry consent for a purpose that isn't obvious. Third, don't treat negative consent as automatically illegal or automatically fine. The lecturer's position is nuanced: technically possible, often invalid, safe only if made unmissable. His "separate statutory opt-out" argument is his own view, not settled law.

注意本周材料容易引发的三个误区。第一，不要把默示同意（通过行为给出的实际同意，如 German European School 案和公寓闭路电视告示）与视为同意（根本没有给出同意时的法定拟制）混为一谈。第二，不要过度扩大"通过行为视为同意"：Actxa 案表明，自愿的行为（站上秤）并不意味着对一个不明显的目的给出了同意。第三，不要把消极同意当成必然违法或必然合法。讲师的立场有分寸：技术上可行，往往无效，只有在让人不可能错过时才算稳妥。他关于"已有法定选择退出机制"的论点是他个人的观点，不是定论。

Build a one-line card for each case using "facts, failing, lesson". Spring College: Facebook success posts about children under 13, no consent sought at all, so minors need sufficient understanding (with 13 as a rule of thumb) or a verified parent's consent. German European School: drug testing under bye-law 5.8, no breach, because access to the rules plus years of enrolment equals implied consent. Actxa: scale data sent to servers, registration data deemed but body data not, because deemed consent by conduct needs an objectively obvious purpose. Then put Actxa next to the spa, clinic and taxi examples so you can see exactly where "obvious purpose" stops.

用"事实、问题、教训"为每个案例做一行卡片。Spring College：在 Facebook 上发布 13 岁以下孩子的成功帖，完全没有征求同意，所以未成年人需要有足够理解（以 13 岁为经验法则），或者取得经核实的家长同意。German European School：依章程第 5.8 条进行药物检测，不违规，因为能查阅规则加上多年就读等于默示同意。Actxa：秤的数据被传到服务器，注册数据可视为同意但身体数据不行，因为通过行为视为同意需要客观上显而易见的目的。然后把 Actxa 和水疗、诊所、出租车的例子放在一起，看清"明显目的"的边界到底在哪里。

Make deemed consent by notification a fixed checklist you can recite: adverse effect assessment (the four steps, ending in "no likely adverse effect remains"), adequate notice (intention, purpose, opt-out period and method, sent through direct channels), a reasonable opt-out period you wait out, and never for direct marketing. Then rehearse the two situations where it fails: the exhibition sensors, where no opt-out is possible, and fraud detection, where adverse effects are inherent. When a fact pattern involves a quiet policy update with a default-on setting, test it against this checklist. That is exactly how the LinkedIn analysis worked.

把"通过通知视为同意"变成一份能背出来的固定清单：不利影响评估（四个步骤，最后要得出"没有剩余的可能不利影响"），充分通知（意图、目的、选择退出期限和方式，并通过直接渠道发出），等过一个合理的选择退出期，以及永远不能用于直接营销。然后演练它失败的两种情况：展览会传感器（无法选择退出）和欺诈检测（本身就有不利影响）。当事实是悄悄更新政策、设置默认开启时，就用这份清单去检验，LinkedIn 的分析正是这样做的。

For withdrawal, separate three questions that students tend to merge. What must the organisation do on notice: explain consequences, stop within a reasonable time (about 10 business days), and instruct its intermediaries and agents. What need it not do: delete the data immediately, or chase independent third parties, as the Y Electronics example shows. What can it legitimately pass on: genuine contractual consequences such as early termination fees or a service that truly depends on the data, but never a fee or degraded service designed to deter withdrawal. Present the fee question as the lecturer did, as a test of substance over label, rather than as a yes or no.

关于撤回，要把学生容易混在一起的三个问题分开。收到通知后组织必须做什么：说明后果、在合理时间内（约 10 个工作日）停止处理、指示其中介和代理。组织不需要做什么：立即删除数据，或去追索独立的第三方，正如 Y Electronics 例子所示。组织可以正当转嫁什么：真实的合同后果，例如提前终止费，或确实依赖这些数据的服务，但绝不能是为了阻止撤回而设计的费用或降级服务。回答收费问题时，要像讲师那样把它当作"看实质而非标签"的检验，而不是简单回答是或否。

When answering scenario questions, follow the lecturer's pattern. State the organisation's best argument first, then the problems, then what it should have done instead, keeping his hedges where the law is open (the Facebook necessity argument, AI proctoring as tying, and discount versus penalty). For "do it properly" questions, compare actual consent and deemed consent by notification on validity and on practical trade-offs: administrative burden versus reputational risk. Finally, mind the scope: the EU GDPR and India DPDPA definitions are non-examinable comparisons, and the Notification Obligation is self-study, so read those slides yourself instead of skipping them.

回答场景题时，沿用讲师的模式。先陈述组织最好的论点，再指出问题，最后说明它本应怎么做；在法律尚未定论的地方保留讲师的保留语气（Facebook 的必要性论点、AI 监考是否构成捆绑、折扣与惩罚）。遇到"正确做法"类问题，要从有效性和实际取舍两方面比较实际同意与通过通知视为同意：行政负担对比声誉风险。最后注意范围：欧盟 GDPR 和印度 DPDPA 的定义只是作为比较，不在考试范围内；通知义务是自学内容，所以要自己读那些幻灯片，而不是跳过。
## Week 3 Lecture
- [18:35:54–18:39:45] **The Consent Obligation: Three Ways to Comply**

  We are now getting into the first of the data protection obligations. As I mentioned, data protection law in Singapore, and in most other jurisdictions, works by imposing a range of duties or obligations on organisations, controllers, or whatever you want to call them.

  Today we are going to look at two of the obligations that apply in Singapore: the Consent Obligation and the Notification Obligation. I'm splitting the Consent Obligation into two parts. I'll cover the first part in this lesson and the second part in the following lesson. The Consent Obligation is a very important component of the regime.

  There are three ways you can fulfil the Consent Obligation. The first, which is the standard way, is getting actual consent. This is where you actually go to the individual and request and obtain their consent. It's the most direct way. There are two alternatives. The first alternative is that in some circumstances you don't actually need to go and get consent from the individual, because you can take it that the individual has given their consent. This is called deemed consent. Finally, the data protection regime contains a large range of exceptions. These are situations where you do not need to get consent at all. In some circumstances, like emergencies, the regime doesn't require any consent because there's an overriding reason or necessity to use the personal data.

  One big note right from the start, about withdrawal. If you get actual consent or deemed consent, the individual always has the right to withdraw that consent. Whether you actually obtained consent or you assume the individual gave it, the individual can always withdraw it later. Of course, if you are relying on an exception, meaning you say you don't need consent at all, then there's nothing to withdraw.

  我们现在进入第一项数据保护义务。正如我之前提到的，新加坡以及大多数其他司法管辖区的数据保护法，其运作方式是对组织、控制者（controller），或者不管你怎么称呼它们，施加一系列职责或义务。

  今天我们会看新加坡适用的两项义务：同意义务（Consent Obligation）和通知义务（Notification Obligation）。我把同意义务拆成两部分，这节课讲第一部分，下节课讲第二部分。同意义务是整个制度中非常重要的组成部分。

  履行同意义务有三种方式。第一种，也是标准做法，是取得实际同意（actual consent），也就是你真的去找个人，请求并取得他的同意，这是最直接的方式。另外有两种替代方式。第一种替代方式是，在某些情况下你不需要真的去取得同意，因为你可以认定这个人已经给出了同意，这叫视为同意（deemed consent）。最后，数据保护制度中还有大量的例外情形（exceptions），在这些情况下你根本不需要取得同意。比如在紧急情况等场合，制度不要求任何同意，因为存在某种压倒性的理由或必要性需要使用该个人数据。

  一开始我要特别强调一点，关于撤回。如果你取得的是实际同意或视为同意，个人永远有权撤回该同意。无论是你真的取得了同意，还是你认定个人给了同意，个人都可以在之后撤回。当然，如果你依赖的是某个例外，也就是说你根本不需要同意，那就不存在可撤回的东西了。
- [18:39:45–18:44:48] **Q&A: Other Jurisdictions, Multinationals, Purchased Data, and Online Publication**

  That's the basic structure of the Consent Obligation. Any questions?

  A student asks whether this applies only in Singapore or everywhere.

  Yes, this is for Singapore. Around the world, consent is generally relevant, but it works a bit differently. For example, under the European regime, consent is regarded as one of the legal bases for processing personal data. They treat consent as one of six different bases for processing. The structure looks different, but functionally it is the same. When you want to process, use, or do something with personal data, one way to do it is to get consent from the individual, unless you rely on something else to go about that processing.

  Another student asks: if a global organisation collects data in Europe and also operates in Asia, does it need to follow all of these rules?

  If you happen to be a multinational organisation doing things in different countries, the rules you need to follow depend on where you are doing the thing. If you are collecting data in the UK, then you must follow the UK rules for that collection, even if your entity is based elsewhere. Generally, yes. Say your base is Singapore, you're ABC Private Limited incorporated in Singapore. If you happen to be doing something in China or Europe or any other country, you will generally need to follow their rules.

  The same student asks: what about purchased data?

  If you are purchasing data from a third party, we need to go a bit more deeply into the mechanics of how you're actually purchasing it. Just a hypothetical scenario: let's say the mechanics are that your seller collects the data in, say, Spain, and then transfers it from Spain to Singapore, and you receive it in Singapore. Here you need to make sure the seller complies with the data collection rules in Spain when they collect the data, and then you comply with Singapore's rules when you receive the collected data.

  If you are publishing something on the internet, you really have to be quite careful, because what you are doing there is disclosing an individual's data. The internet situation is a tricky one, because you need to ask yourself where you are actually making the disclosure. When you publish something online, are you disclosing the information in Singapore, or in all the different countries where it's received?

  The student describes their own practice: when they get consent, they just record the consent; when they purchase data from a vendor, they rely on that, as long as they make sure the relevant options are available.

  If you're a multinational organisation, you will generally rely on some form of consent. If you have a website available to everyone and you happen to be collecting data from all of them, there's usually a standard kind of consent box you can show to get consent in most countries. That would be the usual way a multinational handles this sort of thing. But I'm oversimplifying, because once you involve different countries, the puzzle gets more complicated.

  这就是同意义务的基本结构。有问题吗？

  一位学生问，这只适用于新加坡，还是到处都适用？

  是的，这是新加坡的规定。在世界范围内，同意一般都是相关的，但运作方式有些不同。比如欧洲的制度把同意视为处理个人数据的法律依据之一，他们把同意当作六种处理依据中的一种。结构看起来不同，但功能上是一样的：当你想处理、使用或对个人数据做任何事情时，其中一种方式就是取得个人的同意，除非你依赖其他依据来进行处理。

  另一位学生问：如果一个全球性组织在欧洲收集数据，同时也在亚洲运营，那它是否需要遵守所有这些规则？

  如果你是一家跨国组织，在不同国家开展活动，你需要遵守的规则取决于你在哪里做这件事。如果你在英国收集数据，那么就这次收集而言你必须遵守英国的规则，即使你的实体设在别处。一般来说，是的。假设你的总部在新加坡，你是一家在新加坡注册成立的 ABC Private Limited。如果你恰好在中国、欧洲或任何其他国家做事，你一般需要遵守当地的规则。

  同一位学生问：那购买的数据呢？

  如果你从第三方购买数据，我们就需要更深入地看具体机制，你到底是怎么购买的。举个假设的场景：比如你的卖家在西班牙收集数据，然后从西班牙传输到新加坡，你在新加坡接收。这时你需要确保卖家在收集数据时遵守西班牙的数据收集规则，然后你在接收这些数据时遵守新加坡的规则。

  如果你在互联网上发布东西，你真的要相当小心，因为你在做的是披露个人的数据。互联网的情况比较棘手，因为你需要问自己：你到底是在哪里进行披露？当你在网上发布东西时，你是在新加坡披露信息，还是在所有接收到它的国家披露？

  这位学生描述了他们自己的做法：取得同意时就把同意记录下来；从供应商购买数据时就依赖这一点，只要确保相关选项是可用的。

- [18:44:48–18:47:33] **Validity of Actual Consent and Unreasonable Tying**

  Let me now focus on the first way to comply with the Consent Obligation, which is actually getting consent. What do you need to do to get valid actual consent? Basically, two things. First, you need to make sure the individual knows your purposes for the collection, use, and disclosure of the data. You'll see later that this is essentially the Notification Obligation, which is the second obligation we're covering today. For your actual consent to be valid, you need to tell the individual, "Here is what I want to do with your personal data," and then the individual must give consent for those specific purposes. So it's a purpose-based regime.

  Actual consent is very straightforward to obtain, as long as you're clear about your purposes and the individual is okay with them. But there are specifically two ways of getting actual consent that would make it invalid. The first is if you engage in what I would call unreasonable tying. Meaning, you are an organisation providing some product or service, and you tell the individual, "Unless you consent, I will not provide you with this product or service." If you do this, and the consent is not reasonably necessary for you to provide the product or service, this is unreasonable.

  只要你清楚说明目的、个人也接受，实际同意是非常容易取得的。但具体有两种取得实际同意的方式会使其无效。第一种是我所说的不合理捆绑（unreasonable tying）。也就是说，你是一家提供某种产品或服务的组织，你告诉个人："除非你同意，否则我不向你提供这个产品或服务。"如果你这样做，而该同意对提供该产品或服务并非合理必要，这就是不合理的。

If you use weasel words to try to fool the individual, vague or inaccurate terms, that will still be deceptive. Even if you're not technically lying, if you state your purposes in illegible fonts, so small they cannot possibly be read, that's also deceptive. - [19:03:29–19:08:14] **Consent from Minors: Spring College International and Representatives**

  Another problem, especially difficult in online settings, is that if you try to obtain consent from a minor, a young person, the consent may also be invalid, because generally we understand that children may not have the capacity to give consent to things.

  The case that demonstrates this is the Spring College International case. The organisation here was a private educational institution. It maintained a Facebook page, which it used to market itself. The complainant was a parent of a student at the school. The complainant was looking at Facebook, came across the organisation's page, and saw a post with her son's picture proclaiming that this child they teach had gained admission to a particular secondary school. So they were promoting their success story. The post contained details about the son, such as his full name, his primary school, and how long he had been studying with the organisation. The complainant complained to the PDPC. The PDPC investigated and found that the organisation had done something wrong. All the students showcased were minors, young children below the age of 13. The PDPC found a breach.

  This case is one where no consent was given; there wasn't even an attempt to obtain consent. But the question is, even if they had tried, what would happen? Here the PDPC discussed how you actually obtain consent from minors. The general principle organisations must follow when obtaining consent from anyone below the age of 21, so a minor, is that you need to consider whether the person has sufficient understanding of the nature and consequences of giving consent. So if you're obtaining consent from someone below 21, you need to make sure that person is mature enough to understand what they're doing when they say yes.

  But of course, this is very vague and hard to apply as a standard, so the PDPC also gives a practical rule of thumb: you can assume, as a starting point, that anyone who is at least 13 years old typically has sufficient understanding to consent. But again, you cannot just assume this in every case. For example, if you are asking for consent for something quite complicated that may potentially harm this person in the future, it needs to be looked at more carefully. The rough number is thirteen.

  A student asks: for minors, the consent may be invalid. If the guardian of the minor gives the consent, would that change the situation?

  Yes. That actually brings us to the next slide. If you think the individual cannot validly consent, say because they are a minor, you may get consent from their representative, which for a child would be their parents or guardians. But if you do this, you need to conduct some measure of due diligence to make sure the person can actually validly represent the child, some proof that this person is the parent or guardian of this particular child. That's how you solve the problem. If you really want to be extra careful, you can consult both the child and the parent, so you cover all the bases.

  另一个问题，在网络环境中尤其棘手，是如果你试图从未成年人（minor）、年轻人那里取得同意，这个同意也可能无效，因为一般我们认为儿童可能没有能力对事情给出同意。

  说明这一点的案例是 Spring College International 案。本案中的组织是一家私立教育机构。它维护着一个 Facebook 页面，用来推广自己。投诉人是该校一名学生的家长。投诉人在浏览 Facebook 时看到了这家机构的页面，发现其中一条帖子放了她儿子的照片，宣称他们教的这个孩子考进了某所中学。也就是说，他们在宣传自己的成功案例。帖子包含了关于她儿子的细节，比如他的全名、他就读的小学，以及他在该机构学习了多久。投诉人向 PDPC 投诉。PDPC 调查后认定这家机构做错了。所有被展示的学生都是未成年人，是 13 岁以下的小孩子。PDPC 认定存在违规。

  Any other questions? That takes us to the next variation, which I sort of mentioned: express versus implied. Express means you use words to convey the consent. Implied means you don't use words; instead, the consent is understood from your conduct, your behaviour, or the circumstances.

  One good example is the German European School Singapore case. The organisation here was a private international school. The complainant was the parent of one of the students. The school conducts random drug testing, and they happened to pick this particular child, AB. The school told the parent that they would expel the child if he refused to provide a hair sample for the drug test, or if the test happened and the result was positive. There is some discussion in this case about unreasonable tying, and in the end the PDPC says it is not unreasonable. But the point we are focusing on here is implied consent.

  The PDPC says that even though it might look like the school didn't get consent, the school could be understood as having obtained implied consent. How is the consent implied? The school's bye-laws included a particular clause, 5.8, saying the school will conduct drug testing on its students. Plus, the parents of this child did have access to the school rules, so they were notified of this drug testing rule. So by enrolling the child in the school for ten years, knowing this rule exists, we can assume they impliedly consented to the drug testing and the collection of personal data for it. The PDPC found no breach of the Consent Obligation, because there was implied consent.

  And as with every complaint, in this case the parent complained after the whole drug testing, and whenever someone complains about a data protection matter, the PDPC gets involved.

  Question: why do you need to be careful when getting implied consent?

  A student says one point is that you really have to ensure people have the means to access the documents and are able to understand that they are giving implied consent.

  So even if you're getting implied consent, there is a need to ensure that the individual knows what they're getting into.

  Another student says people often don't really know; you'd want to make sure they actually know what they're in for. In this particular case, for instance, maybe the parents read the bye-laws a long time ago and forgot, and weren't checking through what they had signed up for.

  Also, with implied consent there are difficulties of proof. There's no signature, no tick box to indicate "yes, I read this, yes, I agree." So you need to find some other way to prove that consent was given.

  A student asks: when you go to private estates like condos, sometimes there are signs saying "CCTV in operation." Is that an example of implied consent?

  That would be an example of implied consent, because you never actually say, "Sure, record me." You just walk in. But in that case, the condo or office has to be careful to put the sign where you cannot possibly miss it. When you walk in, it's clear you saw the sign and you still walked in anyway. If you hide the sign somewhere, obviously that won't be okay.
