  A student asks: in this case, if I fail to uncheck certain boxes on a form, is that implied consent?

  You can think of that as implied consent, but I would treat it under a different dimension, which I'll get to now. This is the difference between positive and negative consent. Positive consent is consent obtained through some positive action the individual takes, for example signing a form or ticking a box. Negative consent is the opposite: the consent is obtained because the individual failed to do something. For example, failing to untick a box that has already been ticked, or when asked "Do you object?", the individual says nothing. That would be negative consent.

  Let me show you an example. On the left-hand side is the positive, good example, where the organisation obtains positive consent. The organisation is collecting data and asking, "Would you like to receive promotions through these means?", and it expects the individual to tick the boxes. On the other side is a negative example. Again they collect the data, but you can see the boxes are pre-ticked, and they assume that if the individual didn't untick them, the individual agrees. The PDPC is fairly clear here: you should avoid doing this. The question is, why should we avoid it?

  A student answers that inaction doesn't necessarily mean agreement. It could mean a number of things: I misunderstood; the text was too small; I might have been in a rush and signed up by mistake. So in any sense it isn't an expression of consent, because it doesn't prove I understood the entire clause.

  So the fundamental problem with negative consent is that it is ambiguous. When I fail to untick the box, it might well be that I agree, but it might also be that I didn't want to and missed it, or I was too busy to untick it. It can mean all sorts of things, and who knows what the real intention was? That's the problem with negative consent.

  It's not an unsolvable problem. You can still obtain negative consent, but you really have to make it super obvious. If you make it really prominent, like this, then maybe you might get away with it. But if you just do something unobtrusive like this, I think it's a bit risky.

  A student asks: so negative consent is okay? It's not a legal issue?

  I would say there is a legal argument that negative consent of this kind is legally invalid. The explanation involves bringing in other aspects of the PDPA. The argument is that the PDPA already provides for an opt-out mechanism elsewhere, so it cannot be that there is a separate opt-out mechanism like this. Since the PDPA elsewhere prescribes a specific opt-out mechanism, which we'll talk about, that's my legal argument. But in terms of what the cases and guidelines have said so far, the answer is still that you can use negative consent, as long as you are somehow able to show that the only reason the individual didn't untick the box is because they agreed. So, as I said, one way to do it is to make it super big and super obvious, so the individual couldn't possibly have missed it.

  A student suggests something their organisation does: there are two tick boxes, an OK button, and then a repeated statement that you are consenting to the collection and use of your information.

  That will make it clearer. It makes it more evident that the individual has seen this and has chosen not to untick.

  Another student raises language: say the entire thing is in Chinese, and I'm really not sure what it says, so I can only guess. But later on, they argue that I actually understood.

  So you're asking about the language problem. Generally speaking, I think Singapore law doesn't care much about whether you were able to read what you were signing. In general, I think there's a bias in that direction. Of course, the language problem makes negative consent even more dangerous, because it's another reason why people might not untick the box: they didn't understand it, not that they agreed.

  Some jurisdictions do specify what form consent must take in their legislation. For example, look at the EU version. They define consent as freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous, by a statement or by a clear affirmative action. The Indian version is quite similar. So you can see these provisions explicitly rule out negative consent, because they require a clear affirmative action, which is positive action. That's just for comparison; it isn't examinable.

  一位学生问：那么消极同意是可以的？这不是法律问题？

  一位学生提到他们组织的一种做法：有两个勾选框、一个"确定"按钮，然后再重复一遍你同意收集和使用你的信息的声明。

  你问的是语言问题。一般来说，我认为新加坡法律不太在意你能否读懂你所签署的东西。总体上，我认为存在这方面的倾向。当然，语言问题会让消极同意更加危险，因为这是人们可能没有取消勾选的另一个原因：他们没看懂，而不是他们同意了。

- [19:52:31–19:56:20] **Deemed Consent from a Third Party**

  Let me move on a little faster. We've talked about actual consent, so we move on to the second part, which is deemed consent. As I said, deemed consent is where you don't actually go and ask for consent, but you are allowed to assume that the individual gave consent. There are a few situations where you can deem consent.

  The first one is the most straightforward: deemed consent from a third party. When is this allowed? If the individual gave consent A to one organisation, saying "you may disclose my personal data to another organisation," then logically the individual should be deemed to give consent B for that other organisation to collect the data. Why else would they give consent A to disclose the data? That's a very logical basis for consent B. So if I say, "You may disclose my personal data to this person," I am deemed to consent to this person collecting my personal data. Very straightforward.

  But if you are relying on this kind of consent, you do need to do a bit of due diligence. When you receive personal data from the other organisation, you need to check that the other organisation actually got my consent to disclose it. As to what due diligence means in this context, you can have a look at the guidelines. In many cases, it basically amounts to obtaining some sort of written undertaking from the first organisation saying, "Yes, we promise that we did in fact obtain consent from the individual before we sent you the data." Of course, if you want to investigate further, you can request evidence: if they signed the form, where is the form? Those are the ways of doing due diligence.

  For example, here you have Sarah, who provides the personal data of her friend Jane to the spa as part of a referral programme. Here Sarah is the third party disclosing the individual's personal data. Before the spa can assume that Jane consented to the collection, the sales consultant does a bit of due diligence. He asks Sarah, "Did Jane actually know that you are disclosing her personal data to us?" After doing this very light level of due diligence, the spa then assumes that Jane consented to them collecting her personal data. That's one example of how this provision works.

  我讲快一点。我们已经讲了实际同意，现在进入第二部分，视为同意。正如我说的，视为同意就是你不用真的去请求同意，但法律允许你假定个人已经给出了同意。有几种情况可以视为同意。

  第一种是最直接的：来自第三方的视为同意（deemed consent from third party）。什么时候可以这样做？如果个人向一个组织给出了同意 A，说"你可以把我的个人数据披露给另一个组织"，那么从逻辑上讲，这个人应当被视为对另一个组织收集该数据给出了同意 B。不然他们为什么要给出同意 A 去披露数据呢？这是同意 B 非常合乎逻辑的依据。所以如果我说"你可以把我的个人数据披露给这个人"，我就被视为同意这个人收集我的个人数据。非常直接。

  但如果你依赖这种同意，你确实需要做一点尽职调查。当你从另一个组织收到个人数据时，你需要核实那个组织确实取得了我的同意来披露它。至于尽职调查在这里是什么意思，你们可以看指引。在很多情况下，基本上就是从第一个组织那里取得某种书面承诺，说"是的，我们保证在把数据发给你之前确实取得了个人的同意"。当然，如果你想进一步调查，可以要求提供证据：如果他们签了表格，表格在哪里？这些就是做尽职调查的方式。

  例如，这里 Sarah 在一个推荐计划中把她朋友 Jane 的个人数据提供给水疗中心。这里 Sarah 是披露个人数据的第三方。在水疗中心能假定 Jane 同意被收集数据之前，销售顾问做了一点尽职调查。他问 Sarah："Jane 真的知道你在把她的个人数据披露给我们吗？"在做了这种非常轻度的尽职调查之后，水疗中心就假定 Jane 同意他们收集她的个人数据。这就是这条规定如何运作的一个例子。
- [19:56:20–20:02:36] **Deemed Consent by Conduct: Spa, Clinic, Taxi, and the Actxa Case**

  The next situation is known as deemed consent by conduct. You are allowed to deem consent if the individual voluntarily provides his personal data to the organisation for a particular purpose, and it is reasonable that he would voluntarily provide that personal data. The reason for this provision is that there are some situations where the individual volunteers his personal data and it is obvious that he would consent.

  Let me show you some examples. First example: Sarah again goes to a spa for a facial treatment. After completing the treatment, the facial costs $49.99. Sarah doesn't say anything; she just hands over her credit card to the cashier to make payment. In this case, the cashier doesn't need to ask Sarah for consent to use her credit card number and other details to process the payment transaction. The consent is simply assumed, because it's obvious she would consent for this purpose.

  Another example: Eva goes for a health check-up at a clinic and is told the tests will collect certain information. If she proceeds with the tests, Eva is deemed to have consented to the collection of that personal data. The clinic doesn't even ask for specific consent to collect this data, because that's the only reason she's taking the test: to obtain this information.

  One more example. Tina calls a taxi operator's hotline to book a taxi. The customer service officer requests her name and contact number in order to inform her about the taxi. Tina provides this information voluntarily. So again, this is a scenario where Tina is deemed to consent to the taxi company using her name and number to inform her when the taxi arrives. But we cannot stretch this too far. Let's say the taxi operator also wants to use her information to do some marketing. They cannot simply deem consent for that marketing purpose, because she provided her name and number for only one obvious purpose, which is to get a cab, not for the non-obvious purpose of receiving marketing from the taxi operator.

  So the main question that arises is: at what point are you allowed to deem consent? The basic rule for this provision is that you are only allowed to deem consent if the purpose is so clear that a reasonable bystander would assume the individual would ordinarily give consent. From the circumstances, the purpose must be very clear.

  Here is the Actxa case. The organisation sold smart weighing scales, which measure certain types of body data like weight, total body fat, muscle mass, and so on. Users could also download the organisation's app, and when they linked the app to their smart scale, they could access the data through the app. But note that the scale could be used by itself, without the app. To register for the app, users had to provide certain basic registration data, like date of birth, height, weight, and so on. What happened here is that the complainant used a scale, which I think was purchased by someone else, and he later discovered that the app had transferred both his body data and his registration data to the organisation's servers without asking him for permission.

  The PDPC said this was a breach of the Consent Obligation, and they looked at the two types of personal data. Number one, the registration data. Here, the complainant could be deemed to consent to the organisation collecting the registration data, because he provided it for the purpose of registering for the app. The purpose is very obvious: when you register for the app and provide data voluntarily, obviously you consent to the organisation collecting it for that purpose. However, there was no deemed consent as far as the body data was concerned. Although you could say he voluntarily provided the body data by standing on the scale, the organisation's purpose for collecting it was not clear. There's no obvious reason why the organisation needs to collect this body data.

  So when you are relying on this type of consent, you need to be a bit careful and make sure you only deem consent when the purpose is very obvious from the circumstances.

  下一种情况叫作通过行为视为同意（deemed consent by conduct）。如果个人为了某个特定目的自愿向组织提供他的个人数据，而且他会自愿提供该个人数据是合理的，你就可以视为他已同意。这条规定的理由是，在某些情况下，个人主动提供了个人数据，而他会同意这一点是显而易见的。

  我给你们看几个例子。第一个例子：Sarah 又去水疗中心做面部护理。做完护理后，面部护理的费用是 49.99 元。Sarah 什么也没说，只是把信用卡交给收银员付款。在这种情况下，收银员不需要请求 Sarah 同意使用她的信用卡号码和其他资料来处理付款交易。同意被直接假定，因为很明显她会为了这个目的给出同意。

  另一个例子：Eva 去诊所做健康检查，被告知检查会收集某些信息。如果她继续进行检查，Eva 就被视为同意收集这些个人数据。诊所甚至不需要为收集这些数据请求具体的同意，因为她做检查的唯一原因就是获取这些信息。

  再举一个例子。Tina 打电话给出租车公司的热线叫车。客服人员要她的名字和联系号码，以便通知她出租车的情况。Tina 自愿提供了这些信息。所以这同样是 Tina 被视为同意出租车公司在车到时使用她的名字和号码通知她的情形。但我们不能把它延伸得太远。假设出租车公司还想用她的信息做营销。他们不能简单地视为她同意了这个营销目的，因为她提供名字和号码只是为了一个显而易见的目的，也就是叫车，而不是为了接收出租车公司营销信息这个不显而易见的目的。

  所以主要的问题是：在什么情况下你可以视为同意？这条规定的基本规则是，只有当目的清楚到一个合理的旁观者（reasonable bystander）会认为个人通常都会同意时，你才可以视为同意。从情境来看，目的必须非常清楚。

  这里是 Actxa 案。这家组织销售智能体重秤，可以测量某些身体数据，比如体重、总体脂、肌肉量等。用户还可以下载该组织的应用程序，把应用程序与智能秤连接后，就可以通过应用程序查看数据。但要注意，这个秤本身不用应用程序也可以使用。要注册应用程序，用户必须提供某些基本的注册数据，比如出生日期、身高、体重等。本案中发生的事情是，投诉人使用了一个秤，我想是别人买的，后来他发现应用程序在没有征求他许可的情况下，把他的身体数据和注册数据都传到了该组织的服务器上。

  PDPC 认定这违反了同意义务，并分别审视了两类个人数据。第一类是注册数据。在这里，投诉人可以被视为同意该组织收集注册数据，因为他是为了注册应用程序而提供这些数据的。目的非常明显：当你注册应用程序并自愿提供数据时，你显然同意组织为此目的收集数据。然而，就身体数据而言，不存在视为同意。虽然你可以说他站上秤就自愿提供了身体数据，但组织收集这些数据的目的并不清楚。没有显而易见的理由说明组织为什么需要收集这些身体数据。

  所以当你依赖这类同意时，需要小心一点，确保只有在目的从情境中非常显而易见时才视为同意。
- [20:02:36–20:06:00] **Deemed Consent by Contractual Necessity and Data Intermediaries**

  That's the second type of deemed consent. The third one is deemed consent by contractual necessity. When does this work? Let's say I, the individual, contract with an organisation, say a company, which we call A, and I provide my personal data to A for this particular contract. Let's say it is reasonably necessary for A to disclose my personal data to B in order to perform this contract. In that case, I would be deemed to consent to that disclosure, because it is necessary for A to perform the contract. In addition, I'm also deemed to consent to further disclosures to C, D, E, and so on, as long as all of it is necessary to perform the contract between me and A.

  I think it's easier to explain with an example. Going back to the spa: Sarah has given her credit card details to the spa for the purpose of payment. But of course, when you pay by credit card, it's not just the business that's involved, because the business needs to disclose your payment details to the bank and other financial institutions. This is an example where this type of deemed consent applies. You are deemed to consent to the spa transferring your personal data to the bank, the payment processors, and so on.

  A student asks whether this is the same as a data intermediary relationship, for example with the payment processor.

  This would be an example where the payment processor would be a data intermediary as well.

  The student asks whether all data intermediaries would be covered.

  Not always. In this case, it so happens that the data intermediaries are also doing things necessary for the contract, because they are the ones processing the payment. But of course there will be certain data intermediaries that are not doing anything necessary for any contract. In that case, they wouldn't be able to fall back on this. There are a couple of other examples, but I won't belabour this point. I think you understand deemed consent by contractual necessity.

  这是第二种视为同意。第三种是基于合同必要性的视为同意（deemed consent by contractual necessity）。它在什么时候适用？假设我，作为个人，与一个组织签约，比如一家公司，我们称它为 A，我为了这份合同向 A 提供了我的个人数据。假设为了履行这份合同，A 把我的个人数据披露给 B 是合理必要的。在这种情况下，我会被视为同意这次披露，因为这对 A 履行合同是必要的。此外，我还被视为同意进一步披露给 C、D、E 等等，只要这一切都是履行我与 A 之间的合同所必要的。

Here it is possible to deem an individual's consent where the organisation notifies the individual about the collection, use, or disclosure of his personal data, and the individual then fails to take any action. It's a rule that allows an explicit opt-out regime.

  So again, you can deem consent if you notify the individual, saying "I am going to collect, use, or disclose your personal data," and the individual doesn't respond. But it's not so straightforward, because the law introduces certain safeguards. As we discussed earlier, negative consent is a bit risky, so here the law introduces some additional requirements.

  What are the requirements? Number one: the organisation needs to conduct an assessment to make sure this collection, use, or disclosure does not create adverse effects, so that it's not a risky process. Even if it so happens that people just go along with the notification, it's no big deal, because in any case it's not harmful. Number two, of course, the organisation needs to take reasonable steps to notify the individual, because that's the basis for this consent. And number three, the organisation must give the individual a reasonable opt-out period. So those are the three conditions.

  Plus, you are not allowed to use this for direct marketing. You cannot use this consent provision for the purpose of sending direct marketing to individuals. The reason is simple: if the law allowed this, every direct marketer would use it, which would then create even more unwanted messages for people.

  Let me briefly explain each of the three safeguards. The first one is that you must conduct the so-called adverse effect assessment. What are you supposed to do? Number one, consider whether what you are proposing is likely to have any adverse effect. Is there a chance that you are harming the individual? If yes, you are expected to implement measures to eliminate, reduce the likelihood of, or mitigate the adverse effect. And you must get to a point where there is no more likely adverse effect. If you get to that point, then you're fine.

  The guidelines do provide some examples. If you look at the Key Concepts guidelines, Annex B, which I've highlighted, you will see a sort of ready-to-use assessment checklist if you want to use deemed consent by notification. Within the checklist is basically your adverse effect assessment, so you don't need to create your own table.

  If you look at this flowchart, this is how the PDPC recommends you apply this provision. Step one, you determine your purposes: what are you doing? Step two, you determine how you will notify. Step three is where you assess whether there is any likely adverse effect. In step three, you can consider some factors. Number one, what type of personal data are you processing? Is it sensitive? Number two, is your purpose reasonable? Number three, what are the likely impacts or effects, and how might this affect the individual's interests? And number four is where you decide how to reduce the likelihood of harm to the individual. After you have done all this, you go to step four: after implementing all the measures, you decide whether there is still a likely adverse effect. If the answer is yes, then you must not do it; you cannot use this deemed consent. But if your answer is no, there is no likely adverse effect, you can proceed with this mechanism. So that's the first condition, the assessment.

- [20:11:25–20:16:59] **Adequate Notification and a Reasonable Opt-Out Period**

  Second, you need to provide appropriate notification to the individual. What do you need to include in the notification? Obviously the first thing is your intention, which means you need to tell the individual, "I would like to collect, use, or disclose your personal data." Number two, indicate what the purpose is. Number three, indicate a reasonable period and a reasonable method to opt out. So you tell the individual, "I want to use your personal data for this purpose. If you don't like it, you have fourteen days to opt out."

  There is no real prescribed method, meaning the law doesn't say exactly how you should give this notification. You simply need to make sure it is effective, which means the individual is likely to read and understand it. There are a few things you can consider. Number one, how you usually communicate. If you usually communicate by email, then logically you should send this by email. Number two, you should consider using so-called direct channels of communication, meaning email, telephone, SMS, WhatsApp, whatever. What to avoid is indirect channels, meaning you just put a notice on your website, because then it's very easy for people to miss it. Number three, consider how many individuals you are going to notify, because that determines how you notify. If you're going to notify a million people, hypothetically, maybe you do need broader channels. But if it's three people, you can probably just send them a text.

  What would be an example of appropriate notification? Let's say you have this health app that collects personal data about individuals' wellness, such as how many steps they walk, their height, weight, and gender. Users can view their activity data, like their sleep patterns. What this company wants to do is use all this data to provide a personalised weight loss programme for its users through the app, and it wants to use deemed consent by notification. So what it has to do is ensure there is no likely adverse effect with respect to the users. And then here is where they decide the correct way to notify the users, in the last paragraph. The health app company decides the best way to notify is through the app itself, because that's the direct way to communicate and also the most effective way, since users usually open the app and would then see the notice. To ensure inactive users are notified, it also notifies users through other channels, email and social media. So this would be an example of how to provide notification for this deemed consent process.

  The third safeguard is that we need to give the individual a reasonable period to opt out. The statute doesn't say how long, but there are some factors you can consider. One is how frequently you interact. The more frequent your interaction, the shorter your period can be. If you only talk to this individual once a year, you probably need a longer period. Number two, how are you communicating, and what opt-out channel are you using? If you are communicating directly, meaning you can expect the individual to read the notice quite quickly, and you provide an opt-out channel that is very convenient, then your period can be shorter. If you make things difficult for the individual, then naturally it will need a longer period. And obviously, you need to wait until the opt-out period has expired before you actually start the processing.

  第二，你需要向个人提供恰当的通知。通知里需要包括什么？显然第一是你的意图，也就是你要告诉个人："我想收集、使用或披露你的个人数据。"第二，说明目的是什么。第三，说明一个合理的期限和合理的选择退出方式。所以你告诉个人："我想为这个目的使用你的个人数据。如果你不喜欢，你有十四天时间选择退出。"

  这里没有真正规定的方式，也就是说法律没有具体说你应该如何发出这个通知。你只需要确保它是有效的，也就是个人很可能会阅读并理解它。有几件事你可以考虑。第一，你通常怎么沟通。如果你通常用电邮沟通，那么按逻辑你应该用电邮发出。第二，你应该考虑使用所谓的直接沟通渠道，也就是电邮、电话、短信、WhatsApp 之类的。要避免的是间接渠道，也就是你只在网站上贴一个通知，因为那样人们很容易错过。第三，考虑你要通知多少人，因为这决定了你如何通知。假设你要通知一百万人，也许你确实需要更广泛的渠道。但如果只是三个人，你大概直接给他们发短信就行了。

- [20:29:28–20:36:51] **Withdrawal of Consent: Policy, Notice, Consequences, and the Y Electronics Example**

  As I mentioned previously, if you have actual or deemed consent, there is the possibility of individuals withdrawing that consent. The rule is that organisations have to allow individuals to withdraw consent at any time. Consent is never permanent.

  To facilitate this withdrawal, organisations should have a clear and accessible withdrawal policy, which should indicate a few things to individuals. First of all, how they can express their withdrawal. Number two, the person or the mechanism by which they can submit the notice to withdraw: which party will handle it, what website they can go to. And number three, telling individuals which purposes are needed for us to provide services to you, and which purposes are optional. Individuals can then choose to withdraw consent for optional purposes while keeping their consent for necessary purposes. When you develop this withdrawal policy, you need to make sure you don't do it in a way that indirectly restricts people from withdrawing consent. That would be the case if you make it unnecessarily complicated to withdraw.

  How does withdrawal happen? There is a specific process. It starts with the individual giving notice to the organisation: the individual needs to tell the organisation, "I would like to withdraw my consent." How much notice is reasonable? The law doesn't really give any indication. But generally, the rule of thumb in the guidelines is ten business days. When you receive a notice to withdraw, you can allow yourself ten business days to give effect to it. And if for some reason you need more than ten business days, the best practice is to tell the individual how long it will take. Of course, you shouldn't take too long, but you can extend somewhat.

  So what happens when you receive a notice to withdraw? You need to do certain things. The first thing you must do is tell the individual what the likely consequences of withdrawing are. Often it will be something like, "If you withdraw, we can no longer provide the same level of service," or there are other consequences. After that, you have the reasonable period, the ten business days, to give effect to the withdrawal, which means you stop collecting, using, or disclosing the individual's personal data. In addition, if your data intermediaries or other agents are also processing the individual's personal data, you need to tell them to stop. That is giving effect to the withdrawal.

  However, and this is something organisations sometimes get wrong, just because an individual withdrew their consent doesn't mean you need to delete the data. In Singapore, there is no right for individuals to require organisations to delete their personal data. All they can do is say, "Please stop," or rather, "I'm no longer consenting to the use of my personal data for further purposes." They can't force organisations to delete the data immediately.

  A student asks about the time frame: if the organisation doesn't delete immediately, is there some time frame or period by which it must?

  So not immediately. There will be a point where you must delete the data, even if the individual didn't ask, because there's a separate rule saying you can only hold on to data for a certain period of time. That's another obligation.

  Let me concentrate on how this withdrawal of consent mechanism works. Let's say you have Andy. Previously he consented to Y Electronics collecting, using, and disclosing his contact details to provide him with promotions. So that was consent given. Y Electronics then goes on to disclose these contact details to its marketing agent, plus some other third-party partners. Andy subsequently regrets this decision and submits a notice to withdraw, saying, "I don't want to receive any of your marketing anymore."

  At this point, what Y Electronics must do is tell Andy what happens if he withdraws consent. For example: Y Electronics and its agents will stop sending marketing information to Andy; Y Electronics will stop disclosing Andy's personal data to any other person; and Y Electronics will stop using Andy's contact details for marketing and will tell its agent to do likewise.

  That being said, why does Y Electronics not need to inform the third parties to which it already disclosed the personal data that they should also stop processing Andy's personal data? Because unless those third parties are data intermediaries or agents, Y Electronics is not responsible for them. It only needs to stop its own use, and stop disclosing to them.

  Also, again, this clarifies the point I was making: withdrawal doesn't affect Y Electronics' ability to retain the data it needs to keep, as long as it complies with its other obligations on retention.

  正如我之前提到的，如果你取得的是实际同意或视为同意，个人就有可能撤回该同意。规则是组织必须允许个人随时撤回同意。同意从来都不是永久的。

  为了方便撤回，组织应当有一份清晰且易于获取的撤回政策（withdrawal policy），向个人说明几件事。首先，他们可以如何表达撤回。第二，他们可以通过什么人或什么机制提交撤回通知：由哪一方处理，可以去哪个网站。第三，告诉个人哪些目的是我们向你提供服务所需要的，哪些目的是可选的。这样个人就可以选择撤回对可选目的的同意，同时保留对必要目的的同意。在制定撤回政策时，你需要确保不会以间接限制人们撤回同意的方式来制定。如果你把撤回弄得不必要地复杂，就属于这种情况。

  撤回是怎么发生的？有一个特定的流程。它从个人向组织发出通知开始：个人需要告诉组织"我想撤回我的同意"。多长的通知期是合理的？法律其实没有给出任何指示。但一般来说，指引中的经验法则是十个工作日。当你收到撤回通知时，你可以给自己十个工作日来执行。如果因为某些原因你需要超过十个工作日，最佳做法是告诉个人需要多长时间。当然，你不应该拖得太久，但可以适当延长。

  那么收到撤回通知后会怎样？你需要做几件事。你必须做的第一件事是告诉个人撤回可能带来的后果。通常会是类似"如果你撤回，我们就无法再提供同样水平的服务"之类的，或者其他后果。之后，你有一个合理期限，也就是十个工作日，来执行撤回，也就是停止收集、使用或披露该个人的个人数据。此外，如果你的数据中介或其他代理也在处理该个人的个人数据，你需要告诉它们停止。这就是执行撤回。

  然而，这是组织有时会弄错的地方：个人撤回了同意，并不意味着你需要删除数据。在新加坡，个人没有权利要求组织删除他们的个人数据。他们能做的只是说"请停止"，或者更确切地说，"我不再同意为后续目的使用我的个人数据"。他们不能强迫组织立即删除数据。

  一位学生问时间框架的问题：如果组织不立即删除，是否有某个时限或期限必须删除？

  所以不是立即删除。会有一个你必须删除数据的时间点，即使个人没有要求，因为另有一条规则规定你只能在一定期限内保留数据。那是另一项义务。

  我集中讲讲撤回同意的机制是如何运作的。假设有一个人叫 Andy。他之前同意 Y Electronics 收集、使用和披露他的联系方式，用来向他提供促销信息。这就是给出的同意。Y Electronics 随后把这些联系方式披露给它的营销代理，以及其他一些第三方合作伙伴。Andy 后来后悔了，提交了撤回通知，说"我不想再收到你们的任何营销信息了"。

  这时，Y Electronics 必须做的是告诉 Andy 撤回同意会发生什么。例如：Y Electronics 及其代理将停止向 Andy 发送营销信息；Y Electronics 将停止向任何其他人披露 Andy 的个人数据；Y Electronics 将停止使用 Andy 的联系方式进行营销，并告诉其代理也这样做。

  话虽如此，为什么 Y Electronics 不需要通知它已经披露过个人数据的那些第三方也停止处理 Andy 的个人数据？因为除非这些第三方是数据中介或代理，否则 Y Electronics 不对它们负责。它只需要停止自己的使用，并停止向它们披露。

  另外，这再次澄清了我之前提到的一点：撤回不影响 Y Electronics 保留它需要保留的数据的能力，只要它遵守其他关于数据保留的义务。
- [20:36:51–20:42:44] **No Prohibiting Withdrawal; Can Organisations Charge a Fee?**

  Something I mentioned earlier is that you cannot prohibit individuals from withdrawing consent. For example, you cannot put inside your contract with an individual a term saying you are not allowed to withdraw consent. However, the legislation also says this does not affect the legal consequences of withdrawal. This point can be a bit complicated and perhaps a bit contradictory, so let me explain.

  This is a common example. Say you're an individual who wants to obtain services from a telco and goes through the usual consent process. The telco can say that in order to provide services to you, you must consent to certain types of processing of your name, address, and so on. The individual gives the consent, and later on wants to withdraw. What happens when he withdraws? The operator cannot provide services to the individual, because without this personal data they cannot continue providing the service. This in turn entails early termination. Most telecommunication plans are for two years, for example, and if you terminate early there's a certain fee to be paid. So the withdrawal has the legal effect of early termination of the contract, which may then incur early termination charges. The telco here is allowed to impose that kind of charge.

  I suppose one question that arises from this is whether organisations can actually impose a fee for withdrawal of consent. Any thoughts?

  A student guesses that, for the withdrawal itself, if you withdraw you should know there will be some additional charges associated with it.

  For the act of withdrawal by itself, I would guess not. That's probably the correct first step. You cannot say, "If you withdraw consent, I am charging you a lot of money," because that basically amounts to a prohibition. But you are allowed to charge fees that are a consequence of the withdrawal. Of course, at the second level, the next question is: why is that different? In the end, you are still charging a fee for the withdrawal; it's just that the reason is different. This is where the contradiction arises. Again, I suspect that how this would be resolved in practice is that the regulator would look at the structure of the transaction between you and the individual to see whether the fee is a real one. Are you really charging a fee for early termination, or is the intention behind the fee really to deter people from withdrawing consent? I think that's how this question is generally approached.

  A student asks a quick question: does the termination fee have to reflect the actual cost, or does it just have to be reasonable? An organisation could make it a bit elaborate to make it less obvious.

  There isn't a clear answer. But I think if you charge a fee that is far in excess of what the termination actually costs, it is less likely that a judge or regulator would regard it as a genuine fee, and they would probably take issue with it.

  Another student asks: does that mean organisations can impose a fee for withdrawal?

  Not directly. You cannot directly impose a fee for withdrawal. But if the withdrawal results in legal consequences, such as termination of a contract that has a fee attached, that seems to be okay.

  The same student suggests a workaround: the company could say that if it has to process the withdrawal, it will incur costs in doing so, and charge for those costs.

  No, not for that. Because that again is charging a fee for processing the withdrawal.

  我之前提到过，你不能禁止个人撤回同意。例如，你不能在与个人的合同中写上一条说你不得撤回同意。然而，法律也规定，这不影响撤回的法律后果。这一点可能有点复杂，也许还有点矛盾，我来解释一下。

  这是一个常见的例子。假设你是一个想从电信公司获得服务的个人，走了一遍通常的同意流程。电信公司可以说，为了向你提供服务，你必须同意对你的姓名、地址等进行某些类型的处理。个人给出了同意，后来想撤回。撤回时会发生什么？运营商无法向这个人提供服务，因为没有这些个人数据，他们就无法继续提供服务。这进而导致提前终止合同。比如大多数电信套餐是两年的，如果提前终止就要付一笔费用。所以撤回具有提前终止合同的法律效果，进而可能产生提前终止费用。这里电信公司是被允许收取这种费用的。

  我想由此产生的一个问题是：组织是否真的可以就撤回同意收取费用？大家有什么想法？

  一位学生猜测说，就撤回本身而言，如果你撤回，你应该知道会有一些相关的额外费用。

  就撤回这个行为本身而言，我猜不可以。这大概是正确的第一步。你不能说"如果你撤回同意，我就收你一大笔钱"，因为那基本上等于禁止。但你可以收取作为撤回后果的费用。当然，到了第二层，下一个问题是：为什么这就不同了？归根结底你还是在为撤回收费，只是理由不同。矛盾就在这里产生。同样，我猜在实践中这个问题的解决方式是，监管机构会审视你与个人之间交易的结构，看看这笔费用是否真实。你真的是在收取提前终止费，还是这笔费用背后的意图其实是阻止人们撤回同意？我认为这个问题一般就是这样处理的。

  一位学生快速问了一个问题：终止费是否必须反映实际成本，还是只需要合理？组织可以把它设计得复杂一点，让它不那么明显。

  这没有明确的答案。但我认为，如果你收取的费用远远超过终止实际产生的成本，法官或监管机构就不太可能把它视为真实的费用，他们很可能会对此提出质疑。

  另一位学生问：这是否意味着组织可以就撤回收费？

  不能直接收。你不能直接就撤回收费。但如果撤回导致了法律后果，比如终止一份附带费用的合同，那似乎是可以的。

  同一位学生提出一个变通办法：公司可以说如果它要处理撤回，就会因此产生成本，然后就这些成本收费。

  不行，不能为那个收费。因为那同样是在为处理撤回收费。
- [20:42:44–20:49:00] **Q&A: Degrading Service, Incentives, and Stating Consequences**

  A student asks: instead of charging a fee, what if the company changes the quality of the service? Withdrawal may mean a revenue loss for the company.

  I think that one is a bit easier to answer, because the question then is: is there a relationship between the personal data and the quality of service? If the inability to process the personal data does affect how you provide the service, there's some connection, and then that's fine. But if you purposely degrade a service for no reason other than to punish the individual, then I think that again amounts to an attempt to prohibit withdrawal.

  The student adds that this is something to consider: evaluating the case where the organisation genuinely cannot deliver the same quality of service as normal.

  If the organisation cannot continue to provide the service, or a high quality of service, I think the natural and correct consequence is that you stop providing the service or the service degrades.

  Another student raises credit cards. Sometimes when you sign up for a credit card, they make you give marketing consent, for example linked to lucky draws. Two questions: first, does this marketing consent really affect the quality of the credit card service? Second, if you withdraw after a certain period of time, does that change things?

  That one is interesting, because here you have incentivised people, in the sense that you actually bought their consent.

  Another student suggests that charging a fee for withdrawal would still amount to an attempt to deter individuals from withdrawing, regardless of the background that there was originally an incentive or inducement to get them to consent to the marketing.

  I think as long as you try to charge a fee to deter the individual from withdrawing, you risk falling foul of the rule that you cannot prohibit the individual from withdrawing. But I guess in such situations you have to take the risk. Either you keep providing incentives so that people don't withdraw, or you take the risk that the individual might take your inducement and immediately withdraw.

  A student asks: so it's okay for the company to give incentives to stop people from withdrawing, as compared to charging them?

  To stop them from withdrawing, yes. If you keep giving incentives, saying that as long as you continue to consent, we will continue to give you this benefit, that's fine.

  Another student asks: does that mean that, as part of the original contract, the organisation is expected to make a very clear statement that withdrawing consent would result in services being interrupted? Something like, "If you withdraw your consent, I can't provide you services." Does it have to be clearly stated in the contract?

  You don't have to state it upfront, but you do need to state it when you receive the notice. When I, the individual, send you the notice saying I want to withdraw, you should tell me what the consequences are, because then it makes me think it over before I proceed. That's it.

  This would then come down to the question of whether it is really a discount, or whether that's actually the standard price and everyone who withdraws is made to pay more. Assuming everyone else is paying the standard price, that should be fine, because this is more of an inducement.

  一位学生问：如果公司不收费，而是改变服务质量呢？撤回可能意味着公司的收入损失。

  我认为这个问题比较容易回答，因为问题在于：个人数据与服务质量之间有没有关系？如果无法处理个人数据确实影响到你如何提供服务，存在某种联系，那就没问题。但如果你故意降低服务质量，除了惩罚个人之外没有其他理由，那么我认为这同样等于试图禁止撤回。

  这位学生补充说，这是需要考虑的一点：评估组织确实无法提供与平常相同质量服务的情况。

  如果组织无法继续提供服务，或者无法提供高质量的服务，我认为自然而正确的后果就是你停止提供服务，或者服务质量下降。

  另一位学生提到信用卡。有时办信用卡时，他们会要你给出营销同意，比如与幸运抽奖挂钩。两个问题：第一，这个营销同意真的会影响信用卡服务的质量吗？第二，如果你在一段时间后撤回，会不会有所不同？

  这个很有意思，因为这里你激励了人们，某种意义上你实际上买下了他们的同意。

  另一位学生提出，就撤回收费仍然等于试图阻止个人撤回，不管背景是当初曾有过激励或诱因让他们同意营销。

  我认为只要你试图收费来阻止个人撤回，你就有违反"不得禁止个人撤回"这条规则的风险。但我想在这种情况下你只能承担风险。要么你持续提供激励，让人们不撤回；要么你承担个人可能拿了你的好处然后立即撤回的风险。

  一位学生问：所以与收费相比，公司提供激励来让人们不撤回是可以的？

  为了让他们不撤回，是的。如果你持续提供激励，说只要你继续同意，我们就继续给你这个好处，那是可以的。

  另一位学生问：这是否意味着作为原始合同的一部分，组织应当非常清楚地声明撤回同意会导致服务中断？比如"如果你撤回同意，我就无法向你提供服务"。这必须在合同中清楚写明吗？

  你不必事先写明，但在收到通知时你确实需要说明。当我，作为个人，给你发通知说我想撤回时，你应该告诉我后果是什么，因为这会让我在继续之前三思。就是这样。

  那么这就归结为一个问题：它真的是折扣，还是其实那才是标准价格，而每个撤回的人都要多付钱。假设其他人都在付标准价格，那应该没问题，因为这更多是一种诱因。

  Let's have a look at this scenario. We can stop there.

  Let's think about what LinkedIn might argue from their perspective. Looking at this fact situation, LinkedIn would possibly say, "Well, we did mention in our data collection policy update that we are going to use some of this for training. We actually mentioned that, and we gave users the right to opt out if they are not comfortable." That would be their best case. What do you think? Would they say they have deemed consent, or that they obtained actual consent? What do you think would be the problems with that?

  One problem is that this is relying on negative consent: if you don't opt out, we will carry on using your data. In fact, it's even worse, because technically speaking, users weren't even given the option to effectively opt out. You can see here that you can opt out, but when you opt out, it doesn't affect the training that has already been done. So it's not as if opting out is a real option.

  The other problem is that, while they did say what they were doing, it's a bit hidden inside the data collection policy. That's another important point.

  A student adds that this goes to notification: simply changing the privacy policy isn't adequate notice to the people you're dealing with.

  Yes, it's an indirect way of notifying, in the sense that users weren't personally given some sort of notification saying, "Here's what we're going to do with your data."

  I suppose this goes back to the problem we saw earlier: when you amend the data protection policy, people don't read it again. So there's that additional problem. Then there's the question of how you deal with inactive users, which makes negative consent a problem. One reason people fail to uncheck the box is simply that they are inactive. They're not actually using the network. That is another difficulty.

  Another student points out that the original purpose was essentially networking with your colleagues on the platform, but now it's a different purpose altogether, so notification of this new purpose is needed.

  So you might call it an unexpected purpose. Expected purposes are okay, but when you have a purpose that people wouldn't reasonably expect, you actually need to make it prominent, because people generally don't expect it. Even now that things have changed, people generally did not expect their data to be used to train generative AI.

  我们来看这个场景。就到这里吧。

  我们想想 LinkedIn 从它的角度可能会怎么论证。看这个事实情况，LinkedIn 可能会说："嗯，我们在数据收集政策的更新中确实提到了会把部分数据用于训练。我们确实提到了，而且我们给了用户在不舒服时选择退出的权利。"这会是他们最好的论点。你们怎么看？他们会说自己取得的是视为同意，还是实际同意？你们觉得这有什么问题？

  一个问题是这依赖的是消极同意：如果你不选择退出，我们就继续使用你的数据。事实上情况更糟，因为从技术上讲，用户甚至没有被给予有效选择退出的选项。你可以看到这里你可以选择退出，但当你选择退出时，它不影响已经完成的训练。所以选择退出并不是一个真正的选项。

  另一个问题是，虽然他们确实说了自己在做什么，但这有点被藏在数据收集政策里面了。这是另一个重要的点。

  另一位学生指出，原来的目的本质上是在平台上与同事建立人脉，但现在是一个完全不同的目的，所以需要就这个新目的进行通知。

  所以你可以称之为一个意料之外的目的（unexpected purpose）。意料之中的目的是可以的，但当你的目的是人们不会合理预期到的，你实际上需要把它突出地提出来，因为人们一般不会预期到。即使到了现在情况已经变了，人们一般也没有预期自己的数据会被用来训练生成式 AI。
