We're basically just helping you do better what we promised to do."

  That's interesting. So LinkedIn might possibly say that this new thing, training the AI, fits within the purposes users already consented to. Here a clever data protection officer would look back at the list of purposes people already consented to and say, "Oh, it kind of fits inside this provision here." I think that would be a possible argument, depending on what users actually consented to at the time they signed up.

  Another student raises one more point: the content may be trained by another company, such as OpenAI. That's likely a transfer from the original user, and even though the original user agreed to LinkedIn's use, it doesn't mean they also agreed to their content being used for training by an outside company. The last sentence shows the training may also be done outside.

  I suppose that would also be something unexpected. You wouldn't expect your data to be shared with some third-party AI company to feed their generative AI. So I think the difficulties with this scenario are fairly substantial.

  Another student asks to confirm: negative consent may possibly be okay in some cases, but there are bad forms of negative consent that shouldn't be done, so some cases are okay and others are not?

  Just to go back to this point and clarify: what the guidelines and cases suggest is that technically, negative consent can be valid, but it will often not be valid. It will often not be valid because, as we saw in this question, the failure to uncheck the box can be explained by several reasons, only one of which is that the individual actually agrees. So in a sense it can be very risky, and in this case even more risky because of the other characteristics. It is really not recommended, because you will likely breach the Consent Obligation if you use negative consent. And if you do insist on using it, you have to be very careful to make it super clear to the individual that they must uncheck this, before you process their personal data.

  It seems that ultimately nothing really came of this controversy. I think they probably did backpedal a little, which is perhaps why nothing came of it, and I don't think there was much to fear subsequently. I suppose because this was a fairly novel kind of situation, the PDPC may have taken a more cautious approach: ask them questions first and see what the situation is. But of course there was some negative reaction.

  一位学生说，LinkedIn 可以主张这并没有超出他们最初的服务范围。不管从用户角度多么难以接受，他们可以主张业务的整体目的是一样的："我们并没有推出新的业务线或产品线。我们基本上只是帮你把我们承诺做的事情做得更好。"

  这很有意思。所以 LinkedIn 可能会说，这件新事情，也就是训练 AI，符合用户已经同意过的目的。在这里，一个聪明的数据保护官（data protection officer）会回头看人们已经同意过的目的清单，然后说："哦，它大概可以归入这里的这一条。"我认为这会是一个可能的论点，取决于用户在注册时实际同意了什么。

  另一位学生又提出一点：内容可能由另一家公司训练，比如 OpenAI。这很可能是从原始用户那里转移出去的，即使原始用户同意了 LinkedIn 的使用，也不意味着他们也同意自己的内容被外部公司用于训练。最后一句表明训练也可能在外部进行。

  我想这也会是意料之外的。你不会预期自己的数据会被分享给某家第三方 AI 公司，去喂养他们的生成式 AI。所以我认为这个场景的问题相当大。

  另一位学生请求确认：消极同意在某些情况下可能是可以的，但有一些不好的消极同意形式是不应该做的，所以有些情况可以，有些不行？

  我回到这一点澄清一下：指引和案例表明，从技术上讲，消极同意可以是有效的，但它往往是无效的。它往往无效，是因为正如我们在这道题中看到的，没有取消勾选可以有好几种解释，其中只有一种是个人真的同意。所以某种意义上它可能非常有风险，而在这个案例中，由于其他特点，风险就更大了。这真的不推荐，因为如果你用消极同意，很可能会违反同意义务。如果你坚持要用，就必须非常小心，在处理个人数据之前，要让个人非常清楚地知道他们必须取消勾选这一项。

  看起来这场风波最终并没有什么结果。我想他们可能稍微退让了一点，这也许就是没有下文的原因，而且我认为之后也没有什么可担心的了。我想因为这是一种相当新的情况，PDPC 可能采取了更谨慎的做法：先问他们一些问题，看看情况如何。但当然，还是有一些负面反应的。
- [21:08:12–21:14:16] **Doing It Properly: Actual Consent vs. Deemed Consent by Notification; Organ Donation Opt-Out**

  Let's press on. Say you go back in time and you want to do AI training. How would you go about it? What's the logical way to get consent from users for training?

  One possibility is actual consent: present some sort of agreement and ask the users, "Okay?" This would be a typical way of getting consent for this.

  A student suggests starting by asking users to confirm that they are comfortable with it.

  So that would be the second method, which is deemed consent by notification. Here you need to do the adverse effect assessment, assess the likely adverse effects, give a reasonable period for them to opt out, and then, once you've done all that, for those individuals who did not opt out, you can use their personal data.

  The student asks: what if we want to withdraw?

  They could withdraw, of course. But almost certainly, what they could not do is say, "You must consent, otherwise we stop providing you with the service." That much I think we all agree on.

  Another student suggests offering something to incentivise users to consent, for example giving them access to a new AI feature.

  Yes, give them some kind of incentive. Both of these are valid methods, and it's simply a business decision which one you want to use. Both approaches are common. The con of actual consent is that it's very troublesome, especially as your number of users gets into the hundreds of thousands or millions, because now you have to handle every single one and keep track of it. The con of deemed consent by notification is that it's more of a reputational thing, because as you can see from the reaction here, people did not react well to this kind of opt-out system. It would be better if you actually notify them properly, but some will still miss out, since instead of giving them a choice upfront, you are making them act. I think the other forms of deemed consent are probably not really relevant to this kind of situation.

  A student asks about the Singapore government: for things like organ donation, we are all opted in by law. What kind of consent process applies there?

  I think for organ transplantation, the human organ transplant regime has quite different public policy considerations. In that case, I think what the Singapore government has chosen to do is adopt a stronger touch: "We will assume you are okay with it by default, and if you want to opt out, you can." And those who opt out get lower priority.

  The student asks how many people actually know that they can opt out of organ donation.

  As far as the human organ transplant regime is concerned, I suppose the government here makes a trade-off in terms of personal autonomy. But I think I'll just release you now.

  我们继续。假设你回到过去，想做 AI 训练。你会怎么做？从用户那里取得训练同意的合理方式是什么？

  一种可能是实际同意：给出某种协议，问用户"可以吗？"这会是取得这方面同意的典型方式。

  一位学生建议，先请用户确认他们对此感到可以接受。

  那么第二种方法就是通过通知视为同意。在这里你需要做不利影响评估，评估可能的不利影响，给他们一个合理的选择退出期，然后在完成这一切之后，对于那些没有选择退出的人，你就可以使用他们的个人数据。

  这位学生问：如果我们想撤回呢？

  他们当然可以撤回。但几乎可以肯定的是，他们不能说"你必须同意，否则我们就停止为你提供服务"。这一点我想我们都同意。

  另一位学生建议提供一些东西来激励用户同意，比如让他们使用新的 AI 功能。

  是的，给他们某种激励。这两种都是有效的方法，选择哪一种只是一个商业决定。两种做法都很常见。实际同意的缺点是非常麻烦，尤其是当你的用户数量达到几十万甚至几百万时，因为你现在要处理每一个人并加以追踪。通过通知视为同意的缺点更多是声誉方面的，因为正如你们从这里的反应看到的，人们对这种选择退出的机制反应不好。如果你真正恰当地通知他们会好一些，但仍会有人错过，因为你不是事先给他们选择，而是要他们自己采取行动。我认为其他形式的视为同意大概和这类情况并不相关。

  一位学生问到新加坡政府：像器官捐献这类事情，我们都依法被默认加入了。那里适用的是什么样的同意流程？

  我认为就器官移植而言，人体器官移植制度有相当不同的公共政策考量。在这种情况下，我认为新加坡政府选择了采取更强有力的做法："我们默认假定你是同意的，如果你想选择退出，你可以选择退出。"而那些选择退出的人会获得较低的优先次序。

  这位学生问，到底有多少人真正知道自己可以选择不捐献器官。

    就人体器官移植制度而言，我想政府在这里是在个人自主方面做出了取舍。不过我想今天就到这里，下课吧。
# Seminar 4
## Week 4 Readings
  - AGKCP at 12.55-13.4.
## Week 4 Summary
- **Exceptions to Consent: Overview 同意的例外：概览**
  - **Third route to compliance:** Besides actual consent and deemed consent, an organisation can comply with the Consent Obligation by relying on an **exception to consent**.
  - **Scope this week:** The PDPA has a long list of exceptions, some of them straightforward (e.g. emergencies). The course covers only four, because in practice organisations rely on these most:
    - **Legitimate interest exception**
    - **Business improvement exception**
    - **Research exception**
    - **Public availability exception**
  - **第三种合规途径：** 除了实际同意和视为同意之外，机构还可以依赖**同意的例外**来履行同意义务。
  - **本周范围：** PDPA 列出了很长一串例外，其中一些很直白（如紧急情况）。课程只讲四个，因为实践中机构最常依赖这四个：
    - **正当利益例外**
    - **业务改进例外**
    - **研究例外**
    - **公开可得例外**

- **Legitimate Interest Exception: Concept and Three Requirements 正当利益例外：概念与三项要求**
  - **Rule:** An organisation may **collect, use, or disclose** personal data without consent if this is in the **legitimate interests** of the organisation or another person.
  - **Not automatic:** Saying "I have a legitimate purpose" is not enough. You must satisfy three requirements:
    - **(1) Identify and articulate** the legitimate interest.
    - **(2) Conduct an adverse effect assessment.**
    - **(3) Disclose reliance** on the exception. You cannot rely on it secretly.
  - **规则：** 如果符合机构或他人的**正当利益**，机构可以在未取得同意的情况下**收集、使用或披露**个人数据。
  - **并非自动适用：** 只说“我有正当目的”是不够的，必须满足三项要求：
    - **（1）识别并阐明**正当利益。
    - **（2）进行不利影响评估。**
    - **（3）披露**正在依赖该例外，不能偷偷依赖。

- **Step 1: Articulating the Legitimate Interest 第一步：阐明正当利益**
  - **Benefit:** Identify the concrete benefit pursued (e.g. student safety, fraud prevention).
  - **Beneficiary:** Identify who benefits: usually the organisation, but it can also be other people or the public.
  - **Real and present:** The benefit must be **real and present**, not **speculative**. You must show it will arise if the processing is allowed.
  - **Specificity:** A generic aim such as "revenue" is likely **too broad**, since every profit-making business wants it. Articulate the specific benefit instead.
  - **Hard limit:** The exception **cannot** be used to send **direct marketing messages**. This is the same as for deemed consent by notification.
  - **好处：** 识别所追求的具体好处（如学生安全、防止欺诈）。
  - **受益人：** 识别谁受益：通常是机构本身，但也可以是其他人或公众。
  - **真实且当下：** 好处必须**真实且当下存在**，而非**推测性的**。你必须证明只要允许处理，好处就会出现。
  - **具体性：** 像“收入”这样的笼统目标很可能**过于宽泛**，因为每家营利企业都想要。应阐明具体的好处。
  - **硬性限制：** 该例外**不能**用于发送**直接营销信息**，这一点与通知视为同意相同。

- **Step 2: Adverse Effect Assessment 第二步：不利影响评估**
  - **Clear adverse effects:** Physical harm, harassment, serious alarm, and distress clearly count. No further analysis is needed.
  - **Other effects:** Whether these count depends on **prevailing social norms**. An effect can look harmful but be socially acceptable. Example: a bank refusing a loan after a creditworthiness assessment is not regarded as an adverse effect.
  - **Factors for predicting likely adverse effects (consider all circumstances):**
    - **Impact** on the individual, covering both **severity** and **likelihood**.
    - **Type of data:** sensitive data is more likely to cause harm.
    - **Vulnerable groups:** e.g. groups prone to discrimination, or children.
    - **Extent** of the processing and **how** the data will be processed.
    - **Reasonableness** of the purpose.
    - Whether **predictions or decisions** about the individual are likely to cause physical harm, serious alarm, and so on.
  - **Whose harm counts:** Only harm to the individuals **whose personal data is processed**. Benefits to others (the company, passengers' safety) go on the **legitimate interest side** of the scale.
  - **明显的不利影响：** 人身伤害、骚扰、严重惊恐和痛苦明显属于不利影响，无需进一步分析。
  - **其他影响：** 是否算不利影响取决于**当下的社会规范**。有些影响看似有害，但社会可以接受。例如，银行经信用评估后拒绝贷款，不被视为不利影响。
  - **预测可能不利影响的因素（综合考虑所有情况）：**
    - 对个人的**影响**，包括**严重程度**和**发生可能性**。
    - **数据类型**：敏感数据更可能造成伤害。
    - **弱势群体**：如容易受歧视的群体、儿童。
    - 处理的**范围**以及数据将**如何**被处理。
    - 目的的**合理性**。
    - 针对个人的**预测或决定**是否可能造成人身伤害、严重惊恐等。
  - **谁的伤害才算：** 只算**个人数据被处理的那些人**受到的伤害。对他人的好处（公司、乘客安全）放在天平的**正当利益一侧**。

- **Mitigation, Balancing, and Retention 减轻措施、权衡与保留**
  - **Mitigate:** Implement reasonable measures to **eliminate, reduce the likelihood of, or mitigate** adverse effects.
  - **Key contrast with deemed consent by notification:**
    - **Notification:** adverse effects must be **completely eliminated**.
    - **Legitimate interest:** a **balancing test** applies. Residual adverse effects are allowed if the legitimate interest **outweighs** them. If it does not, you cannot use the exception.
  - **Retention:** Keep the assessment for the **whole period** of reliance on the exception.
  - **Balancing is uncertain:** Interests rarely have a clear monetary value, so the weighing is **impressionistic**. The practical advice is to rely on the exception only when the scale is **heavily tilted** in your favour. If it is finely balanced, the PDPC could take a different view.
  - **Not a headcount:** "More people benefit" does not automatically win. A slight, speculative public benefit may not outweigh serious harm to a few individuals.
  - **Alternatives matter:** If the benefit can be achieved another way, the balance tilts **against** the organisation.
  - **减轻：** 采取合理措施**消除、降低可能性或减轻**不利影响。
  - **与通知视为同意的关键对比：**
    - **通知视为同意：** 不利影响必须**完全消除**。
    - **正当利益：** 适用**权衡测试**。只要正当利益**压过**残余的不利影响，就允许存在残余影响。如果压不过，就不能用该例外。
  - **保留：** 在依赖该例外的**整个期间**都要保留评估。
  - **权衡具有不确定性：** 各种利益很少有清晰的金钱价值，权衡是**印象式的**。实务建议是只有在天平**明显倾向**于己方时才依赖该例外。若两边差不多，PDPC 可能有不同看法。
  - **不是数人头：** “受益人数多”并不必然胜出。微小且推测性的公共利益，可能压不过少数人受到的严重伤害。
  - **替代方案很重要：** 如果能用其他方式实现该好处，天平会**不利于**机构。

- **Step 3: Disclosure of Reliance 第三步：披露依赖情况**
  - **Reasonable access:** Give individuals reasonable access to information about the collection, use, or disclosure, typically through the **data protection policy** or an app notification.
  - **Contact person:** Provide the business contact information of someone who can answer queries, usually the **DPO**.
  - **Assessment stays confidential:** You need **not** disclose the adverse effect assessment itself. You show it only when the **PDPC asks**.
  - **合理获取：** 让个人能合理获取有关收集、使用或披露的信息，通常通过**数据保护政策**或应用内通知。
  - **联系人：** 提供能解答疑问者的业务联系方式，通常是**数据保护官（DPO）**。
  - **评估可保密：** **无需**披露不利影响评估本身，只在 **PDPC 要求**时提供。

- **Examples and Q&A on Legitimate Interest 正当利益的例子与问答**
  - **Insurance fraud:** An insurer processes customers' past claims data for fraud detection and prevention. If the legitimate interest outweighs the adverse effects, consent is not needed.
  - **Hotel skippers blacklist:** Several hotels jointly compile a blacklist (names, passport numbers, etc.) of guests who repeatedly fail to pay. This is a legitimate interest.
  - **Common thread:** In these situations the individual would **never consent**, because consent would lead to negative consequences for them.
  - **EU comparison (non-examinable):**
    - **Singapore:** legitimate interest is an **exception**, so consent is the default.
    - **EU GDPR:** legitimate interest is a lawful basis **on par with consent**, still subject to balancing against the data subject's rights.
    - **Lecturer's view:** the hotel-skipper balance would likely still favour the hotels. The counter-argument that skippers would have nowhere to stay is weak, because they are at fault.
  - **Flock cameras question:** Balancing is notoriously uncertain. US constitutional law offers balancing principles that Singapore lacks. The Flock scenario would not transfer directly to Singapore, because it involves a private–public relationship and Singapore's public sector is exempt from the PDPA.
  - **Frequency of use:** No studies exist. The regulator's position is that **if you can rely on consent, you should**. The case for the exception is stronger when consent is not an appropriate mechanism.
  - **No limit on interests:** Any interest can qualify, depending on the activity. Example: an online grocery platform's interest in **food safety** (hygienic, untampered groceries).
  - **保险欺诈：** 保险公司处理客户过往理赔数据用于欺诈检测和预防。如果正当利益压过不利影响，就无需同意。
  - **逃单住客黑名单：** 多家酒店联合编制屡次不付款住客的黑名单（姓名、护照号码等），属于正当利益。
  - **共同点：** 在这些情况下，当事人**绝不会同意**，因为同意会给他们带来负面后果。
  - **与欧盟比较（不考）：**
    - **新加坡：** 正当利益是一项**例外**，默认应取得同意。
    - **欧盟 GDPR：** 正当利益是与同意**同等地位**的合法基础，但仍要与数据主体的权利进行权衡。
    - **讲师观点：** 逃单住客案的权衡结果很可能仍偏向酒店。“逃单者将无处可住”这一反驳很弱，因为过错在他们自己。
  - **Flock 摄像头问题：** 权衡出了名地不确定。美国宪法提供了一些权衡原则，新加坡没有。Flock 的情形不会直接照搬到新加坡，因为它涉及私营与公共部门的关系，而新加坡公共部门豁免于 PDPA。
  - **使用频率：** 没有相关研究。监管机构的立场是**能依赖同意就应依赖同意**。当同意不是合适机制时，依赖该例外的理由更充分。
  - **利益类型无限制：** 任何利益都可能成立，视具体活动而定。例如：网上杂货平台对**食品安全**（卫生、未被动手脚）的利益。

- **In-Class Exercise: RHC and the BARG App 课堂练习：RHC 与 BARG 应用**
  - **Scenario:** RHC, a ride-hailing company, suspects (on anecdotal evidence) that drivers are making **off-platform arrangements**, which its T&Cs prohibit. It runs an algorithm on drivers' **location data**, originally collected for **passenger safety**. If the tool estimates a **≥80% probability** of an off-platform arrangement, the driver is **automatically expelled**.
  - **Articulating the interest:**
    - "Protecting the business" or "revenue" is **too broad**. The specific interest is eliminating off-platform arrangements.
    - Stronger, more believable framings are **passenger safety** (off-platform trips are untracked) and preventing **overcharging**.
    - Pure revenue protection is questionable where it looks like **unreasonable control** of drivers, even with a contractual prohibition.
  - **Adverse effects:**
    - Distinguish **correct expulsions** from **wrongful expulsions**.
    - An 80% threshold means **meaningful uncertainty**, so innocent drivers will be expelled, and this is hard to sort out afterwards.
    - "Off-platform arrangement" is **ill-defined** (e.g. ferrying relatives, or a child to school), which raises the risk of wrongful expulsion further.
    - Arguably, even correctly identified drivers should not be expelled immediately.
  - **Balancing points:** Ask whether the benefit could be achieved **another way** (e.g. requiring drivers to keep the app on). If so, the balance tilts against RHC.
  - **Purpose of reuse:** If the tool can genuinely be fitted within the **passenger safety purpose already consented to**, RHC may not need the exception at all. But having already collected the data **does not by itself** permit a new, unconsented use.
  - **Implications:** In its current form the adverse effects are likely too strong. RHC can either use **consent**, or add **mitigation** (human review, warnings, letting drivers explain) to swing the balance.
  - **Disclosure:** Through the data protection policy or an in-app notification.
  - **Method:** Run the three steps and put each interest in the **correct bucket**: company and passenger interests on the legitimate interest side, drivers' harms on the adverse effect side.
  - **情景：** 网约车公司 RHC 基于零星证据怀疑司机在做其条款禁止的**场外安排**。它对司机的**位置数据**（原为**乘客安全**而收集）运行算法；若工具估计场外安排概率**≥80%**，就**自动开除**该司机。
  - **阐明利益：**
    - “保护业务”或“收入”**过于宽泛**，具体利益是消除场外安排。
    - 更有力、更可信的表述是**乘客安全**（场外行程无人追踪）和防止**乱收费**。
    - 如果看起来是在**不合理地控制**司机，即使有合同禁止，纯粹的收入保护也值得怀疑。
  - **不利影响：**
    - 区分**正确开除**和**错误开除**。
    - 80% 阈值意味着存在**相当大的不确定性**，无辜司机会被开除，事后也难以纠正。
    - “场外安排”**定义不清**（如载亲戚、送孩子上学），进一步增加了错误开除的风险。
    - 可以说，即使正确识别出违规司机，也不应立即开除。
  - **权衡要点：** 问能否用**其他方式**实现该好处（如要求司机始终开着应用）。如果能，天平就不利于 RHC。
  - **数据再利用：** 若该工具真能纳入**已获同意的乘客安全目的**，RHC 可能根本不需要该例外。但已经收集了数据，**本身并不**允许未经同意的新用途。
  - **结论：** 按现有形式，不利影响很可能太大。RHC 可以改用**同意**，或增加**减轻措施**（人工复核、警告、让司机解释）来扭转权衡结果。
  - **披露：** 通过数据保护政策或应用内通知。
  - **方法：** 走完三个步骤，把每种利益放进**正确的一栏**：公司和乘客利益放在正当利益一侧，司机受到的伤害放在不利影响一侧。

- **Business Improvement Exception 业务改进例外**
  - **Rule:** **Use only**, not collection or disclosure, of personal data without consent for a **business improvement purpose**. This is distinctly Singaporean.
  - **Four purposes:**
    - Improving, enhancing, or developing goods or services.
    - Improving, enhancing, or developing methods or processes for business operations.
    - Learning or understanding individuals' behaviour and preferences.
    - Identifying suitable goods or services for individuals, or personalising them.
  - **Two conditions:**
    - The purpose **cannot be achieved without** personal data in **individually identifiable form**.
    - The use must be **reasonable**, i.e. customers would not be horrified if it were disclosed to them.
  - **No public proof needed:** These conditions need not be publicised. You explain them to the PDPC if it asks, so confidential internal processes stay confidential.
  - **Marketing:** It **cannot** be used to send direct marketing, but it **can** be used for **preparatory** marketing work (data analytics, market research to understand customers).
  - **Versus legitimate interest:** Generally **more straightforward**, because there is no adverse effect assessment. But it is **not a blank cheque**: the reasonableness condition can bring back the same concerns.
  - **Overrides refusals:** The exception applies **regardless of consent or lack of consent**. Strictly, a narrow permission (e.g. an app store user choosing "necessary use only") can be overridden for these purposes, provided the conditions are met.
  - **AI training:** Training models could fall under the first two purposes. However, the identifiability condition bites. If data can be **anonymised**, it ceases to be personal data and no exception is needed, and **that is what you should do**. LinkedIn-style text training is a practical difficulty, because posts are hard to strip of personal data.
  - **Territoriality:** Processing in Singapore can rely on Singapore's exception, but this is not straightforward, because the **EU** may assert its law extraterritorially.
  - **Examples:**
    - **Credit card company:** analyses payment history and transactions to understand spending habits and design new cards and reward schemes. This is a typical use.
    - **Wearables company:** model training could use **anonymised** data, so it should do that. Personalising the feature for each customer needs personal data, and that part relies on the exception.
  - **Intra-group branch (non-examinable):** A second branch allows **disclosure within a group of companies**, with slightly different conditions.
  - **Why it exists:** No explanation has been given for why only Singapore has it. Its rationale is to facilitate business improvement where it is **safe not to rely on consent**, i.e. where the use is unlikely to affect individuals significantly.
  - **规则：** 为**业务改进目的**，在未取得同意的情况下**仅限使用**个人数据，不包括收集或披露。这是新加坡特有的例外。
  - **四种目的：**
    - 改进、提升或开发商品或服务。
    - 改进、提升或开发业务运营的方法或流程。
    - 了解个人的行为和偏好。
    - 识别适合个人的商品或服务，或进行个性化。
  - **两个条件：**
    - **不使用**可识别个人身份形式的个人数据，就**无法实现**该目的。
    - 使用必须**合理**，即告诉客户时他们不会被吓到。
  - **无需公开证明：** 这些条件无需公开，PDPC 询问时再解释，因此保密的内部流程可以继续保密。
  - **营销：** **不能**用于发送直接营销，但**可以**用于营销的**准备工作**（数据分析、了解客户的市场调研）。
  - **与正当利益相比：** 一般**更直接**，因为不需要做不利影响评估。但它**不是空白支票**：合理性条件可能把同样的问题带回来。
  - **可凌驾于拒绝之上：** 该例外**无论有无同意**都适用。严格来说，只要满足条件，为这些目的可以无视狭窄的许可（如应用商店用户选择“仅必要使用”）。
  - **AI 训练：** 模型训练可能落入前两项目的，但可识别性条件会起限制作用。如果数据可以**匿名化**，它就不再是个人数据，也无需任何例外，而且**就应该这样做**。LinkedIn 式的文本训练存在实际困难，因为帖子很难剥离个人数据。
  - **地域性：** 在新加坡进行处理可依赖新加坡的例外，但并不简单，因为**欧盟**可能会主张其法律的域外效力。
  - **例子：**
    - **信用卡公司：** 分析还款记录和交易，了解消费习惯，设计新卡和奖励计划，属于典型用途。
    - **可穿戴设备公司：** 模型训练可以用**匿名化**数据，所以应当这样做。为每位客户个性化功能需要个人数据，这部分依赖该例外。
  - **集团内部分支（不考）：** 第二个分支允许**集团公司内部披露**，条件略有不同。
  - **存在原因：** 没有解释过为什么只有新加坡有这一例外。它的理由是在**可以安全地不依赖同意**的情况下促进业务改进，也就是使用不太可能对个人造成重大影响的情况。

- **Research Exception 研究例外**
  - **Rule:** Use personal data without consent for **research purposes**, subject to four cumulative conditions, which makes it more cumbersome than the other exceptions:
    - The purpose **cannot reasonably be accomplished** without identifiable personal data. Any data that remains personal data counts, not just names.
    - There is a **clear public benefit**, not a purely private one. This is the condition that excludes most private companies.
    - The results are **not used to make decisions affecting the individual**.
    - Published results **do not identify** the individual.
  - **Additional condition for disclosure:** Seeking consent must be **impracticable**. Factors:
    - **Contact information:** Do you have current contact details, or can you get them? If yes, contact the individual for consent.
    - **Disproportionate burden:** Would seeking consent impose disproportionate resource or time demands (e.g. thousands of subjects) so that the research is no longer viable? Mere inconvenience is not enough.
    - **Exceptional circumstances:** Would seeking consent skew the results or defeat the research? This typically applies to psychology and social science, where subjects change their behaviour if they know they are observed.
  - **In practice:** There are no statistics. The lecturer's impression is that it is mainly used by academic institutions like NUS. Private companies can rely on it in principle, but would usually use the previous two exceptions. Other jurisdictions have similar research exceptions with safeguards (non-examinable).
  - **规则：** 为**研究目的**在未经同意的情况下使用个人数据，须同时满足四个条件，因此比其他例外更繁琐：
    - 不使用可识别的个人数据就**无法合理完成**研究目的。只要仍属于个人数据都算，不限于姓名。
    - 存在**明确的公共利益**，而非纯粹的私人利益。这个条件把大多数私营公司排除在外。
    - 研究结果**不得用于作出影响该个人的决定**。
    - 公布结果时**不得识别**个人。
  - **披露的额外条件：** 征求同意必须是**不切实际的**。考虑因素：
    - **联系方式：** 你是否有现有联系方式，或能否取得？如果能，就应联系本人取得同意。
    - **不成比例的负担：** 征求同意是否会造成不成比例的资源或时间负担（如成千上万的研究对象），使研究不再可行？仅仅不方便是不够的。
    - **特殊情况：** 征求同意是否会使结果出现偏差或使研究落空？这通常适用于心理学和社会科学研究，对象知道被观察就会改变行为。
  - **实践中：** 没有统计数据。讲师的印象是主要由 NUS 等学术机构使用。私营公司原则上也可依赖，但通常会用前两个例外。其他法域也有类似的、附带保障措施的研究例外（不考）。

- **Public Availability Exception: Definition and Key Rules 公开可得例外：定义与核心规则**
  - **Rule:** You may **collect, use, or disclose** personal data without consent if it is **publicly available**. This is especially relevant to **AI development**.
  - **Definition:** "Publicly available" means **generally available to the public**: any member of the public can obtain or access the data with **few or no restrictions**. Some restrictions do not defeat public availability.
  - **Alan vs Bob:**
    - **Alan:** has a publicly searchable profile on an open social network. His data is very likely publicly available. Having to sign up is too low a barrier to matter.
    - **Bob:** limits access to a few known users and restricts reposting. His data is less likely to be publicly available, because the restrictions are significant.
  - **AI search:** If ChatGPT or Gemini can surface the personal data, there is very likely practically no restriction on access.
  - **Exceltec Property Management (2018):**
    - **Facts:** Condo MCSTs or managing agents posted meeting notices with residents' names, unit numbers, and voting shares.
    - **Outcome:** No breach. The **public availability exception** applied.
    - **Reason:** The data was already in the **strata roll**. Access requires an MCST application and a fee, but in practice anyone who pays gets access. Some data was also in the **SLA registry** for a fee. Paying for access does not make data non-public.
  - **Combining sources:** Public data can be combined with data collected with valid consent, provided the consent covers the intended use. A different purpose needs separate consent for the privately collected data.
  - **Later deletion:** If the data was public **at the point of collection** (e.g. John's LinkedIn profile, later deleted), you can continue to rely on the exception. You need not keep re-checking, which would be onerous.
  - **Resale of scraped data:** The PDPC is silent on this. The lecturer's logical view is that a **recipient** should be able to rely on the data's earlier public availability. Do **due diligence**, for example a contractual warranty that the data was public when collected, plus an indemnity.
  - **规则：** 如果个人数据是**公开可得的**，可以在未经同意的情况下**收集、使用或披露**。这与 **AI 开发**尤其相关。
  - **定义：** “公开可得”指**一般公众可以获取**：任何公众成员都能在**很少或没有限制**的情况下获取或访问数据。存在某些限制并不否定公开可得性。
  - **Alan 与 Bob：**
    - **Alan：** 在开放社交网络上有可公开搜索的资料，其数据很可能属于公开可得。需要注册这一门槛太低，无关紧要。
    - **Bob：** 只允许少数熟人访问并限制转发，其数据不太可能属于公开可得，因为限制相当大。
  - **AI 搜索：** 如果 ChatGPT 或 Gemini 能查出这些个人数据，那么获取它们很可能几乎没有限制。
  - **Exceltec Property Management（2018）：**
    - **事实：** 公寓管理委员会（MCST）或管理代理在会议通知中张贴了住户的姓名、单位号码和投票份额。
    - **结果：** 不构成违规，适用**公开可得例外**。
    - **理由：** 这些数据本已载于**分层地契登记册（strata roll）**。查阅需向 MCST 申请并付费，但实际上任何付费者都能查到。部分数据也可付费在**土地管理局（SLA）登记系统**查到。需要付费并不使数据变成非公开。
  - **合并来源：** 公开数据可以与经有效同意收集的数据结合，前提是该同意涵盖拟议用途。用于不同目的的话，私下收集的那部分数据需另行取得同意。
  - **事后删除：** 只要数据**在收集时**是公开的（如 John 后来删除的 LinkedIn 资料），就可以继续依赖该例外，无需反复核查，否则负担过重。
  - **转售抓取数据：** PDPC 对此没有说明。讲师从逻辑上认为，**接收方**应可依赖数据此前的公开可得性。应做**尽职调查**，例如让卖方在合同中保证数据收集时是公开的，并提供赔偿承诺。

- **Publicly Observable Data 可公开观察的数据**
  - **Two components:**
    - Observed by **reasonably expected means**.
    - Observed at a **location or event that is open to the public**, where the individual appears.
  - **Reasonably expected means:** The collection must **not surprise** the individual.
    - **Expected:** mall or store CCTV, photo-taking in a store, filming in a public park.
    - **Not expected:** hidden cameras or microphones in a bush.
    - **Good practice:** put up notices (e.g. "we are taking photos here").
  - **Open to the public:** Accessible with few restrictions. Consider physical barriers and security systems. A paid exhibition can still be open to the public.
  - **Special cases:**
    - **Public space turned private:** e.g. a whole restaurant booked for a private event, or a booked private room. Merely booking a table leaves the space open to the public.
    - **Private stays private:** e.g. the inside of a hired taxi, even though people can look in through the window.
  - **Q&A points:**
    - **Other jurisdictions:** This exception is rarer but not unique. Singapore's regime came from **Canada**, which has a similar but not identical exception. In the US, the position varies by state and is complicated by constitutional case law.
    - **Tourist photos:** Taking photos with strangers in the shot is no problem. You act in a **personal capacity**, so the PDPA does not apply, and people in public expect photo-taking anyway.
    - **Camera-enabled glasses:** It is **debatable** whether these are reasonably expected today.
    - **News media:** They rely on a separate **news-reporting exception**, which is not covered.
    - **Cross-border jurisdiction:** The lecturer was unsure what the rules say.
  - **两个要素：**
    - 通过**合理预期的方式**观察到。
    - 在个人出现的、**对公众开放的地点或活动**中观察到。
  - **合理预期的方式：** 收集方式**不能让当事人感到意外**。
    - **可预期：** 商场或商店的闭路电视、店内拍照、公园里的拍摄。
    - **不可预期：** 藏起来的摄像头、藏在灌木丛里的麦克风。
    - **良好做法：** 张贴告示（如“我们会在这里拍照”）。
  - **对公众开放：** 公众可在很少限制下进入。要考虑物理屏障和安保系统。收费展览仍可算对公众开放。
  - **特殊情况：**
    - **公共空间变私人空间：** 例如包下整个餐厅办私人活动，或预订包间。只订一张桌子，空间仍对公众开放。
    - **私人空间仍是私人的：** 例如已被乘客叫下的出租车车内，即使有人能透过车窗看进去。
  - **问答要点：**
    - **其他法域：** 这一例外较少见但并非独有。新加坡的制度源自**加拿大**，加拿大有类似但不完全相同的例外。美国则因州而异，还受宪法判例法影响，更加复杂。
    - **游客拍照：** 镜头里有陌生人没有问题。你是以**个人身份**行事，PDPA 不适用，而且人们在公共场所本来就预期有人拍照。
    - **带摄像头的眼镜：** 目前是否属于合理预期**存在争议**。
    - **新闻媒体：** 依赖另一项**新闻报道例外**，本课不讲。
    - **跨境管辖：** 讲师不确定相关规则如何规定。

- **Exercise: Bryan Air's Personalised Pricing 练习：Bryan Air 的个性化定价**
  - **Scenario:** An airline builds customer profiles from (1) **social media data** and (2) **passport data and purchasing history** to set personalised prices, e.g. charging more to people who display luxury goods.
  - **Research exception:** Fails quickly. There is **no clear public benefit**, because the benefits accrue to the company.
  - **Public availability exception:**
    - **Public social media accounts:** can rely on the exception.
    - **Passport data and purchase history:** **not** publicly available, since they sit in closed systems.
  - **Remaining options for closed-system data:** **Consent**, or an attempt to **stretch the business improvement exception**. That attempt is questionable, and the big issue would be whether the use is **reasonable**.
  - **情景：** 航空公司用（1）**社交媒体数据**和（2）**护照数据及购买记录**建立客户画像来个性化定价，例如向晒奢侈品的人收更高价格。
  - **研究例外：** 很快就能排除，因为**没有明确的公共利益**，好处都归公司。
  - **公开可得例外：**
    - **公开的社交媒体账户：** 可以依赖该例外。
    - **护照数据和购买记录：** **不是**公开可得的，因为存放在封闭系统中。
  - **封闭系统数据的剩余选项：** **同意**，或尝试**扩张解释业务改进例外**。这种尝试值得怀疑，最大的问题是这种使用是否**合理**。

- **Purpose Limitation Obligation: Rule and Rationale 目的限制义务：规则与理由**
  - **Rule:** You may collect, use, or disclose personal data only for purposes that a **reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances**.
  - **Place among the obligations:** Together with consent and notification, it is one of the three obligations engaged whenever you collect, use, or disclose personal data.
  - **Independent obligation:** It applies **even with valid consent** and **even when relying on an exception**.
  - **Why consent is not enough:**
    - Coerced consent, or consent given without capacity, simply means **no consent**, so that is a Consent Obligation breach.
    - Purpose limitation targets something else: **pre-emptive blanket consent**, where individuals do not read the form, are unaware of the risks, or cannot foresee the problems.
    - It acts as a **safety net** for the limitations of consent.
  - **Other jurisdictions (non-examinable):**
    - **EU GDPR:** specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes.
    - **China PIPL:** definite and reasonable purposes, directly related to the processing, using the least-impact manner.
  - **Guidance:** The PDPC guidelines are thin, so the **cases** supply the guidance. There are three considerations:
    - **Nature** of the purpose.
    - **Kind** of personal data.
    - **Manner** of collection, use, or disclosure.
  - **规则：** 只能为**理性的人在当时情况下认为恰当**的目的收集、使用或披露个人数据。
  - **在各项义务中的位置：** 它与同意义务、通知义务一起，构成收集、使用或披露个人数据时都会涉及的三项义务。
  - **独立义务：** **即使取得有效同意**、**即使依赖例外**，它仍然适用。
  - **为何光有同意不够：**
    - 被胁迫的同意或无行为能力的同意，只是意味着**没有同意**，属于违反同意义务。
    - 目的限制针对的是另一种情况：**预先的概括同意**，即个人没读同意书、不了解风险或无法预见问题。
    - 它是弥补同意局限的**安全网**。
  - **其他法域（不考）：**
    - **欧盟 GDPR：** 特定、明确且正当的目的。
    - **中国 PIPL：** 明确、合理的目的，与处理目的直接相关，采取影响最小的方式。
  - **指引：** PDPC 的指引很简短，主要靠**案例**提供指导。有三项考虑因素：
    - 目的的**性质**。
    - 个人数据的**类型**。
    - 收集、使用或披露的**方式**。

- **Consideration 1: Nature of the Purpose 考虑因素一：目的的性质**
  - **Generally inappropriate purposes:** **Illegal** purposes, and purposes that **harm the individual**.
  - **Neo Yong Xiang (2021):**
    - **Facts:** A phone-shop operator used customers' ID scans to secretly register the maximum number of prepaid SIM cards (the limit was three per person) in their names, then sold the cards to shady buyers who used them for illegal purposes.
    - **Outcome:** **Breach** of purpose limitation.
    - **Reason:** A fraudulent, illegal purpose is clearly unreasonable.
  - **Canada (for knowledge only, not examinable):**
    - **Threshold:** whether there is a **bona fide business interest** or a legitimate business need.
    - **Regulator's "no-go zones":**
      - Unfair, unethical, or discriminatory treatment.
      - Publishing personal information and then charging for its removal (blackmail-like).
      - Requiring employees' social media passwords for screening.
      - Surveillance through the individual's own device (e.g. webcam).
    - **Caveat:** These are not Singapore law. What is unacceptable in Canada may be acceptable in Singapore, and vice versa.
  - **一般不恰当的目的：** **违法**目的，以及**伤害个人**的目的。
  - **Neo Yong Xiang（2021）：**
    - **事实：** 手机店经营者利用客户的身份证扫描，偷偷以客户名义登记最大数量的预付费 SIM 卡（每人上限三张），再卖给可疑买家，用于违法目的。
    - **结果：** **违反**目的限制义务。
    - **理由：** 欺诈性、违法的目的显然不合理。
  - **加拿大（仅供了解，不考）：**
    - **门槛：** 是否存在**善意的商业利益**或正当的商业需要。
    - **监管机构的“禁区”：**
      - 不公平、不道德或歧视性的对待。
      - 公布个人信息后收费才删除（类似敲诈）。
      - 要求员工交出社交媒体密码以供审查。
      - 通过个人自己的设备（如网络摄像头）进行监控。
    - **注意：** 这些不是新加坡法律。在加拿大不可接受的，在新加坡可能可以接受，反之亦然。

- **Consideration 2: Kind of Personal Data 考虑因素二：个人数据的类型**
  - **Rule:** **Sensitive** data calls for **additional care** and a higher threshold. There had better be a good reason to process it.
  - **Galaxy Credit (2018):**
    - **Facts:** A moneylender sent debt collectors with a letter of demand and an attached **photograph of the debtor**. Because of a tagging error, debtor W received a letter carrying debtor T's photo.
    - **Outcome:** **Breach** of purpose limitation.
    - **Reason:** Debtors had **consented**, but the practice was still unreasonable. The photographs were **sensitive in context**, because they revealed the person's **indebtedness** to a moneylender.
  - **规则：** **敏感**数据需要**格外小心**，门槛更高。处理它最好有充分的理由。
  - **Galaxy Credit（2018）：**
    - **事实：** 放贷机构派收债员送追款信，并附上**债务人照片**。由于关联错误，债务人 W 收到的信附的是债务人 T 的照片。
    - **结果：** **违反**目的限制义务。
    - **理由：** 债务人**已同意**，但这种做法仍不合理。照片**在具体情境下是敏感的**，因为它揭示了当事人欠放贷人钱这一**负债事实**。

- **Consideration 3: Manner of Collection, Use, or Disclosure 考虑因素三：收集、使用或披露的方式**
  - **Two key factors:**
    - **Effectiveness:** Does the processing actually serve the purpose? If it is ineffective, it is unreasonable.
    - **Less invasive means:** If a less invasive method exists, the processing is less likely to be reasonable.
  - **Club the Chambers (2018):**
    - **Facts:** A LAN gaming centre posted A4 notices of banned members, with **ID copies** and reasons (skipping class, surfing pornography, stealing, gambling), supposedly so staff could identify them.
    - **Outcome:** **Breach** of purpose limitation.
    - **Reason:** The purpose (keeping banned members out) was appropriate, but the manner was defective:
      - **Ineffective:** the notices were placed **behind the staff**, so they could not serve the purpose.
      - **Invasive:** a **private internal blacklist** would have done the job.
    - **Lesson:** A fine purpose carried out in the wrong way still breaches the obligation.
  - **Q&A: legitimate interest does not cure this.** That exception addresses the **Consent Obligation** only, not the separate purpose limitation obligation.
  - **两个关键因素：**
    - **有效性：** 处理是否真的能实现目的？如果无效，就不合理。
    - **侵入性更低的手段：** 如果存在侵入性更低的方法，处理就不太可能是合理的。
  - **Club the Chambers（2018）：**
    - **事实：** 一家局域网游戏中心张贴被禁会员的 A4 告示，附**身份证件复印件**和被禁原因（逃课、浏览色情内容、偷窃、赌博），声称是为了让员工识别这些人。
    - **结果：** **违反**目的限制义务。
    - **理由：** 目的（不让被禁会员进入）是恰当的，但方式有缺陷：
      - **无效：** 告示贴在**员工身后**，无法实现目的。
      - **侵入性过强：** 用**内部黑名单**就能达到目的。
    - **教训：** 目的正当但方式错误，仍然违反该义务。
  - **问答：正当利益例外无法补救。** 该例外只解决**同意义务**，不解决独立的目的限制义务。

- **Proportionality: Open Question in Singapore 相称性：新加坡尚未明确的问题**
  - **Status:** Canada considers **proportionality**. Singapore has **said nothing** on it, so this point is **uncertain** (non-examinable).
  - **Detective Mode (Canada, 2013):**
    - **Facts:** A laptop lessor installed remotely activated software that captured keystrokes, contacts, screenshots, and webcam photos in order to recover lost or stolen laptops.
    - **Outcome:** **Breach** of purpose limitation.
    - **Reason:** The purpose was **good**, the method was **effective**, and arguably there was **no less invasive alternative** (though a tracker might work today). But the **loss of privacy was disproportionate** to the benefit.
  - **AI relevance:** In AI training, "more data is better". A developer can argue effectiveness and necessity, so **proportionality** may be the **most significant** constraint for AI. Whether Singapore will adopt it remains uncertain.
  - **现状：** 加拿大会考虑**相称性**。新加坡**尚无任何说法**，所以这一点**不确定**（不考）。
  - **Detective Mode（加拿大，2013）：**
    - **事实：** 一家笔记本电脑出租商安装了可远程激活的软件，记录键盘输入、联系人、屏幕截图和网络摄像头照片，用于找回丢失或被盗的电脑。
    - **结果：** **违反**目的限制义务。
    - **理由：** 目的**正当**，方法**有效**，而且可以说**没有侵入性更低的替代方案**（尽管如今或许可以装定位器）。但**隐私损失与好处不成比例**。
  - **与 AI 的关系：** AI 训练讲究“数据越多越好”。开发者可以主张有效性和必要性，所以**相称性**可能是对 AI **最重要**的限制。新加坡会否采纳仍不确定。

- **Take-Home Question: Clarifai and OkCupid 课后思考题：Clarifai 与 OkCupid**
  - **Scenario:** Clarifai obtained OkCupid users' photos to train facial recognition AI. It later deleted the photos and the models trained on them.
  - **Question:** Even if consent had been obtained (e.g. through a sign-up notification), would this breach the purpose limitation obligation in Singapore?
  - **Approach:** Run through the three considerations (nature, kind of data, manner) and the open proportionality question.
  - **Next week:** The course moves beyond collection, use, and disclosure.
  - **情景：** Clarifai 获取 OkCupid 用户照片来训练人脸识别 AI，后来删除了这些照片以及用它们训练的模型。
  - **问题：** 即使取得了同意（如注册时的通知），在新加坡这样做是否违反目的限制义务？
  - **思路：** 把三项考虑因素（性质、数据类型、方式）以及尚未明确的相称性问题都走一遍。
  - **下周：** 课程将超越收集、使用和披露的范畴。
## Week 4 Learning Tips
Start with the "why" behind each exception, because each one solves a different problem. Legitimate interest exists for situations where consent would never be given, like fraudsters or hotel skippers. Business improvement makes low-risk internal uses of data you already hold easier. Research serves the public good. Public availability recognises that you cannot meaningfully protect what anyone can already see. Once you see each exception as a policy answer to a specific problem, its conditions stop looking arbitrary. Research demands a clear public benefit because it is meant for public-good research. Business improvement covers use only, because it is about data the organisation already holds.

先从每项例外背后的“为什么”入手，因为每项例外解决的问题都不同。正当利益例外针对的是当事人绝不会同意的情形，比如欺诈者或逃单住客。业务改进例外让机构对已持有数据的低风险内部使用变得更容易。研究例外服务于公共利益。公开可得例外承认，对任何人都看得到的东西，很难再给予有意义的保护。一旦把每项例外看作针对某个特定问题的政策回应，它的条件就不再显得随意。研究例外要求明确的公共利益，是因为它本就为公益研究而设。业务改进例外只涵盖使用，是因为它针对的是机构已经持有的数据。

The single most testable contrast this week is between the adverse effect assessment for deemed consent by notification and the one for legitimate interest. Under notification, adverse effects must be eliminated. Under legitimate interest, you mitigate and then balance the residual effects against the interest. Students often merge the two. Build a small comparison table with four rows: what must be done with adverse effects, whether direct marketing is allowed, what must be disclosed, and whether the assessment must be shown. Then add the business improvement exception as a third column, noting that it needs no adverse effect assessment but still has a reasonableness check.

本周最可能考的对比，是通知视为同意与正当利益例外中的不利影响评估。在通知视为同意下，不利影响必须被消除。在正当利益下，你先减轻不利影响，再把残余影响与利益进行权衡。同学们常常把两者混为一谈。建议做一张小对比表，列四行：对不利影响必须做什么、能否用于直接营销、必须披露什么、评估是否必须出示。然后把业务改进例外加为第三列，注明它不需要不利影响评估，但仍有合理性审查。

The RHC exercise shows how the lecturer wants you to structure a legitimate interest answer. Go through the three steps in order and put every interest in the right bucket. Harms to the drivers belong on the adverse effect side. The company's revenue and passengers' safety belong on the legitimate interest side, even though students instinctively wanted to list them as "adverse effects". Practise a fixed template: articulate a specific, real benefit (not just "revenue"); list the likely harms, distinguishing correct from wrongful outcomes; propose mitigation such as human review, warnings, or a right to explain; weigh the residue and ask whether there is a less invasive alternative; then state how reliance will be disclosed. Keep the lecturer's practical rule in mind: rely on the exception only when the scale is clearly tilted, and otherwise fall back on consent.

RHC 练习展示了讲师希望你如何组织正当利益题的答案。按顺序走完三个步骤，把每种利益放进正确的一栏。司机受到的伤害属于不利影响一侧。公司的收入和乘客的安全属于正当利益一侧，尽管同学们本能地想把它们列为“不利影响”。练习一个固定模板：阐明具体而真实的好处（不只是“收入”）；列出可能的伤害，区分正确与错误的结果；提出人工复核、警告、解释权等减轻措施；权衡残余影响，并问有没有侵入性更低的替代方案；最后说明如何披露依赖情况。记住讲师的实务规则：只有天平明显倾斜时才依赖该例外，否则就回到同意。

Watch for scope traps that this week's material invites. Business improvement covers use only. It cannot be used for direct marketing, but it can support preparatory analytics. It is unnecessary if you can anonymise the data. Public availability is judged at the point of collection, so later deletion does not matter. Paying a fee, as in Exceltec, does not make data private, but meaningful access controls, as with Bob, do. In Bryan Air, the trap is treating the whole dataset as one: the public social media data and the closed-system passport and purchase data need separate analysis. Train yourself to split datasets by source before choosing an exception.

注意本周内容容易引出的范围陷阱。业务改进例外只涵盖使用。它不能用于直接营销，但可以支持准备性分析。如果能把数据匿名化，就根本不需要它。公开可得性以收集时为准，所以事后删除没有影响。像 Exceltec 案那样需要付费，并不使数据变成私密的，但像 Bob 那样有实质性的访问控制则会。Bryan Air 题的陷阱是把整个数据集当作一回事：公开的社交媒体数据和封闭系统里的护照及购买数据需要分开分析。训练自己在选择例外之前，先按来源拆分数据集。

The biggest conceptual pitfall in the second half is assuming that consent, or an exception, ends the analysis. Purpose limitation is an independent safety net. Galaxy Credit had consent and still breached it. In Club the Chambers, relying on legitimate interest would only have fixed the consent problem. Make one-line "facts / failing / lesson" cards for each case. Neo Yong Xiang failed on the nature of the purpose, because it was illegal. Galaxy Credit failed on the kind of data, because the photographs were sensitive in context and revealed indebtedness. Club the Chambers failed on manner: the notices were ineffective and a private list was less invasive. Detective Mode failed on proportionality, even though the purpose was good, the method effective, and no alternative was available. That last progression is worth memorising, because it shows each factor independently sinking a practice.

下半节课最大的概念陷阱，是以为取得同意或依赖例外，分析就结束了。目的限制是一张独立的安全网。Galaxy Credit 取得了同意，仍然违规。在 Club the Chambers 案中，依赖正当利益只能解决同意问题。给每个案例做一张“事实 / 失误 / 教训”的一行卡片。Neo Yong Xiang 败在目的的性质，因为目的违法。Galaxy Credit 败在数据类型，因为照片在具体情境下敏感，揭示了负债事实。Club the Chambers 败在方式：告示无效，而内部名单侵入性更低。Detective Mode 败在相称性，尽管目的正当、方法有效、也没有替代方案。最后这个递进值得记住，因为它显示了每个因素都可以单独让一种做法站不住脚。

Respect the scope signals the lecturer gave. The EU and India comparisons, the intra-group branch of business improvement, other jurisdictions' research exceptions, and the Canadian no-go zones were flagged as background or non-examinable. Proportionality is explicitly an open question in Singapore. In an exam, you can raise proportionality as a possible further consideration, especially for AI training, but frame it as uncertain under Singapore law rather than as settled doctrine. Likewise, keep the lecturer's hedges: "pure revenue is probably too broad" and "camera glasses are debatable" are arguments to make, not rules to state as absolutes.

尊重讲师给出的范围信号。欧盟和印度的比较、业务改进例外的集团内部分支、其他法域的研究例外，以及加拿大的禁区，都被标明为背景知识或不考内容。相称性在新加坡被明确定位为尚未解决的问题。考试中，你可以把相称性作为一个可能的进一步考虑提出来，尤其是在 AI 训练题里，但要表述为新加坡法下尚不确定，而不是既定法理。同样，保留讲师的保留语气：“纯粹的收入大概过于宽泛”“摄像头眼镜存在争议”，这些是要去论证的观点，而不是作为绝对规则陈述的结论。

Finally, use the Clarifai and OkCupid question as your rehearsal piece, because it ties the whole week together. First ask whether consent or an exception covers the collection, and notice that public availability and business improvement each have limits here. Then, assuming consent was obtained, run the three purpose limitation considerations: the nature of training facial recognition, the sensitivity of dating-app photos, and the manner of bulk transfer. Close with the proportionality question that the lecturer flagged as most relevant to AI. Writing that answer out once in full will consolidate both halves of this week far better than rereading the slides.

最后，把 Clarifai 与 OkCupid 这道题当作你的演练题，因为它把整周内容串了起来。先问收集是否有同意或例外支撑，并注意公开可得例外和业务改进例外在这里各有局限。然后假设已取得同意，走一遍目的限制的三项考虑：训练人脸识别的目的性质、约会应用照片的敏感性，以及批量转移的方式。最后讨论讲师指出的、对 AI 最相关的相称性问题。完整地把这道题写一遍，比反复看课件更能巩固本周上下两部分的内容。
## Week 4 Lecture
- [18:35:37–18:37:04] **Recap and the Exceptions to Consent**

  In the previous seminar, we talked about the consent obligation, and we looked at actual consent as well as deemed consent. For today's lesson, we'll begin with the final way an organisation can comply with the consent obligation, which is to rely on one of the exceptions to it.

  If you look inside the legislation, inside the PDPA (you don't have to, right?), you'll see there's actually a very long list of exceptions to consent. Some of them are pretty straightforward. For emergency situations, for example, you can do away with consent. For our purposes, we're going to look at just four of the more significant exceptions: the legitimate interest exception, the business improvement exception, the research exception, and the public availability exception. In practice, these four are the ones organisations tend to rely on more often than the others.

  在上一次研讨课中，我们讨论了同意义务（consent obligation），讲了实际同意（actual consent）和视为同意（deemed consent）。今天这节课，我们先来看机构履行同意义务的最后一种方式，也就是依赖同意义务的某一项例外。

  如果你去翻法律条文，也就是 PDPA（不翻也没关系，对吧？），会发现同意的例外其实有很长一串。有些很直白，比如在紧急情况下，就可以不需要同意。我们这里只看其中四个比较重要的例外：正当利益例外（legitimate interest exception）、业务改进例外（business improvement exception）、研究例外（research exception）和公开可得例外（public availability exception）。因为在实践中，机构最常依赖的就是这四个例外。
- [18:37:04–18:38:50] **Legitimate Interest Exception: The Basic Idea and Three Requirements**

  Let's begin with the legitimate interest exception. What's the idea behind it? Basically, if the organisation is pursuing some, quote unquote, "legitimate interest", then it may collect, use, or disclose personal data without obtaining consent.

  But it's not so straightforward, right? You can't just say, "Oh, I have a legitimate purpose, so I don't have to get consent." You actually need to satisfy three conditions if you want to rely on this exception. First, of course, you need to identify and articulate your interest: what exactly is the legitimate interest you're pursuing? Second, similar to deemed consent by notification, which we covered in the previous seminar, you need to conduct an adverse effect assessment. That means assessing whether what you're doing is likely to have an adverse effect on the individual. There's a slight difference from the notification version that you need to pay attention to, and I'll go into it a bit later. The last thing you need to do is disclose that you're relying on the exception. So you can't do this secretly. You actually have to tell people, "I'm using your personal data for this particular legitimate interest." So those are the three requirements.

  我们先来看正当利益例外。这个例外背后的思路是什么？基本上就是，如果机构在追求某种所谓的“正当利益”，那它可以在不取得同意的情况下收集、使用或披露个人数据。

  但事情没那么简单，对吧？你不能只说“我有正当目的，所以不用取得同意”。要依赖这个例外，你实际上需要满足三个条件。第一，当然是要识别并阐明你的利益：你追求的正当利益到底是什么？第二，和上次讲过的通知视为同意（deemed consent by notification）类似，你也需要做一个不利影响评估（adverse effect assessment），也就是评估你所做的事情是否可能对个人造成不利影响。不过这里和通知那种情况有一点细微差别，需要留意，我稍后会深入讲。最后，你需要披露你在依赖这个例外，也就是说你不能偷偷摸摸地做，而是要告诉别人：“我正在为了这项特定的正当利益使用你的个人数据。”这就是三项要求。
- [18:38:50–18:41:10] **Step One: Identifying and Articulating the Legitimate Interest**

  Let's look at the first one. The first requirement is for the organisation to actually articulate or state what its legitimate interest is. In other words, what's the big reason, or the important reason, you have for collecting, using, or disclosing the personal data?

  When you're articulating your legitimate interest, there are a few things you should point out. First, you need to identify what exactly the benefit is. What benefits do you hope to get from your collection, use, or disclosure? Something like, "I'm trying to ensure the safety of my students," or "I'm trying to prevent customers from committing fraud."

  You should also identify who exactly the beneficiary is, meaning the person or people who are supposed to benefit. In many cases, that will of course be the organisation itself, but it's also possible for the organisation to be trying to benefit other people or the general public.

  The third thing you need to make sure of is that whatever benefit you're chasing is a real and present benefit, and not something merely speculative. If you're going to highlight a particular benefit, it can't be something that might possibly happen. You need to show that this benefit will arise if you're allowed to collect, use, and disclose the personal data. So no speculative things that you're guessing may or may not happen.

  One important limitation on this exception is that you can't rely on it to send direct marketing messages. Again, that's similar to deemed consent by notification. So that's the first step: identify what exactly your legitimate interest is.

  我们来看第一项。第一项要求是机构必须真正阐明或说明它的正当利益是什么。换句话说，你收集、使用或披露这些个人数据，背后那个重要的理由是什么？

  在阐明正当利益时，你需要指出几点。第一，当然要指出好处到底是什么，你希望通过收集、使用或披露得到什么好处。比如“我要确保学生的安全”，或者“我要防止客户进行欺诈”。

  你还应该指出受益人到底是谁，也就是谁应该从中受益。很多时候受益的当然是机构自己，但机构也有可能是为了让其他人或广大公众受益。

  第三，你要确保你追求的好处是真实且当下存在的，而不仅仅是推测性的。如果你要强调某个好处，它不能是“可能会发生”的东西。你需要证明，只要允许你收集、使用和披露个人数据，这个好处就会出现。所以不能是那些你猜测可能发生也可能不发生的东西。

  这个例外有一个重要的限制：你不能依赖它来发送直接营销信息（direct marketing messages），这一点同样和通知视为同意类似。这就是第一步：确定你的正当利益到底是什么。
- [18:41:10–18:45:19] **Step Two: The Adverse Effect Assessment**

  The second step is to conduct the adverse effect assessment. Again, that means identifying whether what you're doing will cause an adverse effect on the individual. The guidelines do try to give some insight into what counts as an adverse effect, and it's quite interesting because there's a bit of nuance here.

  First, what clearly counts as an adverse effect? Physical harm to the individual, any harassment, serious alarm, or distress. All of these are clearly adverse effects. You don't have to think much more about whether, for example, physical harm counts.

  However, if you're looking at other potential effects, you need to consider the prevailing social norms. This matters because in some circumstances, processing personal data can produce an effect that looks harmful at first, as if it harms the individual, but that society generally regards as acceptable. For example, say you're a bank, and you process personal data to determine an individual's creditworthiness. On that basis, you say, "Okay, I can't grant you this loan because you're not creditworthy." Arguably, that's a kind of adverse effect, because the individual can't get the loan. But based on prevailing social norms, it isn't actually regarded as an adverse effect. It's an acceptable decision to make about an individual. So, very simply, if you're looking at other kinds of adverse effects, you need to consider the prevailing social norms.

  So how do you go about predicting or identifying the likely adverse effects? You look at all the circumstances, but there are some pointers you can consider. First, you look at the impact of the collection, use, or disclosure on the individual, and you consider both how severe it is and how likely it is that the effect will arise. Second, you should consider what type of personal data you're going to process. Naturally, if the personal data is sensitive, it's more likely to cause harm. You should also consider whether the individual belongs to a vulnerable group. Is this individual in a group that's likely to be subject to discrimination? Is this individual a child? And so on. All of these feed into the assessment of whether your collection, use, or disclosure is likely to cause an adverse effect.

  You'd also consider how much you're collecting, using, or disclosing, and how you're going to process the personal data. You'd consider the reasonableness of your purpose. And if you're going to make a prediction or a decision about the individual, you should think about whether it's likely to cause physical harm, or result in serious alarm, and so on. In other words, you should consider all the circumstances, but these are some pointers you can use.

  第二步是做不利影响评估，也就是判断你所做的事情会不会对个人造成不利影响。相关指引（guidelines）尝试说明什么算不利影响，这里挺有意思，因为有一些细微之处。

  首先，什么明显属于不利影响？对个人的人身伤害、任何骚扰、严重惊恐或痛苦。这些都明显属于不利影响，你不需要再多想，比如人身伤害算不算不利影响。

  不过，如果你考虑的是其他潜在影响，那就需要考虑当下的社会规范（prevailing social norms）。这一点很重要，因为在某些情况下，处理个人数据产生的某种影响乍看像是有害的，好像伤害了个人，但社会一般认为它是可以接受的。比如，假设你是一家银行，你处理个人数据来判断某人的信用状况，然后据此说：“好，我不能批给你这笔贷款，因为你信用不够。”可以说这是一种不利影响，因为这个人拿不到贷款。但按照当下的社会规范，这其实不被视为不利影响，而是对个人作出的一个可以接受的决定。所以简单来说，如果你看的是其他类型的不利影响，就需要考虑当下的社会规范。

  那么你怎样预测或识别可能的不利影响呢？你要综合考虑所有情况，不过有一些要点可以参考。首先，看收集、使用或披露对个人的影响，既要考虑有多严重，也要考虑这种影响发生的可能性有多大。第二，要考虑你将处理的个人数据属于什么类型。很自然地，如果个人数据是敏感的，就更可能造成伤害。你还应该考虑这个人是否属于弱势群体：这个人是否属于容易受到歧视的群体？是不是儿童？等等。所有这些都关系到你的收集、使用或披露是否可能造成不利影响。

  你还要考虑你收集、使用或披露的量有多大，以及你将如何处理这些个人数据。你要考虑你的目的是否合理。如果你要对个人作出预测或决定，你应该想想这是否可能造成人身伤害、导致严重惊恐等等。换句话说，你应该考虑所有情况，但这些是可以参考的一些要点。
- [18:45:19–18:47:07] **Mitigation, Balancing, and Retaining the Assessment**

  After going through this assessment, you've determined the likely adverse effects on the individual. There are then two things you need to do with this information. The first is to implement reasonable measures to eliminate, reduce the likelihood of, or mitigate any adverse effects. Again, this is similar to what you do for deemed consent by notification: you find some way to get rid of the adverse effects.

  What's different for this exception is that you don't have to completely eliminate the adverse effects. For deemed consent by notification, you do need to get rid of the adverse effect completely. Whereas for this exception, what the law allows is a balancing exercise. You try to get rid of the adverse effects, and if there are any residual adverse effects, you have to see whether they outweigh the legitimate interest or not. If the legitimate interest is more important and outweighs the adverse effect, you can carry on. If the legitimate interest doesn't outweigh the adverse effect, you can't use this exception.

  Finally, once you've completed this assessment, you have to retain it for the whole period during which you're collecting, using, or disclosing the personal data in reliance on this exception.

  做完这个评估之后，你已经确定了对个人可能产生的不利影响。接下来你需要用这些信息做两件事。第一，必须采取合理措施，消除不利影响、降低其发生的可能性，或者减轻不利影响。这同样和通知视为同意的做法类似：想办法去掉这些不利影响。

  这个例外的不同之处在于，你不必完全消除不利影响。在通知视为同意中，你确实需要完全去掉不利影响。而对于这个例外，法律允许你做一个权衡（balancing）。你先尽量去掉不利影响，如果还有残余的不利影响，就要看它是否超过了正当利益。如果正当利益更重要，压过了不利影响，你就可以继续。如果正当利益压不过不利影响，你就不能使用这个例外。

  最后，完成评估之后，在你依赖这个例外收集、使用或披露个人数据的整个期间，都必须保留这份评估。
- [18:47:07–18:48:15] **Step Three: Disclosing Reliance on the Exception**

  Third point: if you're going to rely on the exception, you need to tell people, to disclose that you're relying on it. Essentially, you need to give individuals reasonable access to information about your collection, use, or disclosure. In many cases, that will simply mean putting a notice in your data protection policy. On top of that, you should also provide the business contact information of someone who can address individuals' questions about your reliance on this exception, and this will usually be your data protection officer.

  One important thing to bear in mind: while you need to tell people you're relying on this exception, you don't have to show them your adverse effect assessment. That you can keep secret, until the PDPC asks for it. Until then, you don't have to show it to anyone.

  Okay, so let me show you some examples of how this exception can apply in practice.

  第三点：如果你要依赖这个例外，就需要告诉别人，也就是披露你在依赖这个例外。基本上，你需要让个人能够合理地获取关于你的收集、使用或披露的信息。很多时候，这只需要在你的数据保护政策里放一条说明。此外，你还应该提供一个能解答个人对你依赖该例外的疑问的人的业务联系方式，通常就是你的数据保护官（data protection officer，DPO）。

  有一点要记住：虽然你需要告诉别人你在依赖这个例外，但你不需要向他们展示你的不利影响评估。这份评估你可以保密，直到 PDPC 要求查看为止。在那之前，你不需要给任何人看。

  好，接下来给大家看几个这个例外在实践中如何适用的例子。
- [18:48:15–18:50:43] **Examples: Insurance Fraud Detection and the Hotel Skipper Blacklist**

  This first example involves an insurance company that wants to do fraud detection and prevention. The company suspects that some of its customers are making fraudulent claims, so it wants to collect, use, and disclose personal data about their past insurance claims to detect potential fraud. Here, the insurance company would go through the process I just discussed: conduct the assessment of legitimate interests, look at the adverse effects, and see whether they outweigh the legitimate interest or not. If the conclusion is that the legitimate interest outweighs the adverse effect, the insurance company can carry on without having to obtain consent.

  Another interesting example of how this exception can be used: here you have multiple organisations, several hotels, and they want to collaborate and put together a blacklist of so-called hotel skippers, meaning hotel guests who repeatedly fail to pay for their rooms. This blacklist would contain personal data like names, passport numbers, and so on, of these recalcitrant hotel skippers. Again, this would be a legitimate interest, so the hotels could use this exception to collect, use, and disclose personal data without getting consent.

  What you can observe from these two examples, fraud detection and prevention of non-payment, is that these are circumstances where it seems really unlikely the individual would give consent. If you're a hotel skipper, or if you're committing fraud when claiming insurance, it's very likely you won't consent to the organisation using your personal data this way, because it would automatically lead to negative consequences for you.

  第一个例子涉及一家保险公司，它想做欺诈检测和预防。公司怀疑部分客户在提出欺诈性理赔，因此想收集、使用和披露客户过往理赔的个人数据，以发现潜在的欺诈。这时保险公司就要走一遍我刚才讲的流程：评估正当利益，看不利影响，再看不利影响是否超过正当利益。如果结论是正当利益压过了不利影响，保险公司就可以继续，而不需要取得同意。

  另一个关于如何使用这个例外的有趣例子：这里有多家机构，也就是几家酒店，它们想合作建立一份所谓“逃单住客”（hotel skippers）的黑名单，也就是经常不付房费的酒店住客。这份黑名单会包含这些屡教不改的逃单住客的姓名、护照号码等个人数据。同样，这属于正当利益，酒店可以用这个例外在不取得同意的情况下收集、使用和披露个人数据。

  从这两个例子，也就是欺诈检测和防止欠款中，你大概可以看出，这些情况下个人似乎非常不可能给出同意。如果你是逃单住客，或者你在申请保险理赔时进行欺诈，你很可能不会同意机构这样使用你的个人数据，因为这会直接给你带来负面后果。
- [18:50:43–18:53:27] **Q&A: Would This Work under the EU GDPR?**

  A student asks whether this example is set in Singapore, and whether the same thing would be acceptable in the EU under the GDPR, or might be judged differently there.

  Yeah. If you want to compare: what I've presented to you is Singapore's version of legitimate interest. Other jurisdictions, like the EU, also have this idea of legitimate interests, but it's phrased slightly differently. In Singapore, legitimate interest counts as an exception to the consent obligation. What that means is that, by default, organisations should get consent, unless there's some reason why they can't rely on consent. Other jurisdictions treat legitimate interest as on par with consent, which means you can choose. The law doesn't care which one you're relying on, consent or legitimate interest.

  If you look at the EU GDPR, what it says is that processing shall be lawful if it's necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or a third party, except where such interests are overridden by the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject. So in the EU, there would also be this sort of balancing process, where you compare the interests of the controller against the interests of the data subject. But if you're looking at hotel skippers, who are arguably doing something either immoral or illegal, I suspect the balancing exercise would tilt in favour of the hotels.

  The student then asks whether you could argue that the skippers risk having no place to stay if every hotel bans them.

  Well, yeah, I guess we could make that argument as well, but I'd still lean towards the hotels in that particular case. I suppose the hotels would probably say it was their own fault for not paying.

  看欧盟 GDPR，它规定：如果处理对于控制者（controller）或第三方所追求的正当利益是必要的，那么该处理就是合法的，除非这些利益被数据主体（data subject）的利益或基本权利与自由所压倒。所以在欧盟，也会有这样一种权衡过程，比较控制者的利益和数据主体的利益。不过，如果看的是逃单住客，他们做的事情可以说要么不道德、要么违法，我猜权衡结果会偏向酒店。

- [19:37:45–19:39:06] **Business Improvement Exception: The Four Purposes**

  This exception is distinctly Singaporean. What it says is that you can use personal data without consent if you're doing so for a so-called business improvement purpose. Note that it covers use only. It doesn't cover collection or disclosure.

  What are these purposes? The first is that you're trying to develop or improve your goods or services. The second is that you're trying to improve, enhance, or develop some new method or process for doing business, such as your digital processes. The third is that you're trying to learn or understand the behaviour and preferences of individuals, who are most likely your customers. The fourth is that you're trying to identify goods or services suitable for individuals. That means you're trying to see, for any particular individual, which of your products are suitable for them. Or you could be trying to personalise or customise your goods or services for those individuals.

  So these are all business improvement purposes, and if you're doing one of them, you don't have to get consent. I honestly think these are quite important.

  这个例外是新加坡特有的。它规定，如果你是为了所谓的业务改进目的（business improvement purpose），就可以在不取得同意的情况下使用个人数据。注意，它只涵盖使用，不涵盖收集或披露。

  这些目的是什么？第一，你在开发或改进你的商品或服务。第二，你在改进、提升或开发某种新的经营方法或流程，比如你的数字化流程。第三，你在了解个人的行为和偏好，这些人最有可能是你的客户。第四，你在识别适合个人的商品或服务，也就是针对某个具体的人，看看你的哪些产品适合他。或者你也可能是在为这些人个性化或定制你的商品或服务。

  这些都是业务改进目的，只要你做的是其中之一，就不需要取得同意。我真心觉得这些相当重要。

  But there are two conditions. First, you have to show that you have no choice but to use the personal data. That is, you must show you couldn't achieve these purposes without using personal data in an individually identifiable form.

  The second is a fairly general condition: you must make sure your use of the personal data is reasonable. I guess that means if you had to disclose it to your customers, they wouldn't be horrified. I think that's the general premise of reasonableness. And just like the legitimate interest exception, you can't use this for sending... sorry.

  不过有两个条件。第一，你必须证明你别无选择，只能使用个人数据。也就是说，你必须证明不使用可识别个人身份的个人数据，就无法实现这些目的。

  第二个条件比较笼统：你必须确保对个人数据的使用是合理的。我想意思是，如果你把它告诉客户，他们不会被吓到。我认为这就是合理性的大致前提。另外，和正当利益例外一样，你不能用它来发送……抱歉。

- [19:48:34–19:50:15] **Examples: Credit Card Company and Wearables Company**

  These are just to show you the actual intended use cases of this exception. In the first example, a credit card company wants to use customers' personal data, for example their credit payment history and transactions, to derive insights on its customers' spending habits so as to develop a new credit card and new reward schemes. This would be one of the typical use cases for this exception.

  Another example is a wearables company, so smart watches and the like, that wants to develop some new functionality in its application to give customers reminders when their vital signs change. This company wants to use its customers' personal data to train its machine learning model to monitor vital signs and develop the new function. In this case, it assesses that it actually doesn't need personal data per se for training, so it can just anonymise the data and train on it. If that's the case, that's what it should do. But it also assesses that it needs the personal data to personalise the product feature for each customer. Then it uses personal data, and here it can rely on this business improvement exception.

- [19:52:14–19:53:09] **Research Exception: Four Conditions**

  Let me move on to the next exception, which is quite straightforward: the research exception. Here, organisations can again use personal data without consent for research purposes, but with four conditions, so it's a lot more cumbersome.

  First, you need to show that your research purpose couldn't reasonably be accomplished unless you use the personal data in identifiable form. Second, and this is the condition that will prevent most private companies from using this exception, you have to show a clear public benefit to using the personal data. It can't just be a purely private benefit. Third, you shouldn't use the results of your research to make any decision affecting the individual. And fourth, if you publish the results, you must do so in a way that doesn't identify the individual.

  我们接着看下一个例外，它相当直白：研究例外。这里，机构同样可以为研究目的在不取得同意的情况下使用个人数据，但有四个条件，所以麻烦得多。

  第一，你需要证明，除非使用可识别形式的个人数据，否则无法合理地实现研究目的。第二，这个条件会把大多数私营公司挡在这个例外之外：你必须证明使用个人数据有明确的公共利益（clear public benefit），不能只是纯粹的私人利益。第三，你不应该用研究结果去作出任何影响个人的决定。第四，如果你发表研究结果，必须以不识别个人的方式发表。

- [19:54:59–19:57:41] **Research Exception: Disclosure and Impracticability of Consent**

  Moving on: if you want to disclose personal data for research, there's one more condition. You must show that it's impracticable to seek the individual's consent for the disclosure. You must show it wouldn't be possible to do the research if you had to go and get consent from every single research subject.

  So how do we decide whether seeking consent is impracticable? We can consider a few factors. First, do you have the contact information, or is it possible for you to get it? If the answer is yes, then you go and contact the individual to get consent. Second, would it impose a disproportionate resource demand, or take up so much time that carrying out the research is no longer viable? Basically, the problem here is that there are too many research subjects, thousands or hundreds of thousands, and trying to get consent from every single one would make the research impossible. Third, you can point to exceptional circumstances where reaching out to the subject for consent would ruin the research. It would either skew the results or defeat the purpose of the research. That's the case if the research has to be done without the subjects knowing they're being researched, which normally happens in more psychological or social science types of research. If you tell individuals they're being observed, they'll change their behaviour.

  That's all I'll say about this exception. I'd also point out that other jurisdictions have similar exceptions for research purposes, again with safeguards. In principle, though, even a private company can rely on this exception, as long as it satisfies those requirements.

  接下来：如果你想为研究目的披露个人数据，还有一个额外条件。你必须证明就该披露征求个人同意是不切实际的（impracticable），也就是证明如果你必须去取得每一位研究对象的同意，研究就无法进行。

  那么怎样判断征求同意是否不切实际呢？可以考虑几个因素。第一，你有没有联系方式，或者能不能拿到联系方式？如果答案是能，那你就应该去联系这个人取得同意。第二，这是否会造成不成比例的资源负担，或者耗费太多时间，以至于研究不再可行？基本上，这里的问题是研究对象太多，成千上万甚至几十万，要逐一取得同意会让研究无法进行。第三，你可以指出存在特殊情况，即联系研究对象征求同意会毁掉研究：要么使结果出现偏差，要么使研究目的落空。如果研究必须在对象不知情的情况下进行，就属于这种情况，这通常出现在偏心理学或社会科学类的研究中。如果你告诉一个人他正在被观察，他就会改变行为。

  关于这个例外我就讲这么多。我还要指出，其他法域也有类似的研究例外，同样附带保障措施。不过原则上，即使是私营公司，只要满足这些要求，也可以依赖这个例外。
- [19:57:41–20:00:28] **Public Availability Exception: Meaning and the Alan/Bob Example**

  Let me now move on to the last one, which is actually more relevant when it comes to AI development: the public availability exception. This one is perhaps a bit better known. It says you can collect, use, or disclose personal data without consent if the personal data is already publicly available, for example things that are already online, or on public social media.

  So what does publicly available mean? It means generally available to the public. And generally available to the public means any member of the public can obtain or access the data with few or no restrictions. In short, anyone should be able to access the data without many restrictions impeding access.

  One thing to note is that something can be generally available to the public even if there are some restrictions. Having a few restrictions doesn't mean it isn't available to the public. For example, here we have Alan, a member of an online social network like Facebook, which is open to the public. His membership profile is publicly searchable, with his name and his personal data, and he regularly updates his profile. In this case, the data he shares on the network is very likely to be publicly available, since any other user of the social network could gain access to it, even if they accessed his profile page by accident. So the fact that you have to sign up to the social network to access this personal data still means the data is publicly available. The restriction is too low in this case.

  But we have a different person, Bob, also a member of the social network, who limits access to a few users he personally knows. He also restricts the reposting of what he puts on his profile. In this case, it's less likely that his profile is publicly available, because the restrictions are now quite significant.

  现在我们来看最后一个，它其实和 AI 开发更相关：公开可得例外。这个可能更为人熟知一些。它规定，如果个人数据已经是公开可得的，比如已经在网上、在公开的社交媒体上，那么你可以在不取得同意的情况下收集、使用或披露这些个人数据。

  那么“公开可得”（publicly available）是什么意思？它指的是“一般公众可以获取”（generally available to the public）。而“一般公众可以获取”是指任何公众成员都能在很少或没有限制的情况下获取或访问这些数据。简而言之，任何人都应该能在没有太多限制阻碍的情况下访问这些数据。

  要注意的是，即使存在一些限制，某样东西仍然可以算作一般公众可以获取。有少量限制并不意味着它不对公众开放。比如这里有 Alan，他是一个类似 Facebook 的、对公众开放的在线社交网络的成员。他的会员资料可以公开搜索，包括姓名和个人数据，而且他会定期更新资料。在这种情况下，他在该网络上分享的数据很可能属于公开可得，因为社交网络的任何其他用户都能访问这些数据，即使是无意中点进了他的主页。所以，虽然你需要注册社交网络才能访问这些个人数据，这些数据仍然属于公开可得。这里的限制门槛太低了。

  但还有另一个人 Bob，他也是这个社交网络的成员，但他只允许少数他认识的用户访问他的资料，还限制别人转发他放在资料里的内容。在这种情况下，他的资料就不太可能属于公开可得，因为现在的限制相当大。

  Yes. If you can just type into something like ChatGPT or Gemini, and the AI service gives you the personal data, it's very likely there's practically no restriction on any member of the public getting access. So that's the principle.

- [20:01:08–20:03:48] **Case: Exceltec Property Management**

  One real case on this is Exceltec Property Management. In this case, the organisations were either the management corporations or the managing agents of three condominium developments. They were holding meetings, and you're required to put up notices of these meetings. So each of them put up details on notice boards containing residents' personal data, including their names, unit numbers, and voting shares. The residents, for various reasons, weren't happy with this, and they complained about the disclosure of their personal data.

  The PDPC said the organisations could rely on the public availability exception. Where was this data found? The personal data they published was already publicly available, because every condominium development has a strata roll, which is the official record of all the residents in the condominium. Although you do need to apply to the MCST for access and pay a fee, so there are some restrictions, practically speaking the restrictions are very low. So it still counts as publicly available data. Also, some of the information could be found on the Singapore Land Authority's registry, which is again accessible as long as you pay a certain fee. So what this case demonstrates is that even if you have to pay for access to personal data, that doesn't mean the personal data isn't publicly available.

  A student points out that you have to apply to the MCST, so there's an inherent risk the application might not be approved. Can that be considered a low restriction rather than a high one?

  In this particular case, what the PDPC found was that yes, you do need to apply to the MCST, and strictly speaking, not everyone is eligible for access. But in practice, anyone who applies gets access. In practice, the MCST isn't going to check whether you're a prospective buyer or whatever. They just see that you've paid the fee, and that's all. So that's why the barrier is low.

  这方面有一个真实案例：Exceltec Property Management。在这个案例中，涉案机构是三个公寓项目的管理委员会或管理代理。它们要召开会议，而法律要求张贴会议通知。所以它们各自在告示板上张贴了包含住户个人数据的详细信息，包括姓名、单位号码和投票份额。住户出于各种原因对此不满，投诉这些机构未经同意披露他们的个人数据。

  PDPC 认为这些机构可以依赖公开可得例外。这些数据从哪里来？它们公布的个人数据本来就是公开可得的，因为每个公寓项目都有一份分层地契登记册（strata roll），也就是公寓全体住户的官方记录。虽然你需要向 MCST 申请查阅，还要付费，所以有一定限制，但实际上这些限制非常低，因此仍然算作公开可得数据。此外，部分信息还可以在新加坡土地管理局（Singapore Land Authority）的登记系统上查到，同样只要付一定费用就能查阅。所以这个案例说明，即使你需要付费才能获取个人数据，也不代表这些个人数据就不是公开可得的。

  一位同学指出，你得向 MCST 申请，所以存在申请可能不被批准的内在风险。这能算低限制而不是高限制吗？

  在这个具体案例中，PDPC 认定，是的，你确实需要向 MCST 申请，严格来说也不是每个人都有资格查阅。但实际上，任何人申请都能拿到。实际上 MCST 不会去核查你是不是潜在买家之类的，他们只看你付了费，就这样。所以这就是为什么说门槛很低。

  That will be fine. Of course, if you're trying to use the data for different purposes, then you'd really need separate consent, as far as that privately collected personal data is concerned.

  可以。如果你从某个来源收集了公开可得数据，同时你另外经个人同意从其本人那里收集了信息，那么只要你的同意对你打算的用途是有效的，就没问题。当然，如果你想把数据用于不同的目的，那么就那部分私下收集的个人数据而言，你确实需要另外取得同意。
- [20:06:10–20:07:23] **Data That Later Ceases to Be Publicly Available**

  Here's an interesting point, something the PDPC says to make the public availability exception a bit more straightforward to use. Look at this example. XYZ collects John's personal data from his public LinkedIn account, so that's publicly available information. But John later deletes his LinkedIn account, so the data is no longer publicly available. The question is: can XYZ still rely on the public availability exception later on, even though the data technically isn't publicly available any more? The answer is yes. XYZ doesn't need to keep checking, every single time it uses the personal data, that the data is still publicly available, because that would be quite onerous.

  Moving on. One of the ways personal data can become publicly available is if it's publicly observable. There are two components. First, the personal data must have been observed by reasonably expected means. Second, it must have been observed at a location or event where the individual appears and which is open to the public.   Two things to highlight. First, what are reasonably expected means? It refers to particular means by which individuals would reasonably expect their personal data to be collected. This is a bit of a word salad, but the simple way to put it is that the personal data must be collected in a way that won't surprise the individual. So if you collect personal data by hiding some sort of camera, or a microphone in a bush, that won't be reasonably expected.

  If you look at this example, it shows you what might be reasonably expected. If you walk into a shopping mall, you can reasonably expect a CCTV camera to be watching you. If you go into a store, again you can expect there's a camera. You can also expect some photo-taking might go on within the store; that's still part of the deal. If you go to a public park and someone is filming some sort of show, that's also reasonably expected. We'd expect that to take place in this kind of location. So all of that counts as reasonably expected means. As long as you're not trying something funny, some secret, surreptitious way of collecting data, you should be able to rely on this.

I won't go through the whole story, but basically, if you book a private room in the restaurant, that space is no longer open to the public.
