  PDPC 的权力之一是向不合规的机构发出指示，包括采取某些行动来纠正违规、减少对个人造成的伤害，或者整改其流程。除了指示——也就是机构必须做的事情——之外，如果机构故意或疏忽地违反 PDPA，PDPC 还可以处以罚款。最高罚款是一百万新元或你在新加坡年营业额的百分之十，以较高者为准。
- [20:38:06–20:44:15] **Financial Penalty Framework: The Marina Bay Sands Case**

  I'll just briefly mention that the PDPC has recently set out the way in which it assesses its financial penalties. This is from the Marina Bay Sands case. The organisation, as you probably know, is an integrated resort. It has a membership programme, and members can access their accounts using a four-digit PIN, which is a very short password. What happened was that some unknown actor used password spraying to compromise six accounts. And then they used those compromised accounts to make HTTP requests to access other people's personal data. This was due to an error made during their migration to a different platform. As a result, the unknown actor got access to the personal data of roughly 665,000 people.

  I'm very much summarising the facts here. The PDPC said this is a breach of the Protection Obligation. In its preliminary decision, which the PDPC will often give to the organisation first, they said they would fine the organisation $450,000. The organisation then had the chance to make representations, saying why it should not be fined so heavily. Here, the PDPC mostly rejected the representations, but because of this, they also went on to explain how they actually assess financial penalties.

  There is this five-step process, plus a preliminary step. I'll just briefly explain how they do it. The first thing is they want to determine the maximum financial penalty in this case. What they do is take the statutory maximum financial penalty, and then multiply it by some undisclosed percentage rate, depending on whether the breach is negligent or intentional. The next step is to determine the level of culpability, which means how wrong or how guilty the organisation is, and the level of harm. Culpability may be low, medium, or high; harm may be slight, moderate, or severe. Based on these two, the next step is to determine the starting financial penalty. Again, they don't really mention the percentages they use; they're just explaining roughly how they arrive at the starting financial penalty.

  From there, the financial penalty can be adjusted using so-called aggravating or mitigating factors. Aggravating factors are factors that make the organisation's behaviour worse; mitigating factors are the opposite. So the financial penalty will go up or go down accordingly. In step four, the PDPC will check to make sure that the financial penalty is not so serious that the organisation cannot continue operating. So if the organisation happens to be a not very well-resourced organisation, and the fine happens to be so big that it will basically shut down, then the PDPC might reduce the financial penalty. And the last step is that the PDPC will take a final look at the number to make sure the financial penalty is big enough to be a deterrent to the organisation, but not so big that it is disproportionate. So this is a sort of common-sense check.

  How did it apply here? In this case, the organisation's statutory maximum financial penalty is ten percent of its annual turnover. Then they apply the negligence percentage to give the case maximum financial penalty. Then the PDPC found that the organisation's culpability was low and the harm was moderate, so they assessed the starting financial penalty at the low-moderate band. So that's the starting point. Then they considered some mitigating factors: for example, the organisation had generally implemented reasonable security measures, they took quick action after discovering the incident, they used the expedited decision procedure where they basically pleaded guilty, and they were generally cooperative. The organisation, in its representations, also highlighted one mitigating factor the PDPC didn't consider, which is that they voluntarily notified individuals of the breach even though they were not required to. So the PDPC acknowledged this and reduced the financial penalty to $315,000. Then the PDPC checks: is this amount too big? The answer is no; Marina Bay Sands can afford it. And then step five is the common-sense check, where there was no final adjustment.

  Here, I'm just giving you a list of the most common types of mitigating and aggravating factors. In general, if you are cooperative and you take action to fix the problems, that will be mitigating. If you are not cooperative, you are profiteering from the breach, or sensitive personal data is involved, then that will be aggravating, so that will increase the financial penalty.

  This slide is just about the process. Whenever the PDPC is going to issue a financial penalty, normally they will give you fourteen days to respond, to explain why you should not get the penalty, and then subsequently they will consider these representations before finalising the decision.

  我简单提一下，PDPC 最近阐明了它评估罚款的方式。这来自 Marina Bay Sands 一案。你们大概知道，这个机构是一家综合度假村。它有一个会员计划，会员可以用一个四位数的 PIN 码登录账户，这是一个非常短的密码。事情的经过是，某个身份不明的人用密码喷洒（password spraying）的方式攻破了六个账户，然后用这些被攻破的账户发出 HTTP 请求，获取其他人的个人数据。这是因为他们在迁移到另一个平台时犯了一个错误。结果，这个身份不明的人获取了大约 665,000 人的个人数据。

  我这里把事实概括得很简略。PDPC 认定这违反了保护义务。在其初步决定（preliminary decision）中——PDPC 通常会先把初步决定发给机构——他们表示会对机构罚款 450,000 新元。随后，机构有机会提出陈述（representations），说明为什么不应该被罚这么重。在这里，PDPC 基本上驳回了这些陈述，但也因此进一步解释了他们实际上是如何评估罚款的。

  有这样一个五步流程，外加一个初步步骤。我简单解释一下他们是怎么做的。第一件事是确定这个案件的最高罚款。他们的做法是取法定最高罚款，然后乘以某个未公开的百分比，具体取决于违规是疏忽还是故意。下一步是确定可责性（culpability）的程度——也就是机构错得多严重、有多大过错——以及伤害程度。可责性可以是低、中、高；伤害可以是轻微、中等或严重。根据这两项，下一步是确定起始罚款。同样，他们没有真正说明所用的百分比，只是大致解释了他们如何得出起始罚款。

  在此基础上，罚款可以根据所谓的加重因素（aggravating factors）或减轻因素（mitigating factors）进行调整。加重因素是让机构的行为显得更恶劣的因素，减轻因素则相反。所以罚款会相应地上调或下调。在第四步，PDPC 会检查罚款是否过重，以至于机构无法继续经营。所以如果这个机构恰好资源不太充足，而罚款大到基本上会让它倒闭，那么 PDPC 可能会降低罚款。最后一步是 PDPC 会对这个数字做最后的审视，确保罚款足以对机构起到威慑作用，但又不会大到不成比例。所以这算是一种常识性检查。

  在这个案件中是怎么适用的呢？在这里，机构的法定最高罚款是其年营业额的百分之十。然后他们乘以疏忽对应的百分比，得出该案的最高罚款。接着，PDPC 认定机构的可责性低、伤害中等，所以把起始罚款定在低至中等区间。这是起点。然后他们考虑了一些减轻因素：比如，机构总体上已经采取了合理的安全措施；发现事件后迅速采取了行动；他们使用了快速决定程序，基本上就是认罪；而且总体上很配合。机构在陈述中还强调了一个 PDPC 没有考虑到的减轻因素，就是尽管没有被要求，他们还是主动通知了受影响的个人。所以 PDPC 认可了这一点，把罚款降到 315,000 新元。然后 PDPC 检查：这个金额是否过高？答案是否定的，Marina Bay Sands 负担得起。第五步是常识性检查，没有作最后的调整。

  这里我只是列出最常见的减轻因素和加重因素。一般来说，如果你很配合，并且采取行动解决问题，这些就是减轻因素。如果你不配合、从违规中牟利，或者涉及敏感个人数据，那就是加重因素，会提高罚款。

  这张幻灯片只是讲程序。每当 PDPC 要处以罚款时，通常会给你十四天时间回应，说明为什么你不应该被罚款，然后他们会在最终确定决定之前考虑这些陈述。
- [20:44:35–20:45:56] **Reconsideration, Appeal, and Comparison with Other Jurisdictions**

  Very quickly, let me just mention the last thing, which is reconsideration and appeal. In brief, if the organisation or the individual doesn't like what the PDPC decided, they can ask the PDPC to reconsider, which the PDPC can do, and it will either affirm, revoke, or vary the decision. You can't ask for reconsideration again, but you can appeal. You can appeal decisions you don't like, and the appeal goes to this tribunal called the Data Protection Appeal Panel. If you don't like that decision, you can appeal onwards to the High Court.

  This slide I'm speeding through a bit. It basically says that most other jurisdictions also have regulators with enforcement powers. The penalties can be a bit different. If you look at the EU's version, the maximum penalty for most infringements is twenty million euros, or up to four percent of total worldwide turnover, which is not the same as Singapore. So if you're looking at a tech company like Google, that can be very big. So that's public enforcement.

  很快地，我再提最后一点，就是复议和上诉。简单来说，如果机构或个人不喜欢 PDPC 的决定，可以请求 PDPC 复议（reconsideration），PDPC 可以这样做，它会维持、撤销或变更该决定。你不能再次请求复议，但可以上诉。你可以对不满意的决定提出上诉，上诉会提交给一个叫数据保护上诉委员会（Data Protection Appeal Panel）的审裁机构。如果你不满意那个决定，可以再上诉到高等法院。

  这张幻灯片我讲得稍微快一点。它基本上是说，大多数其他司法管辖区也有拥有执法权的监管机构。罚款可能会有些不同。如果你看欧盟的版本，大多数违规行为的最高罚款是两千万欧元，或者最高为全球总营业额的百分之四，这和新加坡不一样。所以如果你看的是像 Google 这样的科技公司，这个金额可能会非常大。这就是公共执法。
- [20:46:08–20:48:53] **Private Enforcement: The Statutory Right and Who Has Standing (Reed v Bellingham)**

  Let me finish up with private enforcement, which is the second type of enforcement, but is a lot less common, for obvious reasons. In this case, it's an individual suing the company or organisation using their own resources, which is not likely to happen often.

  So when can an individual sue in private enforcement? The rule is given here, which says that a person who suffers loss or damage directly as a result of a contravention can commence civil proceedings. So there are a few questions to address. The first one: who counts as a person? Number two, it says the person must suffer loss or damage, so what counts as loss or damage? The third question: it says the loss or damage must be directly caused by the breach, so what counts as direct? There are a couple of cases that address these points.

  First question: who gets to sue? The answer is only the individual, not someone else. The case that illustrates this, and I may have touched upon this case before, is the Michael Reed and Alex Bellingham case. In case I haven't covered this before, what happened in this case is that the defendant, Bellingham, was an investment fund manager. He ran a fund called the Edinburgh Fund. Subsequently, he left to join a competing investment firm called Q Investment Partners. And then he went to contact investors he knew had invested in the Edinburgh Fund. Obviously, he knew of them from his previous employment. The individual he contacted, Reed, was surprised and not very happy at being contacted by Bellingham, and he told Bellingham's former employer. The former employer then sued Bellingham for breaching the PDPA, and they later added Reed as an additional plaintiff.

  So one of the questions was whether the employer actually had standing to sue. Here the answer is no. The reason is that when the PDPA says "person", as in a person can sue, "person" refers to the individual. So only Reed in this case had standing, or was entitled, to sue.

  我最后讲私人执法，这是第二种执法方式，但出于显而易见的原因，它要少见得多。在这种情况下，是个人用自己的资源起诉公司或机构，这种事不太会经常发生。

  那么，个人什么时候可以通过私人执法提起诉讼？规则在这里：因违规行为而直接遭受损失或损害的人，可以提起民事诉讼。所以有几个问题需要讨论。第一，谁算是"人"（person）？第二，条文说这个人必须遭受损失或损害，那么什么算损失或损害？第三，条文说损失或损害必须是由违规直接造成的，那么什么算直接？有几个案例处理了这些问题。

  第一个问题：谁可以起诉？答案是只有个人本身，不能是别人。说明这一点的案例——我之前可能提到过——是 Michael Reed 诉 Alex Bellingham 一案。以防我之前没讲过，这个案子的经过是：被告 Bellingham 是一名投资基金经理，他管理一个叫 Edinburgh Fund 的基金。后来他离职，加入了一家叫 Q Investment Partners 的竞争对手投资公司。然后他去联系那些他知道投资过 Edinburgh Fund 的投资者。显然，他是通过之前的工作认识这些人的。他联系的那个人 Reed 很惊讶，也很不高兴被 Bellingham 联系，于是告诉了 Bellingham 的前雇主。前雇主随后起诉 Bellingham 违反 PDPA，后来又把 Reed 加为额外的原告。

  所以其中一个问题是，雇主到底有没有起诉的资格（standing）。这里的答案是没有。原因是，当 PDPA 说"人"可以起诉时，"人"指的是个人本身。所以在这个案子里，只有 Reed 有资格起诉。
- [20:48:53–20:51:09] **What Counts as Loss or Damage: Emotional Distress in Reed v Bellingham**

  The second point is about what counts as loss or damage. Basically, loss or damage can include the usual things like financial loss, and it also includes things like physical injury, which is unlikely to happen here, but it can also include emotional distress. But if you are trying to claim emotional distress, you have to prove it.

  In this case, what Reed was claiming was that he suffered emotional distress because of Bellingham's breach of the consent obligation, since Bellingham used his personal data without consent. The Court of Appeal agreed and said that Reed probably did suffer some emotional distress.

  As to when it is likely that the individual suffered emotional distress, the court will consider a few things. For example, what type of personal data was involved? If it's sensitive personal data, it's more likely to cause distress. What type of breach is it, one-off or repeated? How did the defendant behave? Was it an innocent breach, or was the defendant being malicious? Is there a risk of future breaches causing distress? And finally, what is the actual impact of the breach?

  In this case, Bellingham behaved in a way which was not friendly. He refused to answer Reed's question when he was asked how he was going to use Reed's personal data. He refused to promise not to make unauthorised use of Reed's personal data. The evidence suggested that Reed was anxious enough to report the incident. And finally, the personal data involved sensitive financial data. All these factors suggest that it is more likely that Reed suffered emotional distress.

  第二点是关于什么算损失或损害。基本上，损失或损害可以包括常见的东西，比如经济损失，也包括人身伤害——这在这里不太可能发生——但也可以包括精神困扰（emotional distress）。不过，如果你要主张精神困扰，你必须证明它。

  在这个案子里，Reed 主张的是，由于 Bellingham 违反了同意义务——Bellingham 未经同意使用了他的个人数据——他遭受了精神困扰。上诉庭认同这一点，认为 Reed 很可能确实遭受了一定的精神困扰。

  至于什么情况下个人可能遭受了精神困扰，法院会考虑几点。比如，涉及的是哪类个人数据？如果是敏感个人数据，就更可能造成困扰。是哪种类型的违规，一次性的还是反复的？被告的行为如何？是无心之失，还是被告怀有恶意？将来是否有再次违规造成困扰的风险？最后，违规的实际影响是什么？

  在这个案子里，Bellingham 的表现并不友善。当 Reed 问他打算怎么使用自己的个人数据时，他拒绝回答。他拒绝承诺不会未经授权使用 Reed 的个人数据。证据显示 Reed 焦虑到会去举报这件事。最后，涉及的个人数据包括敏感的财务数据。所有这些因素都表明，Reed 更可能遭受了精神困扰。
- [20:51:09–20:54:09] **Direct Causation: Piper v Singapore Kindness Movement**

  The last point is about directness. It says any person who suffers loss or damage directly as a result of the breach. So what counts as direct? The rule here is that there needs to be a direct causal connection between the breach and the individual's loss. And this can be quite a strict rule, as you'll see here.

  In this case, you have this person called Martin Piper, who made a complaint to the Singapore Kindness Movement. His allegation was that a lady named Carol Loi, who was affiliated with SKM, was promoting discriminatory and false material against transgender people. So he was complaining about this woman. SKM then, for some reason, disclosed his identity to Loi without his consent. Loi then proceeded to retaliate by suing Piper for harassment, and publishing about the affair on Facebook. Sorry, I should say Piper here: Piper then received threatening messages referring to the incident.

  So Piper proceeded to sue for breach of the PDPA, saying SKM disclosed his personal data without consent, and that this caused him emotional distress. In this case, the High Court said that there was clearly a breach of the consent obligation, but unfortunately Piper cannot sue. He cannot sue because the emotional distress, the loss or damage, was not directly caused by the breach. The rule here is that there has to be a strict causal link between the loss and the breach, but Loi's actions, suing him and posting on Facebook, broke the chain of causation. So there's a breach, the breach happened, then Loi did the things that she did, and then this caused Piper to suffer his emotional distress. So there was an intervening step.

  If the third party's action was likely to occur as a result of the breach, or it was glaringly obvious that it was going to happen, then it may not break the chain of causation. But in this case, this was not that kind of action. Loi suing for harassment is not something that is likely to result from the breach of the consent obligation. So, generally speaking, you have to prove that there's a clear, straight line between the breach and whatever loss or damage you suffered.

  最后一点是关于"直接"。条文说的是任何因违规而直接遭受损失或损害的人。那么什么算直接？这里的规则是，违规与个人的损失之间需要有直接的因果关系。正如你们在这里会看到的，这可能是一条相当严格的规则。

  在这个案子里，有一个叫 Martin Piper 的人，他向 Singapore Kindness Movement（SKM）投诉。他指控一位名叫 Carol Loi、与 SKM 有关联的女士，在宣传针对跨性别群体的歧视性和虚假的材料。所以他投诉的是这位女士。随后，SKM 不知出于什么原因，未经他同意就把他的身份透露给了 Loi。Loi 接着进行报复，起诉 Piper 骚扰，并在 Facebook 上发文讲这件事。抱歉，这里我应该说 Piper：Piper 随后收到了提及这件事的威胁信息。

  于是 Piper 以违反 PDPA 为由提起诉讼，说 SKM 未经同意披露了他的个人数据，并给他造成了精神困扰。在这个案子里，高等法院说，这显然违反了同意义务，但很遗憾，Piper 不能起诉。他不能起诉，是因为这种精神困扰，也就是损失或损害，并不是由违规直接造成的。这里的规则是，损失与违规之间必须有严格的因果联系，但 Loi 的行为——起诉他、在 Facebook 上发文——打断了因果链（chain of causation）。所以，先有违规，违规发生了，然后 Loi 做了她所做的事情，然后这才导致 Piper 遭受精神困扰。所以中间有一个介入的步骤。

  如果第三方的行为很可能因违规而发生，或者明显会发生，那么它未必会打断因果链。但在这个案子里，并不是这种行为。Loi 起诉骚扰并不是违反同意义务很可能导致的结果。所以一般来说，你必须证明违规与你所遭受的损失或损害之间有一条清晰、笔直的联系。

# Seminar 10
## Week 10 Summary
- **Lesson Scope and Exam Format 课程范围与考试形式**
  - **Skipped guidelines:** The remaining use-case guidelines (generative AI, recommendation systems) were not taught; they mostly elaborate on material already covered last semester.
  - **DPIA dropped:** The lecturer had planned to test DPIA practice but decided it is not fairly testable, so it will **not** be examined.
  - **Two general question types:**
    - **Compliance advice:** advise an organisation on whether it is, or will be, in breach of the **PDPA**, and if so, what it should do to become compliant.
    - **Enforcement advice:** advise an organisation on handling potential enforcement by the **PDPC** and/or affected individuals.
  - **Specific questions:** These may also appear when the two general types can't cover everything; they will state clearly what is required.
  - **Format:** Plans are for **2 questions in 2 hours**. Each question is a **hypothetical**, and the exam is **open book**.
  - **Non-examinable:** The EU automated decision-making (ADM) rules, plus next week's PETs and telemarketing topics.
  - **跳过的指南：** 其余针对具体用途的指南（生成式 AI、推荐系统）不讲授，因为它们大多是对上学期已讲内容的进一步阐述。
  - **不考 DPIA：** 讲师原计划考 DPIA 实务，但认为无法公平地考，因此**不考**。
  - **两类一般性题型：**
    - **合规建议：** 就机构是否已经或将会违反 **PDPA** 提供建议；如果会违反，说明应如何做到合规。
    - **执法建议：** 就机构如何应对 **PDPC** 和/或受影响个人可能采取的执法行动提供建议。
  - **具体问题：** 在两类一般性题型无法覆盖全部内容时，也可能出现具体问题，题目会清楚说明要求。
  - **形式：** 计划为 **2 小时 2 道题**。每道题都是一个**假设案例**，考试为**开卷**。
  - **不考内容：** 欧盟自动化决策（ADM）规则，以及下周的隐私增强技术和电话营销内容。

- **How to Answer Compliance Advice Questions 合规建议题答题方法**
  - **Be selective:** Don't run through every obligation. Use judgment to pick the obligations **most likely to be at issue** and address only those.
  - **IRAC (optional):** Use **Issue → Rule → Application → Conclusion**. Issue and Rule are straightforward, since the rule can be copied from the slides. **Application** is where the marks and the thinking are.
  - **Take a position:** Conclude that a breach is **likely or unlikely**. Both sides can usually be argued, but don't sit on the fence with "maybe".
  - **Then give solutions:** After concluding that a breach is likely, propose what the organisation should change to be compliant.
  - **有所取舍：** 不要把每项义务都过一遍。运用判断挑出**最可能出问题**的义务，只处理这些义务。
  - **IRAC（非必须）：** 按 **问题 → 规则 → 适用 → 结论** 作答。问题和规则较直接，规则可以照抄幻灯片。**适用**才是需要思考、也是得分的部分。
  - **表明立场：** 结论要说明违规**可能还是不太可能**。通常两边都能论证，但不能骑墙说“也许”。
  - **再提出解决办法：** 得出可能违规的结论后，提出机构为实现合规应作的改变。

- **Practice 1, Issue 1: Dinah / ABC / XYZ and the Protection Obligation 练习一（问题一）：Dinah / ABC / XYZ 与保护义务**
  - **Scenario:** ABC outsources HR and payroll to **XYZ**, a startup in Thailand, and gives it regular direct access to employee files. XYZ's only assurance is an email saying Thai law is "about the same" as Singapore's.
  - **Issues spotted:** The class identified the **Transfer Limitation Obligation** (data leaving Singapore) and the **Protection Obligation** (working with an intermediary).
  - **Rule:** The Protection Obligation requires **reasonable security arrangements**.
  - **Application:**
    - XYZ processes employee data on ABC's behalf, so XYZ is ABC's **data intermediary**.
    - ABC therefore keeps **primary responsibility** for making sure XYZ secures that data.
    - Dinah says nothing about how ABC will ensure this.
  - **Conclusion:** ABC is **likely in breach**.
  - **Solutions:**
    - Put **contractual arrangements** in place requiring XYZ to implement security measures.
    - **Supervise** XYZ, because a startup is not the most reliable intermediary and ABC can't simply rely on its assurances.
    - If supervision isn't feasible because XYZ is overseas, find a **more reputable** intermediary or use a **local** one.
  - **情景：** ABC 把人力资源和薪资外包给泰国初创公司 **XYZ**，并让其定期直接访问员工档案。XYZ 唯一的保证是一封邮件，称泰国法律与新加坡“差不多”。
  - **识别的问题：** 课堂找出了**转移限制义务**（数据出境）和**保护义务**（与中介合作）。
  - **规则：** 保护义务要求作出**合理的安全安排**。
  - **适用：**
    - XYZ 代表 ABC 处理员工数据，因此 XYZ 是 ABC 的**数据中介**。
    - ABC 因此对确保 XYZ 保护这些数据负有**主要责任**。
    - Dinah 对 ABC 将如何确保这一点只字未提。
  - **结论：** ABC **很可能违规**。
  - **解决办法：**
    - 订立**合同安排**，要求 XYZ 落实安全措施。
    - **监督** XYZ，因为初创公司并不是最可靠的中介，ABC 不能只依赖它的保证。
    - 如果因为 XYZ 在海外而无法监督，就改找**更有信誉**的中介或**本地**中介。

- **Practice 1, Issue 2: Transfer Limitation Obligation 练习一（问题二）：转移限制义务**
  - **Rule:** Data transferred overseas must receive **comparable protection**. This is generally achieved by binding the recipient with **legally enforceable obligations**.
  - **Application:**
    - Obligations **imposed by law** (Thai data protection law) are potentially available.
    - But the organisation **cannot simply rely on the foreign law**. It must carry out **its own analysis** of whether that law gives comparable protection.
    - XYZ's emailed assurance and bare "about the same" claim are **unlikely to be sufficient**. No other enforceable obligation is mentioned.
  - **Conclusion:** A breach is **likely**.
  - **Solutions weighed:**
    - **Rely on foreign law after analysis:** possible, but **risky**, because the analysis might be wrong or not comprehensive enough.
    - **Contract:** require XYZ to comply with PDPA data protection obligations. This is the **most likely recommendation**, as the easiest option.
    - **Binding corporate rules:** don't work here, because they need the **same corporate group**.
    - **Certification (CBPR/PRP):** possible, but XYZ, a startup, doesn't appear to be certified, and getting certified could take months or a year.
    - **Consent of every employee:** possible but troublesome. Everyone must consent, and pressured consent ("consent or be fired") may be **invalid**. The lecturer suspects consent is still needed for the overseas transfer even for employment data.
    - **Anonymisation or masking:** hard for payroll, which likely needs bank account details.
    - **Restricting access to relevant data:** good practice, but any personal data sent still triggers the obligation.
    - **Supervision or compliance reviews:** belong to the Protection Obligation (managing an intermediary), not transfer limitation.
  - **Exam tip:** Recommend the best solution, and mention the others in order to **rule them out** with reasons.
  - **规则：** 转移到海外的数据必须获得**可比的保护**。通常的做法是让接收方受**具有法律约束力的义务**约束。
  - **适用：**
    - 可能存在**由法律施加的**义务（泰国数据保护法）。
    - 但机构**不能只依赖外国法律**，必须**自行分析**该法律是否提供可比的保护。
    - XYZ 的邮件保证以及“差不多”的空泛说法**不太可能足够**，题目中也没有提到其他有约束力的义务。
  - **结论：** **很可能违规**。
  - **权衡的解决办法：**
    - **分析后依赖外国法律：** 可行但**有风险**，因为分析可能出错或不够全面。
    - **合同：** 要求 XYZ 遵守 PDPA 的数据保护义务。这是**最可能推荐的方案**，因为最简便。
    - **有约束力的企业规则：** 在这里行不通，因为需要属于**同一企业集团**。
    - **认证（CBPR/PRP）：** 可行，但 XYZ 作为初创公司似乎没有认证，取得认证可能要几个月甚至一年。
    - **取得每位员工同意：** 可行但麻烦。必须人人同意，而被施压的同意（“不同意就解雇”）可能**无效**。讲师认为，即使是雇佣相关数据，出境转移大概仍需要同意。
    - **匿名化或掩码：** 对薪资处理来说很难，因为很可能需要银行账户信息。
    - **只开放相关数据：** 属于良好做法，但只要传送任何个人数据，仍然触发这项义务。
    - **监督或合规审查：** 属于保护义务（管理中介）的范畴，而不是转移限制。
  - **考试提示：** 推荐最佳方案，同时提及其他方案并说明理由**加以排除**。

- **How to Answer Enforcement Advice Questions 执法建议题答题方法**
  - **Both tracks:** Consider **public** (PDPC) and **private** (individual) enforcement.
  - **Most likely outcome:**
    - Private enforcement: does the individual have **standing to sue**?
    - Public enforcement: what approach will the PDPC **most likely** take, and which **powers** will it use?
  - **Response:** Advise on what the organisation should do in response to enforcement.
  - **两条路径：** 同时考虑**公共**（PDPC）和**私人**（个人）执法。
  - **最可能的结果：**
    - 私人执法：个人是否具有**起诉资格**？
    - 公共执法：PDPC **最可能**采取什么做法，会动用哪些**权力**？
  - **应对：** 就机构应如何应对执法提供建议。

- **Practice 2: Reynold / DEF, Private Enforcement 练习二：Reynold / DEF——私人执法**
  - **Scenario:** A branch manager answered Reynold's one-star review by uploading the full, unedited CCTV recording of the incident. The video went viral and Reynold lost his job as a bank relationship manager. He reported DEF to the PDPC and is threatening to sue (Purpose Limitation breach).
  - **Loss or damage:** **Emotional distress** is likely, since a recording of him behaving badly was disclosed even though the data isn't sensitive. There is also **financial harm** from losing his job.
  - **Directness:** Loss must **directly** result from the contravention, and the firing is an **intervening act**.
    - For directness: a bank firing a relationship manager over such publicity was quite likely.
    - Against: the firing may not be a foreseeable consequence.
  - **Conclusion:** Because emotional distress is pretty likely, Reynold likely has **standing to sue**.
  - **DEF's response:** Try to **settle** to avoid court, for example through an apology, negotiated compensation or a settlement agreement.
  - **情景：** 分店经理为回应 Reynold 的一星差评，上传了事件完整、未经剪辑的 CCTV 录像。视频爆红，Reynold 丢掉了银行客户经理的工作。他向 PDPC 举报了 DEF，并扬言起诉（违反目的限制义务）。
  - **损失或损害：** 很可能存在**情绪困扰**，因为即使数据不敏感，他行为失当的录像也被公开了。此外还有失业造成的**经济损害**。
  - **直接性：** 损失必须是违规**直接**造成的，而解雇构成**介入行为**。
    - 支持直接性：银行因这类曝光而解雇客户经理是相当可能的。
    - 反对直接性：被解雇未必是可预见的后果。
  - **结论：** 由于情绪困扰的可能性很高，Reynold 很可能具有**起诉资格**。
  - **DEF 的应对：** 设法**和解**以避免诉讼，例如道歉、协商赔偿或达成和解协议。

- **Practice 2: Public Enforcement and DEF's Response 练习二：公共执法与 DEF 的应对**
  - **Likely sequence:**
    - The PDPC first tries **ADR**, such as mediation, to get the parties to settle.
    - If that fails, it opens an **investigation** and uses its powers to obtain information.
    - If the investigation runs its full course, expect a **decision** with **directions** (e.g. take down the video) and a **financial penalty**. Any exact prediction is a guess.
  - **Suspension:** If Reynold sues, the PDPC will likely **suspend** its investigation to avoid overlapping proceedings, and resume it if he doesn't sue.
  - **No compensation from the PDPC:** The PDPC has no power to order compensation. Compensation is only available through a **private suit**.
  - **Recommended actions:**
    - Negotiate early, avoiding a costly investigation and a lawsuit.
    - **Preserve evidence**, such as the CCTV footage.
    - Take **corrective action** on who can access CCTV.
    - Take **prompt remedial action** by taking the video down.
    - Offer a **voluntary undertaking** so the investigation need not end in a decision against DEF. Its main contents would be a **CCTV footage policy** and **staff training** on that policy and on handling online reviews.
  - **Points rejected or misplaced:**
    - An appeal to the High Court is too far off to need mentioning.
    - Shifting liability to the employee is likely difficult, since he was probably defending the restaurant in the course of his work.
    - "Legitimate interest" arguments belong to the **compliance** stage, not to enforcement advice.
  - **可能的流程：**
    - PDPC 先尝试**替代性争议解决**，例如调解，促使双方和解。
    - 如果不成，就启动**调查**，并动用权力获取信息。
    - 如果调查走完全程，预计会作出**决定**，附带**指示**（例如撤下视频）和**罚款**。具体预测只能是猜测。
  - **暂停调查：** 如果 Reynold 起诉，PDPC 很可能**暂停**调查以避免程序重叠；如果他不起诉，调查则继续。
  - **PDPC 不判赔偿：** PDPC 无权下令赔偿，赔偿只能通过**私人诉讼**获得。
  - **建议行动：**
    - 尽早协商，避免昂贵的调查和诉讼。
    - **保存证据**，例如 CCTV 录像。
    - 针对谁能访问 CCTV 采取**纠正措施**。
    - **迅速补救**，撤下视频。
    - 提交**自愿承诺**，使调查不必以针对 DEF 的决定告终。主要内容是 **CCTV 录像政策**，以及针对该政策和网上评论处理的**员工培训**。
  - **被否定或放错位置的观点：**
    - 向高等法院上诉是很久以后的事，不必提。
    - 把责任推给员工可能很难，因为他很可能是在工作中为餐厅辩护。
    - “合法利益”论点属于**合规**阶段，不属于执法建议。

- **General Exam Guidance and Grading 考试总体指导与评分**
  - **Fair but challenging:** Everything is answerable from the course materials, and nothing outside them is tested. Time pressure is **deliberate**, and you don't need to answer every part to do well.
  - **Rubric-based marking:** Marks reflect which rubric points you address and how well. Unexpected good points are welcome, and you'll likely pass even if you miss a few points.
  - **Sample answers:** These will likely be uploaded, but they are not model answers, only one suggested approach. The rubric itself won't be shared.
  - **Preparation:** Know the materials well, so that you spend less time searching during the exam.
  - **公平但有挑战：** 所有题目都能用课程材料作答，不考材料以外的内容。时间紧张是**刻意设计**的，不必答完每一部分也能考好。
  - **按评分细则给分：** 分数取决于你答到了哪些评分要点、答得多好。意料之外的好观点会受欢迎，即使漏掉几点也可能及格。
  - **参考答案：** 很可能会上传，但它们不是标准答案，只是一种建议思路。评分细则本身不会公开。
  - **准备：** 熟悉材料，考试时就能少花时间翻找。

- **EU ADM: The Article 22 Prohibition (Non-Examinable) 欧盟 ADM：第 22 条禁止规定（不考）**
  - **Relevance:** Matters if you deal with EU consumers, have an EU establishment or work in a large multinational using AI.
  - **Rule:** A data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision **based solely on automated processing** that produces **legal effects** or **similarly significant effects**.
  - **Solely automated:** Means made **without meaningful human involvement**. Token oversight or rubber-stamping doesn't count. The human must have **authority to change** the decision, for example by reviewing an automated recommendation and weighing other factors.
  - **Rule-based filtering (student question):** If a human mechanically applies rules with no discretion, this is technically solely automated. Purely manual processing, however, likely falls **outside the GDPR's scope** altogether. The lecturer considers this an area not properly thought through.
  - **Legal effects:** These affect legal rights, for example voting, cancellation of a contract or denial of social benefits.
  - **Similarly significant effects:** For example, refusal of credit, or denial of health services, employment or education.
  - **Guidelines:**
    - **Targeted advertising** is usually not significant, unless it deliberately exploits **vulnerabilities**.
    - **Personalised pricing** is significant only if it produces **prohibitively high prices**.
  - **相关性：** 如果你面对欧盟消费者、在欧盟设有机构，或在使用 AI 的大型跨国公司工作，就与你相关。
  - **规则：** 数据主体有权不受**仅基于自动化处理**、产生**法律效果**或**类似重大影响**的决定约束。
  - **仅基于自动化处理：** 指**没有有意义的人工参与**。象征性监督或走过场盖章都不算，人必须有**改变决定的权力**，例如审查自动化建议并考虑其他因素。
  - **基于规则的筛选（学生提问）：** 如果由人机械套用规则、没有裁量空间，严格来说属于仅自动化处理。但纯人工处理很可能完全**落在 GDPR 范围之外**。讲师认为这是一个没有被想清楚的领域。
  - **法律效果：** 影响法律权利，例如投票、合同被取消或社会福利被拒。
  - **类似重大影响：** 例如信贷被拒，或被拒绝医疗服务、就业或教育机会。
  - **指南：**
    - **定向广告**通常不算重大影响，除非故意利用**弱点**。
    - **个性化定价**只有在导致**高得令人望而却步的价格**时才算重大影响。

- **EU ADM: Exceptions and Safeguards 欧盟 ADM：例外与保障措施**
  - **Contractual necessity:** You must show that automation was **necessary**, for example to filter thousands of applications for a popular job.
  - **Law:** The decision is authorised by EU or Member State law.
  - **Explicit consent:** Consent must be **expressed**, not inferred from conduct.
  - **Safeguards for contract or consent:** At minimum, the right to obtain **human intervention**, to **express a point of view** and to **contest** the decision.
  - **Human intervention:** Must come from someone with **authority to change** the decision, so that in effect the individual can appeal.
  - **Contesting doesn't force a change (student question):** The controller may keep the same decision, but a human must genuinely reassess it.
  - **Scope:** Unlike the PDPA, the GDPR also binds **government agencies**, such as tax authorities.
  - **合同必要性：** 必须证明自动化是**必要的**，例如为热门职位筛选成千上万份申请。
  - **法律授权：** 该决定获得欧盟或成员国法律授权。
  - **明确同意：** 同意必须是**明示的**，不能从行为推断。
  - **合同或同意情形的保障措施：** 至少包括获得**人工干预**、**表达观点**和**提出异议**的权利。
  - **人工干预：** 必须由**有权改变决定**的人进行，实际上就是让个人可以申诉。
  - **提出异议不等于必须改变（学生提问）：** 控制者可以维持原决定，但必须由人真正重新评估。
  - **适用范围：** 与 PDPA 不同，GDPR 也约束**政府机构**，例如税务机关。

- **EU ADM: Special Transparency Obligation 欧盟 ADM：特别透明度义务**
  - **Three duties:**
    - **Disclose** that ADM is taking place.
    - Give **meaningful information about the logic involved** (explainability).
    - Explain the **significance and envisaged consequences** of the processing.
  - **Black-box challenge:** The guidelines don't really solve it. The controller must give the **rationale** in enough detail for the individual to understand the decision, but need not explain or disclose the **full algorithm**.
  - **Credit scoring example:** The controller explains that the system supports fair, responsible lending decisions, which characteristics and data sources it uses, that the methods are **regularly tested**, and how to request reconsideration or appeal.
  - **Insurance example:** Premiums are based on driving behaviour. The insurer explains that dangerous driving may raise premiums and provides an app comparing **fictional drivers**.
  - **三项义务：**
    - **披露**正在进行 ADM。
    - 提供**关于所涉逻辑的有意义信息**（可解释性）。
    - 说明处理的**重要性及预期后果**。
  - **黑箱难题：** 指南并没有真正解决这个问题。控制者必须提供足以让个人理解决定的**理由**，但不必解释或公开**完整算法**。
  - **信用评分例子：** 控制者说明系统有助于作出公平、负责任的放贷决定，说明使用了哪些特征和数据来源、方法会**定期测试**，以及如何申请复议或申诉。
  - **保险例子：** 保费依据驾驶行为确定。保险公司说明危险驾驶可能提高保费，并提供比较**虚构驾驶者**的应用程序。

- **SCHUFA (2023): ADM Rules Apply to Third-Party Scoring SCHUFA 案（2023）：第三方评分同样适用 ADM 规则**
  - **Facts:** SCHUFA, a credit reporting company, computes scores statistically. A lender denied OQ a loan because of her bad SCHUFA score. SCHUFA gave OQ her score and some general information on the method, but refused to say more.
  - **Issue:** Does Article 22 apply to a scorer that doesn't itself make the decision affecting the individual?
  - **Outcome:** The CJEU held that Article 22 **does apply** to SCHUFA. All three conditions were met:
    - **Decision:** the creditworthiness calculation as a probability of default.
    - **Solely automated:** the probability value is produced by an automatic algorithm.
    - **Significant effect:** the lender draws on that value when deciding on the loan.
  - **Reason:** Otherwise there would be a **gap in protection**. The scorer would escape the ADM rules, while the lender would be bound but lack the information, so OQ could never get the information she is entitled to.
  - **事实：** 信用报告公司 SCHUFA 用统计方法计算评分。一家贷款机构因 OQ 的 SCHUFA 评分很差而拒绝向她放贷。SCHUFA 给了 OQ 她的评分和关于方法的一些一般信息，但拒绝透露更多。
  - **争议：** 第 22 条是否适用于本身不作出影响个人决定的评分方？
  - **结果：** 欧盟法院认定第 22 条**适用**于 SCHUFA，三个条件都满足：
    - **决定：** 以违约概率形式计算信用度。
    - **仅自动化：** 概率值由自动算法得出。
    - **重大影响：** 贷款机构在决定是否放贷时依据该数值。
  - **理由：** 否则会出现**保护空白**。评分方会逃脱 ADM 规则，而贷款机构虽受约束却没有相关信息，OQ 就永远拿不到她有权获得的信息。

- **ADM Wrap-up, Q&A and Next Week ADM 总结、问答与下周预告**
  - **Takeaway:** The EU has a **general prohibition** on solely automated significant decisions, plus a **special transparency obligation** to explain the decision.
  - **Other jurisdictions:** The EU is the **pioneer**. The lecturer knows of no other country with identical rules, though others may have similar ones.
  - **Rationale:** The aim is not to curb AI as such. It guards against **incorrect, unfair or biased** decisions made without human involvement that significantly affect individuals.
  - **Tracking Singapore changes:** The PDPC or IMDA posts changes on its website. Registered DPOs will likely be emailed, but otherwise you need to watch actively, though changes are infrequent.
  - **Law vs IMDA guidance:** The GDPR rules are **legally binding**, with consequences for non-compliance. IMDA guidelines are **recommendations**.
  - **Next week (non-examinable):** **Privacy-enhancing technologies** (how they can be used in AI to avoid having to comply with the PDPA) and rules against **unsolicited telemarketing** (relevant if agents send automated marketing).
  - **要点：** 欧盟对仅基于自动化、产生重大影响的决定实行**一般性禁止**，并规定了解释决定的**特别透明度义务**。
  - **其他法域：** 欧盟是**先行者**。讲师不知道有其他国家制定了完全相同的规则，不过可能有类似规则。
  - **立法理由：** 目的不在于限制 AI 本身，而是防范在没有人工参与的情况下作出、对个人产生重大影响的**错误、不公平或有偏见**的决定。
  - **跟踪新加坡的变化：** PDPC 或 IMDA 会在网站上公布变化。注册 DPO 很可能会收到邮件，否则需要主动留意，不过规则修改并不频繁。
  - **法律与 IMDA 指引的区别：** GDPR 规则**具有法律约束力**，不遵守会有后果；IMDA 指南只是**建议**。
  - **下周（不考）：** **隐私增强技术**（如何在 AI 中运用以避免需要遵守 PDPA），以及禁止**未经请求电话营销**的规则（如果用智能体发送自动化营销就会相关）。
## Week 10 Learning Tips
This week is really about method, and the method rewards judgment over coverage. In the Dinah scenario, the strongest answers named just two obligations, Protection and Transfer Limitation, and went deep on each. The lecturer warned against dumping the whole syllabus into an answer. Before you write anything, spend a minute triaging: which facts in the email are red flags? Direct access to employee files, a foreign startup and an emailed "trust us" each point to a specific obligation. Let the facts choose your issues.

本周的重点其实是方法，而这个方法看重判断而非面面俱到。在 Dinah 情景中，最好的答案只点出两项义务，即保护义务和转移限制义务，并且每项都分析得很深入。讲师明确提醒不要把整个课程大纲倒进答案里。动笔之前，先花一分钟分诊：邮件里哪些事实是危险信号？直接访问员工档案、外国初创公司、一封“相信我们”的邮件，每一点都指向一项具体义务。让事实来决定你要讨论的问题。

Treat IRAC as a way to locate your marks, not a ritual. Issue and Rule can almost be copied from the slides. The Application step earns the credit, because that's where you connect a fact to a legal characterisation. For example: XYZ processes data on ABC's behalf, so it is a data intermediary, so ABC keeps primary responsibility. Build that chain explicitly, link by link. Then commit to "likely" or "unlikely". A conclusion of "maybe" throws away the point of the exercise, even when both sides are arguable.

把 IRAC 当作定位得分点的工具，而不是仪式。问题和规则几乎可以从幻灯片上照抄。真正得分的是适用环节，因为你要在这里把事实和法律定性连接起来。例如：XYZ 代表 ABC 处理数据，所以它是数据中介，所以 ABC 仍负主要责任。要把这条推理链一环一环明确写出来。然后表明“可能”或“不太可能”。即使两边都可以论证，用“也许”作结论也失去了这道题的意义。

A recurring pitfall this week was putting a good point under the wrong obligation or stage. Supervising XYZ is a Protection Obligation answer, not a Transfer Limitation one. Arguing "legitimate interest" for posting the CCTV video belongs to compliance analysis, not enforcement advice. A High Court appeal is too remote to belong in your recommendations. Make a small "where does this belong?" table for your solutions and arguments, sorted by obligation and by stage (compliance, enforcement), so you place each idea correctly under time pressure.

本周反复出现的一个陷阱，是把好观点放到了错误的义务或阶段下。监督 XYZ 属于保护义务的答案，而不属于转移限制义务。用“合法利益”为发布 CCTV 视频辩护属于合规分析，而不属于执法建议。向高等法院上诉太遥远，不应出现在你的建议里。为你的解决办法和论点做一张“这属于哪里？”的小表格，按义务和阶段（合规、执法）分类，这样在时间压力下也能把每个想法放对位置。

For the transfer limitation solutions, practise the "recommend one, rule out the rest" pattern the lecturer modelled. Draw a compact options matrix with a pro and a con for each option: foreign law plus your own analysis (risky), contract (easiest), BCRs (wrong corporate group), certification (XYZ isn't certified and certification is slow), consent (every employee needed, coerced consent invalid), anonymisation (payroll needs bank details) and minimising data (good practice, but still a transfer). Being able to state each option's specific defeater in one line is exactly what the rubric rewards.

关于转移限制的解决办法，要练习讲师示范的“推荐一个、排除其余”模式。画一张简洁的方案矩阵，每个方案写一个优点和一个缺点：外国法律加自行分析（有风险）、合同（最简便）、BCR（不是同一企业集团）、认证（XYZ 没有认证且取得认证很慢）、同意（需要每位员工同意，被迫的同意无效）、匿名化（薪资需要银行信息）、数据最小化（良好做法，但仍属转移）。能用一句话说出每个方案具体被否定的理由，正是评分细则所奖励的。

For enforcement advice, memorise the sequence as a timeline rather than a list of powers: ADR first, then investigation, then directions and a penalty, with a possible suspension if the individual sues. Add the boundary the class discussion made clear: the PDPC cannot award compensation, only a private suit can. On the private side, don't stop at "he was harmed". Walk through loss or damage, then directness, and acknowledge the intervening act (the firing) before concluding. Emotional distress gave Reynold a safer route to standing than his job loss did.

关于执法建议，要把流程当作时间线来记，而不是一张权力清单：先 ADR，然后调查，再到指示和罚款；如果个人起诉，调查可能暂停。再加上课堂讨论厘清的界限：PDPC 不能判给赔偿，只有私人诉讼可以。在私人执法一面，不要停在“他受到了伤害”。要依次分析损失或损害，再到直接性，并在下结论前承认介入行为（解雇）的存在。对 Reynold 来说，情绪困扰比失业更稳妥地支撑他的起诉资格。

The EU ADM material isn't examinable, but it sharpens how you think about AI accountability. Understand the "why": Article 22 targets unfair or biased decisions made with no human able to correct them. That's why token review doesn't count, and why the safeguards centre on a human with real authority to change the outcome. For SCHUFA, write a one-line card: facts (a scorer, a lender and a refused loan), failing (SCHUFA refused to explain), lesson (the scorer is caught too, otherwise there is a protection gap). It's a clean example of a court reading a rule by its purpose.

欧盟 ADM 内容不考，但它能让你更清楚地思考 AI 问责。要理解“为什么”：第 22 条针对的是没有人能纠正的、不公平或有偏见的决定。这就是为什么象征性审查不算数，也是为什么保障措施的核心是一个真正有权改变结果的人。为 SCHUFA 案写一张一句话卡片：事实（一个评分方、一个贷款机构、一笔被拒的贷款）、过错（SCHUFA 拒绝解释）、教训（评分方同样受约束，否则会出现保护空白）。这是法院按立法目的解释规则的一个清晰例子。

Finally, remember the lecturer's framing: the exam is fair but deliberately tight on time, and marks come from rubric points rather than polish. Rehearse full timed answers to the Dinah and Reynold scenarios using a fixed skeleton. For compliance: issues, then IRAC for each, then solutions. For enforcement: private, then public, then response. Know your materials well enough that the open book is for checking, not searching. Missing a few points is survivable, but running out of time from over-writing early issues is the real risk.

最后，记住讲师的定位：考试是公平的，但时间刻意设计得很紧，分数来自评分要点而不是文字修饰。用固定的骨架，限时完整练习 Dinah 和 Reynold 两个情景的答案。合规题：先列问题，再逐项 IRAC，然后给解决办法。执法题：先私人执法，再公共执法，最后讲应对。把材料熟悉到开卷只用来核对、而不是翻找的程度。漏掉几个点还能挺过去，真正的风险是在前面的问题上写太多而用完时间。

  From there, I can say that since XYZ is a data intermediary, ABC has primary responsibility for securing the personal data that XYZ processes. - [19:30:23–19:34:17] **Enforcement example: Reynold's private action**

  This is a question with several possible frameworks and approaches.

  On private enforcement, there are many rules we could bring in, but first we need to work out whether Reynold can sue. The first thing is whether he suffered loss or damage, because the rule requires that the person suffer loss or damage. Here he's likely to have suffered loss or damage, because the breach likely caused him emotional distress, and I think that can be proven, right? The personal data isn't sensitive, but disclosing a recording of him behaving badly is most likely going to cause him distress.

  On top of the emotional distress, he also clearly suffered some financial harm, because he was fired from his job. Here you can argue about whether the financial harm was directly caused by the breach. That's the third point: the loss or damage must be a direct result of the contravention. So you can ask whether the financial harm was in fact directly caused by the breach, because there's clearly an intervening act here. The breach caused the employer to fire him, and the firing caused the financial harm, right? But you could argue that getting fired was directly caused by the breach, because it was quite likely that a bank would fire a relationship manager caught up in this kind of incident, given how much banks care about their public reputation. Of course, you can also argue the other side: being fired may not be such a foreseeable consequence.

  In any case, because the emotional distress is pretty likely, you could argue that ultimately Reynold will have standing to sue.

  That covers the private enforcement side. You could then discuss a bit what DEF could do about this possibility, which is basically to try to settle the matter so it doesn't go to court. They could consider making an apology, negotiating some kind of compensation, or reaching a settlement agreement to put the matter to rest. That's how I'd address the private enforcement side of the question.

  这道题有好几种可能的分析框架和思路。

  在私人执法方面，可以引用的规则很多，但首先我们要弄清楚 Reynold 能不能起诉。第一点是他有没有遭受损失或损害（loss or damage），因为规则要求当事人遭受了损失或损害。在本案中，他很可能遭受了损失或损害，因为这次违规很可能给他造成了情绪困扰（emotional distress），我觉得这是可以证明的，对吧？这些个人数据虽然不是敏感数据，但公开一段他行为失当的录像，很可能会让他感到困扰。

  除了情绪困扰，他显然还遭受了某种经济损害，因为他被解雇了。这里你们可以讨论这种经济损害是否由违规直接造成。这就是第三点：损失或损害必须是违规行为直接导致的。所以你们可以问，这种经济损害是否真的是违规直接造成的，因为这里显然存在一个介入行为（intervening act）。违规导致雇主解雇了他，解雇又造成了经济损害，对吧？但你们可以主张，被解雇是违规直接导致的，因为银行很在意公众声誉，卷入这类事件的客户经理很可能会被解雇。当然，你们也可以论证另一面：被解雇也许不是那么可预见的后果。

  无论如何，由于情绪困扰的可能性很高，你们可以主张 Reynold 最终具有起诉资格（standing to sue）。

  这样就处理了私人执法这一面。接着你们可以稍微讨论一下 DEF 针对这种可能性可以怎么做，基本上就是设法和解，避免闹上法庭。他们可以考虑道歉、协商某种赔偿，或者达成和解协议来了结此事。这就是我处理这道题私人执法部分的方式。

- [19:51:33–19:53:58] **The Article 22 prohibition and "solely automated" decisions**

  So what we're going to talk about are the EU-specific rules on automated decision-making. They're drawn from various parts of the GDPR. Let me talk about the main one, which is the prohibition found in the GDPR. If you look at Article 22, it says: "The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her."

  So this is a prohibition on automated decision-making that affects an individual. Of course, this has direct implications for the use of AI, because organisations often do use AI to make these sorts of decisions very quickly, without thinking.

  I think the basic question is: when does this prohibition apply? There are a few aspects. The first is that the prohibition applies whenever you have a decision based solely on automated processing. What does that mean? Basically, it's a decision made without any human involvement. As long as the decision wasn't made with human involvement, it counts as solely automated processing.

  And what is human involvement? Human involvement refers to meaningful oversight. It can't just be a token gesture. It can't just be a human rubber-stamping the AI's decision. The human actually has to have some authority to change the automated decision. That's what counts as human involvement. If you have human involvement, the rule doesn't apply.

  Here you can see an example. An automated process produces a recommendation concerning a data subject. If a human being reviews it and takes account of other factors in making the final decision, that decision isn't based solely on automated processing.

  我们要讲的是欧盟针对自动化决策的特别规则。这些规则来自 GDPR 的不同部分。我先讲最主要的一条，也就是 GDPR 里的禁止性规定。看第 22 条，它规定："数据主体有权不受仅基于自动化处理作出的、对其产生法律效果或类似重大影响的决定的约束。"

  所以这是对影响个人的自动化决策的禁止。当然，这对 AI 的使用有直接影响，因为机构确实经常用 AI 非常快速地、不经思考地作出这类决定。

  我认为基本问题是：这项禁止什么时候适用？这里有几个方面。第一，只要一项决定是仅基于自动化处理（solely automated processing）作出的，这项禁止就适用。这是什么意思？基本上就是在没有任何人工参与的情况下作出的决定。只要这个决定不是在人工参与下作出的，就算作仅基于自动化处理。

  那什么是人工参与（human involvement）？人工参与是指有意义的监督。它不能只是象征性的姿态，也不能只是人走过场地给 AI 的决定盖章。这个人必须真正有权改变自动化决定。这才算人工参与。如果有人工参与，这条规则就不适用。

  这里有个例子。一个自动化流程针对某个数据主体给出了一项建议。如果有人审查这项建议，并在作出最终决定时考虑了其他因素，那么这个决定就不是仅基于自动化处理作出的。

- [19:56:02–19:58:16] **Legal effects and similarly significant effects**

  So we've talked about how the prohibition applies only to decisions based solely on automated processing. The second condition is that the prohibition only applies to decisions that produce either a legal effect or a similarly significant effect on the individual.

  What's a legal effect? Basically, a decision produces a legal effect when it affects the individual's legal rights, like the right to vote, or if the individual's contract is cancelled, or the individual is denied some social benefits they're entitled to. All of these would be legal effects.

  For non-legal effects that are similarly significant, some examples would be if someone is refused a credit application, or denied health services, employment opportunities or access to education. These would also fall within the prohibition, because the decision similarly significantly affects the individual.

  There are some sub-rules mentioned in the guidelines the EU established. For example, the guidelines say targeted advertising doesn't count as producing a significant effect. But exceptionally, if you're targeting individuals with vulnerabilities, purposely pressing on those vulnerabilities, the decision might still fall within the prohibition.

  Secondly, for personalised pricing, meaning pricing based on your personal data that changes depending on your income and so on, the guidelines say it could produce significant effects and fall within the prohibition if it results in prohibitively high prices that make it difficult to purchase certain products. So actually, it seems the EU is OK with personalised pricing, unless it results in this kind of prohibitively high price.

  我们讲了这项禁止只适用于仅基于自动化处理作出的决定。第二个条件是，这项禁止只适用于对个人产生法律效果（legal effect）或类似重大影响（similarly significant effect）的决定。

  什么是法律效果？基本上，当一项决定影响到个人的法律权利时，就产生了法律效果，比如投票权，或者个人的合同被取消，或者个人被拒绝给予其有权获得的某些社会福利。这些都属于法律效果。

  至于类似重大的非法律影响，例子包括：某人的信贷申请被拒，或者被拒绝提供医疗服务、就业机会或受教育机会。这些也会落入禁止范围，因为该决定对个人产生了类似的重大影响。

  欧盟制定的指南里还提到一些细则。比如，指南说定向广告（targeted advertising）不算产生重大影响。但例外情况是，如果你们针对的是有弱点的人，故意利用这些弱点，那么这个决定仍可能落入禁止范围。

  第二，对于个性化定价（personalised pricing），也就是根据你们的个人数据、随收入等因素变化的定价，指南说，如果它导致价格高得令人望而却步，让人难以购买某些产品，就可能产生重大影响并落入禁止范围。所以实际上，欧盟似乎可以接受个性化定价，除非它导致这种高得令人望而却步的价格。
- [19:58:16–20:01:06] **Three exceptions and the required safeguards**

  OK, so we've talked about the prohibition. If you're caught by it, how do you get out of it? There are three exceptions you can rely on.

  The first is if the decision is necessary for entering into or performing a contract between the individual and the controller. Here you have to show why it was necessary for you to rely on an automated system. Here's an example. Say you're a business advertising a very popular job position, and you receive thousands of applications. You may actually need to use an automated system as a filter, just to get through all of them. So you can argue that automated decision-making is necessary for entering into a contract with the individual, so that you can find the one job applicant you want.

  The other two exceptions are more straightforward. First, if some EU or Member State law allows you to do this, then of course you can use automated decision-making. The last one is if you have the individual's explicit consent. Explicit means expressed, not just by conduct.

  So these are the ways you get out of the prohibition.

  There's a precondition if you're relying on the first or the third exception. If you say, "I'm doing automated decision-making because it's necessary," or "because I have the individual's consent," you must also implement certain safeguards to protect the individual's interests. These safeguards must include at least the right to obtain human intervention, and the individual's right to express their point of view and to contest the decision.

  Human intervention has to be carried out by someone who actually has the authority to change the decision. In effect, you must allow the individual to appeal the automated decision. You can also include other safeguards, but those aren't necessary for this discussion.

  好，我们讲完了这项禁止。如果你们落入了禁止范围，怎么才能豁免？有三个例外可以依赖。

  第一，如果这项决定是个人与控制者之间订立或履行合同所必需的。这里你们必须说明为什么有必要依赖自动化系统。举个例子：假设你们是一家企业，在招聘一个非常热门的职位，收到了成千上万份申请。你们可能确实需要用自动化系统来筛选，才能处理完所有申请。所以你们可以主张，为了找到你们想要的那位求职者、与其订立合同，自动化决策是必要的。

  另外两个例外比较直接。首先，如果欧盟或成员国的某项法律允许你们这样做，那当然可以使用自动化决策。最后一个是取得个人的明确同意（explicit consent）。明确的意思是明示的，而不只是通过行为表示。

  这些就是豁免于这项禁止的方式。

  如果你们依赖的是第一个或第三个例外，还有一个前提条件。如果你们说"我做自动化决策是因为有必要"或者"因为我取得了个人同意"，你们还必须落实某些保障措施来保护个人利益。这些保障措施至少要包括获得人工干预的权利，以及个人表达自己观点和对决定提出异议的权利。

  人工干预必须由真正有权改变决定的人来进行。实际上就是说，你们必须允许个人对自动化决定提出申诉。你们也可以加入其他保障措施，但就这次讨论而言，那些并非必需。
- [20:01:06–20:06:11] **The special transparency obligation and two examples**

  OK, so that was the first special rule on automated decision-making, the prohibition. The second special rule is transparency.

  The rule is this: if you're a controller engaging in this kind of automated decision-making, even if you have an exception you can rely on, you have a special transparency obligation. One, you need to tell the data subject that you're engaging in this kind of automated decision-making. You can't keep it secret, right? The second and third ones are the most controversial. You also need to provide meaningful information about the logic involved. This is the idea of explainability. And you have to explain the significance and the envisaged consequences of the processing.

  Put together, these rules mean that if you're making automated decisions about an individual, you need to explain the automated decision to the individual. That can be quite challenging, especially if you have black-box algorithms that are hard to explain. It's quite difficult to explain why the black box reached the decision it did.

  The guidelines the EU has provided don't quite address the black-box problem. What they say is that the controller basically has to provide the rationale behind the decision. You need to provide enough information for the individual to understand why the decision was made, but you don't have to provide a full explanation of the algorithm or even disclose the full algorithm.

  One example the guidelines give: a data controller uses credit scoring to decide whether to reject or accept an individual's loan application. If you have this sort of automated scoring system, you need to give the data subject information about what you're doing. In this case, the controller explains that the scoring system helps them make fair, responsible, ethical decisions. It provides meaningful information about the logic, so it explains what characteristics were used to create the score, where the information came from, and so on. The controller also explains that the scoring methods are regularly tested, and provides information for the data subject to request reconsideration of, or appeal, any decision, which is required under the prohibition. So that's one example of what a controller in the EU might have to do if they're using this sort of automated credit scoring system.

  As mentioned, there are a couple of important things in giving transparency. The first is providing meaningful information on the logic involved in the decision, and the second is explaining the consequences of the processing.

  On the significance and envisaged consequences of the processing, the controller has to give information about how the decision might affect the individual, and give examples. Here's an example from the guidelines: an insurance company uses an automated decision-making process to set its premiums based on the customer's driving behaviour, which is an example we used in an earlier lesson. The insurance company needs to explain the consequences of this. So it says your dangerous driving may result in higher insurance premiums. Then it provides an app comparing various fictional drivers, including one with dangerous driving habits, to show the customer what might happen if they drive dangerously.

  好，这就是关于自动化决策的第一条特别规则，也就是禁止。第二条特别规则是透明度。

  规则是这样的：如果你们是从事这类自动化决策的控制者，即使你们有可以依赖的例外，也负有一项特别的透明度义务。第一，你们需要告诉数据主体你们在进行这类自动化决策，不能保密，对吧？第二和第三项是最有争议的。你们还需要提供关于所涉逻辑的有意义信息（meaningful information about the logic involved），这就是可解释性（explainability）的概念。你们还必须说明该处理的重要性及预期后果（significance and envisaged consequences）。

  综合起来，这些规则意味着，如果你们在对某个人作出自动化决定，就需要向这个人解释这个自动化决定。这可能相当有挑战性，特别是如果你们用的是难以解释的黑箱算法。要解释黑箱为什么作出那样的决定是相当困难的。

  欧盟提供的指南并没有真正解决黑箱问题。它说的是，控制者基本上要提供决定背后的理由。你们需要提供足够的信息，让个人理解为什么作出这个决定，但不必完整解释算法，甚至不必公开完整的算法。

  指南给出的一个例子是：某数据控制者用信用评分来决定拒绝还是接受某人的贷款申请。如果你们有这类自动化评分系统，就需要告诉数据主体你们在做什么。在这个例子中，控制者解释说，这个评分系统帮助他们作出公平、负责任、合乎伦理的决定。它提供了关于逻辑的有意义信息，也就是解释了评分用了哪些特征、信息从哪里来等等。控制者还说明评分方法会定期测试，并提供信息让数据主体可以要求复议或对任何决定提出申诉，这是禁止条款所要求的。所以这就是欧盟的控制者如果使用这类自动化信用评分系统可能需要做的事情的一个例子。

  如前所述，提供透明度有几件重要的事。第一是提供关于决定所涉逻辑的有意义信息，第二是说明处理的后果。

  关于处理的重要性及预期后果，控制者必须说明该决定可能如何影响个人，并举出例子。指南里有个例子：一家保险公司用自动化决策流程，根据客户的驾驶行为来设定保费，这是我们之前一节课用过的例子。保险公司需要解释这样做的后果。所以它说明，危险驾驶可能导致更高的保费。然后它提供了一个应用程序，比较各种虚构的驾驶者，包括一个有危险驾驶习惯的人，向客户展示如果危险驾驶可能会发生什么。
- [20:06:11–20:11:42] **The SCHUFA case: scoring by a third party**

  Because these rules are quite new, there haven't really been many cases on how they work. But one interesting case that came up fairly recently is the SCHUFA case. What it illustrates is that the automated decision-making rules apply even if the decision affecting the individual is made by a third party, not by the one that actually did the automated processing.

  Let me explain with the case. Here you have SCHUFA, a credit reporting company. SCHUFA is the organisation that comes up with credit scores for individuals, using some sort of mathematical and statistical analysis. Then you have OQ, the data subject, the individual. OQ was denied a loan by a lender because she got a bad credit score from SCHUFA. So you have the lender and OQ, and the lender denies OQ the loan because SCHUFA gave the lender negative information about her.

  What happens next is that OQ asks SCHUFA to send her information about her personal data, and asks SCHUFA to erase some personal data that was incorrect. SCHUFA gave her her score and some general information about how the score was calculated, but refused to give any more. So SCHUFA basically says, "I'm not going to tell you how I computed this."

  One question that arose was: do the automated decision-making rules apply to a company like this, in a case where the one doing the automated processing of personal data isn't the one that actually makes the decision affecting the individual? So there's a separation here, right? This one does the automated processing, but that one actually makes the decision.

  In this case, the CJEU said yes, the rules do apply. They still apply to SCHUFA, and here's the reason. As I mentioned earlier, Article 22 applies when three conditions are met. First, there must be a decision. Second, the decision must be based solely on automated processing. Third, the decision must produce a legal effect or a similarly significant effect on the individual.

  The CJEU went through the three elements. First, there's a decision in this case, because SCHUFA calculated OQ's creditworthiness in the form of a probability value of how likely she is to default. Second, the decision was based solely on automated processing, because the probability value comes from an automatic algorithm. And finally, the decision significantly affected the individual, because the third party, the lender, draws on or is influenced by that probability value in deciding whether to give OQ a loan.

  So essentially, the CJEU is saying that even if there's a third party making the final decision, the automated decision-making rules still apply to the scoring company. And of course this makes sense, because if the CJEU hadn't decided this way, there would be a gap in legal protection. The company doing the automated processing wouldn't be bound by the automated decision-making rules. On the other hand, the company making the decision, the lender, is bound by the rules but doesn't have the information to give to the data subject. In that case, OQ would never get the information she needs, or is entitled to, under the GDPR.

  由于这些规则相当新，关于它们如何运作的案例其实不多。但最近出现了一个有意思的案子，就是 SCHUFA 案。它说明的是：即使影响个人的决定是由第三方作出的，而不是由实际进行自动化处理的一方作出的，自动化决策规则仍然适用。

  我用这个案子来解释。这里有 SCHUFA，一家信用报告公司。SCHUFA 是用某种数学和统计分析为个人计算信用评分的机构。然后是 OQ，也就是数据主体、个人。OQ 被一家贷款机构拒绝了贷款，因为她从 SCHUFA 那里得到了很差的信用评分。所以有贷款机构和 OQ，贷款机构拒绝向 OQ 放贷，是因为 SCHUFA 给了贷款机构关于她的负面信息。

  接下来，OQ 要求 SCHUFA 把有关她个人数据的信息发给她，并要求 SCHUFA 删除一些不正确的个人数据。SCHUFA 给了她她的评分，以及关于评分如何计算的一些一般性信息，但拒绝提供更多。所以 SCHUFA 基本上是说："我不会告诉你我是怎么算出来的。"

  由此产生的一个问题是：在进行个人数据自动化处理的一方并不是实际作出影响个人决定的一方的情况下，自动化决策规则是否适用于这样的公司？这里存在一种分离，对吧？这一方做自动化处理，而那一方实际作出决定。

  在本案中，欧盟法院（CJEU）说，是的，规则适用。规则仍然适用于 SCHUFA，理由如下。正如我之前提到的，第 22 条在满足三个条件时适用。第一，必须存在一项决定。第二，该决定必须仅基于自动化处理。第三，该决定必须对个人产生法律效果或类似的重大影响。

  欧盟法院逐一分析了这三个要素。第一，本案存在一项决定，因为 SCHUFA 以概率值的形式计算了 OQ 的信用度，也就是她违约的可能性有多大。第二，该决定仅基于自动化处理，因为概率值来自自动算法。最后，该决定对个人产生了重大影响，因为第三方，也就是贷款机构，在决定是否向 OQ 放贷时会依据或受到这个概率值的影响。

  所以本质上，欧盟法院是在说，即使有第三方作出最终决定，自动化决策规则仍然适用于评分公司。这当然是合理的，因为如果欧盟法院不这样判，就会出现法律保护的空白（gap）。进行自动化处理的公司将不受自动化决策规则约束；另一方面，作出决定的公司，也就是贷款机构，虽然受规则约束，却没有可以提供给数据主体的信息。这样一来，OQ 就永远得不到她需要的、也是她根据 GDPR 有权获得的信息。
- [20:11:42–20:13:22] **Q&A: contesting a decision, and whether the rules bind government**

  So that was a very quick overview of the rules here. Any questions?

  A student asks: if the data subject contests the decision, can the company still make the same decision?

  So you're referring to this one, right? Here we're talking about the safeguards the data controller needs to implement. The question is, if the individual appeals, can the data controller still take the same position? The answer is yes. The fact that the data controller has to allow the individual to contest the decision obviously doesn't mean the controller is obliged to change it. What it does mean is that they need a human individual to actually look at the decision that was made and assess, on his or her own, whether it was correct.

  The student follows up that the human in the loop could still end up making the same decision, and asks whether the rule also applies to the government. Yes, this rule does. One way the GDPR differs from the PDPA is that the GDPR also applies to government agencies, like tax authorities and so on.

  这就是对这里规则的一个非常简短的概述。有问题吗？

  一位同学问：如果数据主体对决定提出异议，公司还能作出同样的决定吗？

  你指的是这一条，对吧？这里讲的是数据控制者需要落实的保障措施。问题是，如果个人提出申诉，数据控制者能否维持原来的立场？答案是可以。数据控制者必须允许个人对决定提出异议，这显然不意味着控制者有义务改变决定。它的意思是，他们需要有一个人真正去审视已经作出的决定，并自行判断这个决定是否正确。

  这位同学追问说，所以人工参与环节（human in the loop）最后可能还是作出同样的决定；他又问这条规则是否也适用于政府。是的，这条规则适用。GDPR 和 PDPA 的一个不同之处在于，GDPR 也适用于政府机构，比如税务机关等等。
- [20:13:22–20:14:11] **Main takeaway**

  Any other questions on this? OK. So again, none of this is examinable. The rules are a bit complicated, but the main takeaway from this part of the lesson is that in the EU there's a general prohibition on automated decision-making, and when you are making automated decisions, there's a special transparency obligation requiring you to explain the decision to the individual. I'll upload the guidelines I went through for this part later, along with these slides. Any final questions before we end?

  关于这部分还有其他问题吗？好。再说一次，这些都不考。规则有点复杂，但这部分课程的主要收获是：在欧盟，自动化决策受到一般性禁止；而当你们作出自动化决定时，负有一项特别的透明度义务，要求你们向个人解释该决定。我稍后会把这部分讲到的指南连同这些幻灯片一起上传。结束之前还有最后的问题吗？
- [20:14:11–20:18:39] **Q&A: other jurisdictions, the rationale, tracking Singapore changes, and IMDA guidelines**

  A student asks whether other regions have similar regulations. Not that I know of. The EU is definitely the pioneer here. Offhand, I don't know whether any other country has followed suit in this way. There may be other countries that have recently implemented similar rules on automated decisions, but I haven't seen any country do something exactly like this.

  Any other questions?

  A student asks whether this is a clear attempt at limiting the use of AI. No, it's not really that. The rationale behind this set of rules is the concern that individuals will be affected by decisions made incorrectly, or made in a way that's unfair, because there's no human involved, because whatever decision-making system the controller has in place is flawed or biased in a certain way. So this approach is designed to make sure these sorts of bad outcomes, which significantly affect individuals, are guarded against.

  Another student asks whether regulators are looking into something like this. You mean other countries, or Singapore? Oh, you're talking about potential changes to Singapore's rules. Normally the PDPC or IMDA, depending on who is making the rules, will announce changes on its website. Sometimes the announcement isn't widely publicised, so you'd need to look out for it. If you sign up and register as a DPO, they'll probably send you an email if they intend to make any changes. Otherwise, you need to actively watch for these announcements, although they don't change the rules that often.

  A student notes that this overlaps with AI governance, and that the difference is that this is law, whereas the IMDA's material is guidance. Yes. I think many of you have already done the AI governance course, and you'll have encountered guidelines published by Singapore's IMDA. The difference between those guidelines and the rules here is, as you mentioned, that these rules are legally binding, in the sense that if you don't comply, there will be consequences. Whereas the IMDA only provides suggestions or recommendations.

  Any other questions about this?

  一位同学问其他地区有没有类似的法规。据我所知没有。欧盟在这方面绝对是先行者。我一时想不起是否有其他国家以这种方式跟进。也许有其他国家最近实施了关于自动化决策的类似规则，但我还没见过哪个国家做得和这完全一样。

  还有其他问题吗？

  一位同学问，这是否明显是在限制 AI 的使用。不，其实不是。这套规则背后的理由是担心个人会受到错误作出的、或以不公平方式作出的决定的影响，因为没有人工参与，因为控制者所使用的决策系统存在某种缺陷或偏见。所以这种做法是为了防范这类对个人产生重大影响的不良结果。

  另一位同学问监管机构是否在研究类似的东西。你是指其他国家，还是新加坡？哦，你说的是新加坡规则可能的变化。通常 PDPC 或 IMDA，视乎由谁制定规则，会在其网站上公布变化。有时公告不会广泛宣传，所以你们需要留意。如果你们登记注册为 DPO，他们打算作出任何修改时大概会给你们发邮件。否则，你们就需要主动关注这些公告，不过他们并不经常修改规则。

  一位同学指出，这和 AI 治理有重叠，区别在于这是法律，而 IMDA 的材料是指引。是的。我想你们很多人已经修过 AI 治理的课程，会接触过新加坡 IMDA 发布的指南。那些指南和这里的规则的区别正如你所说：这些规则具有法律约束力，也就是说如果不遵守，就会有后果；而 IMDA 只提供建议或推荐。
